title: A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know it | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: Anger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generation, says former prime minster Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: Anger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generation, says former prime minster Gordon Brown
Content: Celebrations in Belgrade last week following Student List’s victory in the Serbian election.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersView image in fullscreenCelebrations in Belgrade last week following Student List’s victory in the Serbian election.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersOpinionProtestA global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know itGordon BrownAnger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generationMon 2 Nov 2026 10.17 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.32 ESTShareWe have not yet reached a 1968 moment, when students at the Sorbonne lit a fuse that detonated a crisis that eventually brought downthe De Gaulle government. But in late 2026, starting with the symbolic act of young French peopleclimbing the July Columnat Paris’s Place de la Bastille, the world is experiencing the biggest outbreak of student demonstrations for 60 years.When Italian students subsequently occupied a high school in Rome, they opened their demand for change with the words “like in France”. Youth demonstrations are now raging from India – where the government hasresponded with repressive forceto theCockroach movement– to Albania, where, after being out on the streets for nearly five months, students are demanding not only an end to corruption, but thereplacement of the government.But the most momentous set of protests has been in Serbia, where theStudent List of candidatesfor national parliamentary elections has succeeded not just in dislodging a long-established, corruption-tainted government alleged to have links with organised crime, but insecuring an electoral mandate. It is now poised to form a new administration. Nothing of this kind has ever happened before.View image in fullscreenProtesters at the base of the July Column in Place de la Bastille, Paris, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockStudent List is not only changing the political leadership of Serbia but popularisingnew methods of organising; it isbuilding a systemfor selecting candidates from outside its own ranks, using methods such as open public assemblies with rotating delegates and specialised working groups. Eighty-five student assemblies selected the candidates, as ananalysis of their internal rulesexplains. And the results are often surprising: the rector of Belgrade university, Vladan Djokić, wasnot selected as a candidate, despite being a longterm supporter of the movement and expected by many to play a major role in government.Student List has beencompared by the Croatian philosopher Srećko Horvat, who situates the movement within a longer tradition of direct democracy and collective self-organisation, to the Paris Commune of 1871. Its fundraising activites, however, are very much up to date:it reportedly crowdsourcedalmost €2m (£1.7m) from more than 26,000 individual donors during the election campaign.The wave of youth protests comes after mobilisations inKenya in 2024and acrossNepal,Indonesia,the Philippines,Madagascar,MoroccoandPeruin 2025. How far the Serbian grassroots model of organising will shape youth movements elsewhere remains to be seen. But according to Olivier Ertzscheid, a senior lecturer at the University of Nantes, “young people’s sense of belonging and social interaction is at play”, with social media now actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters – and driving momentum.September and October have seen youth protests inBelgium,Austria,GreeceandItalyover education funding; inGermanyover the threat of compulsory military service; and inSpainandPortugalover the lack of affordable housing. But the protests have also spread well beyond Europe, toIndonesia, where youth demonstrations are focused on pollution; toArgentinaover austerity; and toChileandColombiaover funding cuts. Last weekend in Germany, a group called Gen Z regeltled demonstrations in 21 cities.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators march through Berlin’s Mitte district on Saturday, demanding action on rising living costs, cuts to education and conscription.Photograph: Nikos Kanistras/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe protests will only intensify this month. In Australia, a big student demonstration is planned for11 November, andstudent unions in Britain and Italyare planning a joint day of action protesting against the rising cost of education on 20 November.Some years ago I wrote about anew generation of youth activists– of Bangladeshi schoolgirls campaigning against forced child marriage who had declared “child marriage-free zones”, and of Nigerian and other young people in Africa demanding their right to education. But the current youth rebellions are of a different order, breaking out in a new and more dangerous global environment and challenging authorities on issues well beyond education. Young people face an AI-led unemployment crisis; they lose out from the skewing of public spending towards older people, from restricted provision of education; they face a housing crisis and governments underplaying the importance of the climate emergency and intergenerational justice.The youth jobs crisis will grow. The number of UK graduate jobs postings advertised on one big employment agency has declined from about180,000 four years ago to 50,000 today. AI is thought to be a factor.Hi-tech employment of 18- to 24-year-olds declined by 30%between December 2019 and December 2025, whereas the sector itself expanded by 33% in that period. So as the government prepares to announce itsreview into youth employment, it is urgent we get nearly 1 million unemployed under-25s into work, giving priority to pre-apprenticeship training and restoring educational maintenance allowances, as well as radically reshaping a benefits system that is failing the younger generation.Butthis is a worldwide problem. Because of ever-rising debt burdens andspiralling expenditures on defence and energy subsidies, governments are trapped in such a fiscal straitjacket that they will struggle to find the resources to meet young people’s aspirations. A large portion of public spending is captured by older generations, with schools and universities losing out as a result. Across the OECD, about half of health and social security spending goes to elderly people – those over 65 – despite them making up only 18.5% of the total population. In this tally, pensions are the biggest item, accounting for38% of all social spending– but an understandably high portion of all health spending goes to older people, too. And with young people now taking home afar smaller share of income than earlier generations,income and wealth gaps between young and oldhave widened.It’s time to join the dots.Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author of Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation, warns that the protests are morphing into awider social movement. “There are inequalities at all levels,” she says, “with gaps widening between different social groups.” The triggers for the demonstrations vary from country to country, but the basic complaint is strikingly similar. Young people believe that any promises that they would do better than their parents’ generation have already been broken – and that case is a strong one.Liberal democracy itself is now on trial.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010, and is United Nations special envoy for global educationExplore more on these topicsProtestOpinionYoung peopleStudentsCost of living crisisHigher educationHousingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Gilded Age review – what did we do to deserve such a terrible stinker? | Television | The Guardian
description: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show
Content: Looking as if someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle … Cynthia Nixon (right) as Ada Brook, with Christine Baranski as Agnes van Rhijn.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenLooking as if someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle … Cynthia Nixon (right) as Ada Brook, with Christine Baranski as Agnes van Rhijn.Photograph: HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Gilded Age review – what did we do to deserve such a terrible stinker?Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful showLucy ManganMon 2 Nov 2026 17.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdoctor with a fully qualified moustache races up a carriageway towards an immaculate stately home. “I fear we should have sent for you sooner!” says the lady who greets him on the doorstep as the screams of a woman in drug-free labour rattle the windows in their frames.Oh, ya think?is not Dr Moustache’s reply.When this many cliches assemble so quickly, it can only mean one thing: Brownstone Abbey – AKA Julian Fellowes’ Revenge, AKA What Did We Do to Deserve This?, AKA The Gilded Age if you insist on its official title – is back for a fourth and, no one has said let alone promised, final season.The labouring woman is Gladys (Taissa Farmiga), daughter of the nouveau riche Russells of Fifth Avenue and now married to Hector (Ben Lamb – I’m sorry, actors, it’s Guardian policy to identify you), 5th Duke of Englandshire and living in England Hall in England after some plot last season. “She’s bleeding!” cries an astute maid, staring at a blood-soaked bed. “What’s wrong?” cries someone crackingly stupid. “She’s haemorraghing!” says the doctor, which is medical moustache for “She’s bleeding!”, so really, we are no further along. That’s the Gilded Age dialogue promise.‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreRead moreMeanwhile, back in America, the costume budget is assembling in church for the wedding of Oscar (Blake Ritson – again, I’m sorry but I don’t make the rules), scion of the old-money Van Rhijn family, and Enid (Kelley Curran), wealthy widow of Mr Winterton and former lady’s maid to Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon). Enid has mastered the constipated diction of the US aristocracy enough to fool Oscar’s mother, Agnes, into thinking that she is a suitable wife for Oscar. (Agnes is played by Christine Baranski, whom one imagines praying nightly before a shrine to Maggie Smith, the patron saint of actors’ retirement funds, begging for a sign that she has done the right thing.)“At last my son is married!” says Agnes, for viewers who have just watched the wedding but still need a bit of help. “And to a fine-looking woman with enough money for them to live well! And soon I shall entertain the president of the United States!” She’s not having a stroke – Grover Cleveland is indeed due to be hosted at Brownstone Abbey. All signs point to it being the equivalent of the opera house wars from season one, so do hold on to your hats.Enid has not, however, fooled either herself or Oscar into thinking she is the right woman for him. He is a dedicated homosexual; theirs is a marriage of convenience and much the healthiest setup of the bunch.View image in fullscreenJack Gilpin (Mr Church), Carrie Coon (Bertha Russell), Taissa Farmiga (Gladys de Vere) and (Ashley Atkinson) as Mamie Fish.Photograph: HBORight, what else is happening? Cynthia Nixon’s Ada is wealthier than Agnes now, since her rich reverend died, but she remains in constant facial rictus, a smile-thing happening beneath a permanently wrinkled nose so she looks as though someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle. Her niece Marian (Louisa Jacobson, daughter of Meryl Streep and honestly, family Thanksgivings must be so awkward whenever this is airing) is still yearning after the Russells’ (heterosexual) scion Larry (Harry Richardson), and I’m afraid no good comes of them being forced to stay in a hotel overnight after a coach accident. (Thunder, lightning, shot of horse rearing, wheel breaking, Larry saying “The horse must have been spooked by the storm!”, fealty to the dialogue promise rewarded by later nakedness with Marian.)Peggy (Denée Benton) is engaged to William (Jordan Donica) and happily so, apart from his interfering mother (Phylicia Rashad). If my bingo card of as-yet-unused-tropes does not deceive me, Peggy is soon to experience problems in terms of reconciling her professional success with her imminently increasing domestic duties. She and the Kirklands remain a conduit for Fellowes’ and his co-typer Sonja Warfield’s take on turn-of-the-century race relations, which is as subtle as their take on class distinctions, Anglo-US relations and human relations, on which we shall not dwell.George Russell (Morgan Spector plus beard, such a beard!) is still in financial difficulties: “And if I deal with him, I have to pay most of the transportation costs of the oil?” “Without his business, your railroad cannot survive!” He is also busy trying to track down the person who shot him before the Newport ball at the end ofthe last series. Something to do with copper mines, I think. I cannot be expected to remember everything.Bridget, the Irish maid (Taylor Richardson), still hasn’t mastered her accent (“Halp me get the kek!”) and is still pining for Jack, the young inventor (Ben Ahlers). He is following up on his alarm-clock success with an electric mixer he assures potential investors will take the world by storm. Meanwhile, Gladys loses her uterus (“What’s wrong?” “The script using the word ‘uterus’”) and – do you know what? I’m too exhausted to go on. In short, all is as it was. Uniformly terrible and likely to outlive us all.This stuff won an Emmy. America is a failed state. E pluribus zilch.The Gilded Age aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now in the UK, and on HBO in the US and Paramount+ in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewJulian FellowesCynthia NixonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Half-witted at best, a people-pleaser at worst: step forward, Chris Philp | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Responding to Shabana Mahmood’s changes to indefinite leave to remain, the shadow home secretary was detached from reality
Author: John Crace
Headline: Responding to Shabana Mahmood’s changes to indefinite leave to remain, the shadow home secretary was detached from reality
Content: The Philpster’s reply will feature heavily in any lowlights reel.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenThe Philpster’s reply will feature heavily in any lowlights reel.Photograph: House of Commons/PAThe politics sketchPoliticsHalf-witted at best, a people-pleaser at worst: step forward, Chris PhilpJohn CraceResponding to Shabana Mahmood’s changes to indefinite leave to remain, the shadow home secretary was detached from realityMon 2 Nov 2026 14.27 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.39 ESTShareBetter late than never. It had seemed as if some apologies from the prime minister were more sincere than others.The one that he has planned to deliver for Britain’s role in the slave tradeat the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua fell on the right side of genuine. There had been no need to make one at that time. Indeed Kemi Badenoch saw it as a sign of weakness. There again, she would refuse to apologise for running someone over on a pedestrian crossing. Somehow it would have turned out to be the victim’s fault.Andy Burnham’s apology for not being able to turn up in the Commons to lend support to his home secretary might rather fall into the “sorry, not sorry” category. Making life more difficult for migrants was more one for Keir Starmer’s legacy than part of the new government’s agenda. Andy couldn’t have been more thrilled to be on a plane asShabana Mahmoodstood up to make her statement on “earned settlement”. It was almost as if the statement had been timed for when Burnham was away. At the very least, it was the perfect coincidence. If not divine intervention.Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlashRead moreEven on Monday lunchtime, the prime minister’s spokesperson was refusing to give Burnham’s wholehearted support for Shabana’s proposed changes to indefinite leave to remain (ILR). Even after he and other cabinet colleagues had managed to water them down a little. The best that Andy would say was that “It was a good thing that immigration had fallen”.Nothing about the home secretary’s role in this. Nothing that hinted at an endorsement. It felt as if Mahmood had been rather hung out to dry. Even more so when Angela Rayner, another of the home secretary’s critics, pointedly left the chamber by the far door so she wouldn’t have to look the home secretary in the eye after housing and communities departmental questions. No need for an awkward “That cup of tea isn’t going to drink itself”.But at the very last minute – as if by magic – a short, unequivocal message of support from Burnham was released. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” he said. Shabana was not being abandoned, after all. Not that she wouldn’t have coped if she had. Even if she had not come to the house with Lou Haigh and Lucy Powell as her outriders, Mahmood is more than capable of looking after herself. She is a woman who knows her mind.The statement was all much as we had expected. A reaffirmation of previous proposals with a few important concessions to Burnham, Rayner and backbenchers from the left of the Labour party. There would be a five-year route to settlement for care workers who had arrived prior to March 2025: a 10-year process for those who had arrived afterwards. Otherwise all was as it had been, plus or minus a couple of tweaks. New safe routes for refugees and a 30-year wait for those who had arrived in the country illegally. All with the usual caveats of speaking English, national insurance contributions and no criminal record.We haven’t seen much of the shadow home secretary,Chris Philp, in recent months. A relief to us all. Partly because even he had begun to have a sense of his own ridiculousness, partly because immigration had ceased to be such a hot topic for the country. There was more than a sense that the government was legislating for a problem that no longer really existed. Legal immigration has fallen to the tens of thousands a year from its high point of one million during Boris Johnson’s time in office. And the small boat crossings have more than halved. But Shabana doesn’t believe in taking chances. Happy to double-lock the doors to the country.But this was The Philpster’s time to shine. To remind us all that he is at best half witted; at his worst, a people-pleaser par excellence. The ultimate nose in search of a bum. And so we got Philp at his most absurd. A joy to behold. A performance to make the whole statement worthwhile. A chance to give the entire Commons its Proustian madeleine moment. The Unbearable Lightness of Chris. Just when you think you’ve seen it all, The Philpster searches for the futility inside himself.It had taken a whole year for Mahmood to establish her credibility, Philp declared. And she had destroyed it all in the space of her 12-minute statement. There will come a time when Chris compiles a show reel of all his political lowlights. A chance for him and his therapist to try to make sense of his career. How can someone of so little ability have come so far? Would Kemi really be daft enough to make him her home secretary if she won an election? Luckily she will never have to answer that one.But know one thing. The Philpster’s reply will feature heavily in any lowlights reel. Above all else for his lack of self-awareness. The government should be ashamed of itself. This was virtually an open-doors policy. There would be foreigners everywhere if we weren’t careful. You could not be more detached from reality if you tried. It had been the Tory government that had presided over the mass wave of immigration. A Tory government that had failed to secure the country’s borders. And who had been a Home Office minister while this was going on? Step forward, Chris.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMahmood scarcely bothered to grace The Philpster’s delusions with a reply. She would have been doing him a favour to offer him a prescription of some anti-psychotic drugs. Nor was it just Labour who put the boot in. The Tory father of the house, Edward Leigh, is becoming increasingly disinhibited in opposition. Determined to make up for a decade or more of supporting a failing government by telling inconvenient truths.The former Tory government should be holding its head in shame, Leigh said. And anyone who had been in the Home Office should wear sackcloth and ashes. It was a complete evisceration of The Philpster and his empty words. Enough to almost make you feel sorry for Chris. Almost. Philp gestured half-heartedly towards Robert Jenrick, another former Home Office minister. Anything to try and mitigate the shame.For the rest of the statement, various Labour backbenchers protested about the lack of fairness to immigrants; the retrospective nature of some proposals. Shabana really wasn’t bothered. She had given away as much as she was going to. The Labour party would just have to live with it. Elsewhere, Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf were holding a press conference on ILR. The government had been weak, they claimed. The only answer was to deport every immigrant. It would have been nice if, to show he meant what he was saying, if Zia had promised to deport himself. Not for being brown or Muslim. But for being thoroughly unpleasant.On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026.
