title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?  | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives
Content: A shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersView image in fullscreenA shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersCybercrimeExplainerWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motivesShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackRobert BoothandMiatta MbriwaMon 2 Nov 2026 14.07 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.56 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countrieshave malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F).The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean?The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia.It appeared to be a reprise ofattacks three weeks agowhen French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software.Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, dispose of spoiled food.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAThis is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control.Who is doing it?No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat.“The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos.The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea isbelieved to have beenbehind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame.Western intelligence chiefs sayMoscow is waging acampaign of sabotage in Europethat takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months.View image in fullscreenA worker at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden disposes of spoiled food.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ShutterstockDiscerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”.How is it possible?The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates.Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read moreNick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline – an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”.In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France.What can shops do to defend themselves?The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France.In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NSCC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.Why have British supermarkets not been hit yet?Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout.Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”.A spokesperson for the NCSC said it was “working with its international partners and industry to fully understand details of an incident”.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeSupermarketsRetail industryEuropeSwedenBelgiumEstonianewsShareReuse this content

title: Five dimensional chess: inside James Talarico’s extraordinary bid to break Texas Democrats’ losing streak | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Texan could pull off a historic victory in the Lone Star state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988
Author: David Smith
Headline: The Texan could pull off a historic victory in the Lone Star state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Callaghan O'Hare/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Photo by Callaghan O'Hare/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Five dimensional chess: inside James Talarico’s extraordinary bid to break Texas Democrats’ losing streakThe Texan could pull off a historic victory in the Lone Star state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988David Smithin Austin, TexasMon 2 Nov 2026 18.32 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen a young, untested former school teacher stood up to address a modest gathering of local donors in Austin, the state capital of Texas,Wendy Davisfelt sorry for him. “Poor kid,” she remembers thinking.Then James Talarico began speaking. “He was like five or six sentences in and I knew that something was different about him,” recalls Davis, a former Democratic state senator. “He was as articulate and unique then as he is now. From that day, I started calling him ‘Baby Obama’.”Eight years after that first fundraising event, “Baby Obama” is no longer a precocious candidate for the state house with paper slogans that read “A future as bright as Texas”. Now 37, Talarico will aim to redraw the political map next week by becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the Lone Star state since 1988.The threat that he poses to Republicans’ grip on power has become clear in the final stretch of a fraught campaign. Over the past month Donald Trump rallied in Texas and branded him “James Talafreako”; JD Vance implied that Talarico is gay (he has a girlfriend); and rightwing influencersspread a baseless liethat he checked into a mental health clinic in Ohio (he was ill with flu).Despite the desperate attacks, most opinion polls give Talarico a narrow edge. On Tuesday the voters will have their say on whether the four-term state representative, a Presbyterian seminarian preaching a gospel of hope, can overcome RepublicanKen Paxton, a scandal-haunted state attorney general and Trump ally who has financial backing from tech billionaire Elon Musk.Facing a barrage of culture war attack ads funded by the world’s wealthiest man, Talarico has responded with an unorthodox blend of economic populism, progressive politics and an unapologetically Christian message that challenges the religious right on its own turf. His campaign raised a record $64m in the third quarter, including donations from a vast number of small-dollar contributors.Last weekTalarico told a crowdof young voters and local activists gathered at his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, that Republicans’ billionaire donors were starting to fret.“They are terrified because they see what we see: we are about to win this election,” he said.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico speaks to supporters during a rally at the University of Texas on 23 October 2026 in Austin.Photograph: Sergio Flores/Getty ImagesAn eighth-generation Texan, he was born James Dell Causey in Round Rock, a small town north of Austin, in 1989. His mother, Tamara Causey, was a preacher’s daughter who left home at 19 and met his biological father, whom she has described as an alcoholic prone to violence.One night the abuse became too much. Tamara drove James and all her belongings in a small Ford Escort to the hotel where she worked as a sales assistant. They lived in an empty room at the hotel until they found an apartment in Austin. Tamara subsequently married a sales manager named Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname.At school, Talarico was a keen debater and actor, with roles including Danny Zuko in the musical Grease. Allegra Hobbs, author of a profile in Texas Monthly magazine,reported: “His high school theater director, Aaron Johnson, joked to me that the young Talarico did not so much inhabit the character as play a version of himself. When the theater department handed out superlatives, ‘Jimmy’ was voted most likely to be president – a running joke among his friends that he would laugh off.”Getaway cars, affairs, Dubai fugitives: Trump’s pick Ken Paxton brings baggage to Senate race in TexasRead moreTalarico studied at the University of Texas at Austin, where Mike Garcia, a 38-year-old lawyer and former legislative staffer, firstencountered his political ambitions. In 2009, Garcia presided over the College Republicans while Talarico led the University Democrats. Despite their ideological differences, the pair initially found common ground in nonpartisan voter drives and a campaign for tuition relief.Speaking from Fort Worth, Garcia recalls: “It was a little strange but I was glad that we were putting our differences aside and doing something that would help everybody.”The goodwill did not last. During student government elections, Talarico’s organisation endorsed establishment candidates who opposed tuition re-regulation, according to Garcia. The move provoked outrage amongDemocratswho had supported the campaign, some of whom turned up at a College Republicans meeting to protest.Garcia suspected Talarico hadcalculated that the endorsementwould win him favour with university administrators ahead of a possible run for student body president. “That sounds like exactly something Jimmy would do,” he says.Years later, when the two crossed paths again at the Texas capitol – Garcia working for Republican legislators and Talarico now an elected representative – Garcia felt he saw a similar gap between political rhetoric and personal charm. Talarico would “routinely just rail against all these people I work for, calling us the worst names ever”, he recalls, before greeting him warmly in the corridor minutes later.Garcia remains unconvinced by Talarico’s current presentation as a moderate. “He is probably one of the types that is willing to tell you exactly what you want to hear, especially if it helps him politically. Right now he’s running as a moderate and he’s doing a very good job of it,” Garcia says.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico with supporters at a campaign rally in Kerrville, Texas, on 31 August 2026.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesBut othersdispute Garcia’s account. In a statement provided by Talarico’s campaign,Muneezeh Kabir, who was at the University of Texas with him and involved in student government, said: “James has always raised his hand to serve others. Throughout his time in student government at UT, James worked with everyone, even those he disagreed with, to make life on campus better for all of us. He delivered for his classmates at UT, then his community in Austin, and now, he’s ready to step up and serve Texans from every corner of the state.”After college, and before the state house, Talarico went into education. His first job was teaching sixth-grade language artsat the Rhodes middle schoolon the west side of San Antonio, a predominantly Latino neighbourhood.Edward Garcia, 56, who wasprincipal of Rhodes at the time, remembers hiring Talarico during the summer of 2011. In a high-poverty school district where teacher turnover was relentless, Garcia was struck by the young applicant’s poise and purpose. “He knew what his mission statement was in terms of working with students that are in high poverty and high need. He was ready to start the next day,” he says.Even before the academic year began, Talarico turned up at the school accompanied by his sister, hauling enlarged prints of Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr and Gandhi to create a classroom display devoted to human freedom.“Teachers are supposed to be universal,” Garcia explains. “There wasn’t an approach in terms of partisan politics. It was just the concept of freedom and what it means for students to truly acquire freedom and leadership in their lives.”Talarico’s connection with his middle schoolers was immediate. In a profession where novice teachers frequently struggle with classroom management and rely on administrative referrals, Talarico never wrote up a single student or sent one to the principal’s office. “He was an exemplary teacher. Kids were enthralled with his presentation and took a shine to him,” Garcia says. “What you see is what you get: smart, articulate and guided by his heart.”When Garcia walked into Talarico’s room during his second-year formal observation, he discovered that the young teacher had physically removed his official administrative desk from the room.“I went in to do his evaluation,” Garcia recalls with a laugh. “I looked around and said, ‘Where’s your desk?’ He goes, ‘Oh, I took it out and turned it into a reading space.’ He put a carpet down right where his desk should be.”After two years in San Antonio, Talarico returned to the Austin area to lead an education non-profit before making his leap into elective politics in 2018. Winning a state house of representatives seat in a suburban swing district, he quickly established a reputation in the Texas capitol as an authority on public school finance and an exceptionally persuasive orator.View image in fullscreenSupporters listen as James Talarico speaks at a rally on 13 July 2026 in Eagle Pass, Texas.Photograph: Brenda Bazán/APHis Republican colleagues in the house began calling him “Baby Gov”, recognising that his ambitions might extend well beyond the state legislature. Talarico focused heavily on public education, prescription drug pricing and property tax relief.During bitter legislative battles over voting rights and school vouchers – proposals to restrict access to the ballot and use public funds to help families pay for private education – Talarico emerged as a prominent opponent of Republican priorities.In 2021, he joined fellow Democratsin leaving Texasto block a vote on Republican-backed voting restrictions by denying the state house the minimum number of members needed to conduct business. He later returned to the chamberbefore the standoff had ended, drawing criticism from some of his own party.He also repeatedly clashed with conservative committee chairs over LGBTQ+ rights. Talarico used the phrase “God is non-binary” while opposing a bill concerning transgender children in school sports. Republicans have sought to weaponise it against him. Talarico has defended the underlying theological argument while acknowledging that he was being provocative.While serving in the state legislature, Talarico enrolled at theAustin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, which has a picturesque downtown campus of neat lawns, light-filled buildings and functional classrooms with blackboards and rows of desks. He pursued a master of arts in theological studies, diving into church history, ethics, systematic theology and ancient biblical languages.The seminary’s president,José Irizarry, says: “We are not an assembly line for dogma. We are a place of faith formation which requires people to think deeply and thoughtfully about their faith practices. What does it mean to take your belief system and actually do the work of justice in the world?”Irizarry recalls working in his office across from the classroom building during Talarico’s first year. “I had no door when I arrived here – an actual open-door policy. He was studying Hebrew across the hall. I could hear the whole Hebrew class because it was with a rabbi and he started the class singing in Hebrew. I would go out during the breaks and see him interacting with all the students. He was a student like everybody else around here, engaged in ministry.”When Talarico called Wendy Davis in late 2023 to disclose his intention to surrender his safe house seat and launch a long-shot bid for the US Senate, she tried to stop him. Davis, now executive director of the theBlueprint Texaspolitical action committee, admits: “I tried hard to talk him out of it. I told him that my fear was he’d been so impactful in the legislature and I thought it would be a big loss for him. I told him he was probably going to lose and he was going to regret leaving his office. And now look at him.”Talarico went on to defeatJasmine Crockett, another rising star of the party, in a bruising Senate primary election. He has since been working hard to unify the Democratic coalition, including Black voters who supported Crockett.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico is hugged by a supporter during a Juneteenth march in Fort Worth, Texas, on 19 June 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesHis theological training has proven not merely a personal spiritual exercise but the construction of a political armour. In a state where conservative evangelicals have long dominated public discourse on religion, Talarico’s fluid command of scripture has allowed him to carry out a counteroffensive.He attacks Christian nationalism, opposes state-mandated displays of the Ten Commandments in public schools and argues that Jesus’s core commandment – to love one’s neighbour – demands support for healthcare, public education and marginalised communities.Cal Jillson, a professor of political science at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, says by phone: “Usually the vote that takes religion seriously in Texas is an evangelical conservative Republican vote. There’s a possibility that he has a little more purchase beyond the Democratic base into moderates and independent voters in the middle. With Talarico, there’s more of a Sermon on the Mount vibe as opposed to this ‘I’m an angry God’.”Talarico demonstrated that approach during a legislative committee hearing on a bill requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in Texas classrooms. Rather than offering a standard secular objection, Talarico quizzed the author on the text of the Commandments themselves – showing on camera that the politician could not recite them.For Democrats, there have been plenty of false dawns in Texas. In 2018 Beto O’Rourke’s charismatic campaign for Senate against Republican Ted Cruz attracted national attention and record-breaking fundraising, but he ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points.Bill Minutaglio, a prominent Texas author and political historian whose books include A Single Star and Bloody Knuckles, argues that Talarico’s campaign represents a far more calculated and controlled evolution of Texas Democratic strategy.“Beto was deemed to be the chosen one who would break the spell and obviously it didn’t happen,” Minutaglio observes. “He was a victim of inflated expectations. He seemed too ambitious and too coated with endorsements that didn’t resonate well outside the borders of Texas. People here don’t take kindly to the sense that a candidate is being shaped and endorsed by places like California or New York.”View image in fullscreenBeto O’Rourke campaigns in San Antonio, Texas, on 31 October 2018.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesTalarico, Minutaglio contends, studied O’Rourke’s missteps to avoid repeating them. “O’Rourke appeared on the cover of Vanity Fair magazine. Talarico has learned his lessons. I don’t mistake his quietude and his seminarian step for him not being a truly shrewd politician. He is that and then some. The ability to walk that fine line is rather amazing to me. I find it almost Obama-like. There’s a calmness about him and a thoughtfulness in public. He’s playing right now five-dimensional chess in Texas,” he says.Part of that strategy involved building a political identity of his personal narrative and Christian faith. “It’s become that sense of armour – holding up the Bible – and people can’t get around it,” Minutaglio says. “Paxton, of course, is the greatest foil that anybody could pray to have. Talarico has found the cheat code in Texas.”The contrast between the two candidates could hardly be starker. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted overwhelmingly to impeach Paxton on 20 articles alleging misconduct, including bribery, abuse of office and obstruction of justice. The state senate later acquitted him.A long-running state securities fraud case ended in 2024 with an agreement requiring Paxton to perform community service, pay restitution and complete legal ethics courses in exchange for prosecutors dropping the charges. Paxton has remained bogged down by public revelations regarding his personal life, including an alleged extramarital affair and a high-profile divorce.Paxton, 63, has also been lethargic on the campaign trail with even Trump poking fun at his dress sense and speaking style.Jon Taylor, a professor of political science at the University of Texas at San Antonio, says: “Paxton is afraid to meet people. He tries to stay in this shell and avoid voters.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump looks on as Ken Paxton speaks at a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on 27 October 2026.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images“Everywhere Talarico goes, he attracts a substantial crowd. He’s got rock star status. Talarico is charismatic, personable and tells stories that resonate. Meanwhile, his opponent is basically screaming that Talarico believes God is non-binary and that he’s ‘far left’. The message is viewed by voters as shrill and ineffective.”As the race entered its final lap, national Republicans realised that Paxton’s vulnerability risked forfeiting a seat crucial to maintaining their narrow Senate majority. In response, conservative Super Pacs launched an unprecedented financial bombardment.Musk, who moved Tesla, SpaceX and his personal residence to Texas, gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The Republican Super Pac subsequently transferred the money to the Texas Pac, which has blanketed the state’s 22 media markets with anti-Talarico advertising. The blitz focused almost entirely on trans culture-war themes, falsely claiming Talarico supported taxpayer-funded gender reassignment surgeries for minors.At the same time, cracks have emerged in the conservative coalition along the Texas-Mexico border. While Trump made significant inroads among Latino voters in 2024, recent aggressive immigration raids and agricultural disruptions appear to have produced widespread buyer’s remorse.Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, a political consultant and former Democratic US Senate candidate, says: “I always say that the portion of Latino voters up for grabs are neither Republicans nor Democrats – they’re poor, and they need candidates who speak to their poverty, their pain and their power.View image in fullscreenJames Talarico prepares to speak to members of the mediain Laredo, Texas, on 14 July 2026.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty Images“Talarico leans more on a moral calling than a political persuasion, and that vision connects to people across a much larger swath of political persuasions than Democrats historically have reached. People are sick of the brazen political corruption and the system not working for ordinary working people.”Democrats are taking nothing for granted in a state that Trump won by 14 percentage points against Kamala Harris in 2024. Talarico is still careful to characterise himself and his movement as the people-powered underdog against the oligarchy, the David taking on a Goliath that includes the world’s most powerful man and the world’s richest man. For supporters who have spent decades enduring Democratic defeats in Texas, the prospect of a Talarico victory feels less like an ordinary midterm result than a profound turning point.Minutaglio comments: “If Talarico wins, it will be huge – a sea change in modern Texas history. The reverberation will rocket from the Fortune 500 companies in Dallas to the oil barons in Houston and the high-tech moguls around Austin. For decades, Texas has been addicted to deregulation and unfettered capitalism. Here’s a quiet seminarian who says, ‘Pump the brakes. Let’s think about oversight.’ It will challenge every perception of what Texas is.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026DemocratsUS politicsTexasKen PaxtonUS SenateUS CongressfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’
Content: ‘I’m still carrying the scars of her creation’ … a later incarnation of Lara Croft.Photograph: AspyrView image in fullscreen‘I’m still carrying the scars of her creation’ … a later incarnation of Lara Croft.Photograph: AspyrHow we madeCultureTomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’Interviews by Sean ColeMon 2 Nov 2026 09.40 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Douglas, lead programmer and co-creatorI joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches forTomb Raider. He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols.I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life.double quotation markWe worked till 2am every day for a year – and managed to bottle lightningWe had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis.Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefactsjust for fun.Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints.View image in fullscreen‘I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of how Lara was sexualised’ … the 1996 Tomb Raider title screen.Photograph: MobyGamesIt was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress.We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised.We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation.Heather Stevens, level designerWe developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life.View image in fullscreen‘Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that’ … Heather Stevens’ level concept sketches.Photograph: Heather StevensToby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before.Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together.double quotation markI was able to buy a house with the royaltiesBefore designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru!Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her.I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties.Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog. Feeling as if you’ve left a mark, and connected with millions of people through something you’ve created, is amazing.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeTomb RaiderGamesAdventure gamesPlatform gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years
Content: Most of the hardline plans drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMost of the hardline plans drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockImmigration and asylumShabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlashException for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five yearsRajeev SyalandJessica ElgotMon 2 Nov 2026 14.06 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.04 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade.Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to faceup to 30 yearsbefore being able to apply for settlement.The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”.But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement.She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”3:24Shabana Mahmood sets out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants – videoIn particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by someLabourMPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.View image in fullscreenDiane Abbott, the Labour MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, criticised the retrospective changes.Photograph: House of Commons/PAThe Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”.She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element.“People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.View image in fullscreenChris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said Mahmood’s decision would cost the country up to £10bn.Photograph: House of Commons/PAHome Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood’s softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years.The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds.Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn’t unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”View image in fullscreenEdward Leigh, the MP for Gainsborough, was among the Conservatives who acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed legal migration numbers to rise so significantly.Photograph: House of Commons/PABusiness groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood’s decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodRefugeesHome OfficeLabourCare workersSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology | Commonwealth summit | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
Content: Andy Burnham said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersCommonwealth summitPM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apologyAndy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and BarbudaPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 17.30 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 19.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event tolaunch a “structured dialogue”into what form an apology might take.UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate.In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs.“In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past.”View image in fullscreenKing Charles visits Nelson’s Dockyard in Antigua and Barbuda. No 10 denied Burnham’s remarks had potentially embarrassed the monarch.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/PABurnham set out his intention to look at a possible apology in anarticle for the Guardianon Saturday, in which he said the UK should “show leadership again today” as it had done in efforts to end the transatlantic slave trade.Asked why Burnham believed an apology was needed, his official spokesperson said: “The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration.” Having conversations about an apology would do this, and was also the right thing to do, he said.Tony Blairexpressed “deep sorrow”about the slave trade and Britain’s role in it in 2006, but stopped short of a formal apology.Burnham intended to go further, his spokesperson said. “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today.Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?Read more“That is distinct from a formal apology. We are opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.“We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they have asked for.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham plays cricket on a visit to Bullets cricket ground in Powells, Antigua and Barbuda, on Monday.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APBurnham is scheduled to take part in a series of assemblies at Chogm, as well as bilateral meetings with other leaders.There was no single event set aside to discuss slavery or an apology, but discussions would take place “throughout the next couple of days”, No 10 said, adding that the Foreign Office would lead talks over the form of an apology.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is already at the summit. One Foreign Office official said other Commonwealth countries “are responding positively to our offer of a structured dialogue” on an apology.“The conversations at Chogm have been focused on the positive work this alliance can do together on issues like climate and trade,” they said. “By not shying away from difficult discussions about our past, we are building trust with our allies to focus on the big issues of the future.”No 10 denied that Burnham’s comments had potentially embarrassed King Charles, who is already inAntigua and Barbudafor a pre-Chogm visit.Buckingham Palace “was made aware in a timely manner”, Burnham’s spokesperson said. “The prime minister believes that being true to British values of decency and honesty means not shying away from these conversations.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth summitSlaveryReparations and reparative justiceCaribbeanAntigua and BarbudaColonialismBritish empirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues
Content: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark crown court on Monday. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and denies the allegations against him.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arrives at Southwark crown court on Monday. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and denies the allegations against him.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court toldDefence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continuesEmine SinmazMon 2 Nov 2026 14.57 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.52 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand is not a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” and is respectful when women say no, a court has heard.In his closing speech at Southwark crown court, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why Brand’s accusers had not fought back when they were allegedly raped, saying “not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.Winter said allegations about the comedian’s sexual conduct in 2023 had “poisoned the wells” of justice. He also said there had been “monstrous delays” in the women in the criminal trial coming forward to police.He also questioned why Brand had been accused of “only three rapes in 10 years” out of all the women he had slept with.He said: “It is an extremely curious feature of this case that out of the many, many women that Mr Brand had sex with during this period only three of them say they did not consent to anal, oral or vaginal sex.”Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Winter began his closing speech by reciting an 1864 quote from the theologian and philosopher John Henry Newman, saying: “What I insist upon here, now that I am bringing this portion of my discussion to a close, is this unmanly attempt of his, in his concluding pages, to cut the ground from under my feet … this I call poisoning the wells.”He said the 2023 reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times and Sunday Times stories had “poisoned the well of justice” in Brand’s case by prompting the women to come forward with accusations afterwards.Winter told jurors: “They poisoned the wells in the hope and intention that other people come forward and make allegations against him.”In her closing speech on Friday, the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, denied that the 2023 reporting had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.Winter told jurors on Monday that Brand had an “immense amount of sex” and none of it was unlawful.“The question for you is, can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand between 1999 and 2009, he raped just three of them?” he asked.“Living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful however morally distasteful you may find it,” he continued. “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral – who cares? It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”Winter said another “curious feature” of the case was that the three rape complainants had alleged Brand was “normal” after the alleged incidents.“That, we suggest, is something that simply cannot have occurred if he is guilty,” the barrister said. “He obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that’s the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal.”The barrister said there was “no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”.He also questioned why the women had not screamed, kicked out or slapped Brand during the alleged attacks. He asked why a woman who accuses Brand of anal rape “didn’t just roll over and kick out in any way” and said she “didn’t scream or resist or call out”. He also questioned why a woman who says she was orally raped did not “slap [Brand] in the face” and suggested she had not “sufficiently” resisted.He also questioned how none of the women came forward during the #MeToo movement.Winter said: “How is it that it’s only three out of the many, many women, how is it that not even these ones, not even these allegations on this indictment came to light during #MeToo?“Many women were questioning whether they had a bad experience sexually at the hands of a famous person. It could not have been more publicised.“How is it that not one of them thought what happened to them involved a crime during the #MeToo movement?”The court has heard the earliest allegation dated back to 1999, when a woman accused Brand of raping her after he had performed in a fringe cabaret event during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth.The woman told the court Brand had left his email address after raping her, while asking her if she was enjoying herself.Winter said the woman was not a “naive and wilting flower” as he questioned her account of events. “You would have to be a psychopath to be raping someone and asking them if they were enjoying it,” Winter said. “He [Brand] said he was trying to please her but he wasn’t successful.”Winter said rapists did not try to please their victims. He also said Brand respected when a woman said no, and sought “approbation and adoration” from women.“He respects it when a woman says no so that makes him someone who is not a rapist,” Winter said. “He was seeking the approval in the sex, it’s the approval, it’s the ‘Yes I will have sex with you’, and that’s what he said in his evidence.”Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: EHRC raises concern with Reform about ‘racial and sexual remarks’ in documentary | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Watchdog writes to Nigel Farage’s party to ask what action it is taking to comply with the Equality Act
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Watchdog writes to Nigel Farage’s party to ask what action it is taking to comply with the Equality Act
Content: While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, councillors and candidates were filmed expressing racist and misogynistic views.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWhile Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, councillors and candidates were filmed expressing racist and misogynistic views.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianReform UKEHRC raises concern with Reform about ‘racial and sexual remarks’ in documentaryWatchdog writes to Nigel Farage’s party to ask what action it is taking to comply with the Equality ActPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.28 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.18 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe official equalities watchdog has written to Reform UK to raise concerns after an undercover TV documentaryshowed councillorsand candidates for the party expressing racist and misogynistic views, with one of the party’s MPs complaining about ingrained sexism.The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it had written to Nigel Farage’s party in the wake of revelations in ITV’s Undercover: A Year in Reform, which was broadcast in October.While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, footage in the programme included Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.In another section, the Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown complaining that the party was “chauvinistic” and riven with “alpha male shit”.An EHRC statement said its letter had asked Reform to provide information, “including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act”.In the wake of the documentary, the statement said, the EHRC “received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns about racial and sexual remarks expressed by councillors, prospective councillors and members”.It went on: “As with every complaint we receive, we will assess the information provided carefully and, following that consideration, take action where appropriate.“Political parties, like all duty-bearers, must comply with the Equality Act and take steps to avoid discrimination or harassment including on the grounds of race, religion or belief and sex. We have guidance advising parties on their responsibilities under the act and urge them to consider it. This could include reviewing party policies or practices to identify areas of potential discrimination, harassment or victimisation that need to be addressed.”It comes weeks after the EHRC wrote to the Greens in England and Wales to seek more information about a new party policy whichequates Zionism with racismand calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.Reform hassaid itreported ITV and the reporters concerned to police, with separate threats of civil legal action against the broadcaster.Responding to the EHRC letter, a party spokesperson said: “We are confident we have fully complied with our obligations under the Equality Act. There is no room for racism inReform UK.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKEquality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC)RaceNigel FarageLocal governmentIslamophobianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s really, really unusual’: tender bond between male donkey and bull baffles scientists | Animal behaviour | The Guardian
description: Patroclo and Achille’s interspecies affair sheds new light on social and sexual relations between animals, scientists say
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Patroclo and Achille’s interspecies affair sheds new light on social and sexual relations between animals, scientists say
Content: Bull and male donkey seen licking, nuzzling each other in rare same-sex interactionAnimal behaviour‘It’s really, really unusual’: tender bond between male donkey and bull baffles scientistsPatroclo and Achille’s interspecies affair sheds new light on social and sexual relations between animals, scientists sayNicola DavisScience correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.53 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.27 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn ancient myth, Achilles and Patroclus were two Greek heroes of the Trojan war whose intense bond was believed by some to have turned into a sexual relationship.In modern science, they are a bull, Achille, and a donkey, Patroclo, whose tender interspecies affair has helped to shed new light on social and sexual interactions between animals.Researchers say the two males have been spotted licking and rubbing each other, with the bull sometimes mounting the donkey.The team said while other donkeys attempted to avoid Achille’s attentions and showed threatening facial expressions towards him, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nibbled him.“It is really, really unusual,” said Dr Elisabetta Palagi of the University of Pisa in Italy, who co-authored the study. “And it is the first time it is reported in literature.”View image in fullscreenAchille with Patroclo.Photograph: André B da Cruz, UNIPIAndré da Cruz, a PhD student at the University of Pisa and another author, said the relationship had been discovered by accident while the researchers studied geladas, or bleeding-heart monkeys, inEthiopia.“We were having a little break for lunch, and in the distance I see something – it seemed a bit odd,” said da Cruz. “I told colleagues: ‘I think I saw a bull mounting a donkey.’ And they didn’t believe me.”Writing in the journal Current Biology, the researchers said the bull and the donkey belonged to different owners and only came into contact with each other when, as part of their daily routine, their herds used the same pasture.The researchers studied Achille and Patroclo over four days when they were both grazing in the same area, and four days when only one was present.The team not only recorded 51 mountings of Patroclo by Achille, but noted licking and rubbing often occurred before and, more surprisingly, after such events.“Rather than being solely attributable to sexual arousal, these interactions appear to play a role in prolonging the social interaction beyond the sexual act,” they wrote.Despite ample opportunity, neither Achille nor Patroclo tried to mount a member of their own species of either sex, although Achille did show courtship behaviours towards some female cattle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnimal homosexual behaviour under-reported by scientists, survey showsRead moreWhile rare, there have been other examples of interspecies hanky-panky, including a case of amale snow monkey attempting to have sex with female sika deer, and anAntarctic fur seal that not only sexually harassed king penguinsbut engaged in necrophilia.However, Palagi said there was no indication that the relationship between the donkey and the bull involved force.“We interpret our data as a special relationship,” Palagi said, adding that the two males searched for each other. “When Achille approached someone else in the plateau, Patroclo went to him and tried to distract him,” she said.Da Cruz said the mounting behaviour of Achille was unlikely to simply be a case of the bull exerting dominance.“We saw on several occasions what might have been semen from the bull, or he might have been orgasming, although we cannot verify [that] completely,” da Cruz said, adding that Patroclo was highly aggressive to bulls other than Achille.Palagi added that the relationship was an example of a sexual interaction that was disentangled from reproductive function.“When two individuals belonging to the same species or different species need to develop a special relationship, they fish simply from their entire [behavioural] repertoire,” she said.Palagi said it was unclear whether the sexual and social relationship between Patroclo and Achille had always co-existed or if one had led to the other. But, she added, the bond appeared to bring benefits, both in terms of attention but potentially also support.Josh Luke Davis, the author of A Little Gay Natural History, said interspecies relationships were not necessarily unusual and that the widespread and common nature of queer behaviours in the natural world meant it was “probably not that surprising” that they overlapped.“There is obviously value in reporting these kinds of behaviours,” Davis added. “But I would caution against reading too much into the significance of it and would be concerned about how it could be misconstrued or twisted by those who already deem homosexuality ‘unnatural’.”Explore more on these topicsAnimal behaviourAnimalsZoologyFarm animalsBiologyEthiopianewsShareReuse this content
