title: Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing | Fishing | The Guardian
description: Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations
Content: Greenpeace has declared the 'boulder barrier' zone an ‘ocean park’, in the spirit of Britain’s onshore national parks.Photograph: Andrew McConnell/GreenpeaceView image in fullscreenGreenpeace has declared the 'boulder barrier' zone an ‘ocean park’, in the spirit of Britain’s onshore national parks.Photograph: Andrew McConnell/GreenpeaceFishingGreenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishingAction taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populationsDamien GayleEnvironment corresponentMon 2 Nov 2026 08.10 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.37 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area.Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA.View image in fullscreenBoulders were loaded on to the Arctic Sunrise in Le Havre.Photograph: Andrew McConnell/GreenpeaceThe Southern North Sea isan area of importance for harbour porpoises, supportingnearly 20% of the UK North Sea population. But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily.Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said.Greenpeace campaigners drop boulders onto the seabed to create anti-trawler barrier“Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.”The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks.Greenpeace campaigner explains the “boulder barrier” on the seabedThe Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective.“We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said.View image in fullscreenThe boulders form an underwater barrier to prevent bottom-trawling fishing in the ‘ocean park’ zone.Photograph: Andrew McConnell/GreenpeaceThe action coincided with thenationwide premiere of Blue Planet III, the latest BBC wildlife documentary narrated by David Attenborough to focus on the oceans and the human-made threats they face. In 2025 bottom trawlers and dredgers tore through a cumulative 55,600 sq km of MPA seabeds, an area 58 times the size of Dartmoor national park, according to a Greenpeace analysis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries,’ said Kerry McCarthy, an MP and former climate minister who has supported the campaign.Photograph: Andrew McConnell/GreenpeaceBottom trawling to continue in English protected waters, government rulesRead moreA number of notable figures added their names to boulders tipped from the Arctic Sunrise into the North Sea. Among them was the Labour MP Kerry McCarthy, a former climate minister and a member of the all-party parliamentary group for the ocean, who said: “Industrialised fishing is having a hugely destructive impact on our marine environment, yet less than 1% of our seas are protected from it.“[Fishing boats] can legally tear through supposedly protected areas of the ocean, wreaking havoc upon the seabed, precious habitats and the sea life that lives there. Progress is too slow and nature can’t wait, which is why I’ve added my name to one of Greenpeace UK’s boulders. We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries, both here in UK waters and right across the Atlantic Ocean.”The government has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsFishingMarine lifeConservationPorpoisesSharksBirdsActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in California | California | The Guardian
description: Latest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballots
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: Latest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballots
Content: Bill Essayli, US attorney for the central district of California, at a news conference in Los Angeles, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenBill Essayli, US attorney for the central district of California, at a news conference in Los Angeles, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APCaliforniaTrump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in CaliforniaLatest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballotsUS midterms – live updatesSam LevinMon 2 Nov 2026 18.22 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.38 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Justice (DoJ) in California has charged six more people with alleged voter fraud crimes, an escalation of the Trump administration’s campaign against the state’s election processes on the eve of the midterms.Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles and aclose ally of the president, announced on Monday that his office was prosecuting six lawful permanent residents accused of unlawfully registering to vote and casting fraudulent ballots. The DoJfiled similar chargesagainst 28 people across California last month and arranged for adramatic on-camera arrestof one 72-year-old defendant, editing the footage into a DoJ promotional video.The six new defendants are all green card holders, according to criminal complaints filed in federal court, meaning they are immigrants who have legal status, but are barred from voting.Voting by noncitizens is extremelyrare, and experts say when noncitizens do end up on the voter rolls, it is usuallydue to confusion.The pro-Trump prosecutor trying to stop California ballots from being countedRead moreThe latest arrests come as the DoJ pushes ahead with its lawsuit seeking to force California election officials toset aside roughly 20,000 ballotsthat federal prosecutors say may belong to noncitizens who fraudulently registered. The DoJ has said the ballots should not be counted until California can confirm their citizenship status. State election leaders have countered that prosecutors’ list and methodology was unreliable and that complying with the demands in the middle of an election would be logistically impossible and would risk disenfranchising US citizens. Multiplejudgeshaverebuffedthe DoJ’s efforts asunconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and the US supreme court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s appeals.Five of the six people charged in the latest round of prosecutions have been arrested, Essayli said at a press conference on Monday. The six defendants include people originally from Mexico, Israel, the Philippines, Canada and Iran, prosecutors said.All six are accused of a single charge each of making false statements on a naturalization application, with affidavits alleging they unlawfully registered to vote, and then when they later applied for citizenship, they falsely claimed that they had never previously registered. The complaints said the defendants cast ballots in recent years, but they are not facing charges specifically relating to fraudulently voting.The defendants are facing a maximum of five years in prison, according to prosecutors. The charges were outlined in initial complaints written by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents. The defendants have not been formally indicted, and it was not immediately clear if any of them had obtained lawyers. The federal public defender’s office in Los Angeles did not immediately respond to an inquiry.One 52-year-old defendant from Canada was accused of voting unlawfully twice, then seeking to cancel his registration. The complaint says he has been in the US for more than 40 years. A 43-year-old defendant from the Philippines has been in the US since 1992 and was accused of voting several times since 2020.Experts have said it was extraordinary for the DoJ to bring these cases in the middle of an election, with federal prosecutors traditionally avoiding taking steps that could be seen as politically motivated or potential interference with an upcoming race. Former prosecutors and defense lawyers have said it was especially galling to see the government present the arrests in such a showy manner, blasting mugshots and parading defendants in front of news cameras.The Associated Press and other news outlets were present for a pre-dawn arrest of the 72-year-old last month on a quiet residential street, and a Fox News reporter on Mondayposted photos of two arrests, including one who appeared to be an Amazon worker handcuffed on the sidewalk. Democrats have accused the DoJ of trying to sow doubt in the results of the election and create a false impression that voter fraud is widespread.Essayli said the newly arrested defendants were on federal prosecutors’ list of 20,000 voters who might be fraudulently registered, arguing the cases further supported their push to stop ballots from being counted. But an immigrants’ rights group, which sued the government over its use of federal immigration data to challenge voters, analyzed the list and said in a filing over the weekend thatmore than 40%of the people flagged as potentially fraudulent voters could not be found on the state’s voter rolls.The 20,000 names represent a tiny fraction of the more than23 million registered votersin California.County election officials who have received threatening letters from the DoJ with demands that they set aside certain ballots have also said the lists handed to them wereriddled with errors.When questioned about the prosecutors’ list on Monday, Essayli told reporters the government had used “third-party databases” to identify potentially fraudulent voters, and that it “may not be 100%” accurate, but there was a “very, very high confidence rate”. At a press briefing during the first round of arrests last month, Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, said: “There may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens. We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve askedCaliforniato cooperate with us.”The DoJ in recent days has also repeatedly threatened to criminally prosecute election officials who process fraudulent ballots, prompting arebuke from a federal judgeon Friday, who said the DoJ’s “intimidation, threats, and attempts at coercion force election workers daily to choose between acceding to [the DoJ’s] unlawful demands or adhering to their duties and thereby subjecting themselves to a serious risk of criminal investigation and prosecution”. The judge blocked the administration from continuing to threaten election officials.Essayli has continued his crusade against California’s elections even after a federal judge ruled last week thathe was “unlawfully” servingas the head of the US attorney’s office since he was not formally appointed and confirmed by the Senate. The DoJ is appealing that ruling.Sam Levine contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaTrump administrationWest CoastUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Republicans were hoping to flip this New Hampshire Senate seat – will Trump get in the way? | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Republican John Sununu tries to distance himself from unpopular president in race against Chris Pappas that has gone from ‘toss-up’ to ‘lean Democrat’
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: Republican John Sununu tries to distance himself from unpopular president in race against Chris Pappas that has gone from ‘toss-up’ to ‘lean Democrat’
Content: Democratic US Senate candidate Chris Pappas, center,  campaigns in New Hampshire, on 31 October.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenDemocratic US Senate candidate Chris Pappas, center,  campaigns in New Hampshire, on 31 October.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersUS midterm elections 2026Republicans were hoping to flip this New Hampshire Senate seat – will Trump get in the way?Republican John Sununu tries to distance himself from unpopular president in race against Chris Pappas that has gone from ‘toss-up’ to ‘lean Democrat’Shrai Popatin Manchester, New HampshireMon 2 Nov 2026 10.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.03 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChris Pappas is stopping himself from getting too excited ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.“I take nothing for granted,” said the four-term US representative and Democratic nominee for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat. “This is a very purple, competitive state. Elections are never in the bag here.”The race to replace the retiring Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen has emerged as a source of 11th hour anxiety for the party.In their attempt to gain four seats and reclaim control of the Senate, Democrats can’t afford to lose one they already hold. But September polling showing Pappasvirtually tiedwith his Republican opponent, former senator John Sununu, rattled party strategists and raised the prospect that New Hampshire could become an unexpected battleground.The warning signs were striking in a state Donald Trump has lost in each of his three presidential bids.The blessing and curse of Trump’s shadowWhile Pappas has regained a narrow advantage in most polls, and the Cook Political Report moved the race in early October from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat”, his closing message has focused heavily on tying Sununu to an unpopular president.Trump’s approval rating sits at just 32% in the state, according to a recent University of New Hampshirepoll, giving Democrats hope that voter frustration with the administration will ultimately benefit Pappas’s run.“Sununu has spent most of the last year on team Trump, and now that we’re getting within range of the election, he’s recognizing how unpopular the president is,” Pappas said as he traveled the state in the final days on the trail, often joined by party heavyweights, like Arizona senator Mark Kelly and former vice-president Kamala Harris.View image in fullscreenChris Pappas at MaryAnn’s Restaurant in Derry, New Hampshire, on 31 October.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersDemocrats believe political headwinds facing Republicans have been strengthened by rising high gas prices and heating-oil costs linked to the war with Iran.More than a thirdof New Hampshire households rely on heating oil, and colder temperatures have pushed the issue to the forefront of voters’ minds ahead of election day.“People are now starting to get really angry,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist. “I think a lot of people see Sununu as just one more Republican who will try to talk a good game, but when push comes to shove, he will not stand up to Trump becauseRepublicansin Washington have a record of not doing it.”For voters like Randy Marchand, who is supporting Pappas, but considers himself an independent, the Republican party is ultimately a rubber stamp for the president’s agenda. “I’m afraid for our democracy … right now the Republican party is no more,” said the 54-year-old flight attendant, who lives in Manchester. “They will say one thing to get in, and will ultimately come down to what Trump wants.”Sununu, however, has spent much of the campaign arguing that independence, not loyalty, defines his political record.The former senator has emphasized his criticism of Trump’s trade war with Canada, which has affected several industries in the state, and in a recent campaign advertisement, he even claimed to have “never met” the president.The former senator’s anti-Trump bona fides do have some roots. In 2024, he voiced his support or Nikki Haleyin an op-edduring Republican primary campaign, and also branded Trump a “loser”.This week, during the final televised Senate debate, Pappas argued that Sununu initially backed the administration’s decision to launch strikes on Iran. Sununu countered that the congressman “exaggerates” his position and noted that he has consistently opposed putting American troops on the ground.View image in fullscreenChris Pappas (left) and John Sununu debate in Manchester, New Hamphire, on 28 October.Photograph: Reba Saldanha/APDemocrats dismiss those distinctions as largely tactical. “Sununu has spent most of the last year on Team Trump, and you know now that we’re getting within range of the election, he’s recognizing how unpopular the president is,” Pappas said in an interview. (The Sununu campaign did not respond to the Guardian’s request for an interview.)Sununu’s Trump problem is also causing consternation for some Republican operatives in the state.While New Hampshire voters like “local Republican control”, it might “be a little too much to send Trump an additional senator when the president’s numbers are just so low. It’s very difficult to articulate why a Republican should win that seat,” said one New Hampshire strategist who spoke on the condition of anonymity to comment candidly on the race.“The war in Iraq is what broke the back of the Republican party in New Hampshire 20 years ago,” the operative added, noting that Sununu’s support for the initial authorizationcontributedto his failed re-election bid in 2008. “Now we have a war in Iran, and while it’s asymmetric, it is economic. That psychological toll certainly doesn’t help.”A history of ticket splittingNew Hampshire’shabit of ticket-splittingcomplicates any effort to view the Senate race solely through a national lens.The state’s congressional delegation is all-Democratic, while Republicans control the state legislature and the governor’s office. In 2024, votersbackedKamala Harris for president whileelectingRepublican Kelly Ayotte as governor.View image in fullscreenVoters during a primary election in Hooksett, New Hampshire, on 8 September.Photograph: Mel Musto/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesThis year, that same kind of mixed vote is prevalent throughout the state. John McAllister, a firefighter in Nashua, said that he and his association were supporting Pappas this election, while also backing Ayotte – who is leading the polls in her re-election race against Cinde Warmington.Pappas has been a “true supporter” of firefighters’ issues “as long as he’s been in the House”, McAllister said. Meanwhile, Ayotte’s work on pension restoration for public safety employees in New Hampshire has put “thousands of dollars” back into first responders’ pockets, he said. As a result, a consistently blue or red vote is never guaranteed. “We have proven time and time again to go either Republican or Democrat,” McAllister said.Two establishment figures fight it outUnlike many of this year’s Senate contests, New Hampshire’s race pits two deeply familiar political brands against one another.Pappas has represented the state’s first congressional district since 2019 and previously served on the executive council. His family also owns the Puritan Backroom restaurant, a fixture of New Hampshire political campaigning, and the alleged birthplace of the chicken tender. If Pappas wins this year’s election, he will be the first out gay man to serve in theUS Senate.Sununu, who served as a congressman before winning his upper-chamber seat in 2002, comes from one one of the Granite state’s best-known political dynasties. Both his father and younger brother, Chris, served as governor.The latter even joked that he would be “up by 30 points” if voters thought he was running for Senate this year. Sununu responded bysaying: “I love my brother but he’s totally wrong.” If he triumphs, Sununu would also be the first Republican senator that New Hampshire has sent to Washington since 2010.View image in fullscreenJohn Sununu greets a voter at Oktoberfest in Loudon, New Hampshire, on 3 October.Photograph: Sophie Park/Getty ImagesIn a national midterms cycle that is characterized by energy for insurgents and anti-establishment energy, the New Hampshire race appears to be an outlier. Two familiar names with robust records to scrutinize.At their final televised debate this week, Sununu chided Pappas for his eight years in office where he “hasn’t gotten the job done” and accused him of siding with his party leadership too frequently.But Pappas made sure to list the ways in which he has broken ranks when necessary and crossed the aisle, pointing to“yes” votefor the Laken Riley Act, the Republican-led legislation that requires the detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related crimes, and hissupportfor a congressional stock trading ban.Meanwhile, Pappas targeted Sununu’s previous support to privatize social security when he was last in the Senate. “I’ve never voted to cut social security benefits, I never will,” Sununusaid. “But Chris attacks me for introducing legislation 20 years ago that would have made the system solvent.”The campaign has also occasionally veered into personal attacks. In September, Pappas referenced a 2010 emailreleasedas part of justice department files related to Jeffrey Epstein, in which the late sex offender wrote that “John Sununu has great stories” in a message to his associate Boris Nikolić.The exchangefollowed attacksfrom national Republicans mocking a photograph of Pappas on a Zoom call with his cat. Pappasrespondedon social media: “I have a cat, and John Sununu’s name is in the Epstein files.”It remains unclear whether Epstein was referring to the Republican nominee or his father, former governor John H Sununu. Earlier this year, Sununu’s campaign said neither man had “ever met or communicated in any way” with Epstein or Nikolić.Looking ‘beyond the next two years’Some Republicans argue that Democrats are betting too heavily on antipathy toward Trump to defeat a candidate they view as genuinely independent.“As someone who is a fiscal conservative … and wants to make every penny count, Sununu is a brilliant guy, and he really cares about the bottom line,” said Kate Day, a 69-year-old retiree from Chesterfield. “He’ll let you know if he doesn’t agree with the rest of the Republicans. I think his number one job is going to be standing up for New Hampshire, which is how it should be.”Republicans also contend that voters are evaluating the race through a longer lens than the remainder of Trump’s presidency. “[Voters] know that this is an election for the next six years,” said Joe Sweeney, a state representative and deputy majority leader in New Hampshire’s Republican-controlled house of representatives.View image in fullscreenChris Pappas with Kamala Harris at a campaign field office in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, on 24 October.Photograph: John Tully/Getty Images“I think that the Democrats have been in this pattern for the last 10 years, where every other word they talk about is about President Trump,” Sweeney added. “They have this sort of obsession with him, and I think New Hampshire voters are wiser than that.”Some Republicans argue that Sununu would really be the state’s only opportunity to elect a stronger voice to check Trump in his final years in office.“If you really want to modify what the president’s doing, you need someone in his own party fighting back, not someone who’s going to be a rubber stamp,” said David Carney, a longtime New Hampshire Republican strategist, pointing to senators such as Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.Yet even Carney acknowledged the challenge facing Sununu in a state where Trump remains deeply unpopular.“We’re not immune in New Hampshire from the national environment,” he said. “We get influenced by what we see and what we feel is happening across the country.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026New HampshireUS politicsRepublicansUS SenatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What can Democrats actually do if they win Congress? | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Democrats are fighting to win control of the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms. Here’s what winning would mean for them – and Donald Trump
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Democrats are fighting to win control of the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms. Here’s what winning would mean for them – and Donald Trump
Content: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries at a press conference at the US Capitol on 27 March 2026.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHouse minority leader Hakeem Jeffries at a press conference at the US Capitol on 27 March 2026.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026ExplainerWhat can Democrats actually do if they win Congress?Democrats are fighting to win control of the House and Senate in the midterms. Here’s what winning would mean for them – and Donald TrumpGuardian staffMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Democrats win back the USHouse of Representativesor the Senate in the midterm elections on Tuesday, the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency will look markedly different from the first half. But what would the Democrats’ actually be able to do with either – or both – chambers of Congress in their control?What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections and why do they matter?Read moreWhat can Democrats do if they win the House?IfDemocratstake the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump for a third time.Democrats will have ‘field day’ with Trump inquiries if they win House, legal experts sayRead moreWhat can Democrats do if they win the Senate?The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.‘A sense of energy’: Our politics team answered your questions on Democrats’ midterms hopesRead moreWhat if Republicans win?Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.What will Democrats investigate if they win?Political reporterJoseph Gedeonlaid out the most consequentialinvestigations Democrats could launchif they take back Congress. Here are a few of the investigations:The family business:Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked Trump family corruption first on his list of priorities, while Representative Jamie Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.Epstein and the emails:Thanks to a tag-team effort by Representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it had deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is nowfacing a lawsuitfrom journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (butnot always) acting in concert tosubpoena witnessesandhold them in contemptwhen they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress.The Pentagon and the war:Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, sayshe will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family.Impeachment:House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing out regarding impeachment this time around, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”.Targeting Trump: how Democrats plan to investigate the president if they win CongressRead moreWhat did the Democrats do last time they flipped the House under Trump?In 2018, halfway through Trump’s first term, theDemocrats flipped the House of Representatives in a sweeping blue wave. House committeesquickly launched dozens of inquiriesinto his businesses, his handling of the Russia probes and possible conflicts of interest.Just over a year after the 2018 midterms, after months of leftwing calls for impeachment, the House voted mostly on party lines toimpeach Trump.Democrats had accused Trump of pursuing a scheme to cheat in the upcoming presidential election by pressuringUkraineto manufacture bad news aboutJoe Bidenand then blocking congressional oversight. Trump was lateracquitted in the Republican-controlled Senateon both articles of impeachment.In 2021, Trump wasimpeached– andacquitted– a second time for inciting the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US SenateHouse of RepresentativesUS politicsDemocratsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief | Jo Brand | The Guardian
description: The comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaper
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaper
Content: ‘Maybe anarchy needs to come back’ … Jo Brand.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Maybe anarchy needs to come back’ … Jo Brand.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe big interviewJo Brand‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and griefThe comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaperEmine SanerMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHadJo Brand, who turns 70 next year, been spending a long time thinking about getting older? Had it become the subject that consumed her, and the reason why, now, she felt impelled to write a book about the vagaries of ageing? No, she says, laughing. She was simply asked if she’d like to do it.Still, it encouraged introspection about what she wanted her future to look like. “Now’s the time, if you want things, to get them in place. I think a lot of people say, ‘I really want to do that, but I’ll forget it for now.’ And then they get to a stage where they can’t.” Does she mean bucket-list things? “No, I mean … what do I mean?” Brand pauses. “I mean the ability to perhaps end your own …” She doesn’t go there, but the end to that sentence is obviously: life.“I know it’s not legal yet, but I think it will be, sooner rather than later.” Her mother had procured drugs to end her own life when she was ill, though she didn’t use them. Two minutes in, and we’re already talking about assisted dying. Off-duty comedians – such a laugh.I’m being unfair. Of course Brand is fun, but ageing isn’t, sometimes. In her book, Decline and Falling Over, she calls the point past middle age “your shitter second half”. The book is funny, as you’d expect, but also surprisingly sober, covering such cheering topics as the decision to go into a care home and, yes, assisted dying.double quotation markI’ve never really been a grumpy person. I’ve been a bit friendly, and tried to be pleasant to everyoneDespite thinking about what she wants her future to look like, Brand has not yet come to any solid conclusions. As a teenager, she worked in a residential home (for adults with learning disabilities, rather than older people), and complained after she witnessed some “appalling behaviour” by male staff. It was not investigated; instead, she was sacked. She was left with a fear of care homes. “That was in the 70s. Are they that different now? Who knows?” But, she adds, “I can’t imagine I can persuade any of my family to get interested in looking after me.” (She has two grown-up daughters.)Are there any benefits of getting older? “Being rude to people.” She laughs. “No, not really. But saying what you think, I suppose. I like the whole ‘grumpy old woman’ sort of thing. I do quite like being grumpy. I’ve never really been a grumpy person. I’ve been a bit friendly, and tried to be pleasant to everyone – not on stage, I accept that, because a lot of people think I’m probably horrible, but in my personal life.” It is, she says, “that whole thing that a lot of women suffer from, which is putting everybody first and themselves last”.Brand writes several times that she’s a “people pleaser” – which, given her bolshie stage persona and unflinching attitude, surprises me (although she has always seemed thoughtful, and very kind). “It surprises me as well,” she says. We’re in a meeting room at the Guardian offices, Brand glorious in layers of black with dark pink hair, looking queenly but punk. “I have always been one because … well, why? I’ve no idea. My dad was quite hard to please, so maybe I spent quite a lot of time doing that.”Did the on-stage version of her character not influence the way she was in real life? “I don’t think it really did,” she says. “I think that was because there weren’t many women comics around when I started – you needed a sort of shield.” If she could be more vulgar, more aggressive than the drunk men who heckled her, they’d back off – or at least, she hoped, word would get around that she wasn’t to be messed with. “If you’re heckled, you have to deal with it because audiences lose faith in you if you don’t, so I had a sliding scale of pleasant through to soul-destroying. I never wanted to use soul-destroying, but I occasionally would.”View image in fullscreenHecklers beware … at the Sadler’s Wells theatre in London, 1995.Photograph: Michael Le Poer Trench/ShutterstockGrowing up in Hastings, where the family ended up after moving from London and Kent, the teenage Brand was rebellious rather than people-pleasing. She had unsuitable boyfriends, stayed out, discovered drugs. “But that was more to do with the circumstances we were in,” she says. “At the time my dad was in a very bad place, and so he was really difficult to live with.” He could be violent. “I mean, not as bad as some poor women have it on a regular basis, but quite a few times. Mainly when I answered back to him, or my little brother did.” Brand, I notice, tends to downplay a lot, but it must have been scary. “It makes you a bit jumpy, hypervigilant. So I was only too delighted to get out of home.”She moved into a bedsit at 17. It was quite exciting, looking back. “We had the freedom to behave appallingly, if we wanted to.” Was she in danger of going out of control? “I always had a sense of when the brakes should be applied. So I was never in danger of, let’s say, becoming a heroin addict, even though I was around a lot of people that used drugs. I think I would have quite happily drunk a lot more if I could drink.” But she couldn’t hold it. “When I was at university, I was very cheap to get pissed.”Becoming a comic had been Brand’s ambition since she was a teenager. “I liked making people laugh, but not in any well-formed sense of doing an act.” She became a psychiatric nurse instead, trying standup at 29. “I imposed a pointless line on my life: that you can’t get to 30 and not have tried comedy.” It helped that she was older, she thinks, and that no heckler could ever be as shocking or as aggressive as some of the patients she had dealt with, who suffered with psychosis. “I was a bit hardened.”Still, how did she not let it get to her, listening to drunk men making personal attacks? “My self-esteem had gone as low as it probably could. It’s hard, because it’s embarrassing if someone says something really gross and awful to you in front of a big group of other people. And the way to deal with it, to me, is to come back with something better. It’s like a battle. If we’d had to fight each other, obviously I wouldn’t have done terribly well.” She smiles. “But I might have done.”What was it like to be a young woman on the circuit? Was sexual harassment part of her experience? “Not the way I looked,” Brand laughs. Then she reconsiders: “Actually, there were a few comics occasionally trying to get in my room at two o’clock in the morning. I just shouted through the door, told them to fuck off, and they did. So it was nothing that I couldn’t deal with.”View image in fullscreenWith Joanna Scanlan, left, and Vicki Pepperdine, the cast of Getting On.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianStill, the 80s comedy circuit sounds as if it must have been thrilling. It was, she says. “There was such a variety of people doing such weird things, like melting a block of ice or whatever it was they did,” she says, referring to the performance artist Anthony Irvine, known as the Iceman. “These days, it’s much more uniform. I think there are some really brilliant comics around, but it’s become very stand-uppy.” It’s expected to be more polished now, I venture, less anarchic. “Yes, maybe anarchy needs to come back.”The birth of alternative comedy in the 80s must also have felt exciting, politically, after decades of old-style comedians with their racist and sexist jokes. For a while it must have felt as if a generation of progressive comics could change, or at least help change, society. But it doesn’t feel like that now. “Yeah, the world is in a mess,” says Brand. “But there are an awful lot of good people, and I just hope the good people win out. I’m not an optimist, but then again, I’m not a terrible pessimist, either.”By 1993 Brand had her own show, Jo Brand Through the Cakehole. It was a mix of standup and sketches. In one segment – Drudge Squad, her spoof cop show – two female detectives worn down by domesticity try to fight crime amid laundry baskets and useless husbands.There were men in the tabloids who were unforgivably awful about Brand, especially about the way she looked. But as for the teenage girls (myself among them) who watched her Friday night Channel 4 show, it’s hard to overstate the thrill of seeing Brand, a woman who looked and spoke differently from everyone else: hilariously rude and unapologetic.View image in fullscreenBrand presented The Great British Bake Off: An Extra Slice from 2014.Photograph: Channel 4Is she envious of female comedians starting now? Does she think they get an easier time? “I’m not, actually. There’s a lot more really good competition these days, and because we were quite unusual – I think there were 15 of us out of, like, 200 male comics – we were a bit of a novelty act, so that was a help. And people didn’t quite know what to make of us, and that was a help, too.”Until last year, Brand presented the Great British Bake Off after-show, An Extra Slice, and this year she is doing a book tour. She has already won a Bafta for her role as a kind but harassed nurse in Getting On, the BBC comedy she co-wrote with Vicki Pepperdine and Joanna Scanlan, set in an NHS geriatric ward. Over the years, she has – for television – learned to play the organ at the Royal Albert Hall, performed as Britney Spears and, for Comic Relief in 2016,walked 140 milesfrom Hull to Liverpool.One aspect of getting older, she says, is that she is less adventurous than she used to be. “I used to do quite a lot of stupid things, like jump off things or learn how to rally drive. I couldn’t imagine being a rally driver now. I love a bit of madness like that, but I’m much less mad than I used to be, physically.”Brand also doesn’t do as many live shows. She thinks her memory took a hit during the pandemic, which makes remembering long sets a bit harder. But she has been doing some “work-in-progress shows”, which takes the pressure off a polished performance. “I was so delighted that I could use that tag, which basically means: most of this might be rubbish.”One of the worst things about ageing, she says, particularly as a woman, is that “you get ignored. Putting my job for a moment out of the equation, older men still get much more respect than older women, because we all think older women are just one big blob that looks the same. I think it’s going to take a while longer to cherish older women for the fantastic variety that they are.”Brand has experienced tragedy in the last 10 years – she lost her parents, both brothers, and two of her three best friends. How has she dealt with it? “I’ve been very good at suppressing my emotions,” she says. “I was always taught not to show any weakness in public, which used to be just a bloke’s thing, didn’t it? So I probably haven’t handled it all very well – I just pretended it wasn’t happening for a long time because I couldn’t believe how awful it was.”View image in fullscreen‘Being angry is very good for me.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn her book, she writes about being stuck at the “angry stage” of grief for a while. “I like the angry stage,” she says. “I think anger is just as valid as crying – you can be angry about people leaving you. I think being angry is very good for me.” As for denial, another part of the so-called five stages of grief, Brand says she could probably do it for the rest of her life. “So yes, I’m not terribly good at grief, because I’m not terribly good at acceptance, either – I don’t think I’ve done that yet at all.” Sometimes she’ll think she hasn’t heard from one of those best friends for a while. “And then I remember. That weird stuff happens with grief all the time, doesn’t it?”Has it made her agonise about her own mortality more? “Less! I refuse to think about it. I’m a massive avoider of those sorts of things. I know it’s a bad thing to be, but what’s the point of thinking about it? It’s far too late for me to go down the gym every 10 minutes. At least, I did give up smoking, but now I’m a champion vaper.”Best just to get on with things. Or at least take a tip on ageing from her great-grandmother, “who just went to bed and ate chocolate all day”. Not that retirement holds any appeal. Brand is lucky, she says, in that her job is not one she has to retire from. “There are still enough people to come and see me at shows, so I can do that if I want to.” Long may she reign.Decline and Falling Over is published by Penguin (£22).
