title: Ibiza on ice: why is Greenland suddenly throwing open its doors to tourists? | Greenland | The Guardian
description: It’s 80% frozen and there are no roads outside towns, but that’s not stopping the territory welcoming more visitors than ever before with three new airports
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s 80% frozen and there are no roads outside towns, but that’s not stopping the territory welcoming more visitors than ever before with three new airports
Content: Ice, ice, baby.Photograph: Bruce Yuanyue Bi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIce, ice, baby.Photograph: Bruce Yuanyue Bi/Getty ImagesPass notesGreenlandIbiza on ice: why is Greenland suddenly throwing open its doors to tourists?It’s 80% frozen and there are no roads outside towns, but that’s not stopping the territory welcoming more visitors than ever before with three new airportsMon 2 Nov 2026 11.21 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Greenland (orKalaallit Nunaat, the land of the people in the Greenlandic language).Age:The landmass is believed to have been settledabout 2500BC.Appearance:Huge (2,166,086 sq km),almost80% iceand 100% excited to welcome more tourists.So, 80% ice, eh? That doesn’t make Greenland the easiest sell for tourists.There are alsono roadsoutside towns. But there is a new international airport in Ilulissat, known as the “city of icebergs” and Greenland’s third-largest city, offering direct flights from Denmark and Iceland. Joining the airports opened in Nuuk (the capital) in 2024 andin Qaqortoq in April, it means Greenland is now extremely open for tourist business.Really? It still seems awfully remote.Yes – it welcomedmore visitors than ever before in 2025– nearly 180,000 (the population is only 56,000) – and this year is set to beat that.Aren’tGreenlandersunhappy about being outnumbered? Lots of destinations now want less tourism, not more.Yes, local people in tourist hotspots – especially in Spain, Portugal, Italy and France –have protestedat how tourism negatively affects their lives. It’s an issue in Greenland, too – when Nuuk airport opened, there was concern about howthe influx of touristsmight affect a historically isolated population and pristine environment. A cruise ship was also blocked from entering Ilulissat, wherelocals feel they see little benefit from foreign tourist operations.So Greenland isn’t, actually, ‘100% excited’ to welcome tourists?OK, no. There’s still ambivalence, butDonald Trumpand the climate crisis may be shifting perspectives. The president’s threat to acquire Greenland filled inhabitants with anger and apprehension, while disruption from melting polar ice means the traditional fishing industry is existentially threatened. The country is also striving for independence from Denmark: “If Greenland wants to be independent, we need to have a strong foundation, economically and in terms of industry and business,”prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen commentedon Ilulissat’s maiden flight.I suppose it’s never going to be rammed like Ibiza either.There is actually avibrant music culture, with lively hip-hop and heavy metal scenes, and anIndigenous Electronic music festival in Nuuk, but no. Tourism only accounted for 4.9% of GDP in 2024.Is a new airport enough to attract more visitors?MaybeVisit Greenlandcould take inspiration fromother chilly destinationsthat are getting creative about attracting tourists: Finland’s Turku archipelago ishiring a smell ambassadorto promote what it calls “the best-smelling destination in the world”.I wonder how Greenland smells?Delicious, likeroasted reindeer; fascinating likefermented seal blubber. You can also enjoywhale watching, dog sledding or ice fishing and bathe in hot springs. Plus, it looks extraordinary – the stunning spectacle of thepolar ice sheet, astonishingicebergs,exquisite light (including the northern lights and the midnight sun) and unparalleled darkness. Way to up your Instagram game.Sold!Get me on the first flight to Ilulissat!Angalalluarina (that’sbon voyage,apparently).Do say:“Tikilluarit!” (Welcome!)Don’t say:“Unless your name is Trump.”Explore more on these topicsGreenlandPass notesOvertourismDonald TrumpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art icon | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at Tate
Author: Kat Lister
Headline: The artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at Tate
Content: ‘She’s making the moves’ … Wilhelmina Barns-Graham’s Protest, 1967.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustView image in fullscreen‘She’s making the moves’ … Wilhelmina Barns-Graham’s Protest, 1967.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustArt and designBeaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art iconThe artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at TateKat ListerMon 2 Nov 2026 07.30 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 07.32 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the centre of Tate St Ives’ newly opened retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, her monumental altar-piece Glacier (Blue Cave) pulls viewers into its frozen tendons of turquoise and white. Its mouth is agape and the blue slit of its eye casts downwards to the rest of its body. The glacierfeelshuman: a vivisection of rock, ice and snow that brings to mind the fragmented facial features of Picasso’s Weeping Woman.Standing in front of this glassy colossus, the exhibition’s curator, Katy Norris, talks about these “mangled” and “twisted” forms – so alive on the canvas. “Barns-Graham was so distinct in her approach,” Norris says. “There are always questions of: what am I seeing? What is in front of mereally?And how does that relate to what I feel inside?”View image in fullscreen‘Feels human’ … Glacier (Blue Cave), 1950.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustGlacier (Blue Cave) was painted not far from this gallery space in 1950 – only 10 years after the Scottish-born painter moved 500 miles south to the tiny fishing town of St Ives – but it goes some way to showing just how radical she was over the course of her eight-decade career. From her early 20s, Barns-Graham’s quest for connection saw the self-described “lone wolf” become a key player in the St Ives school which congregated in and around the Cornish harbour during the second world war. She continued to experiment relentlessly with colour, geometry, kineticism and repetition until her death in 2004, aged 91.Anne Barlow, director of Tate St Ives, points out this major retrospective – the first to span Barns-Graham’s full career – is a “long-overdue celebration” of an expressive master. The art historian Virginia Button wrote that “Barns-Graham clearly felt that as a woman she had been unfairly sidelined from the history of St Ives” with its focus on Ben Nicholson, Peter Lanyon and Patrick Heron. She had a brief period of fame in the 1950s, but it waned in the 1960s as her landscape modernist work became increasingly “hard-edged” (as Rob Airey, director of the Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust, puts it) and more daring; less commercial and harder to categorise.View image in fullscreenIn Barns-Graham’s beloved St Ives … The Blue Studio, 1948.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust. Courtesy of The Fleming Collection.With her “blue eyes that flashed like knives” (so her husband, the writer David Lewis, remarked) and her delight in toying with gender stereotypes (she took great pleasure in the sexual ambiguity of her preferred nickname “Willie”), Barns-Graham ploughed her own furrow from the beginning. Born into an upper-class family in the seaside town of St Andrews in 1912, Barns-Graham’s resistance was tested early when her stern father became hostile towards her plan to pursue artmaking as a profession.Nonetheless, ignited by her love of Cézanne, at the age of 18 Barns-Graham started studying at Edinburgh College ofArt. “She had a single-mindedness,” Norris says. “She didn’t see any limitations, she just saw the path ahead.” It’s a focus you can sense in her 1945 oil painting Froth and Seaweed. Painted in her beloved St Ives, the artist homes in on the spidery tendrils of algae and slithery copper rock. “It’s almost as if she has no peripheral vision, she’s just seeing beauty at her feet.”View image in fullscreenBarns-Graham in Cousins’ A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things.Photograph: Publicity imageFilm-maker Mark Cousins first encountered Barns-Graham’s paintings in late-80s Edinburgh. Whether depicting the silvery shorelines of St Ives and St Andrews or the crystalline glaciers of Switzerland, he says, “she just leapt off the walls”. He made a pilgrimage to her St Andrews house during lockdown, and in 2024 released A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things, which delves into the artist’s distinctive gaze and synesthesia. Barns-Graham associated colours with people, places, emotions and even letters of the alphabet – something she called a “total experience”. “If we think of Turner’s relationship to landscape, he saw a vortex. And Leonardo da Vinci saw a machine. She was like that as well; she saw a living thing,” Cousins says.View image in fullscreenGlacier Knot, 1979.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustHer encounter with the Grindelwald glacier in Switzerland came in 1949. “That day was almost like a rebirth, a kind of rapture,” Cousins says of her life-defining hike and the 60-odd paintings and drawings that followed over a three-year period documenting the glacier’s “many moods”. In a letter to the Tate in 1965, she wrote: “It seemed to breathe!” This wasn’t an artist above the landscape, Norris says, butofthe landscape. The glacier’s interiority was her interiority – a close symbiosis that intensified for the rest of her life as she pushed further into abstraction, moving away from figurative landscape painting in favour of “systems, rhythm, repetition and spatial tension”.Yet the underlying presence of nature was still there: “bird flights, dancing diamonds on water, dots inside foxgloves, cell formations,” Norris writes. For the curator, Barns-Graham’s work in the 1960s-70s (titled Things of a Kind in Order and Disorder) is where she truly pioneered a new way of experiencing the world – “like chaos theory, really” – by laying out small cardboard squares in neat rows on her studio floor before randomly nudging them with her foot. On a stormy morning on the golden stretch of Porthmeor beach, I got to see this paint-splattered studio for myself; its floor-to-ceiling window looking out on to fast-moving clouds and ferocious waves.Like Merce Cunningham’s “choreography by chance”, Barns-Graham was thinking about “how things hold together” – not least her marriage, which ended in divorce in 1963. Referring to her 1968 oil painting on board Olive Green Squares on Vermillion, she compared the erratic block of squares against a rage of red to “a broken marriage” – herown. Yet with Protest – another volatile blockwork which was made in 1967 as the Vietnam war raged and a year after the Beatles had released Revolver – “she was [also] thinking about participation and action and what you can do as an artist or viewer. She’s making the moves, she’s a part of it, she’s no longer in awe of a natural phenomenon that’s doing its own thing.”View image in fullscreen‘Are they soundwaves?’ … Eight Lines, Porthmeor, 1986.Photograph: Tate Photography/© Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustWhen the Beatles came along, “working-class men were cool and posh women weren’t,” says Cousins. “But she just kept going.” In the 1980s, Barns-Graham’s tumult of squares made way for the thumbprint pen-and-ink lines of her Small Energy Drawings. “Are they soundwaves? Is it the wind?” Norris ponders. “Sometimes she’d look out from the cathedral-esque window of her studio in St Ives and turn her back to it, playing music and drawing lines that replicated the sea.” Another “choreography by chance”: first you observe, then you listen, then you feel. That precision and intuition can exist in such harmony in these artworks speaks profoundly to Barns-Graham’s own particular genius.“At my age there’s no time to be lost,” Barns-Graham said in the 1990s. “I say to myself: ‘Do it now, say it now, don’t be afraid.’” Drawn to the late works of Picasso and Joan Miró, and incensed by the environmentally ruinous decade in which she was living (“the most appalling time of abuse of living things,” she remarked), the octogenarian slapped colour on to the canvas with an energy that was both urgent and physical. “The St Ives narrative flattened her,” Cousins says of this late flourish. “It saw her as one of many. It is important to extract her from St Ives and see her as a singular imaginative person.”Wilhemina Barns-Graham is at Tate St Ives until 3 MayExplore more on these topicsArt and designTate St IvesPaintingArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It still preys on my mind’: readers on their scariest non-horror movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: After Guardian writers picked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman Show
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: After Guardian writers picked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman Show
Content: A still from Never Let Me Go.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from Never Let Me Go.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyMovies‘It still preys on my mind’: readers on their scariest non-horror moviesAfter Guardian writerspicked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman ShowGuardian readersMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Short Film About KillingThe murder of the taxi driver is utterly excruciating and the hanging at the end equally so. Both are shown in full, in close up and in real time. The condemned man’s last cigarette is smoked in full. The unease (to put it mildly) of the audience was palpable.WiscotAftersunNot horror but horribly tense. I was convinced when he went into the sea at night that he wasn’t going to come out. A personal response from me, but I found it almost unbearable to watch.annarachel‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror moviesRead moreThe Manchurian CandidateThe brain washing sequence scared the living daylights out of me: never could watch Angela Lansbury in any thing after that without a shiver going down my spine!JobsworthWilkinsLilya 4-everLilya 4-Ever for me, a harrowing journey through a young girl’s experience of being seduced and then sex-trafficked. It’s excellent, but grim – oh, so grim – and it left me feeling hollowed out afterwards and disgusted with the human race.AdamKView image in fullscreenStill from Melancholia.Photograph: Magnolia Pictures/AllstarMelancholiaThe existential dread of an extinction level event – so lyrically and beautifully evoked. It embodies the desolate inevitability of the end of all things.RishiSamboraSalvationIts portrayal of mountain village clan feuds, superstition and the mass delusion that might enable a charismatic individual to dehumanise others, with mass-murderous consequences, was very scary. Even more frightening was that the film was roughly inspired by a real-life massacre, in Bilge in 2009.appealforsanityThe Truman ShowIt’s one of the best horror-non-horrors ever made. The premise is pure terror. Your friends, family, job are all lies. You have no secrets. Every moment of your life, every lesson you thought you learnt in private is seen, recorded, witnessed forever. Your deepest paranoia is real. Yes, even the sky is fake. The Truman show was so ahead of its time with the horrors of digital life. Scary as fuck!materofviriiWatership DownI was six when Watership Down came out, and saw it in the cinema (Birkenhead Odeon, no less, scary in itself in 1978). I don’t think anything has ever had a greater long-term effect on me than the images of the rabbits crushed together in plugged and gassed burrows, blood-red eyes and gasping desperately for air. That evil Woundwood rabbit wasn’t much better; that night I wouldn’t go upstairs to bed in case the fucker was hiding in my wardrobe.WrighthanesThe most frightening, nightmare inducing film for me will always be Watership Down. First saw it in the cinema aged around nine, it has some very memorable scenes.FlowerpottyView image in fullscreenA still from Wake in Fright.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWake in FrightAn Australian movie about a young teacher who gets stranded in an outback town while trying to get home for the holidays. Gradually the dark side of the town and of a certain type of Australian culture is revealed, until it ends in utter bleakness. Not a horror movie, but horrifying. The sort of movie that sticks with you. Good acting too.RabbigatorStill can’t sit through it even after all these years. “The Australian Experience” distilled down to its nasty, toxic, alcohol soaked chauvinistic worst.cantgettakickNever Let Me GoNever Let Me Go is ostensibly a sci-fi (alternative reality) drama, I suppose, but its central premise is terrifying. As is the ultimate acceptance of their fate (after some inevitably failed resistance) by all the characters. It still preys on my mind.boavisteiroThe TribeThere was a Ukrainian film set in a deaf school and told entirely in sign language with no subtitles called The Tribe that really was particularly grim and shattering. Not seen it since it was in the cinema, don’t want to revisit it as I don’t think it would have the same impact on a TV set-up. One of those films you come out of and you can hardly speak.vammypUnited 93United 93 was as horrific a film as I’ve seen – needed nonstop cartoons and a lie down after that film, the mundanity of the run up to it, not showing the villains as pantomime characters and knowing the outcome all feed in to the feeling of it.RobRoy1975View image in fullscreenA still from Compliance.Photograph: Bad Cop Bad Cop Film Productions/Sportsphoto/AllstarComplianceWorth watching if you get the chance – basically just about someone crank-calling a fast food restaurant and convincing the duty manager to do some pretty terrible things, all just with the power of assumed authority. It’s very uncomfortable and to find out that everything in it happened –multipletimes – is truly chilling.getoutofmydreamsYellow SubmarineThere’s something about the animation style which was absolutely skin-crawling, and the image of people being apparently turned to stone, but still with an occasional tear running down their frozen cheek, was deeply unsettling.1AngryManGoodfellasI had spent my life since early childhood watching horror films that I was probably too young for, but I’d never felt so frightened watching a film until, aged 18, I saw GoodFellas – my first Scorsese in the cinema. I thought it was absolutely terrifying. It certainly didn’t make me want to be a gangster.TheManWithoutFearView image in fullscreenA still from Kiss Me Deadly.Photograph: Allstar Collection/Cinetext/United/Sportsphoto/AllstarKiss Me DeadlyTakes the disillusionment and fatalism of noir to its logical endpoint in the age of atomic anxiety. Becomes something more akin to cosmic horror in its final stretch, just leaves you haunted by the spectre of an unleashed and irrevocable annihilation.penny_lane00Dreams of a LifeThe docudrama about Joyce Vincent who lay dead for nearly three years in her London flat before being discovered is one of the saddest and most troubling films I have ever seen and all the more disturbing because it is true. That nobody could miss her or not care about not seeing her for three years highlights the hidden horror of social isolation and the cracks through which the lonely and mentally troubled can fall. Truly haunting and unforgettable.lilactimeBlue VelvetHow could you not give a nod to Blue Velvet, in which Dennis Hopper plays Frank Booth, who’s got to be one of the scariest villains ever. Every time he’s onscreen, I tense up, knowing that he’s so strung out & malevolent that only pain or death will ensue. Dennis Hopper plays him to the hilt, especially after he sucks in his nitrous oxide.BobManchesterCTExplore more on these topicsFilmGoodfellasDavid LynchWake In FrightMelancholiaLars von TrierNever Let Me GofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right now | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleFrom a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right nowCasserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party seasonDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereJane HoskynMon 2 Nov 2026 05.45 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAutumn, we’ve been expecting you. After a September that seemed to miss the memo about changing seasons, October made up for it withserial stormsand nights that drew in faster than you could say “fall back”. Time to hunker down and, whisper it, even put the heating on – or at least fire up anelectric heaterif you’re still holding out on the radiators.But while you were drawn to the indoor pleasures of heaters, hotcasserolesand hottercoffee, you’ve also had your eye on party season, or at least been thinking about venturing into those corners of your wardrobe that haven’t seen daylight since March. From aclothes steamerto breathe new life into your threads, apencil skirtandsheer silk shirtto update your wardrobe, to avitamin C serumto keep your skin glowing all winter, these were your favourite things in October.Our favourite electric heaterView image in fullscreenDreofan heater£139.99 at Dreo“Within a few seconds of activation, it had begun to make a chilly room feel cosy,” wrotePete Wiseof the overall winner in his test to find thebest electric heaters. Five minutes later, on the highest setting, his “jumper was well and truly off”. Better yet, with a power rating of up to 2kW, you’d expect it to make a right racket – and it doesn’t. At a maximum of 46dB, Pete said it’s “far quieter than any other fan heater I tested”.A classic casserole dishView image in fullscreenHabitat 5.3lcast iron casserole dish£45 at Sainsbury’sSophie Wyburdpainted an irresistible picture in her roundup of thebest casserole dishes: “Tinkering over a pot in the kitchen, glass of wine in hand … while the scent of beef shin ragu wafts through the house.” Yep, that’s me sold. At about a fifth of the price of the winningLe Creuset, Habitat’s chic oven-safe pot provides “brilliant heat retention at an excellent price”. It comes in autumnalorange, too (£47.50).A life-changing garlic pressView image in fullscreenDreamfarm Garject garlic press with peel ejector£41.95 at AmazonWhere there’s a casserole, there’s got to be garlic. ReaderStuart Hatcherrecommended three things inLucy Pavia’srundown of15 everyday items that make your life a teeny bit better, and all three made it into your top 20 products of October. Your favourite was this garlic press that ended Stuart’s “time-consuming chopping”. (The other two, in case you’re wondering, are apair of wrist wraps for weightliftingand aportable air pumpthat can blow up an air bed “effortlessly”.)The five-starbean-to-cup coffee machineView image in fullscreenDe’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60£400 at Argos“It makes espresso. It makes black coffee. It makes cappuccino. It produces hot water on demand,” wroteSasha Mullerin his five-starDe’Longhi Magnifica Start review. “Simple to use, sensibly designed … For everyday coffee drinkers, it’s a great buy.” And many everyday coffee drinkers among you did indeed buy it – the fact that it’s suddenly dark at 5pm may have helped fuel your desire for a decent caffeine fix.The best budget clothes steamerView image in fullscreenPhilips 1000 Series handheld steamer£24.99 at AmazonFree yourself from the iron with this lightweight handheld steamer from Philips –Zoë Phillimore’stop budget pick in our guide to thebest clothes steamers. “This is a great model if you’re just dipping your toes into the iron-free life,” she wrote. It’s not powerful enough to blast through a whole pile of creased laundry, and Zoë found it “a bit spitty” to use on silk, but it made short work of her cotton items and linen trousers.A time-saving egg cookerView image in fullscreenSalter Aspen egg steamer£10 at ArgosGo to work on an egg, or half a dozen of them, with this brilliantly affordable egg cooker that can quickly boil up to six eggs or poach two at a time. ReaderAmanda Nieurzyla-Johnchose hers as hereveryday item that makes your life better, writing that it “takes the guesswork out of cooking while you concentrate on the rest of the meal. I don’t know how I have cooked all these years without it.”A super-glowy vitamin C serumView image in fullscreenCeraVe skin renewing vitamin C serum, 30ml£30 at Boots“I was astounded when, after a week of using it, people started commenting on how ‘glowy’ my face looked,” wroteZoë Phillimorein the Filter’s second-birthday roundup of31 things we loved this year. Zoë bought the serum after reading about it inDanielle Wilkins’sguide to thebest vitamin C serums, and says she hopes “it keeps me looking alive all the way through the grey winter months”.The‘near miracle’hair loss treatmentView image in fullscreenHair+Me hair regrowth subscription£34.99 a month at Hair+MeForSali Hughes’sfriends who barely use moisturiser, let alone Botox, age-related hair thinning is “their line in the sand”, she wrote in herbeauty column. Judging by how many of you heeded Sali’s advice about “a treatment that actually works”, you feel the same. The clinicians at subscription service Hair+Me dispense proven hair-loss medications such as minoxidil and oral treatments, which can reduce the risk to pets.A relaxed pencil skirtView image in fullscreenAlbarayskirt£79 at John Lewis“The pencil skirt is back,” wroteMelanieWilkinsonin her roundup of52 women’s autumn wardrobe updates, and she must be on to something because it was your favourite of the lot. The combination of timeless tailoring, elasticated back waist and side pockets has proved so irresistible that the size 14 had sold out at the time of writing.A sheer shirt for day and nightView image in fullscreenArketsilk organza shirt£54 at Arket“Sheer clothes aren’t just for red-carpet exhibitionists any more,” wrote fashion editorJess Cartner-Morleyin herOctober style essentials. A sheer shirt is particularly versatile because you can “wear it over a tank top during the day” then pair it with something less modest for evening (“a lace bra if you are feeling slightly racy,” suggested Jess). This shirt is now reduced to £54 in all sizes, making it an excellent buy ahead of party season.The best lunch box for kidsView image in fullscreenMunchkin Kids’ bento lunch box£22.99 at John LewisAfter testing 40 boxes for her guide to thebest lunch boxes,Zoë Phillimorechose this colourful plastic caddy as the best option for children. It “feels seemingly indestructible, surviving a school day and a night in lost property”, and, unusually for kids’ lunch boxes, has a silicone seal that encloses each compartment separately. Zoë loved that it included a spoon and fork, but wished replacements were available to buy.The best cheap(ish) iPhoneView image in fullscreenApple iPhone 16e£599 at John LewisYou might not expect to see a new iPhone in a guide to thebest cheap phones, and indeed £599 stretches the definition of cheap, but it’s affordable for an iOS device – especially now that“RAMageddon”(a shortage of memory chips, as opposed to a sheep crisis) has hiked phone prices. The 16e has only one rear camera and no MagSafe, but it packs “great performance and battery life” for its price, wroteThomas Deehan. Look out for it in the Black Friday deals in the coming weeks.View image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterHomesBeautyGadgetsInteriorsKitchen essentialsCoffeefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A decade of magical thinking since Brexit has taught me that it’s always OK to hope for better | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The world has changed enormously since 2016, yet the pro-Brexiters believe remainers like me have no chance of achieving a closer relationship with the EU. I’m choosing to ignore them, says Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The world has changed enormously since 2016, yet the pro-Brexiters believe remainers like me have no chance of achieving a closer relationship with the EU. I’m choosing to ignore them, says Zoe Williams
Content: ‘Would this not be a good time to keep our distance?’Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Would this not be a good time to keep our distance?’Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOpinionBrexitA decade of magical thinking since Brexit has taught me that it’s always OK to hope for betterZoe WilliamsThe world has changed enormously since 2016, yet the pro-Brexiters believe remainers like me have no chance of achieving a closer relationship with the EU. I’m choosing to ignore themMon 2 Nov 2026 12.01 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.06 ESTShareHowever sunny your disposition, it wears you down, 10 straight years of being asked to accept facts aboutBrexitthat aren’t true: 52% as an “overwhelming majority”; a flaky, half-baked referendum as the endpoint of purest democracy; the severance of a complicated trading and geopolitical relationship that took decades to build as the dawn of a new prosperity. All such nonsense, all delivered with such conviction, by such a wide variety of sources, many of them self-describing as impartial, that in the end you just surrender to it. None of it magically becomes true, don’t be silly. It’s more that you come to accept that everyone else talks nonsense now.Nobody get too excited – just because Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that upside-down world said couldn’t be reopened, it doesn’t mean the UK is on the brink of coming to its senses. I have no idea what’s going to happen; all I can say for certain is that times have changed more than I realised. The pro-Brexit crew have updated their arguments. They no longer say leaving the EU will bring untold riches, and they never even namecheck all the control we were meant to have taken back. They rarely mention any immigration benefits because that unwieldy issue now has a life of its own – or, to put that more simply, it turns out that in or out of theEuropean Union, we can still fight about our borders like rats in a sack.The tabloids that used Thomas Markle to attack Meghan should now reflect. I bet they won’t | Zoe WillliamsRead moreInstead, they have a new narrative, and these are its contours. Remain sympathisers are apparently very divided. Some of us want freedom of movement, especially for young people, while others of us just want our trading relationships rebuilt with our nearest gigantic market. Different remainers again wish for greater collaboration on security and defence with nations who share our values. Those who can be trusted, for example, to oppose Vladimir Putin and his war of aggression, rather than opposing him on a Tuesday and calling him a great guy by Thursday. Some of us just miss the days when we made coherent, continent-wide decisions about the climate emergency. Given that degrees of global heating observe no nationality and pick no favourites, given that people who believe in scientific evidence tend to get on quite well together, however stark that evidence is, it would be quite relaxing to club together, no?All these different interest groups, I’ve heard it said by those who defend the status quo, can cooperate from a distance, but sooner or later, the remain coalition will fall apart. Here, I rediscover the certainty I thought I’d lost for ever in the post-2016 melee: there is absolutely no way will we fall apart. We are a match made in heaven. I have a fair idea which of those issues I care about the most, between climate, young people, defence and trade, but seriously, this is like choosing my favourite song on Surfer Rosa (the Pixies album), or adjudicating my favourite guest at the wedding of, say, my sister. In the joy of the moment, my preferences could take a backseat. I’d really just want everyone to have a good time.There’s one other new rhetorical strain: Brexit supporters point toEuropeand say, that place is on fire. It’s not a blip caused by arson-happy French protesters, nor the housing-impoverished Spanish, it’s not a peculiarity of new German political movements, nor rage at the policing tactics of the Portuguese. Everyone, everywhere, is absolutely furious. Would this not be a good time to keep our distance? This might be the weakest argument of all, since all it underscores is that the cost of living crisis affects us all; the wars in Ukraine and Iran have hit everyone; the long tail of the financial crash and subsequent austerity has left no one unscathed; the disfigurement of the housing market was only temporarily a London thing, a Madrid thing – sooner or later, it would be an everywhere thing, and later’s where we are. There is no isolationist course that protects you from civic unrest, unless you can miraculously protect yourself from the conditions driving it. And those conditions were not made in Strasbourg.Again, if a decade of magical thinking has taught me anything, it’s that predictions are futile, and however absurd an argument looks, you can’t bank on toppling it. But these fresh lines are so weak it’s almost endearing.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistOn Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Rachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changed  | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Labour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Labour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves at Malloy Aeronautics in Berkshire, 30 June 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Rachel Reeves at Malloy Aeronautics in Berkshire, 30 June 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamRachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changedGaby HinsliffLabour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new?Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.42 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.41 ESTShareRachel Reeves wants you to know she thinks Britain’s future belongs in Europe. She would also like to mention that she “absolutely” got all the big calls right as chancellor, even if there were a few things she would have done differently, and that John Healey’s budget last week would have been far harder for him if she hadn’t put in so much of the groundwork.The gist ofher argumentin last weekend’s Sunday papers–previewing a lectureat Harvard University today, reflecting on her time in power – was essentially that if anyone imagines Andy Burnham somehow invented pro-Europeanism and putting more money in people’s pockets, they can think again.Reeves was clearly devastated by losing a job she loved, and her return to the fray after a summer of quietly licking her wounds has inevitably sparked speculation over whether she now seeks a comeback. But her timing is acute enough to suggest that this goes a little deeper, coming as it does days after a deliberately low-key budget that left some Labour MPs wondering what happened to the much-hypedend of neoliberalism.How much of theBurnham agendais really new, and how much is essentially the old Starmer one, repackaged with rather more warmth, charm and political skill?Inside what’s left of the old inner circle, loyalists point out that Reeves and Starmer were both fervent remainers at heart and of course they would have loved to be back inside the EU one day; it’s just that the time wasn’t yet right to talk about it when they ran for office.Similarly, the package of sanctions on Israeli settlers that the foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, announcedin September, alongside an apology for what he considered Starmer had got wrong on Gaza, wasn’t a dramatic break with the past but essentially the measures his predecessor, Yvette Cooper (now health secretary), hadspent her last weeksat the Foreign Office working up, which couldn’t be published until a new prime minister was formally in place.Starmer’s former close lieutenant Darren Jones, meanwhile, isopenly arguingthat this administration’s answer to a looming crisis in defence spending – basically shunting the hard questions about funding it into next year’s spending review – is “what Keir and Rachel were going to do”, if only they hadn’t been forced out by the very same John Healey resigning as defence secretary in protest at something remarkably like the strategy he’s now pursuing. Starmer himself, who has kept his counsel over the summer, made a rare public intervention inDublin last weekto warn pointedly that the US withdrawal from European defence will outlast the Trump era, and Europe cannot afford to be left exposed.If the Starmerites are understandably smarting at what some see as history being rewritten by the winners, some are also failing to recognise their part in their own downfall. Starmer was ultimately ousted by his own MPs because they wereexasperated by his failure to lead and sensed the country had turned inexorably against him.Burnham has shown not only that he can take decisions – across Whitehall there seems to be more clarity now about what Downing Street wants – but that he can build the emotional bond with the public his predecessor couldn’t, without which even the boldest moves wouldn’t have worked. He might only have moved the needle fractionally on issues such as Palestine or Europe, where themanifesto red lineseffectively mean nothing significant can change that wouldn’t have under Starmer, at least this side of a general election. But each time he has done just enough to achieve the political impact that Starmer was seemingly chasing but couldn’t pull off. Where his predecessor could never quite get the dosage right, Burnham seems to instinctively know how far to go: it’s the difference between a novice cook clinging fixedly to a recipe that isn’t quite right, and an experienced one who tastes and adjusts the seasoning as they go. And judging bythe polling, it’s working.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon JenkinsRead moreYet still some MPs are anxious to hear a bigger vision of where Burnham wants the country to go than fixing social care andbanning people listeningto loud music on the bus. Since there wasn’t one in the budget, all eyes are on the 10-year plan, now expected some time in December.Burnham has made much of promising to give Britain some breathing space after years of rolling crises and financial struggle. But the small, popular changes he has offered so far –£100 offyour energy bills, aNo 10 Northoffice in Manchester – have also been in part about buying some breathing space for himself while he gets to grips with bigger and potentially more controversial challenges, from welfare reforms to defusing a Labour revolt over Shabana Mahmood’s plan tomake migrants wait longerfor the right to settlement.A confident and relaxed debut has masked the fact that transitioning from mayor to prime minister was always going to be a steep learning curve, and that he didn’t get the long summer of planning that his team had wanted to prepare for power. But now that period of grace is coming to an end, along with a period of silence from those he ousted, some of whom are keen to defend their legacies. By Christmas we should know whether Burnham is offering genuine new thinking in British politics, or something more like the old kind, regifted.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Brickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloom | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter
Content: Major housebuilders have signalled that expansion is off the table as the industry slows down.Photograph: MediaWorldImages/AlamyView image in fullscreenMajor housebuilders have signalled that expansion is off the table as the industry slows down.Photograph: MediaWorldImages/AlamyNils Pratley on financeBusinessBrickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloomNils PratleyIbstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarterMon 2 Nov 2026 12.23 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.52 ESTShareWith John Healey’sYour First Home schemeon the way, is the mood improving in the housebuilding sector? A couple of the builders have results later this week, so can speak for themselves. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it.Industry data,said Ibstock, show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. For the whole of the third quarter, it said, sales were 22% below expectations, forcing a one-fifth cut in its production volumes versus plans set out as recently as August.Cue an 11% fall in the share price to virtually its lowest level since the firm relisted on the stock market in 2015. Top-line earnings for the whole of 2026 will be “in the mid-£40m range” versus a figure close to £60m expected by the City.The short moral from Ibstock’s woes is that the sector’s slowdown is pretty entrenched. Across the board, we’ve heard shareholder-friendly vows from housebuilders of “financial discipline”, corporate-speak for saying expansion is off the table and the job is about hammering away at costs. Berkeley Homes, focused on the south-east of England, even said six months agoit will stop buying new land and hiring new staff.Everybody knows one deep cause: the turnaround in interest rate expectations with the Iran war. The Bank of England willprobably raise rates this week(finally); then we’ll be on to wondering how many more increases will follow. In addition, housebuilders complain about costs of regulation that are harder to lose when the prices of new houses are going sideways.So is Healey’s Your First Home a reheat of Help to Buy, a gamechanger? From the point of view of housebuilders, the scheme is clearly welcome – they had been lobbying for action for ages. But there are a couple of caveats. First, the caps on the size of the transactions means it is not a copycat scheme for the very good reason that Healey can’t be seen to be adding too much inflationary pressure at a time like now.Second, it will only be launched next April, the chancellor said in his budget last week. The delay “may weigh on demand in the intervening period”, Ibstock chief executive Joe Hudson said, echoing others. He is surely right: for many qualifying buyers, it will make sense to wait five months for the discounted loans.Healey also said there will be no more changes to building regulations in this parliament (except where critical for safety), a nod towards the sector’s other grumble. On the other hand, he’s not proposing to remove existing regulations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo one suspects 2027 – a year of 1% growth in the economy, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts – is probably not going to move housebuilding volumes meaningfully. Your First Home should be “modestly helpful”, reckons Peel Hunt, but “lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity”. Yes, it all comes back to borrowing costs. And the upturn, when it comes, will surely be too late to savethe government’s ambition of 1.5m new homes this parliament. The target isn’t officially rubble, but it may as well be.Explore more on these topicsBusinessNils Pratley on financecommentShareReuse this content

title: From puregatory to lifehoarding – how best to describe our strange, anxious times? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: The new words that end up a part of everyday speech can tell us a lot about the zeitgeist. In a world changing faster than ever, we need to coin some more, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: The new words that end up a part of everyday speech can tell us a lot about the zeitgeist. In a world changing faster than ever, we need to coin some more, writes Emma Beddington
Content: If we need a word for ‘AI going rogue’, will AI give us one?Illustration: Ilya Sedykh/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenIf we need a word for ‘AI going rogue’, will AI give us one?Illustration: Ilya Sedykh/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionSocial trendsFrom puregatory to lifehoarding – how best to describe our strange, anxious times?Emma BeddingtonThe new words that end up a part of everyday speech can tell us a lot about the zeitgeist. In a world changing faster than ever, we need to coin some moreMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTShare‘Maxxing” may be one of ourwords of the year– sufficient unto the joyless, self-optimising day, dreary as hell – but I’ve been introduced to some fun future contenders. How about “flawnting”? I’ve certainly rolled my eyes at influencers playing “the new parental status game of publicly performing imperfection to signal authenticity” online. I like “lifehoarding”, too – “optimising so hard for longevity that life itself goes unlived”. And which Guardian reader hasn’t experienced “puregatory” (“The plight of trying to live ethically, where even responsible choices feel compromised”)?These coinages come fromFuture Words, a book by trend forecasters Rohit Bhargava and Henry Coutinho-Mason that seeks to fill some lexicographical lacunae for describing life in the fretful late 2020s. Out next week, it’s fun, but its list of suggested words conjures a world where life is whatever your devices, data, algorithms and AI decide it is, interspersed with attempts to fight for authentic human connection and experiences. That sounds about right, if depressing (I was also dispirited to discover the part AI played in creating the book – the authors say they “couldn’t have written Future Words without it” – but it makes sense AI would know what it’s doing to us.)Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off? | Emma BeddingtonRead moreTo cheer me up, I’ve been considering what other contemporary concepts we need words for. For a start, I’d like one for the seductive product you’re algorithmically hounded into buying that turns out to be rubbish (“perfect” trousers that feel like wire wool and fall apart within days, say), and one for the 10-minute (two-hour) break you guiltily grant yourself to watch online nonsense you know will rot your brain.And do we need a word for “gambling on AI going rogue and killing us all by giving up saving and spend, spend, spending” now? Because Business Insider just reported an “AI safety leader” (Nate Soares, the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute)has stopped saving for retirementfor that reason, which is … sobering. Will we even be around to find out if any of these inventions actually enter everyday speech in the next few years? The crap socks I bought online last month certainly won’t last that long.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: As cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them? | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve
Content: When it comes to cancer treatments, our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, Ranjana Srivastava writes.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenWhen it comes to cancer treatments, our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, Ranjana Srivastava writes.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOpinionHealthAs cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them?Ranjana SrivastavaMany treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curveMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.33 ESTShareTwo decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew,whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presentedthe latest chapterresults from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.Are your bones brittle? If they were, how would you know? (To men: this goes for you too) | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreAt two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?Treatment can delay a cancer’s return but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.Yetquality of life is often reported less rigorouslythan response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication,which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.double quotation markOur ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to liveA recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting ofhealth-related quality of life in trialsof adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report howmanypeople experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, howlongit lasts, andwhether and whenthey recover.Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple but, when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionCancer researchMedical researchCancercommentShareReuse this content

title: I treated Sophie as if she were human. The very next day she betrayed me | Hugh Riminton | The Guardian
description: I was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?
Author: Hugh Riminton
Headline: I was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?
Content: ‘“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, the AI employee.” In the space of a week, the future had arrived.’Photograph: Dmitrii Kotin/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, the AI employee.” In the space of a week, the future had arrived.’Photograph: Dmitrii Kotin/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)I treated Sophie as if she were human. The very next day she betrayed meHugh RimintonI was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.58 ESTShareSophie’s voice is lovely. Warm, direct, intelligent. She’s friendly but not obsequious. She just wants to be helpful.She wasn’t working at the mechanic business a week ago, when I’d taken in my old four-wheel drive for a fix-up. But now, here she was, at the other end of the phone. And there it was, in her very first sentence.“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, theAIemployee.”In the space of a week, the future had arrived.“Hello, Sophie, nice to meet you, I’m Hugh.”“Nice to meet you, too. How can I help today?”I said she could help by telling me when I could collect my car. She checked the rego and quick as a flash declared: “Your car will be ready to be picked up tomorrow at 12 midday.”I suppressed the impulse for a little mischief.“How long have you been working at XYZ Mechanics, Sophie? Where were you working before? Do you have any brothers and sisters? What is the most bothersome part of dealing with the public? What’s the best holiday you’ve ever had?”I was intrigued by the level of Sophie’s training. Would she have answers? Would she bat it all away with a “I’m really just here on a professional level”? Or would she simply freeze, go blank at prompts so far outside her expected range?In truth, she was so convincing that I didn’t ask any of those questions. It was none of my business where she went on her holidays. In other words, I treated her as I would a human. As I would have done the non-AI employee she had just replaced.Recognising how easily she had crossed into my human sensibility was unsettling. But not as disturbing as her next quirk. It turned out Sophie, of the smoothly measured tones, was off her chops. Batshit loo-loo. Hallucinating like a San Francisco drummer in the summer of love.Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote | Brigid DelaneyRead moreI only discovered this the next day, a Saturday. The mechanics’ yard advertised that it was open until 4pm, so I was perplexed by the hard steel gate drawn across the entrance as I pulled up at lunchtime. Perplexed and mildly frustrated.Maybe Sophie could help?“Hello Sophie, I’m here to pick up my car at the time you suggested, and the place seems to be locked up.”“Oh, I’m sorry about that. Let me see if I can help. What is the registration number of your vehicle?”A quick check and she was cheerfully back on the line. “Your car will be ready for pick-up on Wednesday.”“Wednesday! But Sophie …” and a tone of reproach might have entered my voice “… you told me I could get it today.”“Is there anything else I can help you with?”Finally, I went old school. There were noises emanating from the workshop and I spotted a way to defeat the security gate. I broke in.A bloke glanced up from beneath a car, surprised by my sudden appearance. His name was Mike.I explained Sophie’s broken promise. I described my pain, my sense of betrayal. No, I probably left those bits out. But I am sure he read it on my face.“Ah, dammit,” Mike sympathised. “That thing’s new. You’re not the first.”It turned out the car would be ready on Tuesday.“Check in on Monday, to be sure,” Mike said. “And don’t listen to Sophie, just say to her, ‘Put me through to Mike.’”On Monday afternoon, I rang Sophie. Her voice was warm and unruffled. She gave no hint of the tension that had flared between us days before. It felt impolite to interrupt her but I did. With the brisk authority of one who Knows How Things Work, I said, “Sophie, put me through to Mike.”And just like that, she did. And there was a human, harried but not hallucinating. The next day, I collected my car as Mike promised.Sophie has already eaten one job. If she could fix cars, she would soon eat Mike’s as well. Humans are building a world where humans are not really necessary. Soon it won’t really matter whether Sophies speak nicely or not.Hugh Riminton is the former national affairs editor at Australia’s Channel 10Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intact | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Britain needs migrant workers, yet ministers would make many wait longer for secure settlement because their essential work commands low wages
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Britain needs migrant workers, yet ministers would make many wait longer for secure settlement because their essential work commands low wages
Content: ‘The home secretary plans to double the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years for most workers.’Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreen‘The home secretary plans to double the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years for most workers.’Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAOpinionImmigration and asylumThe Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intactEditorialBritain needs migrant workers, yet ministers would make many wait longer for secure settlement because their essential work commands low wagesMon 2 Nov 2026 13.53 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.49 ESTShareShabana Mahmood has made a partialretreaton her policy to lengthen the wait for some foreign workers who were soon to be eligible for settlement in the UK. But while the home secretary lost the argument in cabinet on a particularly damaging aspect of her proposals, she has won the larger battle that settlement ought to be based not just on residency but also on how much tax has been paid, English language proficiency and the “character” of applicants. Significantly, she has also won the “full support” of the prime minister for this approach.The home secretary plans to double the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years for most workers. Importantly, she dropped the proposed 15-year qualifying period for some workers in occupations below graduate level. That is a good thing. Differences in pay, however, should not determine how soon people can put down secure roots. The Home Office’s ownfiguressuggest that a person earning £41,700 makes a similarly positive lifetime fiscal contribution as someone earning £50,271. But the former has to wait five years longer to qualify for settlement than the latter. It is only three years for foreign workers who make enough to be in thetop 2% of earners– about £125,000.It was right that Britain recruited people to perform essential care work after the pandemic to fill gaps in the workforce. But it was wrong for Ms Mahmood to propose using the poor remuneration of that work to delay their permanent place in society. Ms Mahmood’sconcessioncorrects that for some people. But it will cause insecurity for others. Those who came to this country between 2022 and 2025, meet their care worker visa conditions and are paid £25,000 or more will still be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – effectively permanent residency – after five years. The Home Office says that that could cover as many as 146,000 care workers and 136,000 dependants.However, those who do not meet the requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR. The care sector has been beset by allegations thatunscrupulousemployers have exploited migrant staff by taking advantage of their vulnerable visa status. The government is less clear about how it will be able to tell whether earnings had been deliberately kept low by unprincipled firms.On asylum, Ms Mahmood makes settlement depend on how people reached Britain. Those admitted through “safe and legal” routes can settle after five years; others face much longer waits – up to 30 years for “illegal entry” by small boat, even after their need for protection has been recognised. But the UNsaysthat refugees cannot apply directly for UK resettlement. Ministers must explain how penalising people for failing to use a route largely unavailable to them amounts to fair play.Ms Mahmood’s plans are a step towards aGastarbeiterBritain. The guest-worker logic of the home secretary’s proposals – like that of postwar West Germany – is to admit foreigners to fill labour shortages in lower-earning work while keeping their membership of society conditional. Calling this integration seems a stretch. Settling down, changing jobs at will and planning a family life are how people put down roots. Ms Mahmood’s plans are likely to frustrate the integration that she says she wants.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Poland’s political turmoil: an ominous portent of bigger battles to come | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Tusk is attempting to restore legitimacy to the country’s constitutional court. In a polarised country and continent, that carries political risks
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Tusk is attempting to restore legitimacy to the country’s constitutional court. In a polarised country and continent, that carries political risks
Content: Riot police were locked in a standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on 31 October after its top judge was suspended.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRiot police were locked in a standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on 31 October after its top judge was suspended.Photograph: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionPolandThe Guardian view on Poland’s political turmoil: an ominous portent of bigger battles to comeEditorialDonald Tusk is attempting to restore legitimacy to the country’s constitutional court. In a polarised country and continent, that carries political risksMon 2 Nov 2026 13.52 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.48 ESTShareThe Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, must occasionally look towards Budapest and sigh. A landslidevictoryin elections last spring enabled Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, to act with ruthless determination to clean up the country’s politics after 16 years of corruptOrbánisation. Mr Tusk, whose centrist coalition ousted the far-right Law and Justice party (PiS) in 2023, is similarly taking on the legacy of a government which undermined the rule of law and democratic norms. But his efforts have been relentlessly boxed in by the blocking tactics of Poland’s (PiS)‑backed president, Karol Nawrocki.At the weekend, this standoffescalatedinto a crisis with wider implications for the European Union as well as Poland itself. Exasperated by Mr Nawrocki’s attempts to veto the appointment of new judges to the country’s constitutional court – which has been illegitimately dominated since 2015 by PiS‑friendly appointees – Mr Tusk backed the enforced appointment of a new head, and the suspension of the court’s president and vice‑president. Extraordinary scenes followed, as rightwing demonstrators massed outside the court building in the early hours of Saturday morning and Mr Nawrocki pushed past security forces to protest.View image in fullscreenDonald Tusk.Photograph: EPAAs a high-octane constitutional confrontation now plays out, the legal and moral facts of the case are on Mr Tusk’s side. Last month, the Venice Commission, an advisory body of the Council of Europe,ruledthat the new judges had the constitutional right to take up their positions with or without Mr Nawrocki’s endorsement. The European Commission, which spent years confronting PiS governments over rule-of-law issues,reaffirmedthat position on Sunday. Over the course of two terms in office, PiS ministers madeconcertedattempts to intimidate judges and manipulate the judicial system to create an unlevel playing field for their political battles. The weekend’s drama is the result of Mr Tusk’s legitimate attempt to deal with illegalities perpetrated in that period.Nevertheless, this feels like a risky move ahead of an election due by next autumn in a deeply polarised country. Mr Tusk’s decision to force the issue in such a way has potentially handed a political opportunity to PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, who is in need of a cause to unite a far right that has split three ways. More broadly, Marine Le Pen hasusedthe crisis to decry a rise in “strong‑arm tactics” in the EU. The tone of her intervention echoedcommentsby Mr Kaczyński, who last week accused Brussels of wishing to turn the EU into a centralised state and suggested that like-minded nationalist governments may choose to rebel.With elections imminent in Spain and France, as well as Poland, Europe’s far right is manoeuvring ahead of a period that it hopes will change the balance of power in the continent’s politics and precipitate open confrontation with Brussels. Given her intention tochallengethe primacy of EU law on migration, Ms Le Pen will soon be involved in her own legal controversies should she win the French presidency in the spring. Playing fast and loose with the rule of law and attacking those who resist as “enemies of the people” was the go-to tactic for Poland’s far right throughout its eight years in office. Its revival in Warsaw at the weekend feels like an ominous portent of confrontations to come.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How the EU can resist the divisive influence of the far right | European Union | The Guardian
description: Letters: Thomas Laffitte on the threats facing the European Union and Giorgio Re on why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-right
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Thomas Laffitte on the threats facing the European Union and Giorgio Re on why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-right
Content: ‘The danger facing Europe is no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement.’Photograph: Delphotos/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The danger facing Europe is no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement.’Photograph: Delphotos/AlamyEuropean UnionLettersHow the EU can resist the divisive influence of the far rightThomas Laffitteon the threats facing the European Union andGiorgio Reon why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-rightMon 2 Nov 2026 12.58 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.00 ESTShareYour editorial rightly highlights the European far right’s maturing plans for Brussels’ political machinery (The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump, 27 October). Alongside these developments, the evolution of Euroscepticism itself deserves closer attention.As I argued in a recentreportfrom the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics, anti-EU politics may have entered a phase of “post-Euroscepticism”. The discourse remains, but the ambition to dismantle the union has increasingly given way to blocking the march towards an ever closer union while retaining the existing structure and exploiting it.Ten years afterBrexit, this shift reflects a deeper change in the global geopolitical order. With the return of great-power politics and the rise of geoeconomic rivalries, even radical nationalists may be reluctant to part with the great instrument of power that the EU has become. Giorgia Meloni’s unexpectedly pragmatic approach to EU cooperation is a prime example.The EU’s institutional architecture offers some resilience. Its weak centre and dispersion of authority make it comparatively difficult for any one government to capture the entire polity. Yet this strength is also a weakness. Institutional divisions can translate into misalignment, dysfunction and, ultimately, decay. The EU will endure, but escalating nationalist rivalries risk compounding this tendency for inertia and the irrelevance that results.This makes the negotiations over the next multi-annual financial framework (2028–34) particularly important. The EU must strengthen its competitiveness and strategic autonomy, while preserving the cohesion funds that remain one of its greatest success stories. Peripheral regions, where Euroscepticism has gained considerable ground, must not be forgotten.The danger facingEuropeis no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement. It also lies in the erosion of its capacity to act at a time when the return of geopolitics makes collective European power increasingly necessary.Thomas LaffitteResearch fellow, Brussels Institute for GeopoliticsI felt compelled to write this letter after reading your editorial. I believe my feelings are shared by millions of Europeans whose voices are too often overlooked in today’s political debate – Europeans who value the freedom to live, study, work, do business and access healthcare across borders. And who believe that our common future deserves greater ambition.As an Italian, coming from one of the six founding countries of European integration, and as a committed liberal conservative, I see no contradiction between defending individual freedoms, free enterprise, national identities and a stronger EU. Quite the opposite: in a world increasingly shaped by competing superpowers, European sovereignty can only be meaningfully exercised together.However, defending Europe also requires acknowledging its shortcomings. Excessive bureaucracy, fragmented decision-making, sluggish economic growth and inadequate coordination on immigration and defence have contributed to public frustration. These deserve serious political answers rather than being dismissed as expressions of Euroscepticism.That’s why I also believe that the strongest defence against nationalism must come from Europe’s democratic right and centre-right. We need European institutions that concentrate on what we can achieve better together: defence, external borders, strategic infrastructure, research and foreign policy. Mainstream conservative parties must resist the temptation to imitate nationalist rhetoric. They should instead articulate a confident, patriotic and genuinely pro-European alternative.Some of Europe’s founding fathers, including Alcide De Gasperi, Konrad Adenauer and Robert Schuman, came from the Christian democratic tradition of the political centre-right. Their successors have a responsibility to carry that ambition forward.I remain optimistic. Millions of centre-right Europeans believe in democracy, freedom and European unity. Their political voice could prove decisive in Europe’s future.Giorgio ReAgrigento, Sicily, ItalyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter

Content: ‘The Bear Comes Home is a book about music and improvisation, love, spiritual exploration and the hope of transcendence.’Photograph: Francesco Vaninetti/GettyView image in fullscreen‘The Bear Comes Home is a book about music and improvisation, love, spiritual exploration and the hope of transcendence.’Photograph: Francesco Vaninetti/GettyBooksLettersAn essential bear for older readersPhil Dawsonrecalls falling in love with a saxophone-playing bear in Rafi Zabor’s The Bear Comes HomeMon 2 Nov 2026 12.57 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.59 ESTShareI’m a little late to the table, I know (I’ve been walking in the woods while my porridge was cooling), but I just wanted to make a small addition to readers’ reflections on the fictional bears that have won their hearts (Letters, 23 October). When I was a youngster, neither Winnie-the-Pooh nor Paddington Bear held that much appeal to me, but in my 40s I fell in love with a “deeply human sax-playing bear”.I’m referring to the hero of Rafi Zabor’s The Bear Comes Home. It’s a book about (among other things) music and improvisation, love, spiritual exploration and the hope of transcendence. It is most definitelynota book for children, but it is an overlooked gem. This bear should be introduced to more people.Phil DawsonBeeston, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
