title: Levelling up projects require long-term commitment | Inequality | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Rob Richardson and Dr Olivier Sykes argue that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary term
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Rob Richardson and Dr Olivier Sykes argue that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary term
Content: ‘Addressing regional inequalities requires stable, long-term funding, and targeted support for local capacity to deliver.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘Addressing regional inequalities requires stable, long-term funding, and targeted support for local capacity to deliver.’Photograph: GettyInequalityLettersLevelling up projects require long-term commitmentDr Rob Richardson and Dr Olivier Sykesargue that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary termMon 2 Nov 2026 12.57 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.01 ESTShareThe fact that the vast majority of levelling up projects are unfinished is disappointing, but not surprising (Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocate, 24 October). Trying to push through such top-down projects in unrealistic timescales, hoping for electoral rewards, was a characteristically misguided approach from Boris Johnson’s government. Decades of UK and EU policy experience show that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary term.Recent research from the universities of Manchester, Liverpool and Salford engages with several local authorities in north-west England that are still committed to these projects. Our findings show that addressing regional inequalities requires stable, long-term funding, and targeted support for local capacity to deliver. One positive from levelling up was that many authorities began to rebuild some of the regeneration skills and capacity lost over a decade of austerity – although such gains were mitigated by the resources needed for competitive bidding, and uncertainty around the rules governing funding eligibility.It is to be hoped that Andy Burnham’s government learns from this, and that local leaders and communities are given the stability and tools to deliver long-term regeneration where it is most needed.Dr Rob RichardsonLecturer in urban planning and placemaking, University of ManchesterDr Olivier SykesSenior lecturer in European spatial planning, University of LiverpoolHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Content: ‘They convey a great deal in tone and intention and the nature of the relationship.’Photograph: izusek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘They convey a great deal in tone and intention and the nature of the relationship.’Photograph: izusek/Getty ImagesEmailLettersSincerely devoted to email signoffsJane RosenthalandSiobhan McGovernrespond to an article advocating for the death of email signoffsMon 2 Nov 2026 12.57 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.59 ESTShareWhat a miserable whinge Tom Gill has subjected us to on the residual flourishes and formalities that linger on in salutations and signoffs in emails (The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, Tom, 25 October).Do let’s keep such greetings. They convey a great deal in tone and intention, and the nature of the relationship, not to mention the character and wit of the writer. True, they are often quaint and archaic, but let’s have them – flourishes and snidely terse signoffs greatly enrich and inform.So, Tom and letters editors, I remain,Sincerely devoted to this newspaper and its often disaffected journalists,Jane RosenthalBetty’s Bay,South AfricaThank you, Tom Gill, for this. title: Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Everton beat Newcastle, who finished with 10 men, for the second time in five days as Thierno Barry’s strike sealed a 1-0 win
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Everton beat Newcastle, who finished with 10 men, for the second time in five days as Thierno Barry’s strike sealed a 1-0 win
Content: Thierno Barry wheels away after his poacher’s finish put Everton a goal up in the second half.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarView image in fullscreenThierno Barry wheels away after his poacher’s finish put Everton a goal up in the second half.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarPremier LeagueNewcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headacheMiles Starforth at St James' ParkMon 2 Nov 2026 17.04 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.48 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Grealish will do well to get back into theEvertonstarting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.Newcastle United 0-1 Everton: Premier League – liveRead moreMoyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game followinga breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”Newcastle fans had made their feelings aboutthe 3-1 Carabao Cup defeataway to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.View image in fullscreenMatthias Jaissle struggles to get his message across to his Newcastle players.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersFrustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJacob Ramsey sees red in stoppage time after coming on as a substitute for Newcastle.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersBy now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNewcastle UnitedEvertonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture
Content: An aerial view of La Bombonera before kick-off in Sunday’sSuperclásico.The absence of away fans have been a fixture of Argentinian football since 2013. Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/Getty ImagesAttending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixtureByMarcela Mora y Araujoat La BomboneraMon 2 Nov 2026 15.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.39 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since the Observer Sport Monthly publisheda listof 50 sporting things you must do before you die withWatch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Airesat No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.Exciting, right?Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the firstSuperclásicowithout away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press areaMoores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.View image in fullscreenFans of Boca cheer from beneath their umbrellas.Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty ImagesOver the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known asLa Doceleads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in byLa Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.Barritta was the infamous leader ofLa Docedecades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with twoRiver Platefans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.View image in fullscreenRiver Plate fans clash with riot police outside the Monumental prior the final of the Copa Libertadores against Boca Juniors in 2018. The match was rescheduled after the bus carrying Boca players was attacked, injuring several players.Photograph: Sebastian Pani/APDeath at theSuperclásicowas not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm ofLa Docein 1981, by which time the rupture was total.In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle theSuperclásicomight be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of theSuperclásicohas remained,if it hadn’t been sucked out already.Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.“I’ve seen betterSuperclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.View image in fullscreenLeonel Flores of Boca celebrates with teammates following the team’s victory in theSuperclásico.Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty ImagesThat must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch theSuperclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.View image in fullscreenRiver Plate’s Gonzalo Montiel leaves the pitch under police protection against Boca.Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty ImagesMaybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all thisSuperclásicononsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to aSuperclásicowith my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.Explore more on these topicsBoca JuniorsRiver PlatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season
Content: Ezri Konsa, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapié and Mikel Arteta look set for another strong title challenge.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEzri Konsa, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapié and Mikel Arteta look set for another strong title challenge.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer DeskArsenalArsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League championsSunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last seasonSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 2 Nov 2026 10.47 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.23 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal are three points clearat the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least amajor points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all overArsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s actionRead moreIf there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. InArsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficientto get them past Fleetwoodin the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsArsenalSoccer DeskPremier LeagueUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stumbling block: Wirtz’s and Liverpool’s costly struggles against tight defences | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Credit to Arsenal for restricting opportunities at Anfield but Iraola will need his side to learn to unpick low backlines
Author: Andrew Beasley
Headline: Credit to Arsenal for restricting opportunities at Anfield but Iraola will need his side to learn to unpick low backlines
Content: Florian Wirtz under pressure from Gabriel in Arsenal’s win at Anfield on Sunday.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz under pressure from Gabriel in Arsenal’s win at Anfield on Sunday.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersLiverpoolAnalysisStumbling block: Wirtz’s and Liverpool’s costly struggles against tight defencesAndrew BeasleyCredit to Arsenal for restricting opportunities at Anfield but Iraola will need his side to learn to unpick low backlinesMon 2 Nov 2026 13.50 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 14.57 ESTShareLiverpool did not have a shot on target intheir 1-0 defeat by Arsenalon Sunday, according to Opta, the first time they have drawn this type of blank in a Premier League game at Anfield since records began in 2003-04. They did not find the target ina goalless drawat the Emirates Stadium this year either, though in both games they struck the woodwork. The margins tend to be fine when recording statistical outliers.If Alexis Mac Allister’s floated ball from distance into David Raya’s waiting arms had actually counted as a shot, would Andoni Iraola’s side have delivered a markedly better attacking performance? Far more concerning for the Spaniard will be that his team had 52 touches in theArsenalpenalty area (which is good) to create only one Opta‑defined big chance (which is bad). The Premier League average this season is five times more efficient; 10.3 box touches per big chance.Credit to Arsenal for restricting the quality of Liverpool’s chances despite them getting repeatedly within range of their goal. Most teams have been able to do this, though. While 12 teams have had fewer touches in opposition penalty boxes thanLiverpool, only Coventry with 11 have generated fewer big chances this season than Liverpool’s 12. Everton’s Thierno Barry alone has had 15, while Manchester City’s Erling Haaland has also had more than Liverpool with 14.Chart showing penalty box touches and big chances for teams in the 2026-27 Premier LeagueLiverpool have not had this issue in Europe. They have 12 big chances in the Champions League in just three games. As two of their opponents, Lask and Villarreal, are rated by Opta as being of lower standard than any side in the Premier League, this is little surprise. The relatively low stakes of a given match in the league- phase of the Champions League encourages those matches to be more open, too.This has not been the case in the 2026-27 Premier League for Liverpool, who have spent more time building up against low defensive blocks than any other team. This is, in part, a problem of their own making as they have conceded first in five of their eight matches. Only against Ipswich and Brighton have they held two‑goal leads, meaning opponents have rarely had compelling need to significantly loosen their defensive grip.Chart showing big chance involvement in the 2026‑27 Premier League for LiverpoolIn his first Liverpool press conference, head coach Iraola spoke of embracing the challenge set by deep-lying defences. “I prefer to face low blocks in terms of: ‘OK, we will be in control of the game, probably we will concede less chances, we will spend a lot of time in the opposition half and those are the scenarios that we have to find,’” he said. Only four teams have had more touches in the opposition half or attempted more final‑third passes than Liverpool this season, but such dominance has not led to higher value chances.This is where Florian Wirtz should be making an impression. He has the ability to unpick the tightest of backlines. Yet he has not created a big chance in the league this season. If his low total of five in his debut campaign was understandable with the problems Liverpool faced on-and-off the pitch, he trailed distantly behind Dominik Szoboszlai (14), Mohamed Salah (11) and Cody Gakpo (10). Wirtz is frequently involved in dangerous areas, as his ranking of ninth in the division for final-third passes completed will attest. His contributions have been far more geared towards ball retention and circulation rather than incision, however.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChart showing percentage of time building up against each block in the 2026-27 Premier LeagueIraola will want Liverpool to make more productive use of their high press. Most of their big chances in the league have come via corners or open-play crosses. Bradley Barcola has had moments; he recovered possessionto go clean through on goal at Brentford, before pouncing on an opposition mistake to assist Alexander Isak against Brighton. But Liverpool have produced shots from only 16.7% of their ball recoveries in the final 40 yards of the pitch, which is below average (18.4%) and the seventh-worst rate in the Premier League. Improvement here will help significantly.Big chances account for 18.1% of shots in the Premier League this season but 59.5% of the goals. They are vitally important. Liverpool’s ambitions for Iraola’s first campaign will be severely limited unless they start fashioning them far more easily.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolArsenalFootball tacticsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Wolff hails world champion Antonelli as role model in blast at F1’s ‘entitled moaners’ | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has described his Formula One world champion Kimi Antonelli as a driver who represents the future of the sport
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has described his Formula One world champion Kimi Antonelli as a driver who represents the future of the sport
Content: The Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff embraces Kimi Antonelli after his win in Mexico.Photograph: Jumeau Alexis/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff embraces Kimi Antonelli after his win in Mexico.Photograph: Jumeau Alexis/ABACA/ShutterstockFormula One 2026Wolff hails world champion Antonelli as role model in blast at F1’s ‘entitled moaners’Mercedes team principal hits out at ‘selfish’ driversAntonelli says he will keep No 12 on his car next seasonGiles Richardsin Mexico CityMon 2 Nov 2026 05.40 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.21 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, has described his Formula One world championKimi Antonellias a new kind of racing driver who represents the future of the sport, com­paring him scathingly to what he called some of the entitled ­moaners on the grid and declaring “selfless, ruthless” drivers now dead to F1.Antonelli secured his first world titlein Mexico City on Sunday, at 20 years old becoming the ­youngest F1 champion in only his second season in the sport. The ­Italian’s attitude, enthusiasm and sense of fair play have been notable in a revelatory season for a driver so young and Wolff believes he has proved to be a gamechanger in more ways than one.How Kimi Antonelli saw off the grid to become F1’s youngest world championRead moreWolff said: “This notion of win at all costs, selfish, opportunistic, ruth­less for your own benefit, that model of ­racing driver has died. We have a new champion that represents ­values: humility, integrity, loyalty, respect. Being himself. He should be a role model for many other young drivers.“He should be a role model for the few entitled ones in Formula One. The endless moaners on the radio. The ones that complain, the ones that crash. Look at this kid of 20 years and then think what you can do in order to improve. That’s the message to these kids.”View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli celebrates with the Mercedes team at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Photograph: Hasan Bratic/DeFodi Images/ShutterstockWolff did not name the targets of his ire but his comments will be lost on no one and clearly he believes Antonelli, who has been with ­Mercedes since he was 12, is an excellent example.Antonelli sealed the title with his third-place finish in Mexico, after a season where he has been on top throughout but has driven clean. Fellow world champions including Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and Lando Norris offered similar plaudits to the young driver who has bested them and his Mercedes teammate, George Russell, roundly beaten by the Italian this year, has ­acknowledged his honest and fair approach to racing.Wolff went further in stating that the most senior figures in the sport felt Antonelli embodied what they wanted inFormula Onedrivers, including Stefano Domenicali, the F1 chief executive, and the president of the FIA, Mohammed Ben Sulayem.“That is how the FIA, that Mohammed, that Stefano, that I would want to see racing drivers in the future,” Wolff said. “That is ­modern ­Formula One. Kimi represents the ­modern ­Formula One driver, because of those values, not only because of his talent. The talent is there with everyone. But you got to be a good person too and he has demonstrated that you can beat everyone out there by being a good person.”Before Wolff had raised the subject in Mexico, Antonelli had already expressed his desire to retain his sense of self, even as world champion. Now entitled to put the No 1 on his car next season, he said he would instead retain his current No 12. Antonelli chose it because of his admiration for Ayrton Senna who used it early in his career with Lotus between 1985 and 1987 and when he won his first title in 1988 for McLaren.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli is held aloft by Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: DPPI/Shutterstock“I’ll stay with No 12 because ­obviously it’s a very special number for me but also it’s a way for me to stay grounded, to stay humble,” Antonelli said when asked if he would adopt the champion’s No 1. “I feel like by keeping No 12, it allows me to have a new point where to start and build on everything again and try to improve.”After what wasclearly a hugely moving experiencein taking the title, Antonelli, was raised aloft on the podium after the race by ­Verstappen and Hamilton, two greats of the sport who finished in first and second in Mexico, which the 20-year-old said he would treasure and immortalise.“I will definitely frame that picture and put it in my house,” he said. “It’s just an incredible moment. To see so much respect from two incredible drivers in the history of the sport is truly special that will live and will always be remembered.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliToto WolffMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Melbourne Cup betting rules show UK the way to prevent illegal gambling boom | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: From January, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulation
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: From January, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulation
Content: Robbie Williams poses for a portrait with the Melbourne Cup after a press conference for Tuesday’s big race in Australia.Photograph: Chris Hopkins/AAPView image in fullscreenRobbie Williams poses for a portrait with the Melbourne Cup after a press conference for Tuesday’s big race in Australia.Photograph: Chris Hopkins/AAPTalking HorsesHorse racingMelbourne Cup betting rules show UK the way to prevent illegal gambling boomGreg WoodFrom January, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulationMon 2 Nov 2026 13.28 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.46 ESTShareThe 2026Melbourne Cupis not due off until 4am GMT on Tuesday – which is 3pm local time on what is still a public holiday in the state of Victoria – but there has already been some spectacular action in the betting market for the “race that stops a nation” over the last few hours, with the Irish punting legend JP McManus, no less, leading the charge.McManus and his fellow owner, Paul Byrne, were among the attendees at the “Call Of The Card” luncheon, a A$340-a-head (£178) event in Melbourne on Monday, which has been a popular feature of the big-race buildup since 1958.Guardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne CupRead moreThe centrepiece of the event sees four leading bookmakers “take on the room”, and give everyone in the 1,000-strong sell-out audience a chance to back each of the 24 runners, starting with the outsiders and concluding with the market leaders.When George Boughey’s Hopewell Rock, the runner-up in the Ebor Handicap at York in August, was offered to the room at $10 – ie 9-1 – Byrne immediately grabbed the microphone (at 2h31min the video of the event here). “We’ve travelled a long way now,” Byrne said, “and this is the horse, we’ve been studying the form on the way down we’re thinking we might try and beat last year’s record [bet of A$500,000] and get us a million dollars win.”A million to win A$10m is a chunky bet even by Australian standards, and after one of the four bookies agreed to lay A$500,000 at 9-1 and another accepted A$30,000, the remaining A$470,000 was laid at 17-2 and 8-1.McManus and Byrne also placed bets on several more runners, including Joseph O’Brien’s James J Braddock (A$150,000 at 20-1), and McManus’s own runners in the race, Trustyourinstinct and Goodie Two Shoes, last year’s runner-up.It is perhaps no great surprise that a lifelong punter (and former bookie) like McManus was in his element as he experienced Monday’s event for the first time. “I certainly enjoyed it. It’s exciting, I must say,”he told the Racing Postafterwards. “It’s something different and I think we can learn from it. I don’t know if anything like this will ever happen in Britain and Ireland, but it certainly adds to the occasion and it creates a lot of excitement. I only wish they would do it elsewhere.”For a punter and racing fan following the event on the other side of the world, meanwhile, it was a fascinating glimpse into a very different betting culture, not least on the bookies’ side of the equation.There are many thousands of racing fans in the UK and Ireland who will greet the sight of a bookie laying a sizeable bet with a hollow laugh. For years, backers – or rather, would-be backers – have seen their accounts closed or restricted to betting in pennies if there is any hint that they might turn a long-term profit from their betting.Australia, though, has an official Minimum Bet Limit (MBL) for racing, which requires an operator to lay an advertised price to lose a standard minimum amount, currently A$2,000 on a major race like the Melbourne Cup.That is, clearly, well below the level at which McManus and Byrne – and many of the other punters at “Call of the Card” – are playing, but establishes the principle that when a bookie advertises a price, the backers deserve a fair crack before it is cut. There were occasional boos, in fact, at Monday’s event in Melbourne when Robbie Waterhouse, perhaps the most familiar name in Australian bookmaking, offered a price that was a half-point or point below his rivals, or accepted only part of a requested stake.View image in fullscreenJP McManus and champion trainer Gai Waterhouse at the ‘Call of the Card’ event ahead of the Melbourne Cup.Photograph: Vince Caligiuri/Getty ImagesThe MBL is not the only aspect of Australian gambling and betting culture and legislation that differs markedly from that in Britain. Operators have been banned from offering online slot-machine gaming to Australian customers, for instance, since 2001, and subsequent legislation passed by the Australian parliament in August will make it much more difficult for Australians to access illegal offshore casinos.We have, of course, heard a great deal about the illegal market in this country in recent years, as the Betting and Gaming Council, the main industry body, has often claimed that tax hikes on gambling will inevitably push gamblers towards unregulated, offshore alternatives.Yet nothing has done more to push racing punters towards the illegal market over the last 20 years than the operators’ own use of restrictions and account closures against punters who are – or simply threaten to be – long-term winners.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowWarwick12.18 Un Sens A La Vie 12.53 Kelly Burn 1.28 Trigg 2.03 Lucy The Wire 2.38 Court In A Storm 3.13 I Love You Sivola 3.48 BallymoreenSedgefield12.44 Jeteye 1.19 Moment Of Light 1.54 Roxy Russet 2.29 Treaty Boy 3.04 Cadillac Ranch 3.39 Curious Mrs FoxLingfield1.02 Burk Flight 1.37 Analogical 2.12 Chosen Hero 2.47 Away For The Night 3.22 Calshot Spit 3.57 A Great ExcuseWolverhampton4.30 Mini Mac (nb) 5.00 Sonbelievable 5.30 Crown Of Ivy 6.00 Red Blue Point 6.30 Fancy Dancer 7.00 Politely 7.30 Lipsink (nap) 8.00 Tiger Beetle 8.30 Man Of DesertWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.From 1 January 2027, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulation, and an essential part of that is the fact that the country’s lawmakers see and understand the distinction between the most harmful forms of gambling – casino-gaming and slots – and betting on sport. They are also taking meaningful steps to protect their citizens from the dangers of the unregulated market, while ensuring that bookies will lay an advertised price to a reasonable sum.There will, surely, be many lessons there for our own government to absorb, if or when a successor to the outdated Gambling Act 2005 finally appears on the horizon.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingTalking HorsesHorse racing tipsMelbourne CupcommentShareReuse this content

title: Alex Mitchell out of Nations Championship opener in fresh England injury blow | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: A hamstring injury has ruled the Northampton scrum-half out of the game against Australia on Sunday, which England will follow by playing New Zealand and Japan
Author: Luke McLaughlin
Headline: A hamstring injury has ruled the Northampton scrum-half out of the game against Australia on Sunday, which England will follow by playing New Zealand and Japan
Content: Alex Mitchell is the latest England player to pick up an injury before the Nations Championship.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex Mitchell is the latest England player to pick up an injury before the Nations Championship.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesEngland rugby union teamAlex Mitchell out of Nations Championship opener in fresh England injury blowScrum-half out of game against Australia on SundayWallabies match followed by New Zealand and JapanLuke McLaughlinMon 2 Nov 2026 14.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 15.32 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Northampton scrum-half Alex Mitchell has been ruled out of England’s November opener against Australia on Sunday, with Bristol’s Harry Randall and Bath’s Ben Spencer called into the squad named by the head coach,Steve Borthwick.Mitchell, established as the first‑choice No 9 under Borthwick, damaged a hamstring inNorthampton’s Prem win against Gloucesteron Saturday and will have a scan on Tuesday to determine the extent of the injury.Borthwick urges England players to improve discipline at Nations ChampionshipRead moreArchie McParland, Mitchell’s uncapped clubmate, is also sidelined for the Wallabies match after sustaining a calf injury training with England last week, following his second call-up to the senior squad. A major scrum-half rethink is consequently needed by Borthwick before a highly significant sequence of fourNations Championshipmatches.The injury-enforced absence of Mitchell and McParland means either Randall or Spencer will be on the bench against Australia, with Leicester’s Jack van Poortvliet expected to start at No 9.While Mitchell is guaranteed to return when he recovers from injury, this week represents a priceless chance for Randall and Spencer to state their respective cases, with the World Cup less than a year away.Borthwick and his staff will consider how swapping Mitchell and McParland for Randall and Spencer may affect tactics against the Wallabies. Randall is famed for a sniping running game with Bristol while Spencer, who recently returned to action for Bath after shoulder surgery, is known for his exemplary tactical kicking.Elsewhere in the backs Gloucester’s Seb Atkinson, Exeter’s Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Fin Smith of Northampton are all named in England’s 36-man squaddespite recent injury concerns. Max Ojomoh of Bath and Saracens’ Noah Caluori drop out of the group named last week.The in-form Harlequins fly-half Marcus Smith is widely expected to push his namesake Fin for the starting No 10 jersey while George Furbank, who is also in scintillating form for Quins, is a strong candidate to start at full-back.Quick GuideEngland squadShowForwards:Fin Baxter (Harlequins), Ollie Chessum (Leicester), Arthur Clark (Gloucester), Alex Coles (Northampton), Luke Cowan-Dickie (Sale), Ben Curry (Sale), Tom Curry (Sale), Theo Dan (Saracens), Ben Earl (Saracens), Greg Fisilau (Exeter), Jamie George (Saracens), Ellis Genge (Bristol), Joe Heyes (Leicester), Maro Itoje (Saracens), Emmanuel Iyogun (Northampton), George Martin (Saracens), Asher Opoku-Fordjour (Sale), Tom Pearson (Northampton), Henry Pollock (Northampton), Will Stuart (Bath).Backs:Seb Atkinson (Gloucester), Fraser Dingwall (Northampton), Immanuel Feyi-Waboso (Exeter), George Ford (Sale), Tommy Freeman (Northampton), George Furbank (Harlequins), Will Joseph (Gloucester), Joe Marchant (Sale), Cadan Murley (Harlequins), Harry Randall (Bristol), Henry Slade (Exeter), Fin Smith (Northampton), Marcus Smith (Harlequins), Ben Spencer (Bath), Freddie Steward (Leicester), Jack van Poortvliet (Leicester).Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.There is one change to the forwards from the training squadnamed last week by Borthwick: the 21-year-old Bath hooker Kepu Tuipulotu, another uncapped player, drops out because of injury, with Theo Dan of Saracens returning.Borthwick’s squad of 20 forwards and 16 backs gathered at Pennyhill Park on Monday night, with the Prem now on a break until December. After kicking off against Australia in round four of the Nations Championship, England will meet Japan and New Zealand in rounds five and six before the finals weekend at the end of the month.“We’re looking forward to getting back to Allianz Stadium for four important Test matches against top-level opposition,” Borthwick said. “These fixtures take on added significance this autumn as they represent our final opportunity to face southern hemisphere opposition before next year’s World Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Facing Australia next Sunday is an exciting challenge. They have played a significant amount of Test rugby in recent months, and we know the quality and experience they will bring.”England’s Nations Championship plans hit by Pepper and Van Rensburg double blowRead moreScotland have had a double injury blow of their own before the conclusion of their Nations Championship campaign, with Jamie Ritchie and Elliot Millar Mills ruled out of all four November matches.Ritchie is expected to be out for four to six weeks after the flanker sustained a suspected medial collateral ligament injury in Glasgow’s United Rugby Championship win against Lions last Friday. The prop Millar Mills picked up a knee injury during Newcastle’s Prem defeat by Saracens on Saturday.Three Edinburgh forwards – the props Ollie Blyth-Lafferty and D’Arcy Rae, and the flanker Freddy Douglas – have been called into Gregor Townsend’s squad. Scotland face New Zealand on Saturday before Tests against Australia and Japan, all at Murrayfield.Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamSteve BorthwickAustralia rugby union teamNations ChampionshipRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: England’s exit from Rugby League World Cup was a disaster years in the making | England rugby league team | The Guardian
description: English rugby league needs systemic change and the national side must be a higher priority after their early exit in Australia
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: English rugby league needs systemic change and the national side must be a higher priority after their early exit in Australia
Content: England’s latest World Cup showing ended with a group-stage departure.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPAView image in fullscreenEngland’s latest World Cup showing ended with a group-stage departure.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPAEngland rugby league teamAnalysisEngland’s exit from Rugby League World Cup was a disaster years in the makingAaron BowerEnglish rugby league needs systemic change and national side must be a higher priority after early exitMon 2 Nov 2026 09.44 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.40 ESTShare“England have gone backwards over the last eight to 10 years.” Damning words about the state of English rugby league, from an Australia head coach, no less. But what should be most troubling for anyone with any sort of power within the sport is that these comments are not recent: they were made by the then Kangaroos coach Ricky Stuart,almost two decades ago.Stuart was speaking after England’s men were beaten in the semi-finals of the 2008 Rugby League World Cup but, as the national team head home from the tournament once again, his stance still holds weight today. England have failed to make it to the last four for the first time, having failed to qualify froma farcical group-stage format.Tonga’s gripping win over Samoa a victory for Pasifika pride at Rugby League World CupRead moreBut to point the blame solely at the format, or even the players and staff involved, would be missing the point entirely. English rugby league has been allowed to coast internationally for years, knowing the only real threat was from Australia and New Zealand and if they lost against either of those sides, well, that’s fair enough given the money and power the National Rugby League possesses.Things are different these days, though. Samoa and Tonga have risen as new powerhouses in the world game; it is not inconceivable to suggest they could contest next weekend’s final. England are now the fifth-best nation in the world and they risk drifting further. English rugby league is in dire need of systemic change, with the early exit the clearest warning sign yet.The Rugby Football League has paid lip service to the humiliation by opening an inquest. If there is one thing at which English rugby league remains best in class, it is a review: the postmortem of 2008 determined things actually weren’t that bad, while a detailed “strategic review” last year was nothing more than a disguise to increase Super League to 14 teams.Here lies the deep-rooted problem for English rugby league. You had to get as low as point 131 in that review to find the first mention of international rugby league and a plan for the England team – below pressing points including, but not limited to, creating a nines event and once again needlessly tweaking the Challenge Cup format. Priorities.That strategic review is a metaphor for how those in charge of the sport – the governing body and the clubs, given how the latter hold most of the power still – view the England team as a priority. Spoiler: it is very low. And in a world where the best are getting better and England’s best players are treated as an afterthought, what do we reasonably expect will happen come 2030?View image in fullscreenTonga have become one of rugby league’s powerhouses while England have drifted.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPPicture the reaction in any other sport where the England team prepared for a World Cup without a single warm-up match, a mid-season Test or even a solitary training camp; where the players and staff met each other in person for the first time days before their first match. The Football Association, the England and Wales Cricket Board or the Rugby Football Union would rightly be ridiculed: the RFL and those responsible must now face the same scrutiny.This is not an easy fix for multiple reasons. As mentioned, the RFL does not hold all the power in this particular scenario; the clubs have ultimate decision-making authority and, in the past year alone, have executed decisions which will set the England programme back further. Expanding Super League to 14 teams – 15 next year when London come up – diminishes the quality on show.The best players from Australia and New Zealand have regular exposure to elite-quality rugby league in the NRL every week. Super League’s standard has gone down. Then there was the outrageous decision to increase the overseas quota from seven to 10 per club. It was a decision made last year out of greed and a desire to fulfil an agenda to expand to 14, to boost the player pool to make 14 teams a viable possibility. It will have a devastating impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn any given weekend in Super League there will be 238 players on the field. As many as 140 of those can now be overseas and when you take out the significant French contingent too, you have a scenario where fewer than 25% of players in Super League could be England‑eligible. Fewer opportunities for English players at the expense of overseas talent. How do we realistically think this is going to pan out long term?View image in fullscreenThe expansion of the Super League to 14 teams has diminished the quality on show.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PAWhat is the immediate fix? An independent commission led by the NRL that takes the power away from the clubs. Critics will say the NRL is hardly a great advocate for the growth of international rugby league, but it would at least be able to ensure clubs are no longer making decisions for their own personal gain which hinder the national team’s prospects.Until that changes, the decline of the national team will deepen. Shorten the Super League calendar, reduce the size of the elite competition and give England’s best talent regular opportunities to play together and progress. Is itreallytoo much to ask to put the England national team higher up on the sport’s priority list?The emergence of Samoa and Tonga feels bad for English rugby league in this precise moment. But it should act as a catalyst for those in charge to wake up and realise that the game cannot coast any longer.Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby league teamRugby League World Cup 2026Rugby League World CupRugby leagueanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Zero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways? | Tampa Bay Buccaneers | The Guardian
description: In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved right
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved right
Content: Baker Mayfield had a busy day handing the ball on Sunday.Photograph: Jason Behnken/APView image in fullscreenBaker Mayfield had a busy day handing the ball on Sunday.Photograph: Jason Behnken/APTampa Bay BuccaneersZero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways?In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved rightDave SchillingMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.21 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t think I’m being cheeky when I say that passing is the most exciting part of football. A solid hit is nice, and a big run can thrill you, but this is a quarterback-centric game. When a QB is bad, teams usually lose and fans get bored. So, Sunday’s performance by Baker Mayfield and theTampa Bay Buccaneershad me positively gobsmacked. I wouldn’t say their 16-0 win over the Atlanta Falcons was thrill-a-minute, but it certainly was historic. By completing a grand total of zero passes out of a paltry three attempts, Baker Mayfield led the Bucs to the first game with no passing offense since the Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 16-12 on 29 September 1974. If you are miraculously old enough to remember the NFL before the advent of the forward pass in 1906, first off, congratulations on being over 120 years of age. Please email me your full diet and exercise regimen. You’re probably on your feet (if standing is still something physically possible), cheering a bit of hard-nosed, classic football. The rest of us young whippersnappers still grinding through our first century are holding our noses.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueNFL roundup: Cowboys and Chiefs suffer late collapses; Lamar Jackson’s season could be overRead moreOf course, Mayfield – a former No 1 overall pick –canthrow. As recently as 2024 he threw for 41 touchdowns and 4,500 passing yards in a season. But Sunday’s game was played in pouring rain thatled to farcical moments like this, and Tampa Bay clearly decided that the ground game was the only way to go. That the Bucs could score at all, let alone 16 points, is a credit to Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell running as though their lives depended on it. Irving finished the day with 170 rushing yards and one touchdown, while Gainwell had 140. Combined with Mayfield, they rushed 56 times for 324 yards – the most ever in a single game for the Bucs. They more than made up for Mayfield’s borderline irrelevance in the pocket. Mayfield made himself useful blocking for his runners, but otherwise, I probably could have started at QB for the Buccaneers and the game would have been the same, other than the high likelihood of me suffering at least one gruesome injury.“If I’m not going to throw the ball, I have to get active somehow,” Mayfield said after the game. He certainly was more valuable for his team than Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr, who had a game that would be front-page terrible if not for the historic passing futility on the other side. Penix went 8-for-24 with four interceptions. The field was wet and as slippery as a greased-up ferret with a sugar rush. But even a wet playing surface wasn’t enough to stop Tampa’s run game, or kicker Chase McLaughlin’s three field goals. Having said that, McLaughlin didn’t even need to make one – Atlanta were just that bad. Next week, the Falcons face the Bengals in Spain. If Atlanta play like this in Madrid, they’ll be the worst American export to Europe sinceDavid Hasselhoff’s first album.MVP of the weekJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.We’ll start with the positives: Burrow threw for five touchdowns, ran for another, racked up 462 passing yards and led his team back from 13 points down to a 43-36 overtime win on Sunday. On the downside, he threw three interceptions and all this came against the Tennessee Titans. But Burrow gets MVP this week for a refusal to do anything dull. And the Bengals are off to their best start since the 2021 season, when they made the Super Bowl.View image in fullscreenJoe Burrow accounted for six touchdowns on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Mack/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockVideo of the weekThe Chiefs-Broncos game was absorbing until the final moments. Kansas City, down 28-24, looked set to pull of a late victory when they had a first and goal on the Denver 4-yard line with 35 seconds left. But stout Broncos defending and a sloppy penalty from the Chiefs when they thought they had scored the winning touchdown meant they needed to score on the final play of the game. When Patrick Mahomes is under center in this type of situation, a Chiefs win is automatic. Not this time, though.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueStat of the week259. That’s the number of career touchdown passes across the regular season and playoffs by Josh Allen for the Bills after his pair during his team’s victory over the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday. In reaching that milestone, he broke the record set by Buffalo legend Jim Kelly. The victory moved the Bills to 6-1 and they now have the best record in the AFC. Sadly, the game was also marked by a thumb injury to the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson. It may end his season, a sad turn of events for one of the most thrilling players in the league.Elsewhere around the leagueThe Vikings are undefeated no more. The Lions pulled out a thriller to end Minnesota’s hopes of a perfect season. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams for a score with 4:35 left in the game to squeak home 19-15. This was Detroit’s third straight victory, but they also lost linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury. Campbell had to be carted off the field on a backboard early in the fourth quarter, which put an undeniable damper on the post-victory celebrations. Instead of reveling in his late-game heroics, Goff wassomber and reflective when speaking about Campbell. “That was definitely scary. He’s a husband and a father.”There’s more heartbreak on display at AT&T Stadium this year than a Kazuo Ishiguro novel. The Dallas Cowboys looked to be in the driver’s seat against Arizona as the fourth quarter began. They led 24-10 and their defense was looking well-prepared to lock down a win. Except, folks, they weren’t. Arizona exploded for 20 points in the fourth, as Gardner Minshew took over from an underperforming Jacoby Brissett. Minshew marched the Cardinals down the field in 63 seconds late in the fourth to tie the game at 30. A simple Chad Ryland extra point would have been enough to win the game, but the PAT flew wide left. This was Ryland’s first extra-point miss in the last 58 tries. To overtime they went. Ryland was able to rescue his no-good, very-bad day by hitting a 42-yard field goal to finally clinch the comeback. The Cowboys are 3-5, and a brutal 1-3 at home as we near the halfway mark of the season. Lucky for Dallas that they play in a division where only one team is above .500.View image in fullscreenGardner Minshew and the Cardinals celebrate a touchdown in their wild comeback.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APAre the Rams back? Or are the Chargers just awful? Time will tell, but in the Battle of Los Angeles, it was the Rams who took care of business, 24-9. The game was close until a pivotal second-half period in which the Rams scored two touchdowns. The Chargers are 0-7. They’re the only team in theNFLwho haven’t scored 100 points or more combined this season – 99 points for, versus 175 against. All this with alleged offensive mastermind Mike McDaniel at OC.The Jacksonville Jaguars remain the most pleasant surprise in the NFL, destroying Indianapolis at home, 42-7. The Jags are top of the AFC South, above three teams with sub-.300 winning percentages. Trevor Lawrence was superb for Jacksonville, sporting a 153.3 rating, 210 yards on 10-of-14 passing and three touchdowns. The Jags’ defense forced three turnovers – two interceptions and a fumble – and surrendered just one pity touchdown in the third quarter. Jacksonville are at the top of a terrible division. Is there any reason to think they won’t stay there?As someone who has dated both a woman from Cleveland and a woman from Pittsburgh (not at the same time), I can attest that Steelers v Browns is one of the most heated rivalries there is, primarily because Pittsburgh and Cleveland are cities with chips the size of dinner plates on their shoulders. Personally, I prefer the food in Pittsburgh (specifically the giant hotdog they sold at Pirates games that has pierogies on top), and so I was pulling for the Steelers on Sunday. They did not let me down. This was the 23rd straight home win for the Steelers over the Browns. Pittsburgh sacked Deshaun Watson eight times. Eerily, the last time I did this column, Deshaun wassacked … eight times by the Jets in Week 5. Maybe next time I’m writing this, I’ll give the Browns a heads-up.View image in fullscreenNick Herbig sacks Deshaun Watson during the Steelers’ win over Cleveland.Photograph: Brent Gudenschwager/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Raiders pulled off another of the day’s improbable comebacks, scoring 24 points in the second half to beat the New York Jets 38-33. Las Vegas broke a four-game losing streak and are 4-4 on the year. Kirk Cousins threw for 247 yards on 19-of-26 passing and three touchdowns, plus a TD run in the third quarter that he punctuated with a peculiarArrested Development-stylechicken dance that he called his “wellness celebration”. The 38-year-old said, “We do a lot of tissue work here. At my age, it’s especially helpful. … So I said someday if I run a touchdown in, I’m going to give a shoutout to all the staff that works so hard to help us feel good and be one of the healthier teams in the league.” Cousins almost forgot to do this peculiar celly, butBrock Bowers reminded him. Perhaps the first and last time anyone will ever say “Hit them with the wellness celebration!” on an NFL field. Or at least I hope so.As for the Jets, they were content to make jokes about themselves. “I think we had some bad penalties, bad mistakes,” their veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick said. “Jets being Jets.”Explore more on these topicsTampa Bay BuccaneersAtlanta FalconsNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Content: A worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAView image in fullscreenA worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPASwedenShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackChains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shopsWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?Jon HenleyEurope correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.39 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.12 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland,Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.The incidents follow anattack in France last monthin which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.Sweden’s Coop chain toldthe daily Aftonbladetthat six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southernSwedenposted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.View image in fullscreenWorkers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ReutersThe head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.View image in fullscreenEmpty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near  russels.Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty ImagesBelgium’sLe Soir newspaper reportedthat dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read more“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.Ikea,famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.View image in fullscreenA customer surveys an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket in Dublin.Photograph: ReutersMany cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.The agency subsequently reportedthat supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.Explore more on these topicsSwedenSupermarketsCybercrimeRetail industryEuropeBelgiumLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Young co-pilot, 20, named as one of nine victims of deadly Florida plane crash | Florida | The Guardian
description: Family of four, two close friends and nanny also died in crash as pilot identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Family of four, two close friends and nanny also died in crash as pilot identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory
Content: Nathalia Filguerias, who worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.Photograph: @itsnatfilg/ThreadsView image in fullscreenNathalia Filguerias, who worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.Photograph: @itsnatfilg/ThreadsFloridaYoung co-pilot, 20, named as one of nine victims of deadly Florida plane crashFamily of four, two close friends and nanny also died in crash as pilot identified as 55-year-old Jeff GregoryRichard Luscombein Miami, andMichael SainatoMon 2 Nov 2026 16.52 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.17 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFamily members on Monday identified a youngFloridapilot as one of nine victims of a plane crash in Palm Beach county that occurred during a heavy thunderstorm.Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, was co-pilot of the private Learjet 60 en route from Austin-Bergstrom international airport in Texas to North Eleuthera airport in the Bahamas on Sunday when it suddenly plummeted out of the sky, killing all onboard, her mothertold the New York Times.Later on Monday, the family of the passengers who died posteda statementon Facebook identifying the victims and paying tribute to them.It named them as Adam Robinson, 45, a Texas-based technology entrepreneur; his wife Helen Sharp, 40; and their children, Emma, four, and Charlie, two. The statement said close family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr were also killed, along with Anita Maria Cetina, the children’s nanny.The pilot in charge of the Learjet was identifiedby TMZand other media outlets on Monday as Jeff Gregory, 55, an experienced aviator from Pennsylvania.The plane crashed at 12.51pm local time on Sunday, exploding on impact, leaving a giant crater in the ground, and scattering debris all around the crash site near a mobile home park in the city of Greenacres.At a briefing on Monday, Tom Chapman, head of a team of about 20 National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) personnel in West Palm Beach, said conditions in south Florida on Sunday were “pretty crazy”, and that the weather would be “a major focus” of the investigation.0:36Burning crater seen on ground after Florida plane crash – video“You all saw what the weather was like here at the surface. What we have to determine is what the weather conditions were like at altitude,” he said.Filgueiras’s mother, Camila Corteleti, told the Times her daughter worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, which owned the aircraft, and that she had been passionate about flying since childhood.“She loved the freedom.
