It was completely different seeing the world from the top,” Cortelini said, adding that her daughter enjoyed plane spotting at local airports as a young girl.Filgueiras graduated high school in Boca Raton, Florida, in 2024, having already obtained her private pilot’s license at the age of 17, according to the Palm Beach CBS affiliate12 News.Aurora Aviation, which operated the aircraft under its trading name of Upper Jets, did not respond to a request for comment.Robinson was the founder of several technology companies, and his wife owned a public relations firm, according to relatives.“Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma and Charlie were the light of their lives,” the statement said.“Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last for ever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.“Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly.“Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.”Chapman of the NTSB said at the press conference: “I want to express our profound, profound condolences to the family and friends of those who were lost in this tragedy. We are truly, truly sorry for your loss.”Air traffic control (ATC) audio from the final moments of the flight feature a female voice reporting a buildup of ice on the jet’s wings, and a request for permission to climb to 37,000ft.“The crew transmitted to ATC that they were encountering light, clear ice, which was manageable, and also moderate turbulence,” Chapman said, noting the plane was at 35,000ft at that point.“The crew reported the outside temperature was -47C (-53F) and they were managing the ice, but were in moderate turbulence. Very soon after, the crew transmitted, ‘We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000ft if able,’ which was approved by FAA air traffic control.”Chapman added: “Less than 30 seconds later, a transmission from the airplane announced a descent, followed by a mayday call. About 12.48pm, the airplane transmitted, “We are in an overspeed condition, descending,’ with the rest unintelligible. Sadly, all aboard were lost.”The female crew member on the recording said the plane, tail number N722BD, was descending at more than 20,000ft a minute, and: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”The recording ends with the woman shouting, “Holy fuck, we’re out of time,” and air traffic controllers trying to re-establish contact.Multiple videos circulating on social media capture the Learjet striking the ground almost vertically, and at a high rate of speed.Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, said on Sunday it was “a cataclysmic plane crash … that looked like a missile going down”. He said it was not believed anybody on the ground was killed or injured, although NTSB staff at the Monday press conference said they believed a car occupant nearby received a minor leg wound.The crash occurred during an outbreak of severe weather and thunderstorms in south Florida that briefly closed Miami international airport and forced commercial airliners to divert to other airports.Chapman said the recovering debris from the crash site was going to be “a real challenge” and “daunting” given the velocity of the impact, and that while on-site investigations would continue for several days, no immediate cause of the tragedy was likely to be imminently announced.“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact, and so some of this is yet to be determined,” he said. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.”The Catholic diocese of Palm Beach dedicated an All Souls’ Day Mass on Monday to the nine people who died, the Palm Beach Postreported.Explore more on these topicsFloridaPlane crashesAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s been a while’: hero’s welcome for UK man after 28-year walk across the world | Hull | The Guardian
description: Former paratrooper Karl Bushby arrives back in Hull and becomes first person to walk continuously across planet
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Former paratrooper Karl Bushby arrives back in Hull and becomes first person to walk continuously across planet
Content: Karl Bushby is greeted by his mother, Angela, in Hull after his 28-year, 36,000-mile walk from Chile.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenKarl Bushby is greeted by his mother, Angela, in Hull after his 28-year, 36,000-mile walk from Chile.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAHull‘It’s been a while’: hero’s welcome for UK man after 28-year walk across the worldFormer paratrooper Karl Bushby arrives back in Hull and becomes first person to walk continuously across planetJosh HallidayNorth of England editorMon 2 Nov 2026 09.49 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.51 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a 28-year odyssey spanning 29 countries, 36,000 miles, facing down polar bears, kidnappers and a spell in Russian custody, Karl Bushby was finally back in the arms of his longsuffering mother, Angela.“Where have I been?” he joked as Angela sobbed into his chest with a mix of relief, pride and no doubt the odd sleepless night.Surrounded by television cameras and with a Sky News helicopter overhead, the 57-year-old was given a hero’s welcome as he completed his record-breaking voyage on foot from Punta Arenas in Chile, the southernmost city on the South American continent, to his home town ofHullon Monday.“There has never been a welcome home quite like this, I’m sure,” said Bushby, shaking his head in disbelief as he greeted a crowd of well-wishers in the city’s Queen Victoria Square. “This is absolutely madness.”View image in fullscreenKarl Bushby spoke at a civic welcome in Queen Victoria Square as he arrived back home in Hull.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAIt has been 28 years since Bushby, then aged 29, left the army to walk the world on what he intended to be a 12-year journey. He finally crossed a misty Humber Bridge back to the city on Sunday – on the same date he set off in 1998.In that time he has stuck by two simple rules: not to return home until he had fully completed his feat, and not to use transport to advance.In all, he walked 36,000 miles across four continents, a frozen sea, deserts, jungles and mountains. Quite a trek for a man not keen on walking. “It’s boring as hell,” hetold the Guardianlast month.View image in fullscreenBushby addresses the crowd in Hull.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAHis return on Monday will make Bushby the first person to have walked continuously across the world, visiting 29 countries, having already exceeded the record for the longest unbroken foot journey (far outstripping the 25,000-mile circumference of the world).The voyage took him across the frozen sea of the Bering strait between Alaska and Russia and across the notorious Darién Gap in Central America. Hedescribed last monthhow he had been threatened at gunpoint, faced down a polar bear, was convicted of being a spy, and been held in custody in Russia and sentenced to deportation.Bushby strode into Queen Victoria Square like a modern folk hero, his passage only slowed by the dozens of people rushing to shake his hand and take photographs.Yet for a man who had navigated much of the planet, he did appear to get a little lost on his way through the crowds of his home city. “I’ve no idea which direction I’m going. Everybody point the way,” he said. “Sorry to keep you all waiting – it’s been a while.”View image in fullscreenBushby with his trolley, Beast 2, as he arrives back in Hull.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAThrough the crowd he pushed his heavily loaded trolley, dubbed the Beast 2 (his first one broke down) laden with essentials such as medicine, sleeping bags, headtorches – and two very worn tyres. “Sorry everybody, sorry,” he said as he manoeuvred through the well-wishers.About three miles away, Angela, 75, was waiting at the gate of Bushby’s childhood home as she had promised. After a tearful embrace, they took a long look at each other.“You’ve changed a bit,” Bushby told her. “I’m older,” his mother replied through tears. “We both are,” he said. “Well done for hanging in there.”He was then whisked inside the small terrace house, festooned with union flag bunting, where he was reunited with his son, now 36, and a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he was meeting for the first time.View image in fullscreenKarl Bushby returned to his childhood home – and his mother – for the first time since 1998.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAEarlier on a makeshift stage, Bushby thanked the city for his hero’s welcome. “It took a world to get me here,” he said. “The kindness of strangers – so many, from individuals to nation states, to get me back here. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth.“We faced down governments, we faced down some of the hardest challenges, we had to create two world records just to get back here. It was a global effort.”At one point, the great German film-makerWerner Herzogappeared on stage alongside Bushby, overseeing what will surely be one of the closing scenes in Herzog’s documentary on the 28-year odyssey.View image in fullscreenThe German film director Werner Herzog joined the welcome-home party in Angela Bushby’s garden.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesKarl Turner, the Labour MP for Kingston upon Hull East, brought with him a message from the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who congratulated Bushby on his “truly remarkable” feat and thanked him for his service as a paratrooper.In a statement read on stage by Turner, Burnham said: “Your journey has taken nearly three decades, crossed continents and tested you in ways most of us can barely imagine.“But today, as you return to the city from which you left 28 years ago, you bring with you something far greater than any world record or a remarkable personal achievement. You bring a story of what can be accomplished through extraordinary determination and self-belief.”As he was ushered away for a big lunch before the walk to his mother’s house, Bushby had one last message for the city he left in 1998: “I guess I’ll be seeing you around.”Explore more on these topicsHullExplorationWalkingMilitaryWerner HerzogDocumentary filmsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: British Gas resumes force-fitting prepay meters months after £112m settlement | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Regulators lift block on supplier, enabling it to install meters in homes of people unable to afford energy bills
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Regulators lift block on supplier, enabling it to install meters in homes of people unable to afford energy bills
Content: Households are bracing for some of the highest energy bills since 2023 this winter.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHouseholds are bracing for some of the highest energy bills since 2023 this winter.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianEnergy billsBritish Gas resumes force-fitting prepay meters months after £112m settlementRegulators lift block on supplier, enabling it to install meters in homes of people unable to afford energy billsJillian AmbroseMon 2 Nov 2026 15.05 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 15.53 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish Gas has resumed force-fitting prepay meters in the homes of people unable to afford their energy bills months after paying the largest settlement on record for sending debt collectors into the homes of vulnerable customers.The industry regulator has lifted a block going back almost four years that prevented British Gas from clawing back unpaid bills by fitting such meters in customers’ homes after extractinga settlement worth more than £100m from the supplierfor its role in the prepay scandal at the height of the Russian gas crisis.The decision means that British Gas agents will be able to force-fit prepay meters in homes from this winter as households brace for some of the highest energy bills since 2023, when the supplierfirst came under fireover its treatment of vulnerable customers.Debt agents working for British Gas at the time had ignored signs of vulnerability in struggling households while fitting meters in their homes, according to an investigation by the Times, including those with severe mental health issues and physical disabilities.The scandal ignited outrage among fuel poverty campaigners and across Whitehall as the government spent billions to help cut bills for energy users and prevent a collapse of the supplier industry.Within a year of the scandal, the regulator lifted its industry-wide moratorium on force-fitting meters to allow some suppliers torestart the installations, although forced fittings in homes with young children or people over the age of 75 remain banned.The regulator said that installing a prepay meter under a warrant “should only be a last resort, with rigorous checks to ensure debt is recovered lawfully, proportionately and safely”.It said smart pay-as-you-go meters were “a positive choice for many customers, helping them stay in control of their energy use and reporting high levels of satisfaction”.Campaigners have said the timing of the change is likely to increase people’s fears of falling behind on energy bills this winter, and will add to the stress that households face.Simon Francis, a coordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “It’s almost as if regulators and ministers are failing to remember the lessons of the last energy price spike.“While more protections are now in place than in 2022, weknowthat magistrates are still approving bulk batches of applications for forced prepayment meter installs and some of the system failures identified in the original investigations are still happening.”British Gas defended its plan to claw back unpaid bills as household energy debt is forecast to exceed £7bn, adding more than £80 to the average household energy bill.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Our industry needs to protect and support customers who genuinely cannot afford to pay while taking appropriate action where people are able to pay but do not engage,” the company said. “We know many households are struggling with energy costs, and we offer significant support to those who need it most.”It said it planned to “engage early, offer targeted support and agree flexible, affordable repayment options” to struggling customers wherever possible, and that involuntary prepay meter fittings would “remain a last resort, with robust vulnerability and affordability checks”.Under Ofgem’s rules, all suppliers must make at least 10 attempts to contact a customer before a prepay meter is installed and carry out a welfare visit before installation. Meters should never be fitted in the homes of the highest risk customers, which include households with people over 75, under two, or those with severe health issues or medical equipment.A government spokesperson said: “This is a regulatory decision by Ofgem. We cannot allow past rogue practices to be repeated, where prepayment meters were wrongly installed in the homes of vulnerable people. We are closely watching to make sure companies protect their customers and act within Ofgem’s rules.”An Ofgem spokesperson said the regulator would continue to closely monitor suppliers and will “take action if we identify instances where our rules are not being followed”.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsConsumer affairsHousehold billsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom | Global development | The Guardian
description: Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports
Author: Benjamin Swift
Headline: Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports
Content: Chang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianView image in fullscreenChang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanGlobal developmentChinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boomMayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exportsSupported byAbout this contentBy Yanzhi Chen andBenjamin Swiftin Mayaya, BoliviaMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon.“Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braisedsábalofish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong.View image in fullscreenZhang Changchun, a Chinese chef and mine investor, at dinner in Mayaya, Bolivia.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianEach man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers.The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money.In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation.Miningequipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street.“We developed this town,” Zhang says between gulps of beer and bites of pork. “Without the Chinese, there would be no Mayaya today.”Asrecord gold pricesdriveAmazonian deforestationand violent conflict, these small-scale, private mining operations are tightening China’s grip on the world’s gold reserves. The Guardian spent five days with Chinese miners, investors and traders.The Bolivian Amazon has long attracted foreign capital, from rubber and timber industries to North American mining companies in the 1950s. But now, Chinese mining is defining a new era of extraction, as a global network of goods, machinery and labour often thrives illegally under Bolivian law.View image in fullscreenThe River Kaka, near Mayaya, has been severely affected by mining in recent years.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianA 2014 national lawlimits mining rights to cooperatives and independent miners, state-controlled firms and domestic and foreign private companies. Such foreign firms must have a registered Bolivian office and operate in their own name. The state permits joint ventures, leases and risk-sharing agreements between foreign and national firms, but only through public-private contracts, in which the state is a shareholder.Chinese mining firms operating outside this framework act unlawfully.Under a 2016 law, cooperatives also risk expropriation if they contract, lease or share mining-concession risks with foreign firms.Chinese goldminers first arrived in Mayaya in 2005, but it was in 2017 that a major wave of immigration took place, after China’s national development and reform commissionbanned domestic small-scale gold mining, citing environmental and national defence concerns. The crackdown sent many miners and investors searching for work globally, and spurred several companies to hire workers from mines closed back home to work at newly opened operations in Bolivia.One of those firms is Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export, which has operated in Bolivia since at least 2011. Officially, the firm does not carry out mining operations,listing only print materialsand manufacturing in a supplier directory.A dredge boat in the Kaka River.Mayaya, Bolivia. Video: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianCampaigners say these companiesskirt the law, “hiding behind”cooperatives to operate in Bolivia’s mining industry. On paper, foreign investors sign service contracts with local cooperatives, provide capital and machinery. In reality, they control the mines end to end, selecting sites, hiring workers, providing machinery, exporting gold and taking 75% to 80% of profits, says Alfredo Zaconeta, a mining researcher atenvironmental thinktank Cedla.Behind these contracts, Zaconeta adds, Chinese investors evade legal responsibilities as the state lacks the resources and political will to oversee the mining lobby. He says it rarely, if ever, enforces existing ownership and permit rules.As a result, in Bolivia, an entire economy has emerged to serve this migration, from La Paz lawyers specialising in Chinese work visas to a local phone store that doubles as an informal bank for exchanging bolivianos and renminbi. In some regions, Chinese miners recruit friends and family, forming home town clusters dedicated to the local mining industry.View image in fullscreenOne of the many Chinese restaurants in Mayaya.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianAlong Mayaya’s main street, shops sell all things Chinese – from bottled tea and cigarettes to pork intestines. Yang Yanbin, a Chinese investor, says: “As long as you have money to invest, this country welcomes you. We stuff all the money straight into our pockets.”Chang Yuequan, a lifelong miner who has mined gold along the China-Russia border since his teens, is another Chinese investor in Mayaya. In 2017, after verifying Mayaya’s gold quality, he ordered 120 shipping containers fromChinaand began assembling machinery.In 2025, he opened his newest mine next to the Kaka River, which he named “Passion Fruit” in Spanish, referencing the wild vines covering the hillside. On one of his periodic visits, Chang and a Chinese employee watched an excavator in a huge pit claw soil into a loader before Bolivian workers blasted it with high-pressure hoses.View image in fullscreenChang Yuequan, a mine investor, near one of his mines in Mayaya.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianChang says the workers then mix the slurry with mercury, then burn it to produce the final product: large, lumpy gold nuggets. Turning to the mine’s Chinese manager, Chang points to the green half of the hill and says: “This whole mountain is ours. Excavate that too.”Chang’s friend and colleague, He Zijian, who ships gold from Mayaya to La Paz during price surges, confirms the Chinese influence in the region. He says: “Everything – down to the tiniest screws – is imported from China.”The trade can be highly lucrative. Much of the gold from Mayaya ends up in Dubai via illegal exports. According to He, Chinese middlemen bring the bullion to Bolivia’s capital, La Paz, before smuggling it to the Gulf state. There, he says, the metal is sold at Murshid Bazar, Dubai’s largest gold market.Gold in Dubai isoften shippedfurtherto Switzerland, where it is laundered into legal supply chains and sold in western markets. In July, police arrested a Bolivian man set to depart to Dubai from Santa Cruz, Bolivia. His four suitcasesallegedly contained 189.5kg(418lb) of high-purity gold worth roughly £18.5m.While the man arrested may not have links to Chinese mining companies, authorities say his arrest highlights the vast quantities of gold illegally exported from the country.View image in fullscreenWorkers at an open-pit goldmine near Mayaya.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The GuardianJaime Sanabria, director ofBolivia’s mining regulator, Ajam, estimates that while Bolivia produces about 100 tonnes of gold a year, only about 10% is sold legally, costing the Bolivian government and the country’s people billions in lost revenue.Alongside illegal exports, the gold-mining boom has brought poor labour conditions and rapid environmental degradation. According to two dredge-boat miners, Bolivian workers are routinely paid a quarter of what Chinese workers doing the same jobs earn.View image in fullscreenVictoriano Piloy, a lifelong resident of Mayaya, at his store by the River Kaka. He says Chinese mining has brought pollution, with little benefit to local communities.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian“They’ve left nothing for us,” says lifelong Mayaya resident Victoriano Piloy. “The money doesn’t stay here – that’s why we’re poor.”In surrounding Indigenous communities,mercury poisoninghas become increasingly common. Already hit hard bythe climate crisis, deforestation and wildfires, residents often struggle to make a living through agriculture and fishing.Many ultimately turn to mining, compounding mercury pollution. With Chinese companies controlling the river, Bolivian artisanal miners increasingly enter Madidi national park, one of the world’s most biodiverse. There have been tensions. In August, residents of a rural village south of Mayayaseized and burnedmining machinery allegedly owned by a Chinese company, denouncing their environmental harms. Nearby municipalities have alsobanned gold mining.“The environmental impact is devastating because no one is inspecting or enforcing the rules,” says Sanabria, the mining regulator, adding that about 80% of mining in the country is illegal.While the government conducts environmental audits every year, Zaconeta says Chinese investors commonly receive advance notice and clean up before inspections. The decentralised nature of gold mining in Bolivia, with 3,117 cooperatives nationwide, complicates state regulation.View image in fullscreenA dredge boat on the River Kaka.Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian“It’s just a good faith declaration; it can’t be verified. Everyone knows they are breaking the law,” Zaconeta says.TheMinistry of Mining and Metallurgydid not respond to requests for comment. Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export Co and the Regional Federation of Gold Mining Cooperatives of Bolivia were also approached for comments.Despite the criticism directed at the mining industry, under the country’s new conservative president, Rodrigo Paz, the trend is toward evenmore permissive policies. In May, Paz signedan agreementwith mining cooperatives that reduces barriers to mining in protected areas and Indigenous territories.‘When the forests burn, the sickness comes’: how protecting trees shields millions from diseaseRead moreYet, government incentives may not be enough to ensure foreign companies’ long-term presence in Bolivia’s mines. Chang Yuequan, one of Mayaya’s early Chinese investors, has spent his life chasing the world’s best gold from Russia to Tibet and North Korea, and finally into the Bolivian Amazon. Twelve years in, he knows Mayaya’s gold is depleting. He expects to move on to his next destination in five or six years – once his boats stop operating.At least a dozenPaceñabeers into one of the Chinese investors’ frequent dinners, one investor sums up their worldwide reach: “You’ll encounter Chinese people in every corner of the world.”Then his friend jokes: “We are just powerful like that – we could conquer the world!”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanMiningGoldAmazon rainforestBoliviaChinafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rare ant nest stolen from last place in England where species survives | Insects | The Guardian
description: Devon nature reserve says ‘reckless’ theft of narrow-headed ant colony sets back years of conservation work
Author: Joe Pinner
Headline: Devon nature reserve says ‘reckless’ theft of narrow-headed ant colony sets back years of conservation work
Content: One possible motive for the theft of the nest could be to ‘rewild’ them, say experts.Photograph: Alex Hyde/PAView image in fullscreenOne possible motive for the theft of the nest could be to ‘rewild’ them, say experts.Photograph: Alex Hyde/PAInsectsRare ant nest stolen from last place in England where species survivesDevon nature reserve says ‘reckless’ theft of narrow-headed ant colony sets back years of conservation workJoe PinnerMon 2 Nov 2026 10.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 10.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA nest containing up to 5,000 of England’s rarest ant species has been stolen from a nature reserve, a conservation charity has said.DevonWildlifeTrust (DWT) said a nest of narrow-headed ants had been dug up and taken from Chudleigh Knighton Heath nature reserve in south Devon, which is the last place in England where the species still exists.A single nest can hold a colony of between 1,000 and 5,000 ants, along with one or more breeding queens, which can live for up to 25 years.View image in fullscreenThe theft was discovered by conservation researchers carrying out regular checks, who found a hole where a known nest had been and ‘clear signs of digging with a spade’.Photograph: Devon Wildlife Trust/PADWT said the theft was discovered by conservation researchers carrying out regular checks in mid-October, who found a hole where a known nest had been and “clear signs of digging with a spade”.Narrow-headed ants, which are named after the distinctive “pinched” look of their heads, were once widespread across southern England in heathlands. However, their numbers have shrunk over the last 100 years due to habitat loss caused by agricultural change and building developments. Now they are classified as a section 41 species, nationally rare, and near threatened on the International Union forConservationof Nature’s red list of species.Stephen Hussey, from DWT, said that whoever had stolen the nest knew what they were looking for and would have needed “prior knowledge” of ant colonies to be able to locate the nest. “We keep a close eye on them, so we know exactly where the nests are, but it’s not obvious to someone who doesn’t know about ants,” he said.He said that while it was difficult to speculate on the motives for such a theft, it could have been an attempt to “rewild” nature by placing the ants back in their former habitats.“It’s still a reckless act because you need a degree of expertise to move ants and prepare new homes for them,” he said. “We have ambitions to move some of the nests to new sites, but that will take a great deal of conservation effort, so relocating one nest to a new site isn’t likely to be very successful.”Smuggled in syringes: how Nairobi became a nexus for the black market in giant harvester antsRead moreAnother possibility was that the ants had been taken by an insect collector, he added.Julia Balfour, the species recovery officer for narrow-headed ants at DWT, said that the removal was a “significant loss” for the species. “Narrow-headed ant colonies develop slowly, and each mature nest, with its long-lived queens, represents many years of growth that cannot quickly be replaced,” she said. “This is a crime every bit as serious as illegal raids on wild bird eggs. It shows the pressures that our nature and wild places are under.“This is the last population of narrow-headed ants in England, and losing even one colony sets back years of careful work by our staff, volunteers and partners.”The theft has been reported toDevonand Cornwall police. It is against the law to deliberately disturb or remove material from a nature reserve. DWT said that it was reviewing the security of its nature reserve and would be continuing regular ant checks.PC Lucy Wyatt, part of the rural affairs team at Devon and Cornwall police, said: “Sites of special scientific interest are legally protected and it is a criminal offence for any person to intentionally or recklessly damage, destroy, or disturb the protected area.”Police are asking the public to report any information about the theft via the Devon and Cornwall police website.Explore more on these topicsInsectsConservationDevonWildlifeEndangered speciesCrimeAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean | Whales | The Guardian
description: A Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceans
Author: Clea Skopeliti
Headline: A Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceans
Content: A sperm whale’s serrated tail fluke rises above the surface of the Mediterranean SeaPhotograph: Mario Gabualdi/Tethys Research InstituteView image in fullscreenA sperm whale’s serrated tail fluke rises above the surface of the Mediterranean SeaPhotograph: Mario Gabualdi/Tethys Research InstituteSeascape: the state of our oceansWhales‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the MediterraneanA Guardian investigation has found that despite a recommendation to slow down, leading shipping companies continue to travel above advised speeds in a key habitat for cetaceansSupported byAbout this contentClea Skopeliti, Federica Rossi and Wouter MassinkMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 00.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarine biologist Alice Barbarioli waits with her camera trained on the horizon. A few minutes earlier, the hydrophone beneath the Pelagos research vessel detected codas – the sequence of clicks sperm whales use to communicate.The sperm whale reveals its head and dorsal fin as those onboard the vessel in the Pelagos sanctuary, a conservation area established to protect marine mammals in the north-western Mediterranean, rush to take photos and note the rhythm of its breathing. After a few minutes, the animal arches its back, and begins to head back into the depths of the sea. They wait to catch a glimpse of its tail.Barbarioli, the lead researcher of the citizen-science expedition, organised by the Tethys Research Institute, immediately notices an injury on its left fluke: “Given how precise the mark is, it’s probably the result of a [vessel] collision,” she says.Collisions have long been recognised as a leading human-induced cause of death for the Mediterranean’s endangered sperm and fin whales. Now, a Guardian investigation using data from the maritime intelligence firm Veson Nautical, has found that large passenger and cargo vessels operated by four companies – the Grimaldi Group, Corsica Ferries, Baleària and Moby Lines – have frequently travelled through a protected habitat that includes the Pelagos sanctuary at 15 knots (17mph) or above –speeds that almost always killcetaceans in cases of a collision. Strikes are unlikely to kill when a vessel is travellingbelow 10 knots.View image in fullscreenA sperm whale’s tail fin rises from the sea in the Pelagos sanctuary.Photograph: Lorenzo Gordigiani/Tethys Research InstituteSlowing vessels is the most effective mitigation strategy when rerouteing isn’t possible,according to conservation NGO Oceancare.The sea between Valencia and Genoa, which includes the Pelagos sanctuary, is akey cetacean habitat,home to about two-thirds of the Mediterranean’s fin whales and more than a fifth of its sperm whales. In July 2023, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) created the north-western Mediterranean Sea particularly sensitive sea area (PSSA). In a voluntary speed recommendation (VSR), it advised vessels weighing 300 gross tonnes and above to sail at 10 to 13 knots in the area to reduce the risk of fatal collisions.Despite the IMO’s recommendation, the Guardian, using additionaldata fromGlobal Fishing Watch, found that ships with IMO identification numbers spent more than 280,000 hours travelling at 15 knots and above through the PSSA in 2025. The data also showed that ships spent more than 6,000 hours travelling above 25 knots. It builds onprevious analysisthat found the voluntary recommendations were largely ineffective.Map of Mediterranean Sea showing the Pelagos sanctuary for whales and cetaceansIn 2022 and 2025, ferries owned by the Grimaldi Group, including Cruise Roma – at more than 250 metres, the world’s longest cruise ferry – dominated the top-20 list of vessels spending the most time at 15 knots or above in the habitat.Speeding remained concentrated among a few operators in the PSSA in 2025, with just seven vessels – four Baleària fast ferries and three Grimaldi cruise ferries – responsible for 70% of the hours spent above 25 knot. Seven Grimaldi cruise ferries amounted to about 8% of all hours recorded for all vessels at 15 knots or above in 2025.The Guardian spoke to six captains – five current and one former – who have sailed in the PSSA since its designation. The seafarers, still or previously at the helm of ships owned by Grimaldi Group and Moby Lines, say their companies have not introduced measures to encourage slow steaming after the IMO’s VSR.View image in fullscreenA Grimaldi Group ferry in the Mediterranean Sea off Italy, one of the companies found to travel above recommended speed limits.Photograph: Diriye Amey/Alamy“As long as it’s only a recommendation, nobody will reduce speed,” says one Grimaldi captain. “It would mean overhauling the whole commercial system. The ferries in the area travel at 25 [knots], especially the ones carrying tourists. They have schedules to follow.”Grimaldi and Moby Lines were contacted for comment but did not respond.Thomas Folegot, the CEO of maritime tech company Quiet-Oceans, says that while slow-moving container vessels could stand to slightly cut speeds in the PSSA, it was far more challenging for ferries: “For their business, it’s a killer. [Passengers] will fly to Corsica.”Quiet-Oceans and Oceancare’sanalysis found that80% of the journeys by merchant ships in the PSSA in 2023 were at speeds above 10 knots.Simone Panigada, president of the Tethys Research Institute and chair of a scientific committee dedicated to the conservation of cetaceans, says it is time to “move, progressively, from voluntary to mandatory” rules on reducing collision risk.“A binding framework would create more level conditions for all operators, encouraging compliance among shipping companies and ensuring the adoption of these measures doesn’t rest solely on individual corporate decisions,” he says.The International Whaling Commission (IWC) told the Guardian it has recorded six incidents since July 2023 in the PSSA: five near-miss events and one collision. It believesmost strikes go unrecorded.While the annual time spent travelling through the PSSA above the key threshold of 15 knots remained high in 2025, it represented an 11% reduction compared with 2022. The time above 25 knots also fell by about a third between 2022 and 2025.View image in fullscreenA fin whale breaks the surface – the area stretching from Valencia to Genoa, which includes the Pelagos sanctuary, is home to about two-thirds of the Mediterranean’s fin whales.Photograph: N Pierantonio/Tethys Research InstituteThese overall declines are probably caused by factors including altered shipping routes, says Olivia Watkins, associate director at Veson Nautical, who adds: “The PSSA recommendation is unlikely to be a significant cause of the year-on-year decline in the data results.”Wei-Jun Mun, director of public policy at the World Shipping Council, says the industry is committed to PSSA’s protective measures, while noting slower navigation involved “commercial trade-offs and operational concerns”, including having to add ships to a service for schedule reliability.How decoding beluga whales’ chitchat may save them – and teach us more about ourselvesRead moreA spokesperson for Corsica Ferries says the company supports Mediterranean marine megafauna research and ship-strike mitigation through measures including continuous monitoring, crew training and the development of whale alert tools. Researchers from programmes includingconservation project Life Conceptu Marismonitor wildlife using its ships, it says.The company says it instructs captains to navigate with particular caution through the PSSA, and to lower speeds to 10 to 13 knots, “while seeking to avoid possible negative impacts of reduced speeds”, including on manoeuvrability. It says its captains have reported a reduced capacity to avoid cetaceans that appear suddenly when navigating at reduced speeds.A spokesperson for Baleària says it is “committed to the conservation of marine biodiversity” and actively working to mitigate the risk of collisions, including through crew training and the use of real-time monitoring systems to allow captains to adjust speed and course where necessary. Baleària says none of its fast ferries had recorded a collision with cetaceans.Baleària adds that it participates in marine conservation programmes, including the Life Conceptu Maris and Life Intemares initiatives.This article was developed with the support of JournalismfundEuropeand in collaboration with Magma magazineExplore more on these topicsWhalesSeascape: the state of our oceansCetaceansMarine lifeShipping industryEndangered habitatsEndangered speciesWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Europe could face colder weather as polar vortex weakens | Environment | The Guardian
description: Disruption to winds above Arctic threatens to alter weather patterns across parts of continent in coming weeks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Disruption to winds above Arctic threatens to alter weather patterns across parts of continent in coming weeks
Content: Storm clouds gather over Naples. Warnings are in place for heavy rain and strong winds across southern Italy.Photograph: Ciro Fusco/EPAView image in fullscreenStorm clouds gather over Naples. Warnings are in place for heavy rain and strong winds across southern Italy.Photograph: Ciro Fusco/EPAWeather trackerEnvironmentEurope could face colder weather as polar vortex weakensDisruption to winds above Arctic threatens to alter weather patterns across parts of continent in coming weeksMatt Andrews and Morgan Thomas for MetDeskMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.50 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe stratospheric polar vortex over the northern hemisphere is facing the prospect of an unusually early weakening. Forecast models suggest it could weaken significantly over the next 10 days, when it would typically be strengthening.A major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event is possible. This could influence weather patterns in the following weeks, increasing the likelihood of persistent areas of high pressure across the mid-latitudes and colder conditions weeks later.The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air high above the Arctic. It weakens during the summer before strengthening during autumn and into winter. Its strong anticlockwise circulation helps contain the coldest air near the pole, although disturbances can allow colder air to spill southwards into the mid-latitudes.An SSW event occurs when temperatures high in the stratosphere rise rapidly, often by as much as 50C in just a few days. This is associated with a dramatic weakening, or even reversal, of the strong westerly winds surrounding the polar vortex, disrupting its circulation. The earliest recorded major SSW, occurred on 28 November 1968, after records began 1958. Current forecast models strongly favour a significant weakening of the vortex, but a complete reversal of the winds required for a major SSW remains uncertain.Such a development would mark a notable early-season disruption, with potential implications for weather patterns into early winter. The likelihood of colder, more settled conditions across northernEuropecould increase, although a spell of severe cold appears unlikely over the next two to three weeks.Meanwhile, an area of low pressure that deepened in the Mediterranean Sea last week is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to central and southernItalyon Monday, prompting warnings being issued for these areas. More than 100mm of rain is forecast to fall in just 24 hours across higher ground in southern Italy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe system is expected to move eastwards across the Ionian Sea, before making its way toGreece, which is still recovering from exceptionally wet and unsettled weather last week.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentWeather trackerItalyGreeceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Newcastle hospital told woman whose unborn baby had died to go home and ‘book a slot to give birth’ | Newcastle | The Guardian
description: Trust admits Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived had she not been sent home from RVI days earlier
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Trust admits Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived had she not been sent home from RVI days earlier
Content: Newcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS foundation trust admitted that Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived if she had not been sent home from her first admission at Royal Victoria Infirmary.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNewcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS foundation trust admitted that Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived if she had not been sent home from her first admission at Royal Victoria Infirmary.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesNewcastleNewcastle hospital told woman whose unborn baby had died to go home and ‘book a slot to give birth’Trust admits Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived had she not been sent home from RVI days earlierJosh HallidayNorth of England editorMon 2 Nov 2026 11.36 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.20 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman whose unborn baby had died was sent home from hospital with a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth.Danielle Brown, 31, was seven months pregnant when she was first discharged from hospital with pre-eclampsia, a potentially life-threatening pregnancy complication. She returned to hospital days later, when scans revealed that her daughter, Maisie, had died.Brown said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive. “When it was confirmed Maisie had died, we burst into tears. Nobody explained what had happened to Maisie,” she said.Brown, from North Shields in north-eastEngland, said she was then “given a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth”. She said: “Hearing that with no compassion angered me so much.”View image in fullscreenDanielle Brown, 31, and her partner, Anthony Miller, were delighted to be expecting a baby.Photograph: Danielle Brown/PABrown and her partner, Anthony Miller, were delighted to be expecting a baby but seven months into the pregnancy, in February 2023, she fell ill and was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia. Monitoring by doctors at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI),Newcastle, had also raised concerns about Maisie’s heart rate.A consultant obstetrician said Brown should remain in hospital until she gave birth, given her potentially life-threatening condition. However, she was discharged 24 hours later on 14 February after a review by a different consultant.A day later, Brown phoned the RVI’s maternity assessment unit with more concerns but was told she probably had a stomach bug.She insisted on being seen and returned to the hospital, waited 90 minutes to be assessed, and was told medics could not find Maisie’s heartbeat. The couple were then told that their baby had died.Instead of delivering Maisie straight away, Brown said she was handed a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth on another day,Brown spoke of her ordeal after being awarded an undisclosed settlement from Newcastle upon Tyne hospitalsNHSfoundation trust. The trust admitted a breach of duty and that Maisie would have survived had her mother not been sent home during her first admission.Faisal Ali, of the solicitors Irwin Mitchell, said pre-eclampsia was serious and required close monitoring.“What happened to Danielle and Maisie vividly highlights the human cost of care failings and how families left needing answers and access to specialist support are left trying to pick up the pieces,” he said. “Sadly, this isn’t an isolated case and we represent hundreds of families nationally affected by maternity failings.“Put simply, maternity services aren’t good enough, resulting in mums and babies being put at risk because of deep-rooted problems nationally.”The couple have since had a son, Harrison, who is two.“While we feel so blessed to have Harrison, it remains difficult knowing Maisie should be here with us too. She will always be part of our family,” Brown said. “More needs to be done not only to improve maternity care but also, when something goes wrong, families need proper and compassionate support.“After saying goodbye to Maisie, we had to walk through a labour ward seeing parents going home with their babies. That will stay with me for ever.”Ian Joy, an executive director at Newcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS foundation trust, said: “Maisie’s family have experienced a devastating loss which has undoubtedly had a profound effect on everyone who loved her.“We fully accept that aspects of the care we provided fell short of the standards the family had every right to expect and offer a heartfelt apology for this. Following a detailed review in 2023, we improved urgent assessment for women who come to our maternity services with unexpected symptoms or suspected complications.”The trust had recently been assessed as performing well against national standards, Joy said.Explore more on these topicsNewcastleHospitalsNHSTyne and WearNorth of EnglandEnglandHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour to end cooperation with Greens in 11 councils over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy | Green party | The Guardian
description: Deals with six Green council groups that have condemned the motion are to remain in place, says Labour
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Deals with six Green council groups that have condemned the motion are to remain in place, says Labour
Content: The Greens have said they are ‘hugely disappointed’ at the move, saying it will result in worse outcomes for residents.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Greens have said they are ‘hugely disappointed’ at the move, saying it will result in worse outcomes for residents.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAGreen partyLabour to end cooperation with Greens in 11 councils over ‘Zionism is racism’ policyDeals with six Green council groups that have condemned the motion are to remain in place, says LabourUK politics live – latest updatesPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 10.31 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.20 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLabour is to stop cooperating with the Green party in 11 councils across England followingan ultimatumfor Greens in local government to disown a new policy stating that “Zionism is racism”.A statement from Labour said coalitions or other deals with Greens would stop in all local authorities where they had refused to condemn the policy motionpassed at their party conferencelast month, which also called for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.Cooperation would cease on Arun, Derbyshire Dales, Havant, Lewes, Sheffield, Stafford, Warwick, Wealden, West Devon and West Suffolk councils,Laboursaid, and had already stopped in Runnymede because of the motion.According to Labour, six Green council groups have condemned the motion, meaning deals will remain in place in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire, West Sussex. The same, it said, had happened with the West of England mayoralty, where the mayor is from Labour and the deputy mayor is a Green.Home secretary Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules – UK politics liveRead moreBridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said the party had been clear that the motion, which has been met with unease by some Greens and has facedsignificant outside condemnation, “crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government”.The Greens said they were “hugely disappointed” at the move, saying it would result in worse outcomes for residents in affected areas.Phillipson said just over a fortnight ago that any Labour groups working with Green party politicians should review their agreements and end them unless they reject the motion, whichAndy Burnham called “antisemitic”.Some Greens, including the party’s former co-leader Adrian Ramsay,had calledon local parties to renounce the policy, a stance that put him at odds with Zack Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales. The party’s official response was that the Greens would “not take lectures” from a Labour government that supplies arms to Israel.The policy equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.The Equality and Human Rights Commission has written to the Greens to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”.Phillipson said: “Any local power-sharing arrangement cannot come at the expense of upholding the moral obligation we have to stand up for everyone in our communities and the values we share.“We are pleased that some local Green parties have rightly opted to disavow this policy and have called on their party’s leadership to do the same. It is disappointing that some local Green parties have not met the conditions Labour has set out. Labour continues to oppose this divisive policy and calls on theGreen partyto do the right thing and rescind it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe added: “The Labour party fought hard to root out antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics.”In a joint statement, the Greens and the Local Government Association Green group said they were “hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents”.They added: “Across the country, Green, Labour, independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change. Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.“Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power-sharing agreements have often ignored the judgments of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.”Under the party’s direct democracy rules, policy is decided by party members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, equating to approximately 0.4% of the total membership. It has been criticised by four of the Greens’ five MPs, as well as the former MP and party leader Caroline Lucas.On Sunday,Ramsay saidthe Greens must fix their internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyLabourLocal politicsBridget PhillipsonAntisemitismLocal governmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trial of nine men accused of abusing woman drugged and raped by husband begins | UK news | The Guardian
description: The husband, who cannot be named to protect his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences spanning more than two decades
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: The husband, who cannot be named to protect his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences spanning more than two decades
Content: The case is being heard at Manchester Minshull Street crown court.Photograph: Ian Nellist/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe case is being heard at Manchester Minshull Street crown court.Photograph: Ian Nellist/AlamyUK newsTrial of nine men accused of abusing woman drugged and raped by husband beginsThe husband, who cannot be named to protect his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences carried out at the couple’s Stockport homeHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 12.56 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.10 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNine men have gone on trial accused of being involved in the abuse of a woman who was drugged, raped and sexually assaulted by her husband while he “lived a double life masked in respectability”.The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences against his wife spanning more than two decades.The offences involving the nine men on trial, who the prosecution say “were [also] leading double lives”, are alleged to have taken place between 2015 and the husband’s arrest in 2025.Two of the men, Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent and David Graves, 59, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire, were described in court as “non-contact offenders”, who are alleged to have encouraged the abuse online.The other seven were described as “contact offenders”, who are alleged to have visited the couple’s home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, and participated in the abuse of the victim.They are Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; and Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester.Three other men, Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee; and Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire, have already admitted to abusing the woman at previous hearings at Manchester Minshull Street crown court.Last week, Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset also pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences at a hearing at the same court on Friday.Opening the crown’s case, prosecutor Louise Oakley KC said: “Unbeknownst to [the victim], for over 20 years, her husband had been abusing her sexually in a variety of ways whilst she was asleep or was unconscious.”Oakley said he had done so “initially taking advantage of occasions when she had drunk enough alcohol herself to put her into a deep sleep, but also on many more occasions, more and more frequently, over that 20-year period, deliberately using a cocktail of stupefying drugs, which he administered to her without her knowledge, with or without alcohol”.Oakley said that “from 2023 onwards at the latest, though he had been talking about it for much longer, [the husband] began actively inviting other men round to their home, and, whilst his wife lay unconscious in their bed, he filmed himself and others raping and sexually abusing her”.“They were well aware, the prosecution say, that [she] was not conscious, that is why they were there, to use her body whilst she was unaware, just as [her husband] had been doing over the preceding years.”Oakley said the men “derived sexual gratification and enjoyment from knowing” that the victim was “unaware” or “out of it”.The victim “had absolutely no idea it was going on”, Oakley said, “that is, until the police came round to her door and identified to her that she had been the subject of the videos” her husband had taken.As the prosecution set out their case in court, a relative of the victim, who was in the courtroom, cried and held their head in their hands, as they were comforted by two companions.Oakley said that while during the course of the trial it maybe be suggested that the victim was “in fact only pretending to be asleep or unconscious as part of a fantasy role play with her husband … the prosecution says that is a smokescreen”.“What these men did”, Oakley said, “was not participation in unconventional, but consensual sexual practices: in this case it was rape and sexual assault, pure and simple.”The court heard that the husband’s offending was discovered after undercover journalists infiltrated a chat on the Telegram messaging platform. He was arrested and his mobile phone was seized.“That telephone was like a confession booth,” Oakley said, adding that it “contained decades’ worth of material” from other devices and cameras.“That description cannot be underestimated,” she said. “It contained [the husband’s] darkest secrets and the barbaric sexual fantasies that he had sought to fulfil going back in time to 2004.”She said the mobile phone contained “over a million photographs and videos, cataloguing not only his abuse of [his wife] but abuse committed by others on her, including those in the dock today”.Oakley said the husband had “lived a double life masked in respectability” and that the nine men on trial were also “leading double lives”.They were, she said, “either creeping in and out of [the marital home] in the hours of darkness, quietly and carefully so that they weren’t seen or heard, or hiding behind the screens of their mobile telephones and computers. No doubt believing they were safe.”The men deny all of the charges against them. The trial at Minshull Street crown court continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Driver who dragged cyclist under his car jailed for life for murder | Greater Manchester | The Guardian
description: Simon Richardson hit Michael Mullins, dragged him for more than a mile under his Volvo XC90, and ran him over
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Simon Richardson hit Michael Mullins, dragged him for more than a mile under his Volvo XC90, and ran him over
Content: Simon Richardson was caught on camera in his Volvo XC90 after hitting Michael Mullins.Photograph: CPS/PAView image in fullscreenSimon Richardson was caught on camera in his Volvo XC90 after hitting Michael Mullins.Photograph: CPS/PAGreater ManchesterDriver who dragged cyclist under his car jailed for life for murderSimon Richardson hit Michael Mullins, dragged him for more than a mile under his Volvo XC90, and ran him overMark BrownNorth of England correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 10.43 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 14.18 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA driver who ploughed into a headteacher who was cycling home from school and dragged him, trapped under his car, for more than a mile has been jailed for life.Simon Richardson, who ignored give-way signs at a junction before the collision, was told he must serve a minimum of 25 years after a jury last weekfound him guilty of murder.His victim, Michael Mullins, 56, was remembered by his family as their “anchor”. His wife said her life had been “brutally and callously torn apart”.Jailing Richardson, 35, on Monday, Mrs Justice Brunner KC said the defendant had shown an “astonishing degree of disregard for human life”.She said: “For every moment you carried on, you were knowingly using your heavy vehicle to cause serious injury to a man who was trapped, injured and completely helpless as a result of your actions.“You did that because you decided escaping from the scene of an accident was more important than a human life.”View image in fullscreenMichael Mullins, 56, was cycling home from Stretford grammar school in Greater Manchester, where he was the headteacher, when he was struck by a Volvo XC90 driven by Simon Richardson.Photograph: GMP/PAMullins was cycling home from Stretford grammar school on the evening of 20 April when the 4x4 Richardson was driving crashed into him. He hit the bonnet and windscreen of Richardson’s Volvo XC90 and then went under it, becoming entangled in the suspension.Richardson continued to drive for more than a mile, knowing that the trapped cyclist was just inches under his feet, a trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court heard.View image in fullscreenSimon Richardson, 35, has been jailed for life.Photograph: GMP/PARichardson had denied knowing the father of two was under his car but the prosecutor Phil Barnes KC said the defendant knew, “and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway”.Richardson’s front-seat passenger, his cousin Gabrielle Debotte, told the trial they had both heard “moaning” from outside as he drove away from the collision scene. Giving evidence for the prosecution, she said Richardson went on to say: “He’s under the car.”The collision happened in the village of Warburton in Trafford,Greater Manchester. The court heard Richardson, of no fixed address, drove to a secluded farm track in Lymm, 1.3 miles away, in an attempt to dislodge Mullins.After he stopped, Richardson twice tried to pull Mullins out, before returning to the car and driving sharply and deliberately from side to side before mounting a grass verge, the court heard. Mullins was finally released but was then driven over again as Richardson reversed and drove away.A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood from the collision spot and discovered Mullins alone and barely breathing on the grass verge, the court heard. Emergency services attended but were unable to save Mullins, from Northwich,Cheshire, who died from multiple injuries.Members of Mullins’s family were in tears when the jury delivered its verdict.Addressing the court on Monday Mullins’s wife, Sarah, spoke of an “all-consuming lethargy that makes it feel difficult to put one foot in front of another” since his death.She said: “My past, present and future have been brutally and callously torn apart, my present is empty and often seems to be without purpose.“The fact that Michael had to endure such a violent and painful death is an open wound that refuses to heal. I am, we are, completely adrift and bereft without our anchor, Michael Mullins.”View image in fullscreenMichael Mullins was ‘beloved in his community, his school, by his family and friends’.Photograph: GMP/PAThe acting head of Stretford grammar school, Elizabeth Baxter, said it had been an “honour and a privilege” to work alongside Mullins, who led the school for 17 years. Describing him as an inspirational leader, she said: “He has left a void and a gulf at every level of our school.”Barnes told the court Richardson had previous convictions for 28 offences, with a “significant history” of driving-related crimes including careless driving and failure to stop or report an accident in 2011, driving with excess alcohol and driving whilst disqualified in 2012, and driving whilst disqualified and uninsured in 2013. In 2023, he had been convicted of driving without a licence and insurance.Det Ch Insp Louise Edwards, of Greater Manchester police, said Richardson chose to “take Michael’s life in one of the most horrific ways I have ever seen”.She said his family should be “proud of the courage they have shown” and added: “Do not remember the offender who has been found guilty of his murder.“Remember Michael – beloved in his community, his school, by his family and friends – a man who should have come home safe and sound to his family but will be remembered forever in the legacy he has left behind.”Explore more on these topicsGreater ManchesterCheshireCrimeNorth of EnglandSentencingEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests | Schools | The Guardian
description: Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Content: Police prevent students from blockading the Lycée Charlemagne in Paris during protests over school conditions.Photograph: Eric Baradat/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice prevent students from blockading the Lycée Charlemagne in Paris during protests over school conditions.Photograph: Eric Baradat/ReutersSchoolsFrench pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protestsMinister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on ThursdayAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 2 Nov 2026 13.17 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.54 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests overschool conditionsand the high cost of living.The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end thelycée blockades, which have been running since September and have promptedone of the biggest protest movements and social crisesof his presidency.From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demandingmore replacement teachers and repairs to buildingsbarricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.View image in fullscreenStudents gather outside a blockaded high school in Paris to protest against a lack of resources.Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/APUniversity students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities acrossFranceto support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.He saidmeasures offered by the government last weekto cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA protester adds a bin to a fire outside the Montebello international high school in Lille.Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty ImagesIn Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.The education ministry said 41 high schools were blocked across France – around 1% of the nationwide total. Students’ unions put the figure at 150.Nicolas Bonnet, of the headteachers’ union SNPDEN-UNSA, said: “It’s time for us to return to our job: teaching and supporting pupils.” He warned that coursework, final-year exams and university applications were at risk.He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said he would meet school students’ unions again next week.Explore more on these topicsSchoolsStudentsProtestFranceEuropeStudent politicsHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists  | Palaeontology | The Guardian
description: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body
Content: Prof Kliti Grice with the fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus, a dinosaur that lived in Brazil 115m years ago.Photograph: Curtin UniversityView image in fullscreenProf Kliti Grice with the fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus, a dinosaur that lived in Brazil 115m years ago.Photograph: Curtin UniversityPalaeontologyFossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientistsChemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around bodyIan SampleScience editorMon 2 Nov 2026 15.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-easternBrazil115m years ago.Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.View image in fullscreenA portion the Aratasaurus’s hind limb. The remains were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil.Photograph: Curtin UniversityIf the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears inProceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants ofblood vessels and soft tissuesin dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.Explore more on these topicsPalaeontologyBrazilFossilsAmericasEvolutionBiologyDinosaursnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past | Hungary | The Guardian
description: From 1945 to 1989 security police relied on tens of thousands of spies to suppress dissent. To rebuild trust, their files will finally be made public
Author: Lili Rutai
Headline: From 1945 to 1989 security police relied on tens of thousands of spies to suppress dissent. To rebuild trust, their files will finally be made public
