Content: An installation in City Hall Park in Budapest shows the toppling of Stalin set against a building projected with wartime ruins.Photograph: Marton Kovacs/EPAView image in fullscreenAn installation in City Hall Park in Budapest shows the toppling of Stalin set against a building projected with wartime ruins.Photograph: Marton Kovacs/EPAHungary‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront pastFrom 1945 to 1989 security police relied on tens of thousands of spies to suppress dissent. To rebuild trust, their files will finally be made publicLili Rutaiin BudapestMon 2 Nov 2026 02.09 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust.From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages.For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks.View image in fullscreenThe ‘agent files’ in the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security in Budapest remained largely inaccessible to the public for decades.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersDuring his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections,Péter Magyarpromised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power.In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.“A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook.Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say.View image in fullscreenPéter Magyar promised during his election campaign to make the files public.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty“We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives.Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956Read more“As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today.For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018.Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now.“People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?”View image in fullscreenZoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, posted on Facebook that ‘a democratic society had the right to know its past’.Photograph: János Kummer/GettyPlaced side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material.Many of the records will be incomplete, as the agent’s motivation, or extent of reporting, will remain unknown. Of the 60,000 people mentioned in the files, the archives include detailed files, background checks and statements for only 9,000 people. These will be released in February, after personal information, including details of health, addictions and sexuality, as well as information about victims, has been redacted in accordance with privacy laws.Alexander Faludy, a freelance journalist and Anglican priest, read the files on his family almost two decades ago. His grandfather, György Faludy, spent more than three years in a Hungarian labour camp on fabricated accusations, and later while in exile wrote his book, My Happy Days in Hell.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFerenc Pallagi and József Horváth, former Hungarian security service generals, appear in court in 1991 in Budapest charged with illegally spying on politicians.Photograph: László Balogh/ReutersOne report in the files, by a Hungarian woman living in London who befriended Faludy’s grandmother as she was dying of cancer, made him particularly angry. “But then, I looked at the details of the informant. There was a really ominous part in her file, with names of relatives living in Hungary, including details of her elderly parents. Suddenly, my anger evaporated. I just felt very sorry for her,” Faludy said.“Exile was very painful for my family, but it also conferred certain moral luxuries. And that makes me hesitant in terms of passing judgment on people for what they did if they had to stay in Hungary,” he added.The identities of secret-service agents have long fascinated Hungarians. Since the 2000s, several partial lists have emerged, naming politicians and prominent artists. Many of them denied involvement, but the allegations alone were enough to plunge governments into political crises.To date, not many former agents have spoken publicly about their experiences, and the subject remains taboo.In July, Szemlélek, an independent, religious online journal, published a call for former agents to come forward. Religious figures were a known target of the state services and they were often blackmailed into reporting on their congregation. According to some estimates,7-10% of themcooperated with the state.So far, no one has volunteered to tell their story. “I think many people feel that there isn’t really much to speak about,” the paper’s editor-in-chief, Szilárd Szőnyi, told the Guardian. “Or they think that their story is so complex that they cannot, do not want to, or are not ready to tell it.”View image in fullscreenAn archivist working in the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security in Budapest.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersDomokos Szokolay, a historian, said he was hopeful that this time “the release won’t turn into a public shaming, but that people will understand that these are complex issues”. His father, Zoltán Szokolay, a poet and politician, was outed as an informant in an unofficial list published in 2005.Szokolay has yet to read all the reports on his father, who died in 2020. By speaking openly about transgenerational trauma, he hopes to reassure others who discover their loved ones were agents that they are not alone, and to encourage them to start conversations about what they find.“There are so many family secrets or traumas that we can already talk about: if someone’s parent is an alcoholic, or a gambling addict. But people worry that they will be judged based on the agent files,” he said. “I know confronting one’s family history can be scary or even painful. But learning about it is always better.”Explore more on these topicsHungaryCold warSurveillanceEspionagePéter MagyarSocial historyEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition | Israel | The Guardian
description: Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
Content: Yousef Jabareen: ‘If [Gadi] Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally.’Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYousef Jabareen: ‘If [Gadi] Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally.’Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelIsrael has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalitionYousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in KnessetJulian Borgerin Umm al-FahmMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 10.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oustBenjamin Netanyahuand his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more thandoubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particularits most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.Chart showing projected seats in the KnessetNetanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli electionRead moreEisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”Yousef Jabareen: ‘I hope we can find partners to make to make this change real’Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister hasalready made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in theresumption of war on Iranas a pretext for putting off political transition.“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”This article was amended on 2 November 2026. An earlier version said that one of Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot’s conditions for a potential coalition partnership with Arab parties was to “accept conscription”. In fact, the condition is to accept compulsory national service, which could be civil or military.Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple posts stronger-than-expected revenue in first earnings report for new CEO John Ternus | Apple | The Guardian
description: Result for the company, which earned $30.71bn and exceeded analysts’ expectations, bucked downward trend for tech firms
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Result for the company, which earned $30.71bn and exceeded analysts’ expectations, bucked downward trend for tech firms
Content: Customers browsing Apple products at a store in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCustomers browsing Apple products at a store in Hong Kong.Photograph: May James/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockAppleApple posts stronger-than-expected revenue in first earnings report for new CEO John TernusResult for the company, which earned $30.71bn and exceeded analysts’ expectations, bucked downward trend for tech firmsAssociated PressMon 2 Nov 2026 18.07 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple Inc posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal third quarter, giving John Ternus, the new CEO, an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech giants this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results.“Apple’s strong earnings come in the wake of a recent tech sell-off, as investors question the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom driven by Apple’s big tech counterparts,” said Jacob Bourne, an Emarketer analyst, adding that record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrate the resilience of Apple’s business.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGoogle owner Alphabet loses $500bn in market value after profit disappoints Wall StreetRead moreThe Cupertino, California-based company earned $30.71bn, or $2.10 a share, in the July-September period. That’s up 12% from $27.47bn, or $1.85 a share, in the same period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included five cents a share from tariff refunds.Revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn from $102.5bn.Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 a share on revenue of $113.4bn, according to a poll by FactSet.While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over huge investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple’s “tepid approach” to AI infrastructure spending helps preserve its cash flow – while partnerships with companies such as Alphabet could help Apple strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.Explore more on these topicsAppleQuarterly resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Control of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startup | Smart meters | The Guardian
description: The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays
Content: The smart meter rollout has faced ‘serious reputational obstacles’, leading to three in 10 households still not having one.Photograph: Alamy/PAView image in fullscreenThe smart meter rollout has faced ‘serious reputational obstacles’, leading to three in 10 households still not having one.Photograph: Alamy/PASmart metersControl of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startupThe handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delaysJillian AmbroseMon 2 Nov 2026 13.13 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.26 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleControl over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network.The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week.The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence granted to Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, to set up the country’s first smart meter data network, a process that has beendogged by costly delays while millions of households faced billing issues.Industry sources said Capita’s subsidiary was effectively blocked from tendering for a new licence to manage the smart meter network after Whitehall officials decided to replace the commercial framework established in 2013 with a not-for-profit public-interest model governed by an independent board.Instead, the network underpinning Britain’s smart meters will become a wholly owned subsidiary of the SmartEnergyCode Company (SECCo) with “a greater focus on cost, transparency and customer and consumer needs”, the new operator said.Its board will include veteran energy and telecoms industry executives as well as Dame Gillian Guy, the former chief executive of Citizens Advice, which claimed in 2024 that households hadbeen “let down” by the rolloutbecause almost a third of smart meters weren’t working properly.Ministers had initially hoped that all households would have a smart meter before 2020 to help modernise Britain’s outdated energy system and make better use of renewable energy andinnovative data-led energy tariffs.But the rollout has faced“serious reputational obstacles”, according to the government’s spending watchdog, which meant that three in 10 households still do not have a meter and another £1.7bn may be required to complete the rollout.The tender process for a new smart network operator ran last summer, at around the same time that the industry regulator opened an investigation into Smart DCC’s procurement contracts, which included deals that were awarded without a competitive process and one which was granted to its parent company, Capita.Smart DCC agreed in July to pay £200,000 into a consumer redress fund, in the same week that its parent company was forced to apologise for its role in administering the crisis-hit Civil Service Pension Scheme, which kept thousands ofretired civil servantswaiting for payments.Capita’s market value has plunged by 97% in the last decade after the outsourcing company once in charge of administering a string of government schemes revealed severely strained finances and mounting debts before undertaking an emergency restructuring of the business.A Capita spokesperson said: “Capita is proud of its 13-year stewardship of DCC. What began as an ambitious programme is now critical national infrastructure, connecting more than 39.2m smart meters across 23m homes and small businesses, with network availability of 99.6%.“We hand over a secure and resilient network that millions of consumers rely on every day and have been working with stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition to DCC’s next chapter.”A spokesperson for Ofgem said Smart DCC had “played a critical role” in delivering “an efficient and secure digital communication structure”, and that the new licence holder would be expected to “build on that solid foundation”.Explore more on these topicsSmart metersEnergy billsConsumer affairsHousehold billsEnergyEnergy efficiencyEthical and green livingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Content: The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersOilOil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran warBrent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeksGraeme WeardenMon 2 Nov 2026 12.14 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.37 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end theIranwar.Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.Over the weekend,Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break inthe inflationary pressures gripping the global economy.Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranShipping industryIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Millions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise looms | Mortgage rates | The Guardian
description: More than 2.3m households face jump in payments in 2027, after expected increase in Bank of England rate this week
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: More than 2.3m households face jump in payments in 2027, after expected increase in Bank of England rate this week
Content: The Bank of England’s base rate has not changed since December last year.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Bank of England’s base rate has not changed since December last year.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockMortgage ratesMillions in UK brace to remortgage on worse deals as rate rise loomsMore than 2.3m households face jump in payments in 2027, after expected increase in Bank of England rate this weekKalyeena MakortoffandHeather StewartMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 10.42 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 2.3m UK households face a sharp rise in mortgage payments as they come off fixed-rate deals in 2027, with theBank of Englandexpected to begin raising interest rates this week.The Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) is widely expected to increase the base rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November afterUK inflation rose further to 3.5%in September.It could be the first of four quarter-point rises over the next 12 months, according to financial market expectations, which would exacerbate the financial pressure on households grappling with higher energy and food bills.Thousands of borrowers are due to come off fixed contracts in the final months of this year, with 700,000 having been forecast to switch over to new rates between July and December.A further 2.3m households will reach the end of their fixed rates next year, according to data collected by UK Finance, a banking industry body.There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets – triggered in part by energy prices and inflation fears linked to the war in the Middle East – has driven up theswap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.An increase in the Bank of England rate could drive those rates, and wider household costs, even higher.Data released last week showed that mortgage approvals in the UK fell to a near three-year low in September as potential buyers were deterred by the jump in borrowing costs.Alongside last week’s budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) warned that householddisposable incomes would fall by 0.6% next yearafter taking account of inflation. The downgrade compares with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes the watchdog had forecast in March – an outlook the OBR’s David Miles described as “a pretty grim picture”.That income squeeze is also being driven by the energy price shock, which the OBR said would push consumer inflation to 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.Ofgem’s energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to rise by more than £400 in January,according to the latest forecast from EDF.John Healey, the chancellor, made a £100 payout to 20m householdsthe centrepiece of his budget, saying he wanted to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”.His cost of living package – which also included cancelling fuel duty rises planned by Rachel Reeves and extending a VAT cut on electricity bills – was paid for by tax rises on banks, savers and landlords.The Bank of England has taken a wait-and-see approach to rising inflation since the start of the Iran war, in contrast to other central banks, including the US Federal Reserve, Bank of Japan and European Central Bank, which have already raised borrowing costs this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAndrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, has made clear that the MPC is watching closely to see if rising prices are being passed through into higher wages for workers – evidence of the so-called “second-round effects” that can lead to inflation becoming embedded.Before the war in the Middle East, the Bank had been expected to cut interest rates several times this year, with inflation expected to drift back down towards its 2% target.But an extended period of historically high oil prices, affected by the closure of the strait of Hormuz choking off supplies, has instead fed through into high and rising inflation.The Bank will publish updated forecasts for economic growth and inflation alongside its interest rate decision this week.The UK economy beat expectations to be the joint fastest-growing in the G7 in the first half of 2026, which the Office for National Statistics said was partly driven by AI-related sectors.But official forecasts for next year have been cut sharply amid fears that the higher cost of energy will eventually start to weigh on economic growth.Although money market pricing suggests the Bank will raise interest rates four times by next July, many City economistssuggest two rate rises are more likely.Explore more on these topicsMortgage ratesInterest ratesBank of EnglandInflationOffice for Budget ResponsibilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama | Movies | The Guardian
description: Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say
Author: Craig McLean
Headline: Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say
Content: Balancing act … Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney.Photograph: BBC/Hilltop ScreenView image in fullscreenBalancing act … Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney.Photograph: BBC/Hilltop ScreenMoviesInterview‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s dramaCraig McLeanWritten by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they sayMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhead of production on their first job together, Rhys Ifans andLaura Linneydidn’t undergo the standard “chemistry read” to make sure they got on. Which is remarkable, given what their characters would have to do to each other in Onwards and Sideways.In the Norfolk-set BBC film directed by John Madden (Shakespeare in Love), Ifans would have to nearly throttle Linney while in the grip of night terrors, she’d have to collapse in his arms in a weeping mess having bankrupted herself with a gambling addiction; both situations arising from the neurological condition afflicting their characters: Parkinson’s disease.But despite being thrown into the deep end in this hugely emotional, often hilarious film, both actors acknowledge an immediate feeling of safety around each other as they embarked on a project that would require them to strip themselves bare. “It’s odd,” says Ifans, “you learn so much about each other so quickly. I couldn’t tell you what kind of car Laura drives. What her home looks like. But we both know how we feel about death and dying.”Linney, 62, is a triple-Oscar-nominated star with a diverse array of roles on her CV, from her breakthrough in The Truman Show (1998) onwards through Clint Eastwood’s Mystic River and Richard Curtis’s Love Actually (both 2003), then the TV series Ozark and The Big C. Ifans, 59, franklyburstthrough in 1997’s Twin Town, AKA the “Welsh Trainspotting”, and went on to play Hugh Grant’s scraggly flatmate Spike in Curtis’s Notting Hill (1999), Daniel Craig’s stalker in Enduring Love (2004) and drug smuggler Howard Marks in Mr Nice (2010).Divergent backgrounds, then. But equally time-served, too. So the actors were able to dive in, no chemistry read required. They did, though, do dance classes. They waltzed together in London, and separately nearer their respective homes, the better to understand one popular form of recreational therapy for people with Parkinson’s. In Brooklyn, Linney was introduced to David Leventhal at the Mark Morris Dance Group. He runs a programme there called Dance for PD.“That’s the mothership of this wonderful organisation that now has offshoots all over the world, including here,” the New Yorker says when she, Ifans and I meet in the central London offices of the producers behind Onwards and Sideways. Both are dressed casually and low-key, each clearly easy in the other’s company, their conversation frequently erupting into gales of laughter.View image in fullscreenIfans and Linney in Onwards and Sideways.Photograph: Jonathan Birch/BBC“I spoke with David for a long time – and then I learned that Juilliard has classes for this once a week,” Linney says of the acting school that’s her alma mater. “So I just started hanging out there. It’s incredibly moving what the arts will do,” she says – in this case, how dance and music could relax people grappling with a condition that, among its 40-plus symptoms, causes uncontrollable shaking, stiffness of gait and involuntary freezing in doorways and thresholds. “How brave it makes people. How it opens up the imagination, and then the body follows somehow, when it shouldn’t. And the difference between someone moving in a dance class and then, when the music stops, to see what happens to their bodies – it’s shattering in a good and a sad way. So … it gets right to the bone of things.”Ifans, meanwhile, attended weekly sessions with a group who meet in Pontio, an “arts and innovation centre” in Bangor, north-west Wales. “There was a harpist accompanying the dance,” says the Pembrokeshire native. “Then there was a support dog running around the room who happened to be a sheepdog.”“Herding!” adds Linney, laughing.“It was peak Welshness!” acknowledges Ifans, to hoots all round. Then, quietly again: “They were so inspiring, these classes. And a great leveller. You’d be sitting next to a nuclear scientist and a school cleaner. Both dancing to the same tune and wrestling with the same diagnosis.”The writer of Onwards and Sideways is Paul Mayhew-Archer. He’s an actor, writer – he co-created The Vicar of Dibley with Richard Curtis – and accidental activist. The 73-year-old is a founder member of the Movers and Shakers podcast, which raises both awareness and laughs, alongside fellow “Parky people”, including journalists Jeremy Paxman and Mark Mardell. He was diagnosed with the disease at 58, with the canary in the coalmine, symptoms-wise, being that “my handwriting was very small and unclear”.His experiences directly inform the experiences of the fiftysomething characters played by Ifans (Tony, a teacher) and Linney (Emma, a musician). They also, full disclosure, inform my writing of this feature: my dad has Parkinson’s and I’m in the age bracket Mayhew-Archer was when he was diagnosed. My handwriting is appalling.View image in fullscreenLove is the drug … Linney with Jason Bateman in Ozark.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTrue to Mayhew-Archer’s mission, Onwards and Sideways is painfully, honestly funny. The scene where Rory Kinnear’s doctor rather cavalierly informs Tony that he has the condition features a joke lifted from Mayhew-Archer’s own diagnosis.“My neurologist told me one of the symptoms is the difficulty of smiling, and that I seemed to have difficulty smiling,” Mayhew-Archer relates to me when we meet on another day in the same office. “And I said: ‘Well, that could be because you just told me I’ve got Parkinson’s.’ As soon as I said that, I knew I wanted to be funny about Parkinson’s, because I saw no point in being serious.”double quotation markThere’s a mercurial element to this illness – it’s bespoke. No one has the same Parkinson’sIfans – who’s been staunchly committed to this project for the duration of its lengthy gestation, stretching back pre-Covid – seconds that emotion. “I loved the way Paul’s story about a life-changing diagnosis was handled, funny and devastating all at once. My attraction to it was also that I have friends and family who’ve been impacted by Parkinson’s. That gave me a fast track into the telling of a story like this.”“You don’t have to scratch very far to find someone somewhere who knows someone who has Parkinson’s,” echoes Linney of a condition that, in the UK, 166,000 people are living with, with one person being diagnosed every 20 minutes according to Parkinson’s UK. “I certainly have friends who do.”To “act” Parkinson’s, Ifans and Linney were aided by the Neuro Heroes, “remarkable women who do physio for people with Parkinson’s and various related conditions”, says Linney. “They helped us with our basic understanding of Parkinson’s, and then also the physicalisation. [Because there’s] a mercurial element to this condition – it’s bespoke. No one has the same Parkinson’s.” Or even the same side-effects from the drugs prescribed to help manage the incurable condition: they can cause increased libido, appetite, and compulsive spending and gambling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThrones is where the heart is … Ifans in House of the Dragon.Photograph: HBO“Parkinson’s was like a physical dialect for us,” continues Ifans. “We had to learn its physical language. They [the Neuro Heroes] could say what was happening at the muscular level, or the skeletal impact, of Parkinson’s. But we needed poetry to understand what that felt like. Whether it felt like moving through tar or sand. Just to be able to arrive at an image that you could apply to the body, that you could take with you to set each day, to help you achieve the shapes and positions that Parkinson’s puts people in.”And those people, ultimately, were always in the actors’ minds. Mayhew-Archer knew the film had to honour those with the condition, but that that noble aim did have its bluntly practical limits. “We knew we couldn’t cast people with Parkinson’s in those two central roles,” he says. “Partly because Laura’s character has [a medical procedure] done which means she stops doing certain things. And it would be very hard for people with Parkinson’s to stop doing some things!” he adds with a laugh. “Once you start freezing, you can’t stop!”“We had the added responsibility in getting Parkinson’s right,” says Ifans. “Not just right, but bang-on. Because there’s a whole demographic watching that deserves to be represented. That was the scary bit, wasn’t it?”Linney, staring intently at her co-star across the table, nods. It was, she says, fundamentally about “doing it justice”. And then, “the possibility of failing at that?” says Ifans. “Huge responsibility. That brought us closer together. That’s the stuff that woke us up at night.”When we meet, Linney is about to be unveiled as one of the cast of DC superhero TV series Lanterns. She’s a Guardian of the Universe, “or so I’ve been told”, she says with spoiler-savvy diplomacy. “But a green beam might come down and evaporate me if I utter a word!” She’s also two weeks into filming, alongside Colin Firth and Julianne Moore, Comfort and Joy (formerly The Joy of Sex), a romcom about the north London throuple who helped produce Alex Comfort’s groundbreaking 1972 illustrated sex manual. So, another unconventional midlife drama but lighter, certainly, than Onwards and Sideways.“There was something about this world of Parkinson’s that forced me to be very present in a way that I normally am not, particularly while working,” she admits. “It forced me to be over my skis a bit. And off-balance, and vulnerable, and experiencing things in very different ways. “This movie rearranged my cellular structure!” she adds, beaming in gratitude. “Most movies don’t do that. I love my work. But very few experiences have literally rearranged my soul. This one certainly did.”As for Ifans, this year we’ve seen him alongside Anna Maxwell Martin in Apple TV’s cold war-era sci-fi thriller Star City. When I meet him, he’s just been beheaded on House of the Dragon. Onwards and Sideways, in stark contrast, is acting in the raw, with no high-concept narrative or CGI to hide behind. Acting of a different order.“Yes. You can have spaceships, lunar landscapes, swords and castles, but you ain’t gonna have a co-star like this,” Ifans says, beaming at Linney. “That’s where the money is. Not the coin … That’s why we go to work. As Laura says: all these [roles] are different and thrilling and enjoyable in their own way. But this film is particularly nourishing.”Having seen Onwards and Sideways in the company of my mum, who cares 24/7 for my dad, I couldn’t agree more. We watched it bathed in both tears and smiles. It’s a beautiful achievement; empowering, educational entertainment, and Ifans and Linney deserve all the credit in the world for how they’ve portrayed the multiverse of Parkinson’s. I would send them a personal note to thank them for what they’ve done for those with, and connected with, the disease. But I’m not sure they’d be able to read my handwriting.Onwards and Sideways is inUKcinemas from 6 November, and on BBC One and iPlayer later this year.Explore more on these topicsFilmRhys IfansLaura LinneyDrama filmsParkinson's diseasefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: One in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting again | Movies | The Guardian
description: Following a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformed
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Following a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformed
Content: Superb … Syrian refugee Israa in One in a Million.Photograph: Keo Films/Jack MacInnesView image in fullscreenSuperb … Syrian refugee Israa in One in a Million.Photograph: Keo Films/Jack MacInnesMoviesReviewOne in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting againFollowing a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformedPhil HoadMon 2 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a startling moment in this BBC refugee documentary when Syrian mother Nisreen – in the apparently miserable situation of hiking across the Balkans towardsGermany, four kids in tow – suddenly explodes with joy. “This is the best holiday I’ve ever had! It’s an amazing adventure. Now I have the chance to walk in the rain – I love it!” Shunted off early into an arranged marriage, never having left Syria until forced out of Aleppo by the civil war, for Nisreen this running jump into the unknown represents total liberation.Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ superb, forthright and highly moving film bypasses the usual refugee dichotomies, that they’re either external threats or history’s victims. Instead of flat abstractions, we get the knotty reality. Focused over a 10-year period from 2015 to 2025 principally on Nisreen’s eldest daughter Israa, it presents an intimate chronicle of how geographical displacement and cultural dislocation reshape families and lives from the inside.Eleven years old in the Turkish city of Izmir, Israa is a quick-smiling street vendor waiting to cross the Aegean; cheery despite the upheaval because of seemingly unbreakable family solidarity. Just a few years later in Cologne, she is a Justin Bieber-worshipping, football-playing teenager who lauds democracy for giving her the freedom to do whatever she wants. Which is increasingly too much for her dad, Tarek, who approves of change “with limits” – so is unaware of her secret boyfriend. He puts his foot down when Israa and Nisreen apply makeup in front of the film-makers’ cameras on the latter’s birthday. Israa is distraught. But soon he has no one to control; Nisreen, who has fanatically embraced western feminism, kicks him out of the house.It’s a wrenchingly immediate demonstration of the neglected flip side to discussions of how immigrants alter host countries – and how the immigrants themselves are also changed in the process. Through the young man who becomes her husband, Israa slowly comes to a rapprochement with her Syrian and Muslim identity – and finally makes an Ithacan return to Aleppo. But the damage is harder to repair for once-respected shawarma chef Tarek, who in his own moment of truth admits he made his family pay for his loss of status. As his daughter says at the start: “War is not as hard as what comes after.”Azzam and MacInnes’ film is so deft at sifting the debris of the years to highlight these breakthroughs for maximum effect, you wish there was another hour to pore over the path leading there. But it stays the course impressively on external and internal journeys as it highlights the family’s hard-won transformations.One in a Million is in UK and Irish cinemas from 6 November.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMigrationSyriaIslamGermanyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ glory | Television | The Guardian
description: High-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: High-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Period piece … The Gilded Age.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenPeriod piece … The Gilded Age.Photograph: HBOTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ gloryHigh-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Jack SealeandGraeme VirtueMon 2 Nov 2026 01.15 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 03.06 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Gilded Age9pm, Sky AtlanticJulian Fellowes’ glossy, airy period confection returns. The Gilded Age has now happily embraced its own lack of real nutritional value and, towards the end of the third season, its ratings swelled as a result. In the opener, Agnes is scheming to retain her position in society and there’s a subplot of real modern resonance as old money starts being threatened by crass, arriviste monopolists.Phil HarrisonA Place in the Sun6pm, Channel 4Now that it’s dark before dinnertime, the show about upping sticks from the UK feels like perfect vicarious viewing. The Dordogne and a gorgeous Greek island feature later in the week but the new run kicks off with a couple contemplating retirement on the balmy Costa Blanca. What can a £450k budget get them?Graeme VirtueEscaping Idi Amin9pm, BBC TwoIn the context of the current hysteria around migration, thistwo-part documentary has been sobering. As it concludes, it’s 1972 and a month after Uganda’s swaggering dictator Idi Amin issued an ultimatum to the country’s Asian population. They must leave within 90 days, taking nothing more than one suitcase and £50 each. Will Britain take them?PHView image in fullscreenDogged … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4 / Olly CourtneyPierre9pm, Channel 4It’s the penultimate chapter of David Harewood’s suave legal drama, and if you think collapsing would keep this dogged duty solicitor down, think again (“It wasn’t a heart attack, it was angina”). He escapes his hospital bed to get back on the case following a new lead on Michael’s death.Hollie RichardsonTrauma: My Broken Brain10pm, Channel 4The documentary’s concluding half follows Dan, Saskia and Dec – all in their 20s – as they recover from life-threatening strokes. As Dan endures surgery to repair a hole in his skull, Saskia goes to great lengths to overcome her neurological fatigue. Dec, meanwhile, finds his psychological recovery more challenging than the physical.Jack SealeDispatches: The Taliban’s War on Women11pm, Channel 4The 2021 US and UK withdrawal from Afghanistan, allowing the Taliban to take control, felt like a shameful betrayal. And the stories that emerge from this remarkable Dispatches documentary confirm that impression. It follows Afghans in exile as they attempt to rescue loved ones from the theocracy; a story of torture, sexual violence, erasure and extraordinary courage.PHLive sportTennis: Paris Masters. title: ‘Funny and self-aware’: why (500) Days of Summer is my feelgood movie | (500) Days of Summer | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaning
Author: Charlie Lindlar
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaning
Content: Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of SummerPhotograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenJoseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of SummerPhotograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMy feelgood movie(500) Days of Summer‘Funny and self-aware’: why (500) Days of Summer is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaningCharlie LindlarMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.13 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is September 2009. Barack Obama is settling into the White House. The global economy is hauling itself gingerly out of the financial crisis. And Keisha has just left the Sugababes.But more importantly, I am on a first date.‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movieRead moreFans of indie music and cinema, both myself and the woman I’m seeing – I still remember the black dress and gold-glitter eyeshadow she chose – are seated to take in (500) Days of Summer, a quirky-looking romcom starring a youthful Joseph Gordon-Levitt and the doe-eyed, Ur-manic pixie dream girlZooey Deschanel.If you’ve not seen the film, how dare you, but here’s a recap: diehard romantic Tom (Gordon-Levitt) meets mysterious lone wolf Summer (Deschanel) in a lift at their workplace, and instantly falls in love when, first, she sings along to the Smiths song she can hear emanating from his headphones, and then, fatally, praises his taste in music. The film then – skipping around in non-linear fashion – recounts the 500 days in which Tom and Summer become close, fall into a relationship of some kind, fall apart in a seemingly sudden argument over what they mean to each other, and ultimately come to part forever as Summer moves jobs and, out of nowhere, marries another man.The heart of the film is the grey area of Tom and Summer’s relationship: were they ever a couple, like Tom believes? Or were they just friends, as Summer insists? While each readily acknowledges they mean something significant to each other, the Rorschach test quality of their dynamic drives the drama.The film is a success: the time-hopping format is a thrill, the rise and fall of their relationship plausible, funny and self-aware. The performances are nuanced career bests from a pair of leads with tangible chemistry. The production is gorgeous too: it combines a glorious indie-poptimist soundtrack, timeless yet squarely 2009 costuming and a sepia-tinged portrayal of Los Angeles which focuses not on the Hollywood Hills and golden beaches but instead on the city’s under-loved downtown, with its plazas, art deco high-rises and many, many car parks.The date, by the way, was a success too. My wife and I have been together ever since, and (500) Days of Summer remains a shared love. Far too many lines have slipped into our lexicon, we have visited a number of key locations on visits to LA, and I at least regularly look back to Tom for office-wear inspo. (Bring back ties and cardigans, but perhaps not those Puma trainers just yet).Most meaningfully, on every anniversary of that 2009 date, we rewatch the film together. We know the thing frame-by-frame now, but the reason we insist on coming back to the story every year stems from something deeper than just loving the script or the setting. To us, each annual rewatch is a chance to look again at the shape, direction and even nature of true love – and perhaps by extent our own relationship.It’s an opportunity to reconsider Tom’s position: is he a true romantic, or just deeply naive? Is his desire to fix a label to what he has with Summer reasonable, or insecure? It’s a chance too to look anew at Summer’s philosophy: is she a woman of principled boundaries, or someone who locks others out to protect herself? Is her desire to avoid labelling things independence, or is it carelessness with the feelings of others?Some years, we like to approach the rewatch with an agenda: last year, we tried to be Summer stans and see only Tom’s foibles. Other times, we theorise if things ever could have worked, or pinpoint the precise moment their relationship goes wrong. This year, we focused only on who was “worse” to the other (it’s Summer, sorry – you can’t invite your ex-lover to an intimate gathering at your apartment andnottell them it’s a party celebrating your engagement to an entirely different man!).The beauty of the film to us is that, though it tends to be more sympathetic to Tom, it forces few conclusions upon you. In the film’s closing moments, when Tom and Summer part for the final time, they find one shared conclusion: he’s right about the existence of true love … but he just wasn’t meant to find it with her.Each year, as we watch and litigate and re-litigate this wonderful film, I too find myself sure of one thing. While Tom was wrong about having found his true love, I know what I knew at that first viewing in 2008: I have found mine.(500) Days of Summer is available on Hoopla and to rent digitally in the US and on Disney+ in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topics(500) Days of SummerMy feelgood movieJoseph Gordon-LevittZooey DeschanelComedy filmsRomance filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ashanti: ‘I’ve had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment’ | Music | The Guardian
description: Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skill
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skill
Content: ‘What gets on my nerves about my husband Nelly? Definitely the thermostat’: Ashanti, who is touring Australia this month.Photograph: Michael Simon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What gets on my nerves about my husband Nelly? Definitely the thermostat’: Ashanti, who is touring Australia this month.Photograph: Michael Simon/Getty Images10 chaotic questionsMusicAshanti: ‘I’ve had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment’Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skillGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailSian CainMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour debut album, Ashanti, turns 25 next year and you’re in the process of re-recording it.How do you feel about that album now?We are re-recording it so I will own my masters. Sonically, it will be a lot clearer. It was 25 years ago so it’ll sound a little more new, obviously, but with the same classic vibe. I’m very excited. What I’ve learned is that I’m just really grateful to have written records that stand the test of time. Foolish is turning 25! That I can still go to an arena and hold the mic in the air and hear everyone sing those lyrics is a beautiful feeling. And a blessing.Owning my masters is really important to me. Nowadays, obviously, things are a lot different compared with back when I first came out as an artist. But after 20 years, you get the right to go in and legally re-record your masters … and take back what’s yours, so to speak. Hopefully it inspires artists to try and take control from the beginning – hopefully you don’t have to wait 20 years! But if you do, you go in, you get it done and you have fun with it.You and your husband, Nelly, have been together for decades. What do you like most about him and what gets on your nerves?He has got to have the biggest heart I know. He is so generous and genuine – he will literally take the shirt off of his back and give it to you. He’s really a beautiful person. And he taught me a lot about staying positive and looking at the glass half full, as opposed to half empty. He has an amazing heart.What gets on my nerves? Definitely the thermostat. He likes it to be cold and I like it to be warm and toasty and cozy. A lot of our beef happens over the thermostat. Our compromise number is 70 degrees fahrenheit (21C) because I would prefer 80, 85 and he would prefer, like, 60. I’m like, “Bro, come on!” So we agreed on 70.What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?Obviously 20 years ago it was very different – you are a new artist so people would come up to me, crying and shaking. And I’m very grateful for that. But being in the game for 20-plus years, teenagers that weren’t even born back then come up to me now. I met a young girl recently and I was like “How do you even know Foolish?” I saw her singing every word in the audience with her mom. It was the coolest thing.Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morningYou want to hear something crazy? This young girl did an interview with me at SiriusXM recently and she said, “Oh my God, I love you! My dad named me after you!”As a millennial, John Tucker Must Die is a very important film to me. Do you find acting easy? How does it compare to making music?It’s just another muscle to flex. I really enjoy acting. I think the difference is you have a lot more control in music, especially if you write your own music. If you’re on stage, you know people are there to see you. When you’re acting, you’re portraying a character that someone else has written and you’re being directed … so although it’s really cool to dip into another version of yourself, it’s kind of limiting because you’re there to portray what they want you to.What’s the most chaotic thing that’s ever happened to you on stage?I definitely have had some – I guess we’re going to call them very excited fans – jump on stage and give me a hug mid-performance. I’ve also had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment. We had to have the band play for a second. I went into the wing and got it together.When you get to a hotel, what’s the first thing you do?I wipe down the phone and the remote with disinfectant wipes – always!If you could collaborate with another artist you haven’t already worked with, who would it be and why?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI like a lot of the newer R&B girls; they are really cool. I love SZA, I think she’s really, really dope. She’s shown me so much love since the beginning. Summer Walker is dope too. And I like women empowerment. Nothing against the guys!What is the best lesson you’ve learned from someone that you’ve worked with?Michael Theo: ‘I want to be on Dancing with the Stars! Would a top hat be too much?’Read moreUsually your gut is right. Sometimes, as artists, we second guess ourselves – but usually your gut is right and you’ve got to follow it. My husband has definitely said that to me, because he’s always like, “You second guess yourself!” But we all do that.Is your baby boy coming along on the Australia tour?Yes, he’s coming to Australia with me. I really thought long and hard about it but I can’t go that long without seeing him. I’m very grateful and blessed to have an amazing nanny. It definitely takes a village. Being a working mom and travelling all over the world definitely takes its toll. And I’m a mom that cooks all of his food from scratch. Everything is organic. Most people have liquor, chips, candy on their rider – and mine is just, like, organic sweet potatoes!What are you secretly really good at?I don’t know if it’s a secret, but I’m actually a really good cook. My go-to dish is Chilean sea bass with rice and vegetables. And I am good at impressions.Who’s your best impression?[In a very convincing Australian accent]Well, I think my best imitation might be you at the moment.Ashanti’s Australian tourkicks off in Perth on 9 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusic10 chaotic questionsR&BfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jail | Music | The Guardian
description: Young, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UK
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: Young, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UK
Content: ‘The energy was there – tons of energy!’ ... HR, centre, performs with Bad Brains in Wetlands in New York in 1999.Photograph: Steve Eichner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The energy was there – tons of energy!’ ... HR, centre, performs with Bad Brains in Wetlands in New York in 1999.Photograph: Steve Eichner/Getty ImagesMusic‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jailYoung, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UKAlex DellerMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOld punks might not agree on much – who was first, who was fastest, where to file the Faith/Void split LP in their record collection – but for those who saw them in their prime, Bad Brains were, unequivocally, the best live band on the planet. YouTube footage bears this out: frontman HR, born Paul D Hudson, is equal parts straining sinew and raw electricity as he bucks and contorts, punctuating rapid-fire snarls and otherworldly croons with impeccably timed backflips. The band surge around him, forging blisteringly fast punk informed by everything from the Damned and Dead Boys to P-Funk, Stevie Wonder and Chick Corea’s Return to Forever.Young, black and fuelled by an ideology that united the 1930s self-help mantras of Napoleon Hill with Rastafari, they were outliers in the already outre 70s punk scene. But while Bad Brains helped change the face of American punk as it morphed into hardcore in the early 80s, and inspired artists as diverse as Rage Against the Machine, Deftones, Lil Jon, the Roots and Beastie Boys, defeat was never far from glory as they balanced feted live performances and a scintillating run of records with an excruciating capacity for self-sabotage.double quotation markI cleaned the floors in jail and got time off on Sundays. I said: ‘Let’s give it a try then’The band’s roots thread back to Central High, a school in Maryland where middle-class military kids HR and his younger brother Earl (drums) met Dr Know (AKA Gary Wayne Miller, guitar) and Darryl Jenifer (bass). Jenifer hailed from Washington DC’s south-east projects. “We had an art teacher that would let us bring in records,” he says. “So you’re making papier-mache, or whatever the fuck, and our clique of musicians met by bringing in things like Billy Cobham’s Spectrum rather than Earth, Wind & Fire.”View image in fullscreen‘It wasn’t like being in a band – it was a mission’ ... from left: Dr Know, Earl Hudson, HR and Darryl Jenifer AKA Bad Brains.Photograph: Atiba JeffersonThe quartet, along with Jenifer’s close friend Sid McCray, began making music, rehearsing in a friend’s house when his mother was out playing bingo. “We were very influenced by all kinds of music,” says Miller. “White, black, rock’n’roll, funk – all the flavours, just like Baskin-Robbins.” Jenifer sums things up more pithily: “My female cousins would say, ‘Darryl listens to white boy music that you can’t dance to.’”The group initially aspired to the jazz-fusion of Return to Forever and the Mahavishnu Orchestra, although Jenifer suggests this era was little more than adolescent daydreaming. “We called ourselves Mind Power, but we never played a show, and we only had one song. It was the delusional teenage phase: it never was serious, it never was real.”Things got real, though, when McCray discovered punk, introducing the band to Sex Pistols, Dead Boys and Ramones. “I just remember listening to the music and feeling liberated,” says Jenifer. “Like, damn, I can make some shit like that.”Mind Power was rechristened Bad Brains, and HR inherited the mic from McCray. “Our first poster said: ‘Bad Brains, the greatest punk rock band in the world’,” laughs Jenifer. While easily chalked up to youthful braggadocio, this radical self-belief was largely the product of the band’s adherence to PMA – positive mental attitude – as a guiding credo.“My father would say, ‘Why do you want to be a musician? Be a doctor or a lawyer or something,’” says HR from his Texas home. “He told me to read a book, so I read Think and Grow Rich.” This was by Hill, the personal motivation guru. “I decided to use PMA as a formula, as a vehicle in my music, and to try to use it to help guide me through what I was going through.” Dabbling with hard drugs, working a dead-end security job and on the brink of fatherhood, it’s perhaps no surprise that PMA seemed like a lifeline for HR, but his interest was shared by the rest of the band. “We wanted to have a purpose and a message,” says Jenifer. “It wasn’t like being in a band – it was a mission.”This sense of focus was apparent at the band’s first studio session, when they entered Don Zientara’s Inner Ear Studio in 1979 to record a six-track demo, a pivotal moment that has now been remastered and released by Trust Records under the title Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording. “They were serious,” says Zientara, speaking from his studio. “The songs were there. The energy was there – tons of energy! – and you hear that coming through. At the time, I didn’t have a chance to think about how good they were. They came, they played, they packed up. It was so quick. It was like, did I record these guys?!”View image in fullscreenA force to be reckoned with … Bad BrainsAfter another demo session, Bad Brains hit their stride with a series of landmark releases: 1980’s brief, brilliant 7-inch Pay to Cum was followed by a self-titled album and then by Rock for Light, produced by Ric Ocasek. These years were turbulent, marked by triumph and tribulation: the band were banned from a number of Washington venues. “They said we incited riots,” says Miller. “The club owners said, ‘You’re making the kids go crazy!’” And, although a scorching 1979 gig with the Damned had led to an invitation to tour the UK, the band tried to enter the country without working papers and were immediately sent back to the US – penniless and with their equipment lost en route.For all the chaos, this period cemented the band’s legend as a force to be reckoned with. The excitement of their music was matched by a zeal amplified by their burgeoning Rastafari beliefs. “The intention has always been to excite people and make them exult,” says Jenifer. “We’re not performing a riff or trying to nail a show. We’re giving the crowd the vibration to destroy Babylon. This music is the spearhead – that’s what we go on stage with. If we didn’t have that revolutionary spirit, we’d probably feel stupid playing the shit that we play.” Miller, more succinct, agrees: “We’re not lost in the moment,” he says. “Wearethe moment.”These sentiments are echoed by many who saw Bad Brains perform. “My friend Bruce and the guys in Autistic Behavior kept telling me, ‘Once you see Bad Brains, your life will change,’” says author and educator Nancy Barile. “They were right.” Barile first saw the band play in Philadelphia in 1982 and had a “physical and visceral” response. “Every time I saw Bad Brains in the early 80s, the audience reaction was insane,” she says. “There’s only a handful of bands I’ve seen get that kind of unrestrained – and totally pure – response and Bad Brains lead the pack. It was chaotic but hypnotic. It was clear that we, the audience, wanted – actually needed – to be participatory in the performance.”Photographer and artist Glen E Friedman concurs. “The first time I saw Bad Brains was just after these early demos were recorded,” he says. “I was in high school. In all honesty, I had never seen anything or heard anything like them. They were incredible in so many ways.”View image in fullscreen‘We’re not lost in the moment. We are the moment’ … the band in 1983The band split for the first time after the release of Rock for Light, with HR wary of major label interest and growing tensions within the band due to his and Earl’s increasing fondness for all-reggae sets. There were also abusive, homophobic clashes with members of the hardcore scene’s gay community – notably with Texas punks Big Boys, whose frontman was gay. The former Hüsker Dü frontmanBob Mouldhas also recalled incidences where his band were subject to homophobia by Bad Brains. And then there was the roundly condemned (and subsequently disowned) 1989 song Don’t Blow Bubbles – perceived to be anti-gay – which continues to cast a pall over the band’s legacy. Neither Williams nor Jenifer are keen to rake over these incidents, though the latter suggests youthful and misguided zealotry were at play. “I was taught to love all people,” he says now. “I’m no homophobe. I respect life. If you got life, I’m loving you.”The band reunited for 1986’s blistering I Against I, which saw them expanding their palette into soul, funk and heavy metal, securing the talents of super-producer Ron Saint Germain despite their label’s limited budget. As well as providing the record with oomph, Saint Germain’s technical skill helped overcome certain logistical difficulties – like HR serving time for a marijuana bust.“I was doing stupid things,” says the singer, “jeopardising my future, and I had to learn the hard way. I was in jail when Sacred Love was recorded. Ron suggested I try to sing some vocals to it over the phone. I was working as a mop, cleaning the floors, and I got in time off on a Sunday. I said, ‘OK, well, I’ll give it a try.’”From the late 1980s onwards, the band existed in fits and starts. Releases were punctuated by breakups, lineup changes and violent incidents that sank both a series of high-profile gigs with Beastie Boys and a deal with Madonna’s Maverick Records. “Everybody can be a handful,” is how Miller rather plainly sums things up. “When we hit the stage, though, all that stuff doesn’t mean anything because the spirit takes over.”With Miller still recovering from a severe stroke and cancer, and HR being treated for both Sunct syndrome and schizoaffective disorder, it’s unlikely Bad Brains will perform again. But their deal with Trust Records at least puts their recorded legacy in safe hands – a legacy the band are very much aware of. “When we first started, we knew it was something unique and not what people expected,” says Miller. “It was like, ‘Who’re these brothers playing some rock’n’roll?’ But what they should’ve done was go to the history of rock’n’roll. It’s all Muddy Waters and them guys, not Elvis Presley.”Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording is out on 6 November via Trust RecordsExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content
