title: Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg review – a BBC reporter’s howl of frustration  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: After more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politics
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: After more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politics
Content: Laura Kuenssberg.Photograph: Jonathan Callery/BBC/October FilmsView image in fullscreenLaura Kuenssberg.Photograph: Jonathan Callery/BBC/October FilmsBook of the dayPolitics booksReviewPay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg review – a BBC reporter’s howl of frustrationAfter more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politicsGaby HinsliffMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaura Kuenssberg always swore she would never write a book. Amid all the vitriol hurled her way, the BBC’s political editor turned presenter has largely kept her counsel. She rarely complained even when she needed security to do her job unobstructed at Labour party conference under Jeremy Corbyn, or had to run the gauntlet of aggressive Brexit protesters outside parliament, or when a creepy unnamed minister tried to inveigle her into his hotel room for what an appalled Kuenssberg concluded was intended to be a threesome. Knowing everything she does is minutely parsed for bias, she keeps her cards close to her chest. Until, apparently, something snapped.Pay Attention is a muted but heartfelt howl of frustration with politicians “who have looked like an absolute shower for a long time” but also,sotto voce, with voters, who she evidently wishes would occasionally take things more seriously. Having covered Westminster since the late noughties, Kuenssberg brings all that weight of experience to bear in spelling out just how far the abnormal is now becoming normalised in British politics.double quotation markShe deconstructs the techniques Farage has developed to dodge questions he dislikesOnce, she points out, there was a cross-party understanding not to inflame racial tensions at sensitive times; now masked men can roam Belfast seeking foreign-born people to burn from their homes, and still Nigel Farage says they shouldn’t be called far right. The Greens, Tories and Reform all selected candidates for this year’s council elections who had previously expressed startlingly flaky views. The rapid turnover of prime ministers over the last decade isn’t normal either, she argues, but nor was the behaviour causing it – from the boozy loucheness of Boris Johnson’s Downing Street to Keir Starmer securing a whopping great majority but no mandate, having never really made a case for what he actually wanted to do.This is a serious and earnest book, not a gossipy insider’s tale, focused on the failures of governance that have radicalised what she argues isn’t naturally a radical country. Kuenssberg describes a politics paralysed by fear, with MPs afraid of telling an angry public the hard truths they’ll happily discuss with her once the camera stops running. (Nobody she talks to, apparently, thinks government operates effectively or spends money well.) But there are glimpses too of journalism struggling to hold politicians accountable, in an era of shrinking audience attention spans – Kuenssberg is notably sniffy about fluffy interviews that focus on a politician’s colourful backstory, not their policies – and Trumpian resistance to scrutiny.She deconstructs the techniques Farage has developed to dodge questions he dislikes: expressing total conviction even when he doesn’t know the facts; turning questions back on his interviewer; and claiming to be persecuted by the media when cornered – an incendiary tactic Corbyn also adopted and which Zack Polanski is beginning to use, though Kuenssberg says at least Polanski has a “swagger and a bluntness” which means he’ll usually answer a straight question. When a politician lashes out at the mainstream media, she argues, pay extra attention to what they’re actually doing: often it’s a distraction tactic.But she also identifies the weaknesses in mainstream politics that she believes gave Farage his opening. Ten years ago, she argues, it would have sounded “distressing and insane” to say there would soon be mass small boat crossings of the Channel: if that reality has changed, alongside the numbers of legal immigrants arriving and arrangements for housing them, perhaps it’s unsurprising that the public mood has changed, too. For Kuenssberg, it started with a wave of eastern European migration in the 2000s that some communities struggled to absorb, followed by the 2015 exodus of refugees from war-torn Syria and European leaders’ apparent impotence in the face of what she calls a “massive migration crisis”.Politicians reacted first too slowly then too bombastically, promising to stop the boats and smash the gangs even when that wasn’t realistically possible, and fuelling the idea that immigration was beyond their control. What’s interesting about this argument – with which readers may agree or disagree – is that itisan argument, one of the few times she seemingly feels strongly enough to advance one.There is a discernible tension here between Kuenssberg’s professional duty as a BBC journalist to remain politically neutral, and the need for a book to say something beyond the bleeding obvious. At times, I wondered if she wouldn’t have been better saving it all for a post-BBC memoir where she could let rip.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs it is, some readers will be outraged that she isn’t taking a stronger stand against extremism, while others will doubtless think she has outed herself as a moderate centrist merely by pointing out that ideas now advanced by both Reform and the Greens would once have been considered completely off the wall. As Kuenssberg knows better than most, you can’t win – though that doesn’t mean it isn’t worth trying. Sadly, I think she’s right that our politics is neither normal nor healthy, and that saying so in plain English is an important part of holding the line. But it will take more than paying attention, I suspect, to bring sanity back.Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg is published by Little, Brown (£22). title: The Rhyl Poster by Tom McCarthy review – is this avant-garde spy drama worth the riddles? | Tom McCarthy | The Guardian
description: The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating reading
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating reading
Content: Prank-adjacent vibe … Tom McCarthy.Photograph: Johannes SchriekView image in fullscreenPrank-adjacent vibe … Tom McCarthy.Photograph: Johannes SchriekTom McCarthyReviewThe Rhyl Poster by Tom McCarthy review – is this avant-garde spy drama worth the riddles?The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating readingAnthony CumminsMon 2 Nov 2026 04.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf the cohort of experimental novelists whose renown grew in the wake of the 2008 financial crash – names includeDeborah Levy,Eimear McBrideandClaire-Louise Bennett– it was Tom McCarthy who first demonstrated the benefit of bypassing orthodox routes to market. When British publishers rejected his 2005 novel,Remainder, about an amnesiac who spends a windfall restaging his past, he released it in a limited edition from a Paris art collective. Three years later, Zadie Smith wrote an essay celebrating it as a path-breaking overthrow of establishment-sanctioned “lyrical realism”. The literary press soon began finding more room for McCarthy, whose regular denunciations of English fiction – not least for its “middlebrow” ignorance of challenging ideas from the continent – did much to shape bookish conversation at the turn of the decade.If his zeal wasn’t to everyone’s taste – the New Statesman once called him Britain’s “most galling interviewee” – anyone lately stepping into a bookshop might well feel the last laugh belongs to McCarthy. Witness the success of Fitzcarraldo Editions: innovative Europeans are hot property. Risk-rewarding ventures such as the Goldsmiths prize, established in 2013 to spotlight formally daring fiction amid panic about the philistinism of award panels, feel a little less urgent when a novel as inscrutable as M John Harrison’sThe End of Everythingsits comfortably on this year’s Booker shortlist, a bestseller to boot. When the mainstream and the avant garde are now kissing cousins, where does it leave McCarthy?The Making of Incarnation(2021), a dense, Pynchonesque espionage yarn about motion capture technology, suggested that he saw the Booker-shortlisted success of both 2010’sCand 2015’sSatin Islandas a green light to push readers harder. Further evidence for the theory is supplied by his riddling new novel, The Rhyl Poster, another abstruse spy drama, this time set deep inside the polyglot operations of Luxembourg’s Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). It’s as if McCarthy – a longtime Berliner who, post-Brexit, holds a Swedish passport – had determined to immerse himself in the minutiae of the institution his native Britain elected to leave.We’re in the company of a pill-popping jurist, Stanton, scarred by his past as a military geographer with the British army in Iraq. Memories of that time, opaque to the reader, don’t help him at work, where he’s meant to be drafting a landmark opinion on a privacy suit against a data analytics firm. His desire for relief from his various war wounds makes him prey to an approach from a shadowy criminal seeking EU documents in exchange for unapproved painkillers from a lab in Rotterdam – home, handily, to Stanton’s long-distance Dutch-Surinamese girlfriend, one among a catalogue of lovers whose pillow talk greases the story’s cogs.double quotation markReading The Rhyl Poster is like trying to fill in a crossword using the wrong cluesThe ensuing double-dealing zigzag around northern Europe plays out as a genre-curious mashup of trauma plot and heist narrative, steadfastly averse to closure. Suspense derives less from events than from the disorientingly stretchy syntax of McCarthy’s narration, a dry blend of legal lingo and lower-slung idiom, like a lecturer wearing a blazer with Nikes. “Interpretation,” we’re told, isn’t the same thing as “advancing to a conclusion from a set of givens guided by parameters that, fixed, are also given: that’s induction. No:interpretation, understood in its profoundest sense, is the plumb opposite … If law in general is the realm where language shapes the world, the European Court of Justice pimps this logic to thenth.”The novel’s interest in law, or its “fundamental propensity for repeatability, its driving imperative towards self-duplication”, eventually reveals itself as another iteration of McCarthy’s abiding preoccupation with repetition. Even the most dramatic scene, a revelatory flashback to Stanton’s days in Iraq, is a replay of sorts, evoking Zadie Smith’s observation about the role Remainder gave to a black man’s fatal shooting (experimental or not, she said, “the non-white subject is still the bad conscience of the contemporary novel”).Remainder remains McCarthy’s best book, its multifunctional concept delivering old-school psychological intrigue while poking fun at literary realism’s mimetic aspirations. Reading The Rhyl Poster, by contrast, is like trying to fill in a crossword using the wrong clues. The endeavour isn’t devoid of quixotic frisson: it’s not unfun to note, for instance, that the defendant in Stanton’s case is named Elrond – like Palantir, a lift from Tolkien – or that the claimant, Kohlhas, described as a “one-man operation”, echoes the wronged justice-seeker Michael Kohlhaas in Heinrich von Kleist’s 1810 novella of that name.Yet these are keys tinkling, not doors unlocked, and while there’s a measure of page-turning urgency in Stanton’s increasingly hallucinatory personal crisis, he’s too plainly a parody of a girl-getting hardman-savant to carry much by way of emotional weight. The mystifying title, poised between enigma and bathos, refers (no spoiler, this) to the protagonist’s half-memory of riding a train in north Wales while watching someone paste up an advert – blank, naturally.The prank-adjacent vibe hardly subsides once the novel’s 240 pages of high-pressure buildup conclude with the word “begin”. Any takeaway perhaps lies in the acronym of the court at the book’s heart, blinking like a beacon through its pages – CJEU,c’est jeu, a game – and if you don’t get a kick out of that, be sure McCarthy does.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
