title: BBCSO/Stasevska review – Caroline Shaw’s cosmic visions meet Barber’s lyrical brilliance | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but occasionally underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall Goosby
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but occasionally underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall Goosby
Content: Violinist Randall Goosby with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Dalia Stasevska in the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenViolinist Randall Goosby with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Dalia Stasevska in the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSO/Stasevska review – Caroline Shaw’s cosmic visions meet Barber’s lyrical brillianceBarbican, LondonThe Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall GoosbyErica JealMon 2 Nov 2026 06.09 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs it hurtles away from Earth – 16bn miles and counting – theGolden Recordon board the Voyager spacecraft continues to fascinate us.Caroline Shaw’s The Listeners – written for San Francisco’s Philharmonia Baroque in 2019 and here receiving its London premiere from the BBCSO as part of Shaw’s Barbican residency – features one of its tracks: spoken greetings in 55 languages. Heard via record player, these resonate through the hall while Shaw’s music forms haltingly underneath, from a pulsing keyboard note to briefly sweeping choral phrases. At times, the music almost eclipses the speech – which somehow emphasises its wonder. Later, Carl Sagan’s “pale blue dot” speech is heard, this time unadorned, via cassette player.Using a wordless choir to express wonderment is a cliche that Shaw skirts deftly, her harmonies avoiding sentimentality even though they often feel simple. Lasting 35 minutes and styled like a miniature classical oratorio, The Listeners starts and ends with movements that grow from a wordless lullaby, sung here hauntingly by the mezzo-soprano Lotte Betts-Dean. There’s a prominent role for keyboard; a harpsichord at the premiere, but an electric piano here, lending the whole thing an aptly Tomorrow’s World feel reinforced by the sight of the audio hardware on a table at the front. A baroque-style orchestral interlude conjures interstellar velocity; as for the texts Shaw sets to music, these include poetry by Whitman and Tennyson along with a striking 2017 meditation on the arbitrariness of borders by Yesenia Montilla.View image in fullscreenLotte Betts-Dean and Florian Störtz with Dalia Stasevska and the BBC Symphony.Photograph: Mark AllanBetts-Dean and the baritone Florian Störtz were communicative soloists, and the BBC Symphony Chorus put the choral passages across compellingly. The movements aren’t necessarily too short – Haydn managed to conjure the vast unknown in just six minutes at the start of The Creation – yet they didn’t all feel developed to full capacity. Given the immensity of its subject, it’s perhaps unsurprising that Shaw’s piece should be enjoyable, thought-provoking and slender all at once.Stasevska and her orchestra had warmed us up with a lyrical first half. Grazhyna, a 1955 tone poem by the Ukrainian composer Borys Lyatoshynsky, was a worthwhile discovery, telling a 15th-century Lithuanian tale in sonorously dramatic style. And Randall Goosby gave us a gratifyingly rich yet unsentimental performance of Barber’s Violin Concerto. His encore, Coleridge-Taylor Perkinson’s Louisiana Blues Strut, was a toe-tapping evocation of bluegrass and slide guitar.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicBarbicanChoral musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Lives of Others review – Keira Knightley brings star power to Robert Icke’s Stasi drama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Theatre wunderkind’s adaptation of the Oscar-winning film has plenty of suspenseful stagecraft but struggles to match its subtlety
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Theatre wunderkind’s adaptation of the Oscar-winning film has plenty of suspenseful stagecraft but struggles to match its subtlety
Content: Overheated, underwritten … Keira Knightley in The Lives of Others at Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanView image in fullscreenOverheated, underwritten … Keira Knightley in The Lives of Others at Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanTheatreReviewThe Lives of Others review – Keira Knightley brings star power to Robert Icke’s Stasi dramaAdelphi theatre, LondonTheatre wunderkind’s adaptation of the Oscar-winning film has plenty of suspenseful stagecraft but struggles to match its subtletyArifa AkbarSun 1 Nov 2026 19.05 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 04.34 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother new show, another old story. This film-to-stage adaptation is from the 2006 German-language romantic thriller about Stasi surveillance and suppression of art in the former GDR. The accompanying, now almost obligatory, high-prestige screen actor isKeira Knightley, presumably whipping up ticket-selling frenzy and stage-door brouhahas.Except this production is helmed by theatre wunderkindRobert Icke, whose work is marked by the utmost integrity and who has a record of making fast-moving, suspense-filled work of canonical material (from the Greeks in Oedipus and Oresteia to Arthur Schnitzler’s Professor Bernhardi reimagined as The Doctor).Icke chooses a difficult story to adapt and direct here. The film follows a Stasi officer who secretly changes sides while spying on a writer and his girlfriend. So much of the power of Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck’s Oscar-winning drama lies in subtlety: a maelstrom of emotion rumbling beneath a taut surface, and the understated brilliance of late actor Ulrich Mühe, who played Stasi captain Gerd Wiesler, and was himself a former East German with a backstory involving the Stasi.View image in fullscreenIntimacy, intrusion … Stephen Dillane in The Lives of Others at Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Manuel HarlanAll that is conveyed by inference and suggestion in the film but takes on the feverish nature of a melodrama on stage. Luke Thompson plays writer George Dreyman, and seems too puppyish in the role. Knightley is his girlfriend, Christa-Maria Sieland, a stage actor and the object of jealous lust for venal government minister Hempf (Andrew Woodall), who seeks to destroy Dreyman so he can claim her. She gives a committed performance, but the character feels overheated and underwritten. She wears glamorous dresses with cinched waists and coiffed hair, looking like a woman who could be from wartime Berlin rather than 1980s East Germany, and quotes lines from Romeo and Juliet which hang oddly: this couple are not star-crossed teenagers but grownups carrying their own secrets.Dillane’s Wiesler sits listening to these secrets after their apartment has been bugged. He also weaves physically between them, and it is a theatrical way of showing the intimacy and intrusion building in his surveillance. But where the film was able to deliver Wiesler’s interiority through lingering closeups and looks, there are fewer ways of opening up his inner world when the story relies on the same mode of suggestion to convey his disenchantment with a system he has believed in, but which he now realises is corrupt or exploited by Grubitz, his boss, and by Hempf.Wiesler stays largely silent, although he interacts with Grubitz (Paul Higgins), who really is grubby.His inner change is portrayed too subtly and not subtly enough. He lies curled and sobbing when he hears Dreyman playing the piano, after the news that his artist friend has hanged himself. The sobbing suggests a new appreciation of the arts but it does not feel enough for his dramatic shift.View image in fullscreenSuspense through stagecraft … Keira Knightley and Luke Thompson in The Lives of Others at Adelphi theatre, London.Photograph: Pamela RaithIcke makes a good decision to centralise the drama so that much of it is enacted from Dreyman’s apartment, but would Hempf really assault Christa-Maria in a place he has instructed the Stasi to monitor? When the Stasi find the hiding place for a smuggled typewriter which is central to the plot, why does Dreyman start shouting at Christa-Maria in front of them about her (presumed) betrayal – wouldn’t this raise further suspicion rather than lead the Stasi to drop their investigation? And is that David Bowie’s Sound and Vision playing in a cafe where Christa-Maria and Wiesler meet? Listening to music from the west might have been a private act of defiance for artists, but wasn’t it publicly banned in the GDR?These are small threads but they do not contain Icke’s signature meticulousness. A penultimate scene features a TV interview with Dreyman, who explains the entire story, twist and all, to his interviewer, and to us. It is a coda we shouldn’t need.“Writers are engineers of the soul,” Hempf says, borrowing a phrase from Stalin about the power, and therefore the danger, of art. You don’t have to be living in the former GDR to find evidence of artistic suppression: Sally Rooney’s work in the UK is one case in point, the Home Office’s ban on the pro-Palestinian Swedish author Andreas Malm from entering the UK, is another. This story should hit home, given its underlying anxiety and anger about the political will to control and diminish art. Sadly, it doesn’t.The best theatre to stream this month: the Gisèle Pelicot trial becomes an all-star play that ‘just floors you’Read moreWhere the production excels is in raising suspense through stagecraft, especially the thuds of sound, lighting and whirl of movement. The face of the stage sometimes becomes a camera shutter, expanding and contracting threateningly. Hildegard Bechtler’s set design transforms from interrogation room to the couple’s revolving home with diaphanous screens that leave all secret activity exposed. These elements become bigger and come faster, bringing their own exciting momentum.Is this enough to justify an adaptation? Some may think so. The osmotic relationship between film and the West End stage is not inherently toxic. Enough adaptations have shown that films can become their own thing on stage. But to me, this does not manage the immensely difficult task it sets itself.AtAdelphi theatre, London, until 9 January 2027Explore more on these topicsTheatreKeira KnightleyRobert IckereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Steve Ellis, frontman of Everlasting Love hitmakers Love Affair, dies aged 76 | Music | The Guardian
description: Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul Weller
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul Weller
Content: Steve Ellis pictured in 1982.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSteve Ellis pictured in 1982.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockMusicSteve Ellis, frontman of Everlasting Love hitmakers Love Affair, dies aged 76Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul WellerBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 2 Nov 2026 06.29 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.31 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Ellis, the singer who found fame as the frontman of 60s pop-rockers Love Affair, has died aged 76. A message on social media announced that Ellis died “peacefully” on 30 October, after “complications from a chronic illness”.With his stirring, heartfelt croon, Ellis gave voice to one of the most enduring hits of the 1960s: Everlasting Love, which topped the UK chart in 1968.Born in Edgware, north-west London, in 1950, Ellis formed the band Soul Survivors when he was 15 years old, inspired by Black US soul and R&B acts including James Brown who Ellis saw perform live: “He blew our socks off, he was phenomenal. I thought, that’s how a singer has to be, so I started doing gymnastics,” he told the Express in 2021.Soul Survivors morphed into Love Affair in the mid-1960s. They were signed to Decca and their debut single, She Smiled Sweetly, was released almost concurrently with the original version by the Rolling Stones, and flopped.But the follow-up Everlasting Love, another cover version, was a major hit – recorded by Ellis between shifts on a building site. Written by Buzz Cason and Mac Gayden and originally recorded by US singer Robert Knight, Ellis’s vocal was arguably more spirited, really selling the song’s pledge of eternal fealty: “Need you by my side, girl, to be my bride / You’ll never be denied everlasting love.”It spent two weeks at No 1 in the UK, and while other versions of the song would become more successful in the US – including Carl Carlton’s No 6 hit in 1974 – Love Affair’s version has endured as the most popular on streaming services, and a staple of wedding ceremonies.Buoyed by bombastic symphonic backings, Love Affair would go on to have three more UK Top 10 hits in the next two years. Rainbow Valley repeated the Everlasting Love formula – a Cason-Gayden song first performed by Knight, anchored by an emotionally wracked Ellis performance – and spent 11 weeks in the Top 40, and it was followed by A Day Without Love and Bringing on Back the Good Times.View image in fullscreenLove Affair perform at Revolution Club, London, in 1970.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesEllis became disillusioned with Love Affair after their fame began to wane later in the decade: “The band wanted to go progressive rock and that wasn’t for me,” he later said. “I’d always been a soul-boy. The main reason we broke up though was the screaming [fans]. We couldn’t hear what we were playing.” In 1972 he formed the band Ellis – their debut album was produced by Roger Daltrey – and then Widowmaker, which also featured ex-Hawkwind member Huw Lloyd Langton and others, recording their self-titled debut in 1976 before they continued without him.He released solo album The Last Angry Man in 1977, followed by Basement Days in 1983. Ellis returned in 2008 with the album Best of Days, which reunited him with Daltrey who appeared on two tracks.That album also kickstarted an enduring collaboration withPaul Weller, who appeared on two tracks including a live acoustic version of Everlasting Love. Ellis and Weller rejoined for 2018’s Boom! Bang! Twang!, with Weller co-writing two tracks and co-producing the album, followed by a one-off co-written song in 2022, Just to Simplify. His most recent album is Baby Faced Assassin, released in September, featuring another three songs co-created with Weller.Weller was among those paying tribute, writing on Instagram: “God bless ya Stevie safe travels everlasting love for sure.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPaul WellernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Screams on the level of a Taylor Swift concert’: horny romp Wicker gets the 4DX treatment | Romance films | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman’s steamy romance, where she plays a woman in love with a wicker man, becomes an unlikely pick for the theme park-like cinema experience
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Olivia Colman’s steamy romance, where she plays a woman in love with a wicker man, becomes an unlikely pick for the theme park-like cinema experience
Content: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAView image in fullscreenOlivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PARomance films‘Screams on the level of a Taylor Swift concert’: horny romp Wicker gets the 4DX treatmentOlivia Colman’s steamy romance, where she plays a woman in love with a wicker man, becomes an unlikely pick for the theme park-like cinema experienceWhat does Olivia Colman’s hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism?‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie WickerAdrian HortonMon 2 Nov 2026 13.29 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.51 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince its introduction in the US in 2014, 4DX, the rollercoaster-ization of the theatrical experience, has primarily been the purview of action movies. And for good reason; the high-speed chases of a Fast and Furious movie, or repetitive battle sequences of an Avatar saga, translate easily to the moving chairs, scent machines and wind/water sprayers of the format, which more closely resembles an amusement park ride than cinema.Wicker review – Olivia Colman finds the perfect lover in intriguing folk-horror romanceRead moreAs a longtime fan of plane turbulence-style seat movement, I thought the immersive pleasures of 4DX – the second most-popular of so-called large premium formats in the US, behind Imax –reached its zenithin the summer of 2024 with the release of Twisters, a perfectly fine action movie about tornadoes that became an 11/10experiencewhen jostled in one’s seat to actual wind and rain. But a recent, unexpected candidate is finally pushing the bounds of 4DX again, making the most of the format’s potential to enhance the sensorial joys of cinema.EnterWicker, the horny medieval fable in which Olivia Colman’s Fisherwoman comes by a wicker-man husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. A relatively small-budget ($10.5m), off-kilter love story from Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, Wicker made waves among curious cinephiles after itsSundance debutin January. But it is not what one might call a prime 4DX candidate. There is nary a mechanized vehicle in sight. Peasant characters don’t so much as ride a horse. Colman’s Fisherwoman at best lumbers about her village, and spends a decent amount of the movie scowling. But trailers did promise some bed-breaking sex between the Fisherwoman and her basket-ready man, prompting a joke on social media and Letterboxd: why notthisin 4DX?Black Bear, the film’s distributor hungry for a box office win (their first US theatrical release, the Sydney Sweeney vehicleChristy, bombed last year), wisely got in on the bit. And so it was that chants of “we want the wick!” filled the Regal Cinemas 4DX theater on a recent weeknight in Times Square, one of 60 “one night only” special screenings for those willing to expand the definition “experiential cinema”. (Due to demand – my screening, like most others, was entirely sold out – Black Bear ended upextendingthe one-night event to a full week.)And it did not disappoint, though viewers did have to endure some very mild 4DX foreplay to get there. Wicker admittedly does not provide much for the chairs to do for the bulk of the movie, which largely consists of characters ambling about. (The scent programmers thankfully spared us the Fisherwoman’s oft-mentioned odor.) Still, I felt the pleasant knock of a door in my back, the light bump of floating down a river and, most evocatively, a splash of moisture when the Fisherwoman empties her chamberpot out the front door.But things take a dramatic turn when Peter Dinklage’s master basket weaver delivers on his promise to make the Fisherwoman a Wicker Husband. Skarsgård’s comically tall, supposedly hollow wicker man exists for one reason and one reason only: to love the Fisherwoman, as physically and deeply as possible. Their bed-breaking post-marriage consummation scene – the reason for any of this hubbub – is probably the hardest I’ve laughed in a theater in years, and produced screams on the level of a Taylor Swift concert.View image in fullscreenAlexander Skarsgård and Olivia Colman in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PAThe women next to me, including one with her own homemade wicker basket dragged there by friends to help get over a breakup, snorted as the seats tossed us, along with the Fisherwoman, with every tightening of the wicker man’s luscious, finely woven shoulders. On the 4DX Richter scale of “fun” to “how are there legally no seatbelts”, this was off the charts. It turns out that the only thing better than losing handfuls of your popcorn to a mock Oklahoma tornado is losing your popcorn to every wicker thrust decimating Colman’s bedposts.This roughly five minutes of sublime action substantiated the next several hours of conversation (many such cases!). Alas, most of Wicker takes place outside the bedroom, which left many in the largely female audience, as one townsman put it, “gagging for a solid log”. Still, it was overall incredibly inspired entertainment; whoever programmed the relatively tame, jackhammer taps for the jealous village normies’ unsatisfying sex, a trot compared to the main couple’s gallop, deserves an award.The undeniable success of Wicker in 4DX (if many giggly“getting that wick” TikToksare to be believed) raises the question: is there a future for 4DX in erotic movies? Could we next see a Fifty Shades of Grey or Basic Instinct rerelease in 4DX? Could the format have saved Emerald Fennell’s should-be horny Wuthering Heights? Wicker may have opened fifth in the North American box office, but it has already achieved the improbable: unlocking new, tantalizing and ridiculous possibilities in the realm of cinema.Explore more on these topicsRomance filmsOlivia ColmanAlexander SkarsgårdSexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disaster | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher
Content: Taika Waititi at the Klara and the Sun premiere at  London film festival last month.Photograph: Zak Hussein/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTaika Waititi at the Klara and the Sun premiere at  London film festival last month.Photograph: Zak Hussein/Variety/Getty ImagesMovies‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disasterThe Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higherAndrew PulverMon 2 Nov 2026 06.38 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.14 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from aKazuo Ishiguronovel.‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the SunRead moreIn a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”He added: “The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit … Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”Pointing to the disparity of thefilm’s audience and critics’ score on review aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes, which currently stands at 74% for the former and 26% (from 90 reviews) for the latter, Waititi also wrote: “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people.”Klara and the Sun, which costa reported $44m(£32.8m) to make, achieved adismal $701,000(£523,000) on its first weekend at the North American box office, working out at just under $800 (£596) per theatre from 880 venues. It came in at 16th place, well below other similarly aimed films such as Wicker, which opened with $5.7m in North America from 1471 venues at an average of $3,906 per cinema. In contrast, You Can See Everything, the celebrated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes scored $18.7m on its second weekend andhas reached a cumulative total of $63.8m.In the UK, the film recordedcomparable figures to Klara and the Sun’s North American results, with an opening weekend of £176,000 from 368 venues, for an average of £477.Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental messRead moreThe Guardian’s chief critic Peter Bradshaw described Klara and the Sun as “unbearably mannered” and “unspeakably acted” in a one-star review, adding: “[It] is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy.” Bradshaw alsonegatively reviewed Waititi’s 2019 film Jojo Rabbit, calling it a “terrible film … a pointless Hitler-spoofy YA adventure with a 12A certificate, obtusely accentuating little-kid cuteness and optimism amid the quaintly imagined non-horror.”Other reviewers have been equally negative towards Klara and the Sun:in the Observer, Wendy Ide called it “a thin and cloying thing that strips away any profundity in the source material and replaces it with self-conscious quirkiness”, whilethe LA Times’ Tim Grierson said: “[Waititi] lacquers the film with a calculated gooeyness that’s stultifying before it becomes downright exasperating”.Its second weekend at the North American box-office saw Klara and the Sun enter a steep decline, dropping 79% to $145,000 (£108,000) from a similar number of venues.Explore more on these topicsFilmTaika WaititiScience fiction and fantasy filmsFilm adaptationsKazuo IshiguroFilm industryFilm criticismnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83 | Doctor Who | The Guardian
description: Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T Davies
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T Davies
Content: John Leeson holding up a picture of K9 at a Doctor Who convention in 2005.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Leeson holding up a picture of K9 at a Doctor Who convention in 2005.Photograph: ShutterstockDoctor WhoJohn Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T DaviesMartin BelamMon 2 Nov 2026 04.13 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.04 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Leeson, the actor best known as the voice of K9, the robot dog inDoctor Who, has died at 83.Leeson’s son, Guy Ducker, shared the news on Facebook. He wrote: “I regret to announce the death of my father … after a summer of illness. The end was peaceful.”In a separate post on social media, Ducker said: “Many thanks to the Whovian community for the love they showed to my father over the decades, it meant a lot to him and me.”Born John Ducker in 1943, he trained at Rada before embarking on a successful career on stage and screen. He was known for his character work across a range of TV shows such as Dad’s Army, Sorry!, Crown Court and Longitude, while other credits included The Bill, Vanity Fair, Doctors and Blake’s 7. He was also a continuity announcer on Channel 4.But Leeson was best known for K9, created by Bob Baker and Dave Martin, who was introduced to Doctor Who in 1977 in a Tom Baker-led story called The Invisible Enemy.Originally only intended to appear in that single script, the production team believed the character would be popular with younger viewers, and decided to have the metallic mutt join the Tardis team. He stayed until 1981 – although K9 was also voiced for a period by David Brierly – establishing the catchphrase “Affirmative, Master” when addressing the Doctor.View image in fullscreenLeeson with wife Judy Griffiths on their wedding day in 1969.Photograph: Gary Weaser/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenK9 flanked by the stars of Doctor Who in 1977.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyView image in fullscreenLeeson standing amid an ITV audience in 1993.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockLeeson reprised the role in the 20th anniversary special of Doctor Who and in a spin-off K-9 and Company, which featured Elisabeth Sladen as popular companion Sarah Jane Smith. Sladen and Leeson were reunited in Doctor Who in 2006 in a David Tennant episode calledSchool Reunion, before featuring in the CBBC spin-off Sarah Jane Adventures, which aired from 2007 until Sladen’s death in 2011.In an Instagram post after Leeson’s death, the former Doctor Who showrunner Russell T Davies said: “There was no question that we’d ask John to provide the voice” when the robot returned. “A posh dog, uppity, haughty, wry, but somehow innocent too, and so funny. Pitched perfectly so that kids could impersonate him. That’s not easy. A true gent, and a great loss.”Keith Barnfather, who first worked with Leeson in the 1980s and who produces behind-the-scenes documentaries about Doctor Who, described the actor as “kind, considerate, professional, charming, talented, unassuming”. Lisa Bowerman, who has credits for work across the Doctor Who universe, remembered him as “an utterly lovely man, excellent company and – and I don’t hesitate to use this word for once – a truly iconic voice”.After leaving school, Leeson worked as a hospital porter before auditioning for Rada. Talking about his career in interviews, Leeson described it as being in two parts: “Half of my career has been pretty much as a stage actor and the television half of my career arose pretty much by accident.”View image in fullscreenThe stars of Rainbow, from left: Bungle, Zippy, George and Geoffrey Hayes. Leeson said he felt ‘really ill inside this bear suit’.Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockLeeson had a stint playing Bungle on the children’s show Rainbow, a job in which he described being “poured out of this costume every evening into a taxi”, because a day’s work in a small studio under the hot lights left him “really ill inside this bear suit”.He also once lamented the haircut he was given when appearing on Dad’s Army, saying: “I was livid because they gave me an army haircut, a real basin job, and then of course put me in a balaclava and a tin hat, so nobody could see the hair anyway.”He was still working as K9, providing voices for Big Finish audio dramas last year. This was despite, he once said, being told by producers at theBBCafter his debut that “under no circumstances would there be anything after the first episode has been shot and is in the can. So don’t expect too much. And here I am in 2025 still attached to Doctor Who … I got to meet a tremendous number of knees doing K9.”View image in fullscreenLeeson with K9.Photograph: ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsDoctor WhoTelevisionBBCChildren's TVFantasy TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested | Christmas | The Guardian
description: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites
Content: Can’t see the wood for the … Here’s your ultimate faux Christmas tree guide.Photograph: Jane Hoskyns/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCan’t see the wood for the … Here’s your ultimate faux Christmas tree guide.Photograph: Jane Hoskyns/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterChristmasReview‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – testedPick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favouritesThe best beauty Advent calendarsJane HoskynUpdatedMon 2 Nov 202610.59 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a realChristmastree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025.Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. TheCarbon Trustsays using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades.To help you choose your forever tree, I rounded up a veritable forest of the best fake Christmas trees, including pre-lit, frosted and mini models. Along with my husband, Alan, I compared them on factors including appearance, durability and whether they could be assembled without causing a breakdown in domestic relations. I also attempted a few on my own to see how easy they were to put up without help.Here I reveal which trees made Christmas come early, and which ones drove us straight to the mini liqueurs.At a glanceBest pre-lit Christmas tree and best overallB&QFull Fraser fir with warm white LEDs£160 at B&QBest budget Christmas treeRobert DyasAlaskan pine with LEDs£49.99 at Robert DyasBest unlit Christmas treeHabitatMixed-tip upswept£120 at ArgosBest realistic Christmas treeChristmas Tree WorldMatterhorn pine£119.99 at Christmas Tree WorldBest small Christmas treeAtkin and ThymeNordmann fir pre-lit potted tree£39 at Atkin and ThymeBest tabletop Christmas treeHomescapesArtificial pinecone & berry in burlap£26.99 at HomescapesWhy you should trust meI’ve spent three decades reviewing products, fromsmartphonestomattresses, so I’m professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically improve our lives by buying their stuff. I also have a solid background inhay feverandcats, both of which are triggered by having a real tree in the house, so I’m on a mission to find the best, greenest and safest alternative.How I testedTree trials: the artificial Christmas trees put to the test – with a little festive magic thrown inArtificial Christmas trees vary in many factors other than height. Foliage style, material, width, number of tips and method of assembly are important considerations when buying, but brands don’t always reveal these specs. My testing of 23 trees, then, involved a lot more measuring and tip counting than anticipated.To keep things simple, I requested the 6ft model of every full-size tree on my shortlist, all sourced from manufacturers and retailers. Taller trees tend to be correspondingly wider, and there was no way I’d fit a forest of 8ft trees in my house (or indeed reach them). I awarded kudos for the range of sizes available, though.While height in feet is the one specification you’re guaranteed to get when buying a tree, I learned not to take it too literally. My “6ft” trees varied in height from 180cm (actually 5ft 11in) to 183cm (just over 6ft).View image in fullscreen‘We timed how long it took to unbox each one, assemble it and arrange its foliage.’Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianMy lawfully wedded testing partner, Alan, helped me put up most of the trees one weekend. I also assembled a few on my own, including the largest and heaviest, to see whether they’d be too much trouble for someone living alone.We timed how long it took to unbox each one, assemble it and arrange its foliage. We looked for clearly marked sections that slotted easily but securely together, sturdy stands, strong, flexible branches that were easy to separate and position, and clear instructions.After measuring each tree, counting its tips and pausing for a much-needed mince pie, we gave them all a good shake. Fake plastic trees shed needles, too. Not nearly as many as a real tree, but some – including our own budget Lidl tree – are litterbugs, screeding the floor with tiny plastic strips. Minimal shedding is a good sign of a tree’s build quality and durability.View image in fullscreenA shining star: Jane’s homemade tree-toppers featured her beloved late cat, Iggy.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianNext, we loaded each full-size tree with decorations to see if the branches drooped or baubles slid off. The smaller trees were subjected to less festive baggage, but we crowned each one with a 150g homemade tree-topper to see how well its vertical top branch remained standing, if at all.Pre-lit trees save time when assembling, provided they have a good number of lights arranged evenly and attractively. There’s no point in spending more on a pre-lit tree (often £20 extra for a full-size model) if you have to then add even more lights. With these models, we also looked for well-concealed wiring, easy-to-connect sections and a long mains cable.Finally, we took each tree apart again and tried to squeeze them back into their boxes, with mixed success. They were collected by Southampton hardship charityScratch, which distributed them to families in need.The best artificial Christmas trees you can buy in 2026View image in fullscreenBranching out: let the tree-testing commence …Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianBest pre-lit Christmas tree and best overall:B&Q full Fraser fir with warm white LEDsB&QFull Fraser fir with warm white LEDs£160£160 at B&QWhat we loveWell-lit, easy to assemble and divine to look atWhat we don’t loveTop branch won’t hold a heavy ornamentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£160 (6ft) at B&QI hesitated to demote Habitat’s beautiful mixed-tip tree from its 2025 position as our best overall Christmas tree, but B&Q’s pre-lit Fraser fir just sneaks in to steal the top spot for 2026. It’s the dreamiest-looking Christmas tree I’ve ever welcomed into my home, and an excellent price for a pre-lit tree of this quality.Why we love itB&Q’s cosy, handsome tree took us less than 10 minutes to get up and lit – no wrestling with fairy lights required. I might have expected such easy assembly from B&Q, but I confess I hadn’t expected such aesthetic flair. The foliage, silhouette and pre-attached lights are simply gorgeous: realistic, stylish and festive enough to raise an “ooh” when you plug it in.A wave of a wand brings B&Q’s pre-lit Christmas tree to lifeThis tree was one of the easiest in my test to assemble. Most branches are on hinges, so they fall effortlessly into place when you hold each of the three sections upright. Slotting the sections together automatically connects the lights, so you never have to go looking for cables to screw together. The only time-consuming bit, as with most full-size trees, is separating and positioning the smaller branches to make the tree look as bushy as you want. The mixed-tip foliage is moderately dense, with plenty of room for ornaments, although the vertical branch at the top isn’t strong enough to hold anything heavy.The lights have a lovely warm white glow, with eight display settings controlled easily from a button on the mains plug. You can also set it to automatically switch on for six hours every day. There’s no remote control supplied, but it’s compatible with B&Q’sMagical Christmas tree wand(£49.49), which works with most pre-lit trees to switch the lights on and off with a wave and an audible twinkle.It’s a shame that …as with all pre-lit artificial trees, B&Q’s tree is likely to last many years longer than its lights, which are wrapped quite securely on to the branches.Dimensions (6ft version):183cm tall by 106cm at widest pointBranch tips:1,262Lights:300 warm white LEDsOther heights available:7ftFoliage material:PVC and polyethyleneB&QFull Fraser fir with warm white LEDs£160£160 at B&QWhat we loveWell-lit, easy to assemble and divine to look atWhat we don’t loveTop branch won’t hold a heavy ornamentBest budget Christmas tree:Robert Dyas Alaskan pine with LEDsRobert DyasAlaskan pine with LEDs£49.99£49.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveGreat value for a full-size pre-lit treeWhat we don’t loveNeedles aren’t very realistic, and they shedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£49.99 (6ft) at Robert DyasA good-value buy isn’t just cheap but built to last. Despite costing less than £50 (or £34.99 for theunlit version), this richly coloured tree is conveniently pre-lit and robust enough to survive several years of use.Why we love itBudget Christmas trees used to be sorry affairs, all droopy neon plastic with bald bits. Not any more, judging by the cheapest trees in my test. The Robert Dyas isn’t quite as bushy as some, but once you fluff up its plentiful branch tips, it’s an impressively verdant pyramid. Plug in the pre-adorned lights, and it’s showy enough to need few further embellishments.The lights are a simple affair. Each of the tree’s three sections has a string of LEDs with cable connectors, and the resulting combined string is mains-powered, so you don’t have to worry about batteries. It’s quick to put together and saves an awful lot of time and fairy-light-based hassle.There are no display options, such as flashing or colours, but the warm white light is a cosy choice. My experience with similar lights suggests these may only last a few years, but the tree itself is sturdy enough to survive many a Christmas and not just end up in landfill.It’s a shame that …it’s not as natural-looking as the Habitat tree below and sheds a few fake needles, although far fewer than a real tree.Dimensions (6ft version):180cm tall by about 90cm at widest pointBranch tips:we counted about 550Lights:we counted about 120 LEDsOther heights available:4ftFoliage material:PVCRobert DyasAlaskan pine with LEDs£49.99£49.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveGreat value for a full-size pre-lit treeWhat we don’t loveNeedles aren’t very realistic, and they shedBest unlit Christmas tree:Habitat mixed-tip upsweptHabitatMixed-tip upswept£120£120 at ArgosWhat we loveQuick and easy to assemble, and looks gorgeousWhat we don’t loveNot pre-lit, and the stand is a bit utilitarianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£120 (6ft) at ArgosThis beautiful tree uses a realistic silhouette and a mix of foliage styles to create a classy, textured look. It made a strong statement in the corner of our living room before we’d even added a bauble.Why we love itHabitat’s magnificent alpine fir lookalike was quick and easy to put together. Its three clearly marked sections slotted together easily, and the metal-hinged branches dropped effortlessly into place. This is one of several trees I tried assembling on my own, and I was pleasantly surprised by how quick and painless I found it – once unboxed, it took six minutes to get to a basic tree shape. It’s quite heavy when assembled, though, so I’d recommend building it in the spot you want it to stand for the next few weeks.This tree can be as bushy as you choose. If you prefer your festive topiary on the dense side, you can go to town sculpting the wired branch tips until there’s little space between them. If you’d rather have plenty of room to hang decorations, leave the branches as they are and fill the gaps with dangly doodads.As with most artificial Christmas trees, this one is “upswept”, which means the tips point upwards and can double as hooks for decorations. The branches supported ornaments well, and the top branch was strong enough to stand proud when adorned with my 150g topper.Most of the fake foliage on this tree is your standard AstroTurf-style slivers of green plastic, but thoughtful details set it apart. Each batch of fluffy fronds has a coniferous shape with shorter blades at the end, and several of the tips are rubbery PVC in a different shade of green to create a natural look. No bits fell to the floor, even when we gave the tree a good wobble.It’s a shame that …the gorgeously wide sweep of the lower branches means you’ll need a fairly spacious room to put it in. You’ll have loads of room for presents underneath, though.Dimensions (6ft version tested):183cm tall by 117.5cm at widest pointBranch tips:1,951Lights:noneOther heights available:5ft,7ft,8ftFoliage material:PVCHabitatMixed-tip upswept£120£120 at ArgosWhat we loveQuick and easy to assemble, and looks gorgeousWhat we don’t loveNot pre-lit, and the stand is a bit utilitarianBest realistic Christmas tree:Christmas Tree World Matterhorn pineChristmas Tree WorldMatterhorn pine£119.99£119.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveStrong, lifelike branches that hold loads of decorationsWhat we don’t loveIt’s heavy and its bristles are sharpView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£119.99 (6ft) at Christmas Tree WorldPreorder now, stock expected 6 NovemberThe dark green foliage of this gloriously lifelike pine will have your neighbours and visitors doing a double take. Its needles feel rather realistic, too, so it’s just as well that you get a pair of protective gloves in the box.Why we love itWhen I read “PVC”, I tend to think of shiny black pleather, but the dense PVC needles of this artificial pine tree are more like wire. It makes the branches feel a bit like bottle brushes, so you wouldn’t want to sit around stroking them, but I concede that Christmas trees are made to look at rather than fondle – and this one is a serious looker.Initial assembly was really quick, but plumping its strong branch tips to their fullest took us a while. Every one of the nearly 900 tips is adjustable and strong enough to support multiple decorations, and if you’re patient, the end result is spectacular.At 14kg, the Matterhorn is one of the heaviest and most robust of all the trees I tested. It comes with a 10-year guarantee, but I expect it will last much longer. As Christmas Tree World says in its excellent instruction booklet, this is far from being single-use plastic. I could even see it being passed down generations. Just don’t be tempted to put it outside because the steel hinges will rust.It’s a shame that …the foliage is darker than your average bright green fake tree. My husband adored it, but I found it a little too dark; it needed plenty of decorations to look camp enough for Christmas.Dimensions (6ft version):180cm tall by 110cm at widest pointBranch tips:856Lights:noneOther heights available:5ft, 7ft, 8ft; pluspre-litFoliage material:PVCChristmas Tree WorldMatterhorn pine£119.99£119.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveStrong, lifelike branches that hold loads of decorationsWhat we don’t loveIt’s heavy and its bristles are sharpBest small Christmas tree:Atkin and Thyme Nordmann fir pre-lit potted treeAtkin and ThymeNordmann fir pre-lit potted tree£39£39 at Atkin and ThymeWhat we loveLooks classy; works indoors or out; no mains cableWhat we don’t loveThe lights get tangled, and batteries aren’t includedView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£39 (3ft) at Atkin and ThymeAnother realistic pre-lit tree, this chic little three-footer ticks all the boxes except “tall”. It’s stylish, festive and lit with 50 warm white LEDs that leave plenty of room for your own decorations.Why we love itPre-lit trees are generally for indoor use only, but this stylish and realistic 3ft fir can go outdoors too. Its lights are powered via a sealed battery pack designed to withstand the elements, and the greenery is a weatherproof, rubbery plastic.Each branch is posable and quite long – this is a wide tree rather than a tall one. It comes firmly embedded in a high-quality pot, so you can pick up the whole thing by the tip without sending the pot crashing to the ground.You don’t even have to remember to switch off the lights. Once on, they’ll stay lit for six hours before automatically switching off – and then come on again at the same start time the next day.It’s a shame that …the light strings got tangled in the branches, so assembling this tree was more trouble than its 3ft size warranted. You also have to supply your own batteries.Dimensions:90cm tall by 86cm at widest pointBranchtips:350+Lights:50 warm white LEDsOther heights available:noneFoliage material:PVC and polyethyleneAtkin and ThymeNordmann fir pre-lit potted tree£39£39 at Atkin and ThymeWhat we loveLooks classy; works indoors or out; no mains cableWhat we don’t loveThe lights get tangled, and batteries aren’t includedBest tabletop Christmas tree:Homescapes artificial pinecone & berry in burlapHomescapesArtificial pinecone & berry in burlapfrom£26.99£26.99 at Homescapes£31.49 at AmazonWhat we loveReady to go out of the box, and the wrapped pot is lovelyWhat we don’t loveNot realistic, and not much room for baublesView image in fullscreen£26.99 (60cm) at Homescapes£31.49 at AmazonTabletop Christmas trees tend towards one of two extremes: ultra-festive straight out of the box, or so modest and realistic that you could use them as fake houseplants all year round.Why we love itHomescapes’ 60cm tree is very much the first of those types. The green foliage is fully decked with frosting, pine cones and faux berries to the point where there’s barely any room for your own decorations, but you could squeeze in a few if you tried. Even the pot is dressed in natural jute and string, looking much more attractive than some of the plastic stands the full-size trees come with.It’s a shame that …the frosting sheds a little, and no one would mistake this artificial mini-tree for the real thing.Dimensions:60cm tall by 32cm (my measure) at widest pointBranch tips:about 120 (my measure)Lights:noneOther heights available:noneFoliage material:plasticHomescapesArtificial pinecone & berry in burlapfrom£26.99£26.99 at Homescapes£31.49 at AmazonWhat we loveReady to go out of the box, and the wrapped pot is lovelyWhat we don’t loveNot realistic, and not much room for baublesThe best of the restView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianThe White Company pre-lit grand spruceThe White CompanyPre-lit grand spruce£375£375 at the White CompanyWhat we loveStunningly stylish and realisticWhat we don’t loveExpensive, and some may prefer warmer white lightsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£375 (6ft) at the White CompanyBest for:low-effort festive luxuryThere’s artificial fir and pine aplenty in this guide, but now it’s the turn of the third big festive tree type: spruce. (Fine Gardening has a handyguide to the differencebetween them.) This gorgeous tree is one of the most realistic I tested, and I also found it to be one of the easiest to put together. The hinged branches fell into place and their tips felt flexible but strong, staying where we’d put them despite being loaded with gaudy cat toys as well as baubles. If you prefer a more minimalist look, the tree looks great with lights only, no other adornments.The 390 white LED lights are distributed generously and evenly, although their white tone is a little on the cool side compared with the warmer, cosier shade of the other pre-loaded lights I tested. The lights’ eight display settings (flickering, slowly glowing and so on) are easy to cycle through using a button on the mains plug, which has a conveniently long cable.It didn’t make the final cut because …£375 for a standard six-footer is a lot to pay for a fake Christmas tree, even one as beautiful as this.Dimensions:182cm tall by 135cm at widest point;branch tips:1,559;lights:390 LEDs;other heights available:7.5ft;foliage material:“man-made materials”The White CompanyPre-lit grand spruce£375£375 at the White CompanyWhat we loveStunningly stylish and realisticWhat we don’t loveExpensive, and some may prefer warmer white lightsPremier Decorations Aspen firPremier DecorationsAspen fir£112£112 at ArgosWhat we loveBeautiful, rich green shade and super easy to assembleWhat we don’t loveFoliage is too thick to accommodate many decorationsView image in fullscreen£112 (6ft) at ArgosBest for:a really lush, verdant tree to adorn with your own lightsThis unlit tree is not quite as realistic or stylish as the Habitat one above, but it costs less – and, despite having fewer branch tips (1,029 to the Habitat’s 1,951), looks and feels much bushier. If you want your Christmas tree to be more tree than bauble, this would be a fine choice.The foliage is a beautifully deep, rich green, and the branches are hinged, so it doesn’t take much time or effort to get this tree up. It took me a fair while, though (20 minutes), to fluff it up by separating all the little branches, and there was less room than usual for large ornaments or dangly decorations in between the lush fake needles. If you wanted more freedom to festoon it with adornments, just separate fewer branches.It didn’t make the final cut because …standing next to the B&Q, Habitat and White Company trees, this one lacked fullness in its middle section and looked a little too triangular – more like a Christmas tree emoji than a real tree.Dimensions (6ft version):180cm tall by 127cm at widest point;branch tips:1,029;lights:none;other heights available:5ft,7ft,8ft;foliage material:PVCPremier DecorationsAspen fir£112£112 at ArgosWhat we loveBeautiful, rich green shade and super easy to assembleWhat we don’t loveFoliage is too thick to accommodate many decorationsDunelm pre-lit potted porch treesDunelmPre-lit potted porch trees£69£69 at DunelmWhat we loveReally easy to move around, indoors or outWhat we don’t loveThe trunks are a little thick for chicView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£69 (4ft, set of 2) at DunelmBest for:Christmassing up the front of your house without looking tackyDunelm’s battery-operated pre-lit potted trees work safely outdoors and indoors. They come as a pair and are designed to frame your front door, but you could just as easily use them in your garden or – if you really want to max out your festive space – as part of a multi-tree indoor display.The foliage is quite sparse, but this gives them a realistic look, and the rubbery needles are soft and natural-looking, in a subtle forest green. The lights are evenly distributed and look lovely, but you have to supply your own AA batteries. The battery packs are weatherproof despite using an easy click-shut mechanism rather than the more fiddly screw type, and the lightweight pots have a matt-white painted finish.It didn’t make the final cut because …the trunks look as if they belong on palm trees rather than Christmas trees, because they’re thick right to the top. Extending the top branch and switching the lights on helps to hide them.Dimensions:101.7cm (tree), 122cm (tree and pot) tall by 28.58cm at widest point;branch tips:about 500 per tree (my measure);lights:about 200 LEDs per tree (my measure);other heights available:none;foliage material:plasticDunelmPre-lit potted porch trees£69£69 at DunelmWhat we loveReally easy to move around, indoors or outWhat we don’t loveThe trunks are a little thick for chicDunelm snowy blue spruceDunelmSnowy blue spruce£99£99 at DunelmWhat we loveWonderfully thick branches and frostingWhat we don’t loveSnow is a microplastics nightmare and gets all over the floorView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£99 (6ft) at DunelmBest for:an indoor white ChristmasThis tree is not just lightly dusted with fake snow: it’s drenched in the stuff, like you’ve dipped it in glue then rolled it down an Alp. That makes its branches much thicker, and we found it hard to hang many baubles without it looking overdone, but at least that means it doesn’t need much work. String it with fairy lights or even just a topper, and it’s good to go.Underneath the frosting is a decent mid-range tree with a mix of tip types, not unlike the Habitat. We found it easy to assemble, and its metal stand is unusually sturdy. The best snowy tree I tested.Itdidn’t make the final cut because …fake snow doesn’t exactly enhance a tree’s sustainability credentials. Flocking can shedplastic particles, potentially contributing tomicroplastic pollution. It’s also an enthusiastic shedder, littering the floor in what looks like the dandruff of a giant.Dimensions (6ft version):180cm tall by 106cm at widest point;branchtips:we counted about 700;lights:none;other heights available:7ft;foliage material:plasticDunelmSnowy blue spruce£99£99 at DunelmWhat we loveWonderfully thick branches and frostingWhat we don’t loveSnow is a microplastics nightmare and gets all over the floorRobert Dyas Westbury multicolour fibre opticRobert DyasWestbury multicolour fibre optic£39.99£39.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveEasy to assemble and loads of colourful funWhat we don’t loveFeels cheap, may not last many yearsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£39.99 (3ft) at Robert DyasBest for:anyone for whom “too much” is never enough at ChristmasThe Westbury (or Woodbury, on the box) is one of the smallest trees I tested, but has the biggest kitsch appeal by far. After minimal adjustment of the fluffy branches, we plugged the tree into the mains, and it threw out so much light and colour that we squealed like excited children.The tree was a breeze to assemble, without a cable to get in the way, because the fairy lights and fibre-optic filaments are firmly embedded in the branch tips. Its handy remote control is ready to go out of the box, so we immediately set about changing colours, playing with effects and testing the timer.It didn’t make the final cut because …every time I went to move the tree it detached from the pot, which got annoying. Pick up the pot, rather than the tip of the tree, and you’ll be fine.Dimensions:90cm tall by 20cm at widest point;branchtips:we counted about 250;lights:80 fibre-optic tips and about 80 LEDs;other heights available:none;foliagematerial:plasticRobert DyasWestbury multicolour fibre optic£39.99£39.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveEasy to assemble and loads of colourful funWhat we don’t loveFeels cheap, may not last many yearsChristmas Tree World pre-lit ultra pop upChristmas Tree WorldPre-lit ultra pop up£149.99£149.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveQuick and easy to assembleWhat we don’t loveNot particularly realistic, if that’s what you wantView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£149.99 (6ft) at Christmas Tree WorldBest for:going from zero to fully lit tree in seconds before guests arriveThis one’s quicker to prepare than eggnog. Open the box and lift out the tree – like a big green crinoline skirt with branches and fairy lights attached – then prop it on to its central pole, switch on the lights,et voilà: your tree.It’s an absolute cracker, too. There’s plenty of room for decorations, but the mix of green shades gives the bendable tips a dense, textured look that means you can get away with a minimal scattering of baubles.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s expensive for what you get, and the uniformly triangular shape of the tree means no one would mistake it for the real thing.Dimensions (6ft version):180cm tall by 60cm at widest point;branchtips:686;lights:200 warm white LEDs;other heights available:7ft;foliage material:PVC and polyethyleneChristmas Tree WorldPre-lit ultra pop up£149.99£149.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveQuick and easy to assembleWhat we don’t loveNot particularly realistic, if that’s what you wantRobert Dyas Duchess slim pre-litRobert DyasDuchess slim pre-lit£49.99£49.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveBushy branches and a good number of lightsWhat we don’t loveNot much room for decorationsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£49.99 (5ft) at Robert DyasBest for:anyone short on time and spaceI expected this tree to be little more than a slimmed-down version of the Robert Dyas Alaskan pine. It’s much bushier, though, and its lights feel more securely attached, giving it a more durable feel.The branches are thickly adorned with deep green plastic foliage, giving a denser look than most other trees I tested – even before you’ve spent time adjusting all the tips. At 75cm wide, it’s big enough to look impressive but small enough to suit smaller living spaces.It didn’t make the final cut because …the thick foliage looks great, but it doesn’t leave much room for decorations.Dimensions (5ft version):150cm tall by 75cm at widest point;branchtips:327;lights:150;other heights available:none;foliagematerial:plasticRobert DyasDuchess slim pre-lit£49.99£49.99 at Robert DyasWhat we loveBushy branches and a good number of lightsWhat we don’t loveNot much room for decorationsChristmas Tree World ultra-lit Montagna firChristmas Tree WorldUltra-lit Montagna fir£449.99£449.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveQuick and easy to assemble but powerfully impressiveWhat we don’t loveExpensive, and possibly too many lights for an indoor treeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£449.99 (7ft) at Christmas Tree WorldBest for:voluminous razzle dazzle with very little workIf you’re going to charge this much more for a pre-lit Christmas tree, you’d better light it more attractively than I could with a string of fairy lights. Christmas Tree World has risen to that challenge and absolutely devoured it with this extravagantly illuminated beast of a tree.There’s not half as much work to do as you may think for a tree this size. It’s heavy but easy to put together, not least because its sections slot together smoothly and automatically connect the lights at the same time, so you don’t have to connect any cables. The tree is nicely balanced, with a lot of width at the bottom to keep it from toppling, and the branches are on hinges so they fall into place. The tips are a nice mix of textures and shades, and there are absolutely tons of lights, slightly more generously scattered at the top of the tree.It didn’t make the final cut because …it all looks “a bit much”, in the words of my visiting sister. That’s a matter of taste, but I do see what she means: the thick foliage, tall height and densely packed lights are overpowering unless you have a large living space.Dimensions (7ft version):210cm tall by 135cm at widest point;branch tips:3,467;lights:3,000 warm white micro LEDs;other heights available:8ft;foliage material:PVC and polyethyleneChristmas Tree WorldUltra-lit Montagna fir£449.99£449.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveQuick and easy to assemble but powerfully impressiveWhat we don’t loveExpensive, and possibly too many lights for an indoor treeOHS Autumn-Christmas burgundy treeOHSAutumn-Christmas burgundy tree£21£21 at Online Home ShopWhat we loveA cool splash of colour at a great priceWhat we don’t loveOne size only, and it’s narrower than premium six-footersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£21 (6ft) at Online Home ShopBest for:a quirky colour scheme in a small spaceIf you, like me, are thoroughly fed up with the greige-ing of modern life, break a few colour rules with this deep magenta tree. It’s much less bushy and decorative than it looks in OHS’s online photos (it doesn’t come adorned with giant pink bows, for starters), and, purpleness aside, it’s a very conventional fake Christmas tree with flat PVC needles. I also found it to shed a little more than the pricier trees in this rundown, and the branches aren’t strong enough to support heavy decorations.Having said that, it’s a lovely sight once assembled. I found it quick to put together, easy to move around on its lightweight but strong plastic stand, and nicely balanced with plenty of room for decorations and lights. It’s not particularly wide at the bottom, so it doesn’t have that luxurious sweep of a wider tree, but it would fit comfortably in a smaller living space.It didn’t make the final cut because …the colour is a little left field, and whether it looks good or not in your home depends on how the space is already decorated. Purple works wonderfully next to yellow walls, but less so next to beige.Dimensions:182cm tall by 100cm (my measure) at widest point;branch tips:500;lights:none;other heights available:none;foliage material:PVCOHSAutumn-Christmas burgundy tree£21£21 at Online Home ShopWhat we loveA cool splash of colour at a great priceWhat we don’t loveOne size only, and it’s narrower than premium six-footersChristmas Tree World black Italian pencilimoChristmas Tree WorldBlack Italian pencilimo£49.99£49.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveA great space-saver and conversation starterWhat we don’t loveDense branches don’t leave much room for decorationsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£49.99 (6ft) at Christmas Tree WorldBest for:an unconventional festive lookIf Coco Chanel were alive today, and assuming she could be persuaded to buy a plastic Christmas tree, this would be the one she’d go for – and woe betide you if you try to add a bauble or fairy light. After all, in her words: “black has it all”.Given that you are not, in fact, Coco Chanel, I’d recommend jazzing up the black a little. This slim, easy-to-assemble tree is a wonderful blank canvas for hundreds of colourful fairy lights and a large, stylish topper, or you could stick with white lights for a cool monochrome look.It didn’t make the final cut because …its tightly packed branches don’t leave much room for dangly decorations.Dimensions (6ft version tested):180cm tall by 58cm at widest point;branch tips:555;lights:none;other heights available:4ft,5ft,7ft,8ftpluspre-lit in all heights;foliage material:PVCChristmas Tree WorldBlack Italian pencilimo£49.99£49.99 at Christmas Tree WorldWhat we loveA great space-saver and conversation starterWhat we don’t loveDense branches don’t leave much room for decorationsDunelm pre-lit tinsel treeDunelmPre-lit tinsel tree£18£18 at DunelmWhat we loveNeeds no decorating whatsoeverWhat we don’t loveNot the most sustainable, and the branches aren’t strongView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£18 (3ft) at DunelmBest for:a minimalist Christmas, or just one part of a mad maximalist YuleDunelm’s tinsel tree is surprisingly versatile and likable. A tree made entirely from “rose gold” tinsel (more silver to my eye) may sound like the apex of kitsch, but it would be the ideal nod to Christmas if you love a cool, bare-home aesthetic. Even the cable connecting the LEDs to the mains has a clear plastic coating, making it almost invisible – and it’s a decent length, too.This tree would also be right at home in an over-the-top Christmas grotto, though. I mean, it’s three feet of fairy lights and tinsel. When listening back to my voice notes, I chuckled at the moment Alan and I switched on the lights and both exclaimed a delighted, “Ooh!” at the glittery cosiness of it all. “It’s actually making me feel Christmassy,” said Alan on a rainy October Sunday.The tinsel feels softer and of better quality than I’d expected, with different shades and types of tinsel to give the whole thing a textured look and feel. The lights are well distributed and ready to go, with no connector, and I didn’t notice any shedding. “It sounds like a contradiction in terms,” said Alan, “but this is quite classy tinsel.”It didn’t make the final cut because …the plastic stand slots together easily and feels sturdy, but I struggled to disassemble it, so I couldn’t fit it back into its box. It’s also worth knowing that the materials used to make tinsel trees tend to be less durable than conventional PVC and PE trees, and can shed microplastics.Dimensions:86.4cm tall by 12.7cm at widest point;branch tips:about 250 (my measure);lights:about 100 (my measure);other heights available:none;foliage material:plasticDunelmPre-lit tinsel tree£18£18 at DunelmWhat we loveNeeds no decorating whatsoeverWhat we don’t loveNot the most sustainable, and the branches aren’t strongDunelm artificial tree in rattan plant potDunelmArtificial tree in rattan plant pot£18£18 at DunelmWhat we loveRealistic and generic enough to display all yearWhat we don’t loveNot particularly festive until you decorate itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£18 (2ft 4in) at DunelmBest for:displaying all year roundThe realistically sparse foliage on this mini fir tree feels lovely and soft, and the flexible branches are easy to position – it’s just a shame there aren’t more of them. It’s hardly the most festive-looking tree I tested, either. But that’s actually something to like about it. You could display this houseplant-sized tree in its lovely woven basket all year, then dress it up in Christmassy whatnots when December rolls around.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a little uneven, with a mad thicket of branches at the bottom but hardly any at the top.Dimensions:70cm tall by 32cm at widest point;branch tips:about 150 (my measure);lights:none;other heights available:none;foliage material:plasticDunelmArtificial tree in rattan plant pot£18£18 at DunelmWhat we loveRealistic and generic enough to display all yearWhat we don’t loveNot particularly festive until you decorate itWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenDurability is key to reducing an artificial Christmas tree’s environmental impact.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianCan an artificial Christmas tree really be more sustainable than a real one?You mean, is a 7ft pyramid of plastic more environmentally friendly than an actual tree? Obviously not. Even if you retire a real tree by setting fire to it – a process not exactly short on pollutants and greenhouse gases – it’s still a greener choice in the short term. “An artificial tree has 10 times the carbon footprint of a natural tree that’s burned after Christmas,” said Alex Robinson, then CEO of UK environmental charityHubbub.An artificial tree is not just for one Christmas, however. “As long as an artificial tree is reused for 10 years or more, its environmental impact will balance out,” said Robinson. This backs up theCarbon Trust’s finding that a fake tree used for seven to 20 years, depending on its weight and materials, produces fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree each year.Real and fake trees have their environmental pros and cons, says Tristan Sissons, head of purchasing at Hillier Nurseries. “Real trees are biodegradable, and they’re grown for years before they’re sold, absorbing carbon dioxide from the air as they grow. But artificial trees can be used for years, so they avoid the ‘one use and dispose of’ mentality.”The best artificial Christmas trees are investment pieces thatcut landfill– you would hope. “Sadly, it’s estimated that artificial Christmas trees are used on average only four times, so it’s important to buy one that gets used year after year,” said Robinson.You don’t have to wheel out the same tree for 55 years like my family, but a decade or more is easily achieved if you choose wisely. Unless I’ve stated otherwise, all the trees I mention above seem robust enough to last 10 years or more, and a few – notably the Christmas Tree World Matterhorn pine, which comes with a 10-year guarantee – are so well built that they probably have a longer life expectancy than I do.How else can I minimise my tree’s carbon impact?View image in fullscreenHanging around: ideally, decorations, including LED lights, should have a similar lifespan to artificial trees. Many don’t, however.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianFlocked trees are trending, according to retailers includingChristmas Tree WorldandWayfair, but the fake snow they’re covered in makes your tree less green in more ways than one. A flocked tree can still have a smaller carbon footprint than an annual series of real trees, though, if you use it every year for long enough. According to the energy supplier100Green, artificial flocking increases the carbon break-even time for an artificial tree to 15 years, and if you spray it on a real tree, it’ll render the tree non-recyclable. It also makes a mess on the floor, albeit more manageable than real tree needles.Pre-lit trees have their green drawbacks, too. LED strings are unlikely to have as long a lifespan as a fake tree, and they’re often attached so securely to pre-lit trees that they can be a hassle to replace.The most frustrating environmental aspect of artificial Christmas trees, though, is where they’re made: China, almost without exception. Not a single tree I was able to source was made in the UK, including those whose brands put a homegrown vibe at the centre of their appeal, such as the Atkin and Thyme Nordmann fir. I’m now redoubling efforts to find UK-made trees to add to this roundup.Starting your Christmas shopping? Check out the Filter’sChristmas gift ideasand thebest beauty Advent calendarsView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.Explore the FilterJane Hoskyn is a features journalist and WFH pioneer with three decades of experience in rearranging bookshelves and “testing” coffee machines while deadlines loom. Her work has made her a low-key expert in all manner of consumables, from sports watches to solar panels.
