title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for sun-dried tomato assassin’s spaghetti | Food | The Guardian
description: A spicy, tomatoey pasta that’s cooked like a risotto, but much, much quicker
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A spicy, tomatoey pasta that’s cooked like a risotto, but much, much quicker
Content: Georgina Hayden’s sun-dried tomato assassin's spaghetti.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s sun-dried tomato assassin's spaghetti.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.FoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for sun-dried tomato assassin’s spaghettiA spicy, tomatoey pasta that’s cooked like a risotto, but much, much quickerGeorgina HaydenMon 2 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePopular in Puglia, assassin’s spaghetti is a rich and punchy dish that I just can’t get enough of. Unlike more familiar pasta recipes, the dried spaghetti is cooked in the sauce itself, and slowly “fed” hot broth, a bit like a risotto. Here, I’ve added sun-dried tomatoes for extra bite and bit of sweetness, and I’ve left the chilli level open, depending on your tolerance – one chilli is just warm, two is my own preference. You could finish with some parmesan, but it really doesn’t need it – there is so much flavour in this dish already.Sun-dried tomato assassin’s spaghettiPrep10 minCook30 minServes43 tbsp tomato puree120ml extra-virgin olive oil,plus extra for serving4 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1-2 red chillies, finely sliced (pith and seeds removed if you prefer less heat)100g sun-dried tomatoes, finely chopped300ml passataSea salt andblack pepper350g spaghettiA few basil sprigs, leaves pickedDilute the tomato puree in a litre of just-boiled water and set aside. Put a large frying pan or saute pan that’s wide enough to hold the spaghetti flat on a medium-low heat. Add the oil, garlic and chillies, and fry for a minute, until lightly fragrant. Stir in the sun-dried tomatoes, cook for a couple of minutes, then add the passata and season generously. Simmer vigorously for five minutes, then, once the sauce looks glossy and rich, lay in the spaghetti, spreading it out to cover the bottom of the pan.Cook on a medium-high heat until the pasta has absorbed the sauce, then ladle in some of the hot tomato broth. Keep cooking until all the liquid has been absorbed, then ladle in more broth. If need be, turn up the heat to high to get a crust underneath and help the pasta absorb the broth. After eight to 10 minutes, use a spatula to flip over the pasta – it should have a slightly charred crust underneath. Keep ladling in more broth, letting it absorb each time before adding more, just like risotto. The pasta should be ready after a further eight to 10 minutes.Flip the spaghetti again – it should now have lovely, crisp, charred edges – then serve with a drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil and the basil leaves torn over the top.Explore more on these topicsFoodPastaTomatoesItalian food and drinkHerbs and spicesMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: Disco cauliflower and bhajis: Maray’s cauliflower recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Cauliflower is a flavour sponge, but miraculously stays satisfyingly al dente. Smother it in chermoula, tahini and harissa, or transform it into spicy bhajis served with a lively chutney
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cauliflower is a flavour sponge, but miraculously stays satisfyingly al dente. Smother it in chermoula, tahini and harissa, or transform it into spicy bhajis served with a lively chutney
Content: James Bates’ disco cauliflower with chermoula, tahini and harissa.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenJames Bates’ disco cauliflower with chermoula, tahini and harissa.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.FoodDisco cauliflower and bhajis: Maray’s cauliflower recipesCauliflower is a flavour sponge, but miraculously stays satisfyingly al dente. Smother it in chermoula, tahini and harissa, or transform it into spicy bhajis served with a lively chutneyJames BatesMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCauliflower is a culinary gem. Often overlooked, it possesses a remarkable ability to absorb complex seasonings and textures while maintaining a satisfying bite. It’s also perfect for braising, frying or roasting, and provides a canvas for bold, herbaceous and spicy flavour profiles that elevate an ostensibly simple brassica into a true centrepiece.Disco cauliflower with chermoula, tahini and harissaThe quantities for the green sauce will make more than you need to dress the cauliflower, but it keeps very well in a jar or sealed container in the fridge for up to a week and is delicious on all sorts, so it’s well worth making extra.Prep10 minCook50 minServes23 tbsp sea salt2 tsp ground turmeric1 largecauliflower(about 1.2kg),leaves trimmed, then cut in half from top to root (900g net)3 tbsp vegetable oilFor the tahini sauce3 tbsp tahini paste1 tbsp lemon juiceFor the green sauce100g fresh coriander, including stalks100g fresh parsley, including stalks, plus a little extra to finish2 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped2 medium red chillies, stalks removed and roughly chopped50g lemon juice10gfinetable salt180ml rapeseed oilFor the honey dressing2 tbsp harissa paste1 tsp honey1 tsp white-wine vinegarTo finish100g natural yoghurtPomegranate seedsand flaked almonds1 tsp paprikaBring a large pan of water to a boil, then stir in two tablespoons of the salt and a teaspoon of the turmeric. Drop in the cauliflower halves, simmerfor about 10 minutes, until just tender, then drain and leave in the colander for 10 minutes to steam-dry and to drain off all the excess water.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. In a small bowl, mix the vegetable oil with the remaining salt and turmeric, then rub this all over the cauliflower. Put the blanched cauliflower halves cut side downon an oven trayand roast for 20-25 minutes, turning once halfway, until charred at the edges.While the cauliflower is roasting, prepare the three sauce toppings. In a small bowl, mix the tahini and lemon juice with a tablespoon of water and set aside.For the green sauce, put the coriander and parsley in a food processor, blitz for a few seconds, then add the garlic, chilli, lemon and salt, and blitz again briefly, so the mix still has some texture. Slowly work in the rapeseed oil, until nicely emulsified.Finally, in another small bowl, loosen the harissa with the honey and wine vinegar.When the cauliflower is ready, transfer it to a large platter. Spoon the yoghurt evenly over the top, followed by drizzles of the tahini, green and harissa sauces. Scatter generously with pomegranate seeds, flaked almonds and chopped parsley, finish with a dusting of paprika and serve hot.Maray bhajisView image in fullscreenJames Bates’ bhajis.Prep20 minCook15 minServes4-6Salt1 tsp ground turmeric1 smallcauliflower(about 500g), leaves trimmed500g white onion, peeled and finely slicedRapeseed oil125gfrozen garden peas65g desiccated coconut20g black onion seeds20g white sesame seeds1 tspchilli flakes2 tsp garam masala60g cornflour65g gram flour1 tsp lemon juice50ml sparkling waterBring a large pan of water to a boil, then stir in two tablespoons of salt and the turmeric. Drop in the whole cauliflower and simmer for about eight minutes, until the cauliflower is cooked but retains a little bite. Drain, leave to cool, then grate the cooked cauliflower on the large holes of a box grater to shred it.Meanwhile, in a pan on a medium heat, saute the sliced onions in two tablespoons of rapeseed oil for six or seven minutes, until just soft. In a large bowl, mix the grated cauliflower, sauteed onions, peas, coconut, seeds, spices, flours, lemon juice and a teaspoon and a half of salt, then slowly whisk in the sparkling water until you have a loose batter that is thick enough to retain its shape when frying. The mixture should feel light, not dense.Pour enough rapeseed oil into a heavy-bottomed pan to come 2½cm up the sides and put on a. medium-high heat. When it’s up to frying temperature, check the seasoning of the bhaji mix by frying a small blob of the batter until golden brown and crisp, then taste and adjust the bhaji mix as required. Working in batches, scoop large dessertspoonfuls of the bhaji mixture into the hot oil and fry for two minutes on each side,until golden brown and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm in a low oven while you repeat with the remaining batter. Season with more salt to taste, and serve hot with some of the chutney below.Kara chutneyView image in fullscreenJames Bates’ kara chutney.A vibrant, tangy and fresh condiment that’s a great accompaniment to the bhajis.Prep10 minCook25 minServesMakes 1 big jar125g banana shallots, peeled and thinly sliced1 tsp cumin seeds25ml rapeseed oil25g red lentils3 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped10g grated fresh ginger30g desiccated coconut, toasted in a dry frying pan until golden10g salt (about 1⅔ tsp)25g sugar35ml white-wine vinegar10g tomato puree100g plum tomatoes, cut into chunky diceTo finish50ml rapeseed oil1 tsp mustard seeds10 fresh curry leaves, or 2 tbsp dried curry leaves, but fresh are by far best1 pinch chilli flakes, or to tasteOver a medium heat, fry the shallots and cumin seeds in the rapeseed oil for 10-15 minutes, until golden, then stir in the lentils, garlic and ginger, and fry, stirring, for another minute. Add 25g of the toasted coconut (save the rest to garnish) and the remaining chutney ingredients, then pour in 75ml water and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook gently, stirring occasionally, for 15-20 minutes, until the lentils are completely soft and the mix has reduced and thickened. Tip the chutney into a blender and blitz to a smooth puree.To finish the chutney, heat the rapeseed oil in a small saucepan, then add the mustard seeds and curry leaves, and cook for about 20 seconds, until they start to pop. Take off the heat, tip the seeds, leaves and oil into the pureed chutney, then fold in thoroughly.Spread the chutney on a platter, top with the cooked bhajis above, scatter over the reserved toasted coconut and some chilli flakes, and serve.James Bates is co-founder ofMarayin LiverpoolExplore more on these topicsFoodVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkSnacksMain courseSide dishesHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patients | Horses | The Guardian
description: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life
Content: Black Pearl with Victoria's daughter Sophie in June 2008.Photograph: Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff NetanelView image in fullscreenBlack Pearl with Victoria's daughter Sophie in June 2008.Photograph: Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff NetanelThe pet I'll never forgetHorsesThe pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patientsBlack Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my lifeVictoria Nodiff-Netanel, as told to Ann LeeMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI trained and competed in dressage for many years and after I retired, I decided to buy a miniature horse for company at home in southern California. I bought Black Pearl from Quicksilver Ranch in Solvang, California, in 2008, when she was six months old. She was a fluffy little thing and would run around at warp speed, then run back to snuggle. She stole my heart from the beginning. I had no idea that Black Pearl would inspire me to change my whole focus in life.I started training her for fun and began to teach her tricks. She learned quickly. I thought of a great way to give back to the community – Black Pearl and I could find ways to help people. I started to wonder where I could visit with my little horse.View image in fullscreenHorse sense … Black Pearl inspired Victoria to set up an  animal therapy charity.Photograph: Terri Miller/Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff-NetanelBlack Pearl inspired me to start my charity,Mini Therapy Horses. If it wasn’t for her outgoing personality, I wouldn’t have attempted it. Now I run a programme with her and eight other miniature therapy horses, visiting patients in the lockdown psychiatric unit at a veterans’ hospital in Los Angeles. The vets have been through so much: they have PTSD, traumatic brain injuries and/or drug addiction and many are homeless. They can pet and hug the horses – they love them. It helps them to feel less lonely and isolated.View image in fullscreenMy little pony … Victoria and Black Pearl with a service veteran in hospital in Los Angeles, circa 2010.Photograph: Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff-NetanelWe also visit several other hospitals – many of the kids and adults are away from home for a long time and the time they spend with our minis is very comforting. If a child is visually impaired we can take their hands and help them to feel our little horses. They can brush their coats and this tactile experience makes them very happy.Black Pearl will also walk beside a patient in a wheelchair while they hold the reins. Some patients are missing their own animals at home, so cuddling her might be just what the doctor ordered.View image in fullscreenHay there … a big horse greets a tiny horse resting in the boot of a car.Photograph: Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff-NetanelOf all our miniature horses, Black Pearl is the biggest show-off. She feeds off everyone’s positive energy and loves to do her tricks. She is by far our best keyboard player – tapping and rubbing her little muzzle back and forth on the keys. She can stand and walk on her hind legs, give a high five with her hoof, smile, nod and shake her head “yes” and “no”, strut with her front legs, and much more.View image in fullscreenGiddy up … Victoria’s therapy horses in their paddock.Photograph: Courtesy of Victoria Nodiff-NetanelWorking with Black Pearl has given me the opportunity to meet people from every walk of life. She inspired me to follow my passion, with her as a partner, in helping others. I love this little horse – she has been a blessing.Explore more on these topicsHorsesThe pet I'll never forgetPetsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They assume the man next to me is the owner’: four women doing business in Africa in their own way | Global development | The Guardian
description: From feeding schoolchildren to recycling tyres, these entrepreneurs are challenging stereotypes while solving social and environmental problems
Author: Sarah Johnson
Headline: From feeding schoolchildren to recycling tyres, these entrepreneurs are challenging stereotypes while solving social and environmental problems
Content: From left: Wawira Njiru in Kenya, Ifedolapo Runsewe in Nigeria, Shine Kyokushaba in Uganda and Chifuno Stevensin Malawi.Composite: Edwin Ndeke/ Valentine Benjamin/Stefanie GlinskiView image in fullscreenFrom left: Wawira Njiru in Kenya, Ifedolapo Runsewe in Nigeria, Shine Kyokushaba in Uganda and Chifuno Stevensin Malawi.Composite: Edwin Ndeke/ Valentine Benjamin/Stefanie GlinskiGlobal development‘They assume the man next to me is the owner’: four women doing business in Africa in their own wayFrom feeding schoolchildren to recycling tyres, these entrepreneurs are challenging stereotypes while solving social and environmental problemsSupported byAbout this contentValentine Benjamin,Stefanie Glinski,Sarah Johnsonand Kenneth ZindondoMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 05.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfrica is thought to havea higher proportion of female entrepreneurs than any other continentand yet manystill struggle to access financing. Four business leaders from Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya and Malawi tell us about the inspiration behind their success – and the challenges women still face.Ifedolapo Runsewe, Nigeria: giving waste tyres a new lifeOn the outskirts of Ibadan in south-westNigeria, thousands of discarded tyres are fuelling an industrial experiment.They arrive at Freee Recycle’s factory where they are sorted, shredded and reduced to rubber granules. Some will become playground surfaces. Others will be turned into gym flooring, paving blocks and interlocking tiles.Ifedolapo Runsewe, the company’s founder, is building an industrial recycling business in a sector where women rarely own factories or lead manufacturing operations.In Nigeria,women own about 40% of small businesses, but56% of female entrepreneurs’ last loan applications were denied, compared with 17% for men, according to the World Bank. In capital-heavy fields such as recycling, this financing gap may prevent female entrepreneurs becoming factory owners.View image in fullscreenIfedolapo Runsewe set up her tyre recycling business after 12 years in banking.Photograph: Valentine BenjaminRunsewe has made that leap. She has built a factory that turns one of Nigeria’s most intransigent waste problems into products. The factory employs about 62 people, collecting tyres from four states in Nigeria: Oyo, Lagos, Osun and Kwara.Nigeria produces millions of waste tyres each year. Many end up in dumps or are burned to recover scrap metal, releasing hazardous pollutants.“Burning tyres releases a complex mix of toxic chemicals – it’s not just pollution, it’s a direct public health threat,” says Oladele Ogunseitan, a presidential chair at the University of California, Irvine.After more than 12 years in banking, Runsewe became interested in tyre recycling after seeing first-hand the impact of burning tyres. What convinced her there was a business opportunity was the fact that almost every part of a tyre can be recovered and reused. She started Freee Recycle in 2020.The challenge has been to convince people that waste can be a business.View image in fullscreenRunsewe displays a bag made from recycled tyres.Photograph: Valentine BenjaminRecycling tyres requires substantial capital. Turning the recovered rubber into finished products requires another layer of machinery, expertise and investment. And unlike collecting waste, manufacturing depends on finding customers willing to buy what comes out of the recycling process.“People view recycling as more of an informal, small-scale activity rather than a serious business capable of generating substantial returns,” she says. “And that is absolutely not true.”Early on, she encountered another obstacle: the assumption that an industrial recycling business was a man’s domain.“I’d go into banks and boardrooms, and investors would assume the man next to me is the owner. As soon as I spoke, the question came up: why should we give a woman millions, hundreds of millions?”Yet she does not want her business reduced to a story about gender. “I don’t think organisations choose to work with us because we’re female-owned,” she says. “They see a brand that is good, transparent, credible and ethical.”Freee Recycle has secured partnerships with organisations including Michelin, Save the Children and the International Committee of the Red Cross. And she is looking into expanding beyond tyres. “There are plans to set up what would be the first in Nigeria dedicated to recycling aerosols, like insecticide cans and spray containers,” she says.Through the company’s Freee art residency programme, launched in 2025, discarded tyres have been transformed into large-scale artworks inspired by African history and culture, including the Bata drum, Ikom monoliths and Benin bronze traditions.The symbolism is deliberate: materials that would otherwise be thrown away are being given another life.Valentine BenjaminKyokushaba Shine, Uganda: building solar-powered irrigation systemsAs a little girl, Kyokushaba Shine would watch her mother get up before dawn, labouring hard all day to tend to the acres of onions she had planted near their house in Kabale, southernUganda.Often her mother’s harvests – the family’s only source of income – would fail. A lack of water or degraded soil could leave them with almost no yield, making it difficult to put enough food on the table.Now, as a water engineer and entrepreneur, Kyokushaba, 31, has made it her mission to help farmers like her mother.“I started my company with the goal of designing small and affordable irrigation systems for smallholder farmers. When I started the business in February 2025, I had neither staff nor capital, but I had a goal in mind and I wanted to work towards it,” she says.View image in fullscreenShine Kyokushaba wants to ensure farmers have reliable access to water.Photograph: Stefanie GlinskiIn just over a year, Kyokushaba says Winta Engineering Solutions has installed 30 water systems across Uganda, most of them solar powered, and more than 10 of them for female farmers. Her business employs a team of people, 80% of them women.The goal, Kyokushaba says, is relatively simple: ensure farmers have reliable access to water using mostly solar-powered pumps, then combine this with modern irrigation technology, such as drip irrigation, that allows water to be used more efficiently. Winta Engineering Solutions designs and installs the equipment, digging boreholes where needed and providing farmers with training on how to operate and maintain the systems.Kyokushaba has started collaborating with local microfinance providers, connecting them with farmers, who are offered loans of about 5m Ugandan shillings (about £1,000), a sum most do not have readily available, but can usually repay within two years.She also runs educational programmes that address bigger challenges, including the impact of the climate crisis and soil degradation on farmers’ ability to produce food.“Farmers want results fast, so they use fertilisers to increase their yields quickly, but sometimes that means they don’t protect the health of their soil,” says Kyokushaba. “It’s not enough to have sufficient water if the soil is degraded, and that’s why we have started working on awareness campaigns.”View image in fullscreenKyokushaba pitches her business idea to potential funders at the African Food Systems Forum.Photograph: Stefanie GlinskiThere is one other issue that matters deeply to Kyokushaba: creating opportunities for women in a sector still largely dominated by men.“As a woman, you can show up in spaces where men are trying to push you out, and where men are trying to set the agenda. This needs to change,” she says.She is also driven by personal reasons. “I have a five-year-old daughter, and it’s just me and her. I want her to see and know that she can do anything she puts her mind to. I want her to know that she’s strong, that women and girls are strong.”Stefanie GlinskiWawira Njiru, Kenya: feeding 700,000 schoolchildren a dayFrom a young age, Wawira Njiru knew she wanted to help people at home inKenya, but it was not until she was at university abroad that her path to feeding the nation’s schoolchildren began.While studying for a degree in nutrition in Australia, she raised A$1,200 (£630) and decided to build a small makeshift kitchen in her home town of Ruiru, 12 miles (20km) from Nairobi. In 2012, it started providing 25 children with one school meal every day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Teachers said food was the biggest need. Kids were fainting. One teacher said they used to keep packs of glucose in the staff room for when a child faints. I thought that was insane. Why don’t we just feed them?”View image in fullscreenMost of Wawira Njiru’s produce comes from local smallholder farmers.Photograph: Edwin Ndeke/The GuardianFood4Education was born, and nearly 15 years later it has 209 kitchens which feed more than 700,000 children daily. Food is distributed using a fleet of motorbikes and trucks.For an operation cooking for hundreds of thousands of children, the emissions could be huge. But the flagship kitchen in Nairobi, which feeds about 60,000 children, runs onsolar and steam.Kitchens have been transitioning to use eco-briquettes made in Kenya from sawdust and agricultural waste, including leaves. “If we were to cook for every child in Kenya using firewood, it would beequivalent to 1.1m acres[0.45 hectares] of forest being cut down. That’s about three times the size of London,” says Njiru.The amount of food waste is small, running at about 2%, because a digital platform verifies who is eating before the next day’s food is produced.In early 2026, there was a mango crisis in Murang’a county when hot weather meant there was a surplus of the fruit and 5,000 farmers were left with produce they could not sell. “The governor reached out and asked if we could absorb the mangoes,” says Njiru. “We bought 1.3m mangoes over a couple of weeks and distributed them to schoolchildren.” The farmers were paid, children were fed and there was minimal waste.View image in fullscreenStudents are served a meal at Salama primary school in Huruma, Nairobi.Photograph: Edwin Ndeke/The GuardianAbout80%of everything Food4Education buys comes from local smallholder farmers. “We make sure we’re aligning what we eat with what’s being grown. When there are more beans, we serve more beans. When there’s more of a certain type of lentil, we serve that,” says Njiru.She says the organisation now has a huge amount of buying power, given that it buys about130 tonnesof food a day.Food4Education, with 6,000 employees, is mostly powered by women. Njiru noticed that men were reluctant to work in kitchens when she started out. “I’ll never forget the man who once told me he’d rather be jobless than work in a kitchen,” she says. Having a predominantly female workforce has affected how the organisation runs, she believes. “I think women want to get things done. I’m not saying men don’t, but it’s very innate to women to focus on what needs to be done and not be paralysed by a big challenge.”Njiru gets emotional when she talks about the impact on their livelihoods. “I meet women and they say, ‘I was able to build my first home’ or ‘I was able to save up to send my child to university’. Now they’re independent and can take care of themselves.”Sarah JohnsonChifuno Stevens, Malawi: turning peanut shells into fuelWhen Chifuno Stevens looks at Dedza town, a bustling district in Malawi’s central region, she sees a landscape caught between natural beauty and severe environmental threat.For years, household waste from the town has been dumped haphazardly across Dedza mountain. At the same time, a heavy reliance on firewood and conventional wood charcoal has rapidly stripped the mountain of its trees.Deeply concerned by the ecological damage, Stevens, 35, decided to step in.“I started the organisation in September 2020 to address two massive challenges: poor waste management and rapid deforestation,” she says. “Many households rely on charcoal and firewood for cooking, which puts enormous pressure on our forests. Meanwhile, agricultural waste is discarded and left to rot. I wanted to find a practical way to address both problems while creating economic opportunities for local women.”Six years later, what began as a community awareness initiative has blossomed into theChifuno Changa Green Initiative(CCGI), a women-led enterprise that fuses environmental conservation with economic empowerment.View image in fullscreenChifuno Stevens’ company sells charcoal briquettes made from agricultural waste.Photograph: Courtesy of  Chifuno StevensThe initiative works directly with 18 local women from the Dauya Ladies Environmental Group.The enterprise’s core activity revolves around producing and selling eco-friendly charcoal briquettes made from agricultural waste, specifically peanut shells. By converting discarded shells into a clean-burning alternative, CCGI provides families with a viable fuel source that actively reduces the pressure on endangered local forests.The business has also found creative ways to integrate into the local economy, partnering with its sister business, Dedza Pottery. The pottery workshop uses CCGI’s briquettes as a supplementary fuel when energy supplies fall short.To build long-term economic resilience, Stevens has expanded the group’s operations beyond green energy. Since early 2026, CCGI has provided sewing classes for its members, enabling them to make and sell reusable tote bags using vibrant local kitenge fabric.View image in fullscreenChifuno Stevens (front row in white T-shirt) with the Chifuno Changa Green Initiative team.Photograph: Courtesy of Chifuno Changa Green InitiativeShe has also begun offering tours of the briquette workshop to tourists, enabling them to interact with the artisans and have a go at making the briquettes themselves.“Some people are hesitant to try charcoal briquettes because they are unfamiliar with them,” she says. “We have found that people need to experience using them to trust their benefits, so we are working to carry out more live demonstrations to build that confidence.”Keeping the products affordable for low-income consumers while trying to grow the business is a delicate balancing act, says Stevens.“As a woman leading an organisation, I want to ensure that business growth translates into meaningful and sustainable income opportunities for the women involved,” she says. “My ultimate aim is for CCGI to become a financially sustainable business rather than one that depends entirely on external aid.”Securing a reliable, year-round supply of peanut shells remains a constant puzzle, compounded by a pressing need to invest in specialised equipment to make production processes more efficient. Like many small enterprises, systemic barriers to accessing finance have at times restricted CCGI’s capacity to scale up and meet growing demand.Despite the uphill battle against these economic and environmental challenges, Stevens’s mission remains unchanged.“I remain deeply committed to this work because I firmly believe that protecting the environment and creating economic opportunities for women must go hand in hand,” she says. “That is the ultimate key to unlocking a sustainable future.”Kenneth ZindondoExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentAfricaWomen's rights and gender equalityRecyclingSchoolsNutrition and developmentSchool mealsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What to look for if you’re buying a smart lock in the UK | Home improvements | The Guardian
description: More people are fitting keyless devices to their front door – but are they worth it and do they affect your insurance?
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: More people are fitting keyless devices to their front door – but are they worth it and do they affect your insurance?
Content: Some locks incorporate the smart feature and handle in a single unit.Photograph: frantic/AlamyView image in fullscreenSome locks incorporate the smart feature and handle in a single unit.Photograph: frantic/AlamyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Home improvementsWhat to look for if you’re buying a smart lock in the UKMore people are fitting keyless devices to their front door – but are they worth it and do they affect your insurance?Shane HickeyMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 10.29 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the nights draw in, thoughts turn to home security. A growing number of British homeowners are choosing to upgrade their front doors with tech-enabled “keyless” smart locks, which allow them to be opened by phone, fob, fingerprint or a number pad.But you need to make sure you have the right lock for the door – and that your insurance isn’t invalidated by installing it.What are they?They allow you to get into your home without a key, instead using a code, a phone, a fingerprint, a voice assistant such as Siri or facial recognition to give you entry.Some can be operated remotely via wifi so that if a tradesman calls to do work, you can let them in wherever you are. Many offer a combination of several options.In South Korea, and some Scandinavian countries, they are becoming the norm, says Steffan George of the Master Locksmiths Association (MLA), a UK trade body. In the UK they are more common on offices, but interest is increasing.View image in fullscreenSkilled burglars can pick typical traditional locks.Photograph: Zoonar GmbH/AlamyThe types vary in complexity. Some have the smart feature and a handle in one unit that fully replaces an existing door handle. Others are made up of a small unit which can be fitted on an existing lock, sitting on top of it, opening the door when activated. This type essentially turns a traditional lock into a smart one.And there is a third type where the existing mechanical lock cylinder is swapped for an electronic one, which opens the lock once activated. Some allow for a physical key to be used in an emergency.How much do they cost?They range from less than £100 to well over £1,000. Shane Hales, of HalesLocks in Sidcup, Kent, puts the starting price for a good quality version at between £200 and £250 for the unit. Getting a professional to fit them will add to the cost.Look out for the Kitemark on the faceplate to ensure that it meets security requirements set by the British Standards Institution.Sold Secure, an agency which judges the performance of locks, has a certification calledSS504. To qualify, locks are tested for physical security, technical performance and cybersecurity.Hales highlights theBlack X(about £200) and theUltion Nuki (£339)as two well-regarded units.George says that a smart lock is unlikely to last as long as a traditional one, which “will last 20 years easily with just a little bit of lubrication”. Hales adds that, in his experience, smart locks will last for five to six years before they need to be replaced.Willit work on my front door?In the UK front doors are made from a variety of materials, including UPVC, timber, and a composite of different types. Checking the lock works with whatever type of door you have is vital. Many US imports will be unsuitable for British doors because of differences in the locking cylinders.Lots of lockmakers have guides on their websites so you can check whether their product would work for your home. For example,Yale has a “smart lock compatibility checker”which uses a visual guide on what your lock looks like to recommend options.You can email in pictures of your existing fitting and door to some installers and manufacturers, and they will advise what is suitable.How are they installed?View image in fullscreenRetrofit smart locks are usually installed on the inside of the door.Photograph: Mikhail Reshetnikov/AlamyRetrofit smart locks are usually installed on the inside of the door and work with the existing cylinder – the barrel in which you insert the key. They have a motorised unit inside which connects to the lock and turns it open.To install one yourself, you will need basic tools. Most people will also want to choose a lock that has been designed to be easy to install, with no modifications needed to the door itself.Things get more complicated when wiring, drilling or carpentry is needed to get the lock to fit properly, or if the door you have is UPVC, composite or non-standard.Checkatrade, the tradespeople’s recommendation site, says installation costs vary; it puts the labour at between £63 for a basic keypad lock and £210 for a Z-wave-enabled lock, a communication system similar to Bluetooth and wifi.Will this affect insurance?If you are considering getting a smart lock, it is important to run it by your home insurer to be sure that what you buy adheres to its standards.The Association of British Insurers (ABI) says you should check the terms of your policy before making any changes. “Some home insurers have specific requirements for the type of lock you use to protect your home, and your provider will be able to advise you,” says its general insurance policy adviser, Charlie Inwood.Your insurer may also require that the lock is put in by a professional.Hales says people should always get professional advice. “There is no one size that fits all doors. For that lock to be compliant, it needs to fit properly, and if it’s not fitted properly, then you know you could leave yourself open to problems.”Explore more on these topicsHome improvementsConsumer affairsPropertyInsuranceCrimeSmart homesHome insurancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be risky
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Health & wellbeingIs it true that … drinking alcohol warms you up?A hot toddy might make you feel toasty, but drinking in cold conditions can be riskyKate LloydMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHot toddies, red wine, a dram of whisky: alcohol has long been a go-to remedy for keeping warm. But while a drink might make youfeelwarmer, does it actually help? “There’s a perception of warmth, but in reality, it doesn’t occur,” says Winston Morgan, professor of toxicology, equity and inclusive practice at the University of East London.Alcohol affects the body’s temperature-regulating system. Our core body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a region of the brain that helps regulate how we respond to changes in temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the surface of the skin widen, a process known as vasodilation. This allows more warm blood to flow close to the skin, where heat can escape into the surrounding air. When we get too cold, the opposite happens. The blood vessels narrow, or constrict, reducing blood flow to the skin and helping to conserve heat.double quotation markAlcohol encourages heat to escape from the body, increasing the risk of hypothermiaAlcohol interferes with this process. It causes blood vessels near the skin to widen, even when our core body temperature has not risen. More warm blood reaches the skin’s surface, which can make us feel hot, and even leave us reaching to take off clothing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … muscle turns into fat if you stop working out?Read more“You’re sending more blood to your skin, which gives you the sensation of feeling warmer,” says Morgan. “But actually you’re not. Your body’s just moving around the blood.”In fact, by increasing blood flow to the skin, alcohol encourages heat to escape from the body, potentially lowering core temperature. That can increase the risk of hypothermia in sufficiently cold conditions, particularly if you start removing clothing.“After some time, what actually happens is your core becomes cooler,” says Morgan. “So, in a cold environment, you don’t really want to be drinking a lot of alcohol.”Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingIs it true that …AlcoholfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A new start after 60: At 26, I saw my dream Porsche. At 68, I built one from scratch | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Bill Drysdale could never afford the sports car he fell in love with as a young man. So when he retired, he went to night school to learn welding, and began assembling it, bit by bit ...
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Bill Drysdale could never afford the sports car he fell in love with as a young man. So when he retired, he went to night school to learn welding, and began assembling it, bit by bit ...
Content: Bill Drysdale at Shelsley Walsh, Worcestershire, in July 2024.Photograph: Joy RichingsView image in fullscreenBill Drysdale at Shelsley Walsh, Worcestershire, in July 2024.Photograph: Joy RichingsA new start after 60Life and styleA new start after 60: At 26, I saw my dream Porsche. At 68, I built one from scratchBill Drysdale could never afford the sports car he fell in love with as a young man. So when he retired, he went to night school to learn welding, and began assembling it, bit by bit ...Paula CocozzaMon 2 Nov 2026 01.55 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen he was 26, Bill Drysdale saw a Porsche 904 at Silverstone racetrack and fell in love. “One day,” he vowed, “I will have one of those.” As the years went by, the price of Drysdale’s dream car rose above £1m. “I realised I was never going to be able to buy one.” But when he retired, still harbouring the dream, he thought: “Why don’t I make one?”Drysdale grew up in Wigtown, Scotland, and cars were in his blood – his grandfather was chauffeur to the local creamery manager, and he first saw a race with his father, when he was 12 – around the time that his mother went into hospital with multiple sclerosis. Drysdale, an only child, grew close to his father. At 14, he taught him to drive. Together they’d huddle in the kitchen to listen to the Le Mans 24 Hour race on the radio.Drysdale was only 21 when his dad died; his mother ended up staying in hospital for 23 years. “That made me very independent,” he says. Determined? “Pig-headed, some would say.”After studying maths and physics at the University of Glasgow, he joined a brake manufacturer as a graduate apprentice engineer. “Oh, it was tremendous,” he says. “As young chaps in the company, there was always this interest in cars and racing and competition.” His favoured form was “sprinting – racing against the clock, competing against yourself”. It was while playing mechanic to a friend in the pit at Silverstone that he saw the Porsche 904 and was floored by “the sound, the look, the line”.Drysdale married and became father to a son and a daughter, at which point he stopped motor racing. While his wife stayed at home in Warwickshire, England, he travelled widely for work – India, South Africa, Brazil, Japan, Argentina, Europe, Australia. By the time he retired at the age of 58, he was international president for a Canadian company, and moved back to Scotland. It was here that he had the idea to build his own version of the famous Porsche.Drysdale went to night school for six months to learn how to weld. Through a friend of a friend of a friend, he got a blueprint of the original Porsche 904. He made the shape of the body in his garage, first from wood, then plaster of paris. From this he made fibreglass moulds; his wife, Lucia, helped him to make the resin. Next came the doors, a bonnet, front and rear wings, the interior and instrument panel.“Once I had the body, I could concentrate on the engineering, fabricating the chassis, designing the suspension. That was all from scratch,” he says. He bought a secondhand engine and transmission – “then started to put all the parts together”.View image in fullscreenDrysdale driving his ‘Porsche 904FF’.Photograph: Joy RichingsThe children “thought I was off my rocker”, he says. Sometimes, the project would defeat him. “For a couple of months I would not go into the garage at all. Then the enthusiasm would come back … I’ve always been interested in broadening myself.” After eight years, the car was finished; Drysdale was 68. He calls his car a Porsche 904FF. The double Fs stand for “effing fake”.When it was done, he transported the car to test days at race tracks, where he did laps to set up the handling. In Scotland, England, France and Switzerland, he competed in speed hill climbs and sprints, right until February this year, when at 87 a stroke affected his sight and put paid to driving.“I’m coming to terms with it but it is very difficult,” he says. Meanwhile, the car continues to compete, driven by friends, while Drysdale takes part as “entrant”. He is already planning the next season. “I intend to be in the paddock, in the pit, next year with my race car, with someone else driving it.”“I think my dad would have said: ‘Yep, that’s my son,’” he says. “The car has given me a dream. I’m a great believer that you must have a dream. A dream to me is something you really would like to do but don’t know if you ever will. That’s my philosophy in life. Look forward. And do the things that you want to do.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleA new start after 60Motor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unable to tell morning from afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up’: a (mostly dark) winter break in magical Swedish Lapland | Lapland holidays | The Guardian
description: With just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lights
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lights
Content: Abisko in the middle of the afternoon.Photograph: Camilla YatesView image in fullscreenAbisko in the middle of the afternoon.Photograph: Camilla YatesLapland holidays‘Unable to tell morning from afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up’: a (mostly dark) winter break in magical Swedish LaplandWith just a few short hours of daylight, the usual boundaries marking time fall away in Abisko, one of the most reliable places to see the northern lightsCamilla YatesMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 03.42 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLooking over the edge of the snow-smoothed canyon down to dark rushing water, we thought we saw a moose or a reindeer, but it could have been a rock. The light was fading fast so it was hard to tell. It was time to turn back; we didn’t want to get lost in the wood, or fall into the river. By the time we’d retraced our steps to Abisko, the blue world had turned to black and dust-like snowflakes whirled around the little village. Back in our hotel room after our expedition, I looked at my phone – it was only 2pm!Travelling to the Arctic Circle in winter had always been a dream, but when I realised the sun wouldn’t get above the horizon on my holiday, it made me twitchy. I usually pack my limited annual leave as tightly as I pack my working life. I was already using up three days’ holiday travelling by train from London to Abisko. How would I make the most of my time there with barely any daylight?double quotation markApart from the icy train tracks cutting a sharp black detail, everything in the landscape appeared icing softMy partner and I chose to stop in this small village in Swedish Lapland almost by chance, when we researched the most northerly stops on thetrain line between Stockholm and Narvik. Abisko looked on the map like a tiny enclave surrounded by lakes and mountains. Reading more about it, we found that it was home to theAbisko blue hole– a unique microclimate where the geography creates frequent clear skies, making it one of the most reliable places on Earth to see the aurora borealis.After a blur of cities and sleeper trains, we arrived at Abisko Ostra, a tiny station comprising just one low platform and a glass shelter over the exit door, at 11am. We jumped down from the high step of the carriage into soft, deep snow, our feet creating the only imprints on the length of the walkway. White mist hung all around us, and the couple of buildings we could see were fading into the sky. Apart from the icy train tracks cutting a sharp black detail, everything in the landscape appeared icing soft.View image in fullscreenAbisko Ostra station.Photograph: Miroslaw Nowaczyk/AlamyWe walked along an empty road that curved up to theAbisko Mountain Lodge, one of a handful of accommodation options we had found online. Our room wasn’t quite ready, so we spent a while in the hotel’s warm, firelit bar watching people change into their outdoor gear then disappear into the cold. Knowing that darkness would soon set in, I was itching to get outside as well – while we could still see our surroundings.By the time we were salopetted up, thick clouds had made the white world grey, but it was still everything my Christmas-film-loving inner child had imagined. The path we followed was lined with low lights glowing yellow against the white landscape, guiding us among houses with bright windows illuminating the dusk. We followed our phone map towards a viewpoint by a river. It was only half an hour’s walk, but in the deep snow it seemed much longer, and felt like walking through a thick white cloud.We had expected to spend the day exploring. Instead, we’d somehow finished our outing before the afternoon had properly begun. Feeling the luxury of time stretching out, we made tea in our room and read for a while, but we still had plenty of time before dinner, so we went for a few rounds in the sauna.View image in fullscreenNorthern lights over Lake Torneträsk.Photograph: Tomasz Wozniak/AlamyIn the restaurant later, we heard an excited murmur among the diners. The aurora! We rushed out, wearing the clothes we’d been eating dinner in, and watched the green glow, our feet growing more and more numb. But the night was still young, so we got back into our cold-weather gear and walked up a path to higher ground where a family were making snow angels while watching nature’s light show. Their enthusiasm added to our excitement, and we found ourselves not wanting to look away from the dancing sky in case it got better or brighter. Our initial walk to the canyon felt like days ago but we’d only arrived 12 hours earlier.double quotation markI have no idea how long we stood admiring the sky. I’d stopped trying to fit the holiday into my idea of what should be done whenThe next day, after a long and leisurely breakfast of pickled herring, gherkins and lots of delicious rye bread, we hiked a few hours along the bank of Lake Torneträsk. The snow on the path was compact enough for us to explore in our hiking boots, but we saw a few adventurous groups snowshoeing through the wilderness. We followed a narrow path through bare silver birches weighed down with bulbous drifts, until we found a picnic spot near a frozen waterfall, where we enjoyed some provisions we’d squirreled away from the generous breakfast.I did a double-take as I looked back at the way we had come. The sunrise-like colour seemed to be glowing in exactly the same way as when we’d set off, hours before. Unable to tell if it was morning or afternoon, I felt my sense of time opening up. The sun remained below the horizon, but its colourful glow hung in the sky for hours. The pinks and oranges slowly brightened, lingered, then imperceptibly began to fade. The ideas of dawn, midday and evening began to fade, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom the waterfall, we walked up to a high viewpoint and ate flapjacks as we watched the hidden sun cast a last ray of deep orange towards the horizon. We warmed up with hot chocolate in theAbisko Turiststation hotel, drying snow-damp clothes on a radiator before heading back into the cold. The stars were out by then – in the mid-afternoon. We took the long path back to the village and headed through the misty gloom towards the red neon sign and strip-light interior of the supermarket to stock up on snacks for the next day’s train journey.The supermarket was designed for people likely to get snowed in, with lots of produce for sale in bulk, but we found delicious jars of pickled herring, cloudberry jam and more of the region’s dense rye bread to tide us over, along with a squeezy tube of cheese spread from the surprisingly varied range that covered almost a whole aisle. Back at our hotel, we had another sauna, then dinner, before a beer in the cosy hotel bar. Then we headed outside again. It had been dark for hours, but it was still only early evening.View image in fullscreenThe aurora over the lávvu-style building.Photograph: Camilla YatesWe were due to take a cable car up toAbisko Sky Station, a mountain viewpoint 900 metres (nearly 3,000ft) above sea level, but high winds meant the 20-minute cable car journey was too dangerous, so our evening’s plans changed shape. Our guide took us to an outcrop above Lake Torneträsk, where we got another spectacular show of the aurora, complete with shooting stars, courtesy ofthe Geminids. I have no idea how long we stood there, admiring the sky. I’d stopped trying to fit the holiday into my idea of what should be done when.Alight here for the aurora borealis: on the Arctic Circle train to northern SwedenRead moreLater, we warmed up with reindeer soup in a building shaped like a traditional Sámi lávvu, a conical structure with a central fire for warmth and light. Our guide told us some of the myths and legends surrounding the aurora: that the lights were ancestors dancing, or a fox spirit running through the sky with snow attached to its tail. He also showed us the best forecasting apps to use, like the Aurora Buddy and My Aurora, and what all the bars on the various graphs meant. The northern lights lit the darkest part of our walk home.I came to Abisko worrying that darkness would take something away from my trip, but instead it removed the boundaries that normally suggest what I should be doing when. When the distinction between night and day dissolved, there unexpectedly seemed to be more holiday in front of me. It felt like a surprisingly liberating way to travel.Explore more on these topicsLapland holidaysSweden holidaysEurope holidaysScandinavia holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: As winter approaches, all eyes here are on heating oil prices | Winter | The Guardian
description: Inkpen and Combe, Berkshire: If the price goes down, the village WhatsApp group lights up
Author: Nicola Chester
Headline: Inkpen and Combe, Berkshire: If the price goes down, the village WhatsApp group lights up
Content: Nicola's heating oil tank.Photograph: Nicola ChesterView image in fullscreenNicola's heating oil tank.Photograph: Nicola ChesterCountry diaryWinterCountry diary: As winter approaches, all eyes here are on heating oil pricesInkpen and Combe, Berkshire:If the price goes down, the village WhatsApp group lights upNicola ChesterMon 2 Nov 2026 00.30 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeyond the reach of the gas mains, there is tension about the coming winter. Many rural homes have an open fire or wood burner, but most rely on kerosene oil for hot water and heating. Since the US-Iran war began, its cost has more than doubled. Currently, 1,000 litres (lasting 10-12 weeks) is £1,219. A year ago, it was £549. Seasoned wood is in demand.We watch the oil price rise, with none of the consumer protections afforded to gas customers. If the price per litre drops, as during the June ceasefire, the village WhatsApp group lights up.Some residents still have a back boiler system: a water tank tucked behind a fireplace that heats and circulates hot water to taps and through radiators. It is possible, if you have access to firewood, to heat your home for nothing. Until recently we supplemented our oil heating with wood we could take from the estate, until that “right” was rescinded by the gamekeeper we fell out with. But this isn’t the first time a villager has had a run-in about collecting wood.View image in fullscreenGranny’s Lane, where ‘Granny’ Bulpitt’s cottage once stood.Photograph: Nicola ChesterIn between rain showers we head out, past the gamekeeper’s old residence, to where the estate woodsman’s cottage once was, on the way to the former Wadsmere Common (now an unfenced field, grazed by pheasants). We step over branches felled by storms Austen and Boelo. It’s mostly ash; the best for burning.Beside the pile of stones where the cottage stood, a tree creaks like a garden gate swinging open. “Granny” Bulpitt, as she was known, was the last occupant. Her father-in-law was the estate bailiff, and after the common and down were enclosed in 1840, he informed on villagers who persisted in collecting firewood.To the estate owners, King’s College, Cambridge, “their” wood was lucrative commerce. Plunged into fuel poverty, the villagers took the estate to court and won, their plight taken up by the Times. But in retaliation, the estate evicted five tenant families into a severe January snowstorm, and pulled down their houses.“Granny” Bulpitt’s associations were not forgotten. When she died in 1903, the college let the house fall to ruin. No one lives on Granny’s Lane now, except her rumoured ghost.Winterfuel is forever a contentious issue.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order atguardianbookshop.comand get a 15% discountExplore more on these topicsWinterCountry diaryRural affairsFuel povertyEnergy billsHousehold billsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Starwatch: Catch the striking trifecta of Venus, the moon and Spica at break of dawn | Astronomy | The Guardian
description: The brilliant planet is about to join the waning crescent moon and the brightest star in the Virgo constellation
Author: Stuart Clark
Headline: The brilliant planet is about to join the waning crescent moon and the brightest star in the Virgo constellation
Content: At 6am on 7 November the view looking east-south-east from London will show Venus, Spica and the moon.Illustration: Guardian GraphicsView image in fullscreenAt 6am on 7 November the view looking east-south-east from London will show Venus, Spica and the moon.Illustration: Guardian GraphicsStarwatchAstronomyStarwatch: Catch the striking trifecta of Venus, the moon and Spica at break of dawnThe brilliant  planet is about to join the waning crescent moon and the brightest star in the Virgo constellationStuart ClarkMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly risers have a beautiful sight to look forward to this week as brilliantVenusjoins the waning crescent moon and the star Spica in the morning sky.The chart shows the view looking east-south-east from London at 0600 GMT on 7 November. Venus will be the easiest object to identify, shining brilliantly. Next to it will be Spica, the brightest star in the constellation of Virgo, the virgin, situated about 250 light years from Earth.The tiny sliver of the waning moon completes the tableau. On this morning, the moon will be just two days away from new, with only 4% of its Earth-facing disc illuminated. It may also be possible to see the faint outline of its unlit portion, illuminated by sunlight reflected from Earth. This phenomenon is known as earthshine.The three objects will form a striking grouping low above the horizon, so you will need a clear view towards the east-south-east to appreciate the spectacle. At 0600 GMT, the sky will still be relatively dark, although the approaching sunrise will gradually wash out the fainter stars.The grouping will also be visible from the southern hemisphere, where Venus, the moon and Spica will appear higher in the eastern sky before sunrise.Explore more on these topicsAstronomyStarwatchSpaceThe moonVenusPlanetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists  | Palaeontology | The Guardian
description: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body
Content: Prof Kliti Grice with the fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus, a dinosaur that lived in Brazil 115m years ago.Photograph: Curtin UniversityView image in fullscreenProf Kliti Grice with the fossilised remains of the Aratasaurus, a dinosaur that lived in Brazil 115m years ago.Photograph: Curtin UniversityPalaeontologyFossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientistsChemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around bodyIan SampleScience editorMon 2 Nov 2026 15.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-easternBrazil115m years ago.Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.View image in fullscreenA portion the Aratasaurus’s hind limb. The remains were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil.Photograph: Curtin UniversityIf the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears inProceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants ofblood vessels and soft tissuesin dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.Explore more on these topicsPalaeontologyBrazilFossilsAmericasEvolutionBiologyDinosaursnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reddit and libertarian group challenge Australia’s under-16s social media ban in high court | Social media ban | The Guardian
description: Social network and Digital Freedom Project, led by NSW state MP John Ruddick, seek to overturn ban on grounds of implied freedom of political communication
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Social network and Digital Freedom Project, led by NSW state MP John Ruddick, seek to overturn ban on grounds of implied freedom of political communication
Content: Under its social media ban Australia forced Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads to deactivate or suspend users they determined to be under 16.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyView image in fullscreenUnder its social media ban Australia forced Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads to deactivate or suspend users they determined to be under 16.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamySocial media banReddit and libertarian group challenge Australia’s under-16s social media ban in high courtSocial network and Digital Freedom Project, led by NSW state MP John Ruddick, seek to overturn ban on grounds of implied freedom of political communicationJosh TaylorTechnology reporterMon 2 Nov 2026 17.09 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s world-leading under-16ssocial media banwill face its first major legal challenge on Tuesday, as Reddit and an advocacy group headed by a libertarian politician seek to overturn the law in the high court.Nearly 11 months ago, 10 platforms – Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram,Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads – were required to deactivate or suspend the accounts of users they determined to be aged under 16 years.Pornhub returns to Australia after banning access due to age verification rulesRead moreSince then, the prime minister,Anthony Albanese, has said more than 5m accounts across the 10 services have been suspended as part of the ban.Whether the ban will stay will be the subject of the high court hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday this week as Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project – led by New South Wales state Libertarian MP John Ruddick – seek to overturn the ban.Australia does not have a guaranteed right to freedom of speech and the case largely focuses on whether preventing under-16s from holding a social media account impermissibly burdens the implied freedom of political communication inAustralian law.Reddit has argued in its submission to the court that online platforms are a “common source of news and political information” in Australia. The company pointed to its “Ask Me Anything” sessions on the site where users have historically asked questions of politicians or candidates.View image in fullscreenNSW MP John Ruddick, the leader of the Digital Freedom Project.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianTeenagers, Reddit said, would not be able to make posts on politics, comment or react to political content, or engage with the social media accounts of the youth wings of the major political parties.“We share the Australian government’s goal of protecting young people online, but there are better, more effective ways to achieve it than the SMMA [social media minimum age]. As we challenge this law in court, we’ll continue to comply with it and advocate for more effective youth safety measures,” Reddit’s chief communications officer, Adam Collins, said in a statement to the Guardian.The Australian government has argued in its defence that the law serves the legitimate purposes of seeking to reduce the risk of harm for under-16s from social media platforms for the “harmful features” including algorithms, infinite scroll, persistent notifications and likes.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhile the Digital Freedom Project adopted many of the same arguments on political communications burden as Reddit in its submission, the group is likely to face an additional hurdle with the government challenging the standing of the group to bring the case to the court.The Digital Freedom Project had initially had two teenagers –Noah Jonesand Macey Nyland – as the original lead plaintiffs for the case as teenagers affected by the ban. However, in July, both were withdrawn from the case, leaving it to the advocacy group.It is understood there were concerns that the teenagers would face potential legal costs against them in the event of a loss.The Digital Freedom Project has argued in its submission that some of its members are between the ages of 13 and 15, and the teenagers are likely to be presented as examples in the case, but the federal government has argued that, as the plaintiff, the Digital Freedom Project does not have standing to bring the case.The federal government’s submission argues the group has not identified any activity of the group that is impeded by the ban.Legal experts have been divided on the prospect of success. The constitutional law expert Prof Anne Twomeywrote last yearthat Reddit could be successful in highlighting the mismatch between the intended purpose of the law and the practical effect – if the restriction is not preventing children from the harms while also restricting their freedom of political communication.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLuke Beck, a professor of constitutional law at Monash University, wrote inthe Guardian last yearthe cases were likely to fail, as the social media account ban only slightly reduces the overall volume of political communication in Australia, and 13, 14 and 15-year-olds were not engaging in much political communication before the ban.Beck said last week the extra hurdle for the Digital Freedom Project to prove standing would also be difficult.“The government is arguing that DFP is not impacted by the law so therefore can’t challenge it,” he said. “We’ll see what the high court says about advocacy groups having standing to challenge laws: traditionally the courts aren’t too keen.”The fight to switch off your algorithm – podcastRead moreMany other countries are considering following Australia’s lead but there have been concerns teenagers have been able to easily circumvent the ban. The federal opposition has also raised concerns that the number of accounts suspended may be inflated, while the government has refused to release numbers broken down by platform.As the legal challengers get their day in court, the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, is also using new powers passed by parliament this year to investigate whether TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook are in compliance with the law, given the number of teenagers still holding accounts.The companies could be facing the prospect of fines of up to nearly $100m a breach if the regulator decides to take the case to the federal court.The federal parliament is also debating the digital duty of care legislation mandating platforms take actions to prevent users experiencing harm on their platforms. Beck has said the passage of this legislation could present a pyrrhic victory for Reddit if it successfully overturns the ban.The Australian government has made this argument in its submission in the case, stating the obligations of the digital duty of care bill would “require the same action” as the social media ban legislation.“Namely, preventing children having accounts or providing children with accounts that do not have any of the [restricted] features.”Explore more on these topicsSocial media banSocial media bansAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseRedditFreedom of speechAustralian lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup | Melbourne Cup | The Guardian
description: Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’
Content: More than two-thirds of Australian polled now say they have low or zero interest in the annual Melbourne Cup horse race.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than two-thirds of Australian polled now say they have low or zero interest in the annual Melbourne Cup horse race.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesMelbourne CupGuardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne CupGrowing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 14.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA record number of Australians are turning their backs on theMelbourne Cup, with more than two-thirds surveyed saying they have low or zero interest in the annual horse race.Support for the Melbourne Cup has been sliding consistently for a number of years, butthe Guardian Essential pollfound just 9% of Australians said they had high interest in the race now – nearly half the proportion in 2025.“The race that once stopped the nation is now just white noise for many,” said Peter Lewis, the chair of Essential Media.The Guardian Essential poll of 1,003 Australians in late October highlights thelatest erosionin popularity of the eventamid growing ambivalence to the event.Guardian Essential poll: One Nation and Labor’s primary vote on par as discontent with Albanese risesRead moreJust 9% of people said they had high interest in the Cup, down seven percentage points from 2025, with another 23% professing moderate interest, also down three points. About 29% of voters said they had low interest (up five points from last year), while another 39% said no interest at all (up eight points).The combined high and moderate interest came to only 32%, the lowest on record since Essential began asking this question in annual polling in November 2022. The combined low and no interest vote was 68%, jumping 12 points from last year to its highest on record.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn November 2022, the low and no interest vote came to a combined 52%; it was 62% in 2023, 52% in 2024, and 56% in 2025.The“Nup to the Cup” movement, backed by some high-profile politicians and celebrities, has contributed to declining support for the race.But 62% of Australians nonetheless agreed the Melbourne Cup was a unique part of Australia’s national identity. That number remains a strong majority view, despite falling from 78% agreement when Essential asked this question in 2019.Half of Australians (50%) believe the Cup promotes unhealthy gambling behaviour, up 3% since 2025, while 36% say they feel the Cup normalises animal cruelty, down three points from 2025.Another 48% said they were less interested in the Cup than they used to be.“The key driver appears to be a growing disdain for gambling, although concern for animal cruelty comes a close second,” Lewis said.“More broadly this reflects the decline in unifying atonal moments in a world where more and more people have their experiences mediated by targeted advertising algorithms.”Just 12% of voters in October’s poll said they regularly wagered on horse races and would bet on Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, down five points from 2025. In contrast, 46% of people said they were not interested in the Cup and would not place a bet, up six points from last year.Another 25% said they rarely bet on horses but would watch the race and place a bet, while 17% said they would watch but not bet.Explore more on these topicsMelbourne CupEssential pollOpinion pollsHorse racingAnimal welfareGamblingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?  | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives
Content: A shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersView image in fullscreenA shopper survey empty fridges at a branch of SuperValu in Dublin.Photograph: Natalia Campos/ReutersCybercrimeExplainerWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motivesShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackRobert BoothandMiatta MbriwaMon 2 Nov 2026 14.07 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.56 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countrieshave malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F).The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean?The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia.It appeared to be a reprise ofattacks three weeks agowhen French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software.Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.View image in fullscreenWorkers at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, dispose of spoiled food.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAThis is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers.
