Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control.Who is doing it?No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat.“The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos.The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea isbelieved to have beenbehind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame.Western intelligence chiefs sayMoscow is waging acampaign of sabotage in Europethat takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months.View image in fullscreenA worker at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden disposes of spoiled food.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ShutterstockDiscerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”.How is it possible?The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates.Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read moreNick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline – an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”.In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France.What can shops do to defend themselves?The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France.In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NSCC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.Why have British supermarkets not been hit yet?Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout.Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”.A spokesperson for the NCSC said it was “working with its international partners and industry to fully understand details of an incident”.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeSupermarketsRetail industryEuropeSwedenBelgiumEstonianewsShareReuse this content

title: French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests | Schools | The Guardian
description: Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Content: Police prevent students from blockading the Lycée Charlemagne in Paris during protests over school conditions.Photograph: Eric Baradat/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice prevent students from blockading the Lycée Charlemagne in Paris during protests over school conditions.Photograph: Eric Baradat/ReutersSchoolsFrench pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protestsMinister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on ThursdayAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 2 Nov 2026 13.17 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.54 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests overschool conditionsand the high cost of living.The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end thelycée blockades, which have been running since September and have promptedone of the biggest protest movements and social crisesof his presidency.From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demandingmore replacement teachers and repairs to buildingsbarricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.View image in fullscreenStudents gather outside a blockaded high school in Paris to protest against a lack of resources.Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/APUniversity students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities acrossFranceto support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.He saidmeasures offered by the government last weekto cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA protester adds a bin to a fire outside the Montebello international high school in Lille.Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty ImagesIn Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.The education ministry said 41 high schools were blocked across France – around 1% of the nationwide total. Students’ unions put the figure at 150.Nicolas Bonnet, of the headteachers’ union SNPDEN-UNSA, said: “It’s time for us to return to our job: teaching and supporting pupils.” He warned that coursework, final-year exams and university applications were at risk.He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said he would meet school students’ unions again next week.Explore more on these topicsSchoolsStudentsProtestFranceEuropeStudent politicsHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Content: A worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAView image in fullscreenA worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPASwedenShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackChains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shopsWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?Jon HenleyEurope correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.39 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.12 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland,Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.The incidents follow anattack in France last monthin which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.Sweden’s Coop chain toldthe daily Aftonbladetthat six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southernSwedenposted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.View image in fullscreenWorkers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ReutersThe head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.View image in fullscreenEmpty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near  russels.Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty ImagesBelgium’sLe Soir newspaper reportedthat dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read more“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.Ikea,famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.View image in fullscreenA customer surveys an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket in Dublin.Photograph: ReutersMany cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.The agency subsequently reportedthat supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.Explore more on these topicsSwedenSupermarketsCybercrimeRetail industryEuropeBelgiumLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ikea among shops affected by fridge cyber-hacks – Europe live | World news | The Guardian
description: Supermarkets across Europe have experienced temperature-control meddling
Author: Frances Mao
Headline: Supermarkets across Europe have experienced temperature-control meddling
Content: 11.13 ESTClosing summaryI’m going to leave the blog there for now, here’s what you need to know:Supermarket chains across Europe are dealing with another wave of cyber-attacks on their refrigeration systemsafter hackers managed to get into the temperature controls, turning the dial past 50C, spoiling huge quantities of frozen and fresh produceThe temperature tampering was reported by chains acrossBelgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, IrelandandEstoniaand affectedSpar, Delhaize, Coop, ICA, Carrefour and SuperValu supermarkets among othersas well as anIkea store’s freezers in BelgiumThis is the second wave of attacks on such a scale targeting fridge and freezer controlsfollowing a cyber-hack of more than 700 supermarkets in France last month. Dutch supermarkets were also affected then.It’s still unclear who or which group is responsible for the latest incidents;if they’re from the same perpetrators of the French attack or if it’s a copycat operationButthe EU food commissioner said it was aimed atundermining consumer confidence in the bloc’s food supplyFewer stores were affected in this roundcompared to the French cyber-hack, and for most of the chains it was only a minority of stores that were affectedSwedish retailer Coop said it did use Danfoss systems in some of its affected stores – the same Danish system that was targeted in the French supermarchés last month.Swedish supermarket employees chuck out spoiled food at an ICA Kvantum supermarket in Sjoebo, Sweden on November 2, 2026 after a hacker attack raised the temperature in the freezers to 50 degrees Celcius.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty ImagesShareUpdated at11.17 EST

title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Content: The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersOilOil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran warBrent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeksGraeme WeardenMon 2 Nov 2026 12.14 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.37 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end theIranwar.Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.Over the weekend,Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break inthe inflationary pressures gripping the global economy.Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranShipping industryIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Most Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll finds  | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Survey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in election
Content: Election banners in the Israeli settlement of Ofra in the occupied West Bank last month.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElection banners in the Israeli settlement of Ofra in the occupied West Bank last month.Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankMost Israelis think settlements policy should change to avoid more sanctions, poll findsSurvey finds UK government’s decision to impose trade ban was not a decisive factor in how Israelis voted in electionPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 01.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government’s decision to impose a ban on trade in goods from illegal settlements was not decisive in how Israelis votedin their general election, but a majority think the Israeli government’s settlements policy should change if it is going to lead to further sanctions, a new poll of Israelis shows.There had been fierce criticism of the UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in September toimpose a trade banand wider sanctions on illegal settlements, with some claiming it would drive Israeli voters into the arms of Benjamin Netanyahu.A survey last month by Israeli social research group aChord shows overall support for foreign sanctions on violent settlers in theWest Bank, but there was little support for the UK’s ban on trade with goods from illegal settlements, with many fearing it would end up being extended across Israel.Israel election: what we know so farRead moreThe survey is unique in showing how much the tougher line onIsraeladopted by Britain and some foreign states was affecting the thinking of Israeli voters, and the extent to which Israelis thought it was a response to Israel’s actions or born of hostility to Israel, or even antisemitism.The survey showed that three-quarters of supporters of the bloc backing Netanyahu said UK sanctions and trade ban policies towards Israel did not affect their vote at all, and to the small extent that they changed anyone’s vote, they shifted voters both ways, leaving no detectable net effect.Just over three-quarters of all those surveyed (76) – had heard of the UK government announcement on settlements, even if 18 % had only heard the broad headline. Four-fifths of those that were aware of the announcement knew that the policy applied to the West Bank, and not the whole of Israel.Israel’s relations with the west were “important or very important” to 60% of the supporters of the Change bloc of parties backing Gadi Eisenkot in deciding their vote. But even then these relationships came fifth in importance in a proffered group of six motives for voting. Only 30% of supporters of the Netanyahu bloc said relations with the west mattered in the same way.1:14'Nothing will change for us': Palestinians react to Israeli elections – videoBut 71% of voters for the opposition Change bloc said the Israeli government should adapt its settlements policy to avoid an escalation of sanctions. Only 14% of Netanyahu bloc voters agreed, most saying instead that the government should continue the policy “whatever the price”.A plurality of the public – 50% – said the settlement and construction policy in the West Bank should be adjusted to avoid sanctions escalation and international isolation, with 71% of Eisenkot bloc supporters agreeing to this proposition. Support for a change in the policy is strongest among supporters of the Arab parties.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe finding prompted Hannah Weisfeld, the director of the British-Jewish organisation Yachad, to claim the research “illustrates that the Israeli public certainly recognises that if there is not a policy shift in relation to settlement enterprise, the international community is likely to try to create an incentive to shift things from the outside. If anything, that highlights the importance of UK and other allies taking action that targets the occupation.”The survey also showed that concerns about foreign sanctions are highest when voters feel they will suffer a high personal price. Only 36% of all those surveyed agreed that the settlement policy should continue even if sanctions on banks that finance construction in illegal settlements led either to higher interest rates, difficulties in transferring money abroad, or using credit cards abroad. The poll suggests that the more people feel they will be damaged personally, the more they oppose the settlement policy.A majority of all Israelis surveyed (52%) support sanctions on individual violent settlers, so long as the sanctions are imposed only on those acting violently, but 70% of Netanyahu bloc supporters oppose foreign sanctions in all circumstances.There is much less widespread support for the policy of banning the import of goods from the illegal settlement, with 63% of all those surveyed opposing the ban and 26% either supporting the measure outright, or saying they would if it were underlined that the ban would not apply to goods from outside settlements.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuForeign policyTrade policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition | Israel | The Guardian
description: Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Yousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in Knesset
Content: Yousef Jabareen: ‘If [Gadi] Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally.’Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYousef Jabareen: ‘If [Gadi] Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally.’Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelIsrael has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalitionYousef Jabareen says he is ready to join forces with opposition bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu after winning record number of seats in KnessetJulian Borgerin Umm al-FahmMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 10.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction.Yousef Jabareen, the head of the Joint List, said he was ready to join forces with the “Change” bloc to oustBenjamin Netanyahuand his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.Turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, 20% of the population) more thandoubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.Jabareen said the first demand of the roughly 840,000 Palestinian Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particularits most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.“This has been an awful four years … in all areas of life: in terms of house demolition, criminal gangs within the Arab community without any [intervention] from the police; not allocating the needed resources for our municipalities, for our education, for our youth in general; racism in all areas of life – physical attacks against Arabs, the brutality of the police,” Jabareen told the Guardian in one of his first interviews since the election. “So this has been really a very dangerous period.”He said the next few days would be critical. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government, with no single grouping commanding a clear claim on power.Chart showing projected seats in the KnessetNetanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving the Arab-Israeli parties as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli electionRead moreEisenkot and his partners have pledged not to form a unity government with Netanyahu, but Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, have signalled it is ready to join an Eisenkot coalition. The Joint List has no intention of joining such a government, but Jabareen said the coalition was ready to keep it afloat from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset.“The conditions that [Eisenkot] speaks of are more relevant for parties who would be in the coalition. We are not planning to be in the coalition … for very clear reasons,” Jabareen said at his family home in the northern city of Umm al-Fahm. “As long as the occupation of our people in the West Bank continues, we cannot be part of a government.“However, in order to use our political power to get rid of the extreme Netanyahu government, we said that we will consider the possibility of supporting from outside. This is an opportunity to change policies, to change attitudes, including towards the Arab community and towards the Palestinian people.“This is really a historic moment and I hope that there will be partners within the opposition to go ahead with that. We are thinking that this could be the start of a change.”Yousef Jabareen: ‘I hope we can find partners to make to make this change real’Jabareen, 54, a former law professor and the leader of the socialist Hadash party, has yet to talk to Eisenkot since Tuesday’s elections, but he confirmed that informal discussions among opposition parties were under way.Forming a new government was unlikely to be straightforward. The party leaders in the Change bloc have to agree on a candidate for prime minister. They would also have to accept partnership with Arab parties, either in coalition or from outside. The rightwing opposition leader, Avigdor Lieberman, is said to be the most resistant. Joint List officials said it was unclear whether partnership with Palestinians really crossed Lieberman’s red lines, or whether he was just holding out for a top cabinet position.Even before a new government could be formed, Jabareen argued, the 67 opponents of Netanyahu in the new Knesset could use their clear majority to wrest control of legislative power. “That would start by changing the speaker of the Knesset,” he said, adding that the opposition could also take control of the committee that oversees the legislative agenda.“That could be very crucially important … even before we reach conclusions on the issue of a coalition and a new government,” he said, adding that one of the priorities of the new Knesset should be to repeal laws passed by the outgoing majority that infringed the independence of Israel’s judiciary.To allow an opposition coalition to oust Netanyahu and function as a minority government, Jabareen made clear it would also have to address deep-seated inequality in Israeli society.“We have suffered from systemic discrimination for years, so if Eisenkot speaks of change, I believe that the change should come also for our community. We need to be treated equally,” he said. “We also ask for a political horizon. We would like to see the war stopped and the resumption of negotiation with the Palestinian leadership. We would like to see a start of a change.”The Joint List leader said he was concerned over what Netanyahu might do to keep his grip on power. The prime minister hasalready made allegations, without evidence, that the Arab parties had used Qatari funds illegally in the election campaign, which Jabareen dismissed as a bid to “delegitimise the political power of the Arab community” and “a dangerous incitement”.One of Jabareen’s concerns was that the Israeli leader would join Donald Trump in theresumption of war on Iranas a pretext for putting off political transition.“This is really a critical period,” he said. “There should be a clear voice from the opposition to go against any attempt by him to initiate war … or dictate a new military agenda in Israel.”This article was amended on 2 November 2026. An earlier version said that one of Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot’s conditions for a potential coalition partnership with Arab parties was to “accept conscription”. In fact, the condition is to accept compulsory national service, which could be civil or military.Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: PM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apology | Commonwealth summit | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Andy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda
Content: Andy Burnham said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/ReutersCommonwealth summitPM to ask countries affected by UK’s role in slavery to help shape formal apologyAndy Burnham to launch ‘structured dialogue’ on issue at Commonwealth summit in Antigua and BarbudaPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 17.30 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 19.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event tolaunch a “structured dialogue”into what form an apology might take.UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate.In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs.“In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past.”View image in fullscreenKing Charles visits Nelson’s Dockyard in Antigua and Barbuda. No 10 denied Burnham’s remarks had potentially embarrassed the monarch.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/PABurnham set out his intention to look at a possible apology in anarticle for the Guardianon Saturday, in which he said the UK should “show leadership again today” as it had done in efforts to end the transatlantic slave trade.Asked why Burnham believed an apology was needed, his official spokesperson said: “The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration.” Having conversations about an apology would do this, and was also the right thing to do, he said.Tony Blairexpressed “deep sorrow”about the slave trade and Britain’s role in it in 2006, but stopped short of a formal apology.Burnham intended to go further, his spokesperson said. “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today.Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?Read more“That is distinct from a formal apology. We are opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.“We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they have asked for.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham plays cricket on a visit to Bullets cricket ground in Powells, Antigua and Barbuda, on Monday.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APBurnham is scheduled to take part in a series of assemblies at Chogm, as well as bilateral meetings with other leaders.There was no single event set aside to discuss slavery or an apology, but discussions would take place “throughout the next couple of days”, No 10 said, adding that the Foreign Office would lead talks over the form of an apology.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is already at the summit. One Foreign Office official said other Commonwealth countries “are responding positively to our offer of a structured dialogue” on an apology.“The conversations at Chogm have been focused on the positive work this alliance can do together on issues like climate and trade,” they said. “By not shying away from difficult discussions about our past, we are building trust with our allies to focus on the big issues of the future.”No 10 denied that Burnham’s comments had potentially embarrassed King Charles, who is already inAntigua and Barbudafor a pre-Chogm visit.Buckingham Palace “was made aware in a timely manner”, Burnham’s spokesperson said. “The prime minister believes that being true to British values of decency and honesty means not shying away from these conversations.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth summitSlaveryReparations and reparative justiceCaribbeanAntigua and BarbudaColonialismBritish empirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Migration is a moral issue for Burnham – but is he trying to please everyone? | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: PM wants to tie Shabana Mahmood’s hard line on borders to recognition of the value of migration, but he may need to shout his conviction
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: PM wants to tie Shabana Mahmood’s hard line on borders to recognition of the value of migration, but he may need to shout his conviction
Content: Andy Burnham has been supportive of Shabana Mahmood’s attempts to limit legal and illegal migration, but he has also sought to reframe those changes.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has been supportive of Shabana Mahmood’s attempts to limit legal and illegal migration, but he has also sought to reframe those changes.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetImmigration and asylumAnalysisMigration is a moral issue for Burnham – but is he trying to please everyone?Pippa CrerarPolitical editorPM wants to tie Shabana Mahmood’s hard line on borders to recognition of the value of migration, but he may need to shout his convictionHow will UK immigration rules change under Shabana Mahmood’s latest plans?Mon 2 Nov 2026 15.39 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.02 ESTShareWhile out on the campaign trail in Makerfield,Andy Burnham gave a glimpseinto where he might land on Labour’s plans for immigration reform, which had already been decried by the left of the party as unfair while described on the right as electorally necessary.Asked what he thought of Reform’s attack on “open borders Andy” – Nigel Farage’s early attempt to define him as soft on migration – the then Manchester mayor dismissed the charge as “ridiculous” and went on the defensive.“I’m not like that. You know me. I was in the Home Office under Tony Blair, and actually, it was my job to return people. That was my specific role,” he said while out knocking on doors in the constituency.“I used to have to travel to governments around the world and persuade them to take back planes of people who had come here with no basis to stay, so you know, I’ve never have been shy of getting to grips with these difficult issues.”But Burnham wasn’t just pitching to the Reform-inclined voters he needed to win the seat; he was already charting whatever path he might need to take if he made it to Downing Street.While he was supportive of attempts by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to limit legal and illegal migration, which had beencriticised by some senior Labour figures as un-British, Burnham wanted to reframe the changes.“I think there’s a different way of thinking about it that might in the end get you to a better position, and one that restores public confidence,” he said.The Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intact | EditorialRead moreThe prime minister’s political allies say he regards migration as a moral issue, showing people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government does have control over the UK’s borders and is prepared to do something about it.But he also wants to tell a positive story about the contribution of migration to the country, they say. Weeks after arriving in No 10, the Guardian revealed thatsocial care workers could be exemptedfrom the plans as he looked for ways to relieve pressure on the sector.In an interview with ITV this week, Burnham again tried to make the case. “When you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say if it’s too high or too low,” he said, arguing that migrants help plug “gaps in the economy”.In the end,Mahmood’s reforms came with a significant carve-outfor almost 300,000 care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.In a further compromise to those on theLabourbenches feeling squeamish, those deemed to be making a “strong contribution” to the UK – high earners, those with strong British connections or who work in health and teaching – will also be able to settle in five years.But that Burnham delivered the bulk of Mahmood’s hardline reforms should not come as a surprise. The prime minister, steeped in the politics of the “red wall”, understands better than many the salience of the issue with voters.The most rigorous ofthe new rules first drawn up a year ago by the Home Office– retrospective changes for many migrants, and forcing small boats arrivals to face up to 30 years before applying for settlement – are still there.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow they land with the public (which polling suggests supports a doubling of the waiting time for most migrants to 10 years) now depends in part on whether ministers can convince them it’s about people making a contribution, rather than a U-turn forced by their own side.The Conservatives and Reform, unsurprisingly, are already pushing the latter narrative, Farage describing the care workers carve-out as “the beginning of the capitulation” on borders.Burnham is, equally predictably, arguing that it’s about fairness. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier,” he said.“Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”But Burnham’s words did not come in the Commons chamber or at a press conference standing alongside Mahmood or even as part of his prolific social media output.They were instead issued in a press release, after the government chose to push ahead with the sensitive policy announcement while he was out of the country – travelling to the Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua.The plans are still likely to face criticism from some on either wing of the Labour party – for going too far or not far enough – although plenty of former critics do now appear to be on board. But without an obvious vote to coalesce around, any major rebellion looks unlikely.Mahmood’s bigger challenge will be convincing the public. She will need Burnham, who has praised her for “gripping this problem”, to help her to do so. But the prime minister will have to accept, on an issue as divisive as this, he won’t be able to please everyone.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumAndy BurnhamShabana MahmoodLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues
Content: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark crown court on Monday. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and denies the allegations against him.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arrives at Southwark crown court on Monday. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges and denies the allegations against him.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesUK newsRussell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court toldDefence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continuesEmine SinmazMon 2 Nov 2026 14.57 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.52 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand is not a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” and is respectful when women say no, a court has heard.In his closing speech at Southwark crown court, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why Brand’s accusers had not fought back when they were allegedly raped, saying “not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.Winter said allegations about the comedian’s sexual conduct in 2023 had “poisoned the wells” of justice. He also said there had been “monstrous delays” in the women in the criminal trial coming forward to police.He also questioned why Brand had been accused of “only three rapes in 10 years” out of all the women he had slept with.He said: “It is an extremely curious feature of this case that out of the many, many women that Mr Brand had sex with during this period only three of them say they did not consent to anal, oral or vaginal sex.”Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Winter began his closing speech by reciting an 1864 quote from the theologian and philosopher John Henry Newman, saying: “What I insist upon here, now that I am bringing this portion of my discussion to a close, is this unmanly attempt of his, in his concluding pages, to cut the ground from under my feet … this I call poisoning the wells.”He said the 2023 reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times and Sunday Times stories had “poisoned the well of justice” in Brand’s case by prompting the women to come forward with accusations afterwards.Winter told jurors: “They poisoned the wells in the hope and intention that other people come forward and make allegations against him.”In her closing speech on Friday, the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, denied that the 2023 reporting had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.Winter told jurors on Monday that Brand had an “immense amount of sex” and none of it was unlawful.“The question for you is, can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand between 1999 and 2009, he raped just three of them?” he asked.“Living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful however morally distasteful you may find it,” he continued. “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral – who cares? It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”Winter said another “curious feature” of the case was that the three rape complainants had alleged Brand was “normal” after the alleged incidents.“That, we suggest, is something that simply cannot have occurred if he is guilty,” the barrister said. “He obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that’s the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal.”The barrister said there was “no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”.He also questioned why the women had not screamed, kicked out or slapped Brand during the alleged attacks. He asked why a woman who accuses Brand of anal rape “didn’t just roll over and kick out in any way” and said she “didn’t scream or resist or call out”. He also questioned why a woman who says she was orally raped did not “slap [Brand] in the face” and suggested she had not “sufficiently” resisted.He also questioned how none of the women came forward during the #MeToo movement.Winter said: “How is it that it’s only three out of the many, many women, how is it that not even these ones, not even these allegations on this indictment came to light during #MeToo?“Many women were questioning whether they had a bad experience sexually at the hands of a famous person. It could not have been more publicised.“How is it that not one of them thought what happened to them involved a crime during the #MeToo movement?”The court has heard the earliest allegation dated back to 1999, when a woman accused Brand of raping her after he had performed in a fringe cabaret event during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth.The woman told the court Brand had left his email address after raping her, while asking her if she was enjoying herself.Winter said the woman was not a “naive and wilting flower” as he questioned her account of events. “You would have to be a psychopath to be raping someone and asking them if they were enjoying it,” Winter said. “He [Brand] said he was trying to please her but he wasn’t successful.”Winter said rapists did not try to please their victims. He also said Brand respected when a woman said no, and sought “approbation and adoration” from women.“He respects it when a woman says no so that makes him someone who is not a rapist,” Winter said. “He was seeking the approval in the sex, it’s the approval, it’s the ‘Yes I will have sex with you’, and that’s what he said in his evidence.”Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years
Content: Most of the hardline plans drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMost of the hardline plans drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockImmigration and asylumShabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlashException for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five yearsRajeev SyalandJessica ElgotMon 2 Nov 2026 14.06 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.04 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade.Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to faceup to 30 yearsbefore being able to apply for settlement.The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”.But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement.She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”3:24Shabana Mahmood sets out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants – videoIn particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by someLabourMPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.View image in fullscreenDiane Abbott, the Labour MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, criticised the retrospective changes.Photograph: House of Commons/PAThe Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”.She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element.“People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.View image in fullscreenChris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said Mahmood’s decision would cost the country up to £10bn.Photograph: House of Commons/PAHome Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood’s softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years.The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds.Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn’t unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”View image in fullscreenEdward Leigh, the MP for Gainsborough, was among the Conservatives who acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed legal migration numbers to rise so significantly.Photograph: House of Commons/PABusiness groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood’s decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodRefugeesHome OfficeLabourCare workersSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A despicable betrayal’: Democrats incensed by Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers | Democrats | The Guardian
description: Stevens’s decision sparked fierce backlash from members of the party, while Donald Trump praised the sudden switch
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Stevens’s decision sparked fierce backlash from members of the party, while Donald Trump praised the sudden switch
Content: 1:38Haley Stevens snubs fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to back GOP Mike Rogers in Michigan  – videoDemocrats‘A despicable betrayal’: Democrats incensed by Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike RogersStevens’s decision sparked fierce backlash from members of the party, while Donald Trump praised the sudden switchEric BergerandChris SteinMon 2 Nov 2026 18.22 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDemocrat Haley Stevens’s shocking last-minute endorsement of Mike Rogers, theMichiganRepublican Senate candidate, in the run-up to Tuesday’s midterm elections has sparked fierce backlash from members of her party.Stevens, who narrowly lost in the Democratic primary for Senate to Abdul El-Sayed, announced her support for Rogers after a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s advertisement, which blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel.Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike RogersRead moreStevens had said she would appear at a campaign event if he denounced the advertisement. El-Sayed’s campaign disinvited her.Following the extraordinary public rupture on Sunday, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised more than $2.4m, a fundraising record in the final days of a race that could determine control of the US senate. The Democrat’s campaign said more than 26,000 people contributed for the first time on Sunday.New York DemocratChuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, described Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.11:32Why did a Democrat endorse a rival Republican in Michigan? - The Latest“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” Schumerpostedon social media.Nancy Pelosi, the Democratic former House speaker,postedthat Stevens had “chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement”.The New York mayor,Zohran Mamdani, said that “working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday”.“Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against,” Mamdaniposted.2:01Trump praises Haley Stevens’ defection while lobbing Islamophobic insults at El-Sayed – videoStevens refused to clearly explain what led to her endorsement of Rogers in aninterview with Anderson CooperonCNN Sunday evening. “I’m just casting my one vote this way,” Stevens said, while insisting she still wanted Democrats to win the majority on election day.“I am not trying to upset anyone,” she added. “I’m just being honest with my constituents and what I’m hearing from people, and in fact, I’ve been hearing from a ton of Dems, Anderson, who said: ‘Thank you, this is how we felt; we haven’t liked this campaign; it’s painful.’”Cooper pressed Stevens, questioning whether being disinvited from El-Sayed’s campaign event triggered her endorsement of Rogers. At one point, Stevens refused to answer the question, allowing several seconds of silence to air.Stevens has continued to defend her decision as she faces accusations of betrayal from Democrats, includingcallsfor her expulsion from the House caucus. Several members of her congressional staff resigned in protest. In an interview on Monday, she compared herself with Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman, a one-time progressive who now frequently breaks with his party, especially over supporting Israel.“You see a Democrat from Pennsylvania, you know, his name’s a lightning rod in the party. His name’s Fetterman,” shetoldconservative commentator Scott Jennings. “They say the same thing about him.”Curtis Hertel, the chair the Michigan Democratic party,said in a postthat Stevens was not a member of the party “nor will she be in the future”.A Detroit journalist, Sam Robinson, shared a video in which Hertel was asked why he thought Stevens made the endorsement.“Obviously there are sour grapes from the election, but there is no reasonable explanation for this. I have known Haley Stevens for a long time, and I know what she has fought for her in her career, and this is the antithesis of all of that,” Hertel said.Debbie Dingell, a veteranMichiganHouse Democrat, dismissed Stevens’s endorsement as a distraction from voters’ concerns about the cost of living.“That’s what they’re talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens’ continued efforts to get attention,” she said in astatement.OnMS Now on Sunday, El-Sayed encouraged undecided Michigan voters to stand with him to protect democracy in the United States. “The divide in our politics isn’t left versus right; the divide in our politics is the people who are locked out versus the people who are locking them out,” El-Sayed said.Speaking to Fox News on Monday, Rogers praised Stevens for her endorsement. “I know Democrats are thumping their chest and saying she has done something other than courageous,” hesaid. “It was nothing but courageous.”Charlotte Clymer, a blogger and activist who supports Democrats, told the Guardian she had considered Stevens a friend for several years, and said the congresswoman’s decision to back Rogers “is like endorsing Donald Trump”.“This is like living through a bad dream. It really is,” Clymer said. “If you had told me there’d be a sitting Democratic member of Congress who would switch like this, Haley would not have come to mind.”She called Stevens a lawmaker of “strident integrity” who has stood up for LGBTQ+ rights, unions and abortion access. As tensions rose with the El-Sayed campaign Clymer said that on on Saturday she texted Stevens, who replied with messages assuring her she still supported the Democratic nominee. Clymer said she texted again after Stevens released a video endorsing Rogers on Sunday, but has not heard back.“It really is bizarre. It feels like there [is] a body snatcher moment. Someone has kidnapped Haley Stevens and replaced her with a completely different person,” Clymer said.What are the races to watch in the US midterm elections and why do they matter?Read moreMeanwhile, Trump praised Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers on his platform Truth Social and described her as a “highly respected Democrat”. He again cheered Stevens during a campaign rally on Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, and encouraged her to switch parties.“I’d love her to join the Republican party, actually, I think that could happen maybe. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan,” Trump said.When asked about Trump praising her, Stevens told CNN: “Well, I impeached him twice,” before criticizingRepublicansfor being “really focused on just letting Trump be the dictator”.Explore more on these topicsDemocratsUS midterm elections 2026MichiganUS SenateUS politicsRepublicansDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in California | California | The Guardian
description: Latest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballots
Author: Sam Levin
Headline: Latest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballots
Content: Bill Essayli, US attorney for the central district of California, at a news conference in Los Angeles, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreenBill Essayli, US attorney for the central district of California, at a news conference in Los Angeles, on Monday.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APCaliforniaTrump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in CaliforniaLatest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballotsUS midterms – live updatesSam LevinMon 2 Nov 2026 18.22 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.38 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Department of Justice (DoJ) in California has charged six more people with alleged voter fraud crimes, an escalation of the Trump administration’s campaign against the state’s election processes on the eve of the midterms.Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles and aclose ally of the president, announced on Monday that his office was prosecuting six lawful permanent residents accused of unlawfully registering to vote and casting fraudulent ballots. The DoJfiled similar chargesagainst 28 people across California last month and arranged for adramatic on-camera arrestof one 72-year-old defendant, editing the footage into a DoJ promotional video.The six new defendants are all green card holders, according to criminal complaints filed in federal court, meaning they are immigrants who have legal status, but are barred from voting.Voting by noncitizens is extremelyrare, and experts say when noncitizens do end up on the voter rolls, it is usuallydue to confusion.The pro-Trump prosecutor trying to stop California ballots from being countedRead moreThe latest arrests come as the DoJ pushes ahead with its lawsuit seeking to force California election officials toset aside roughly 20,000 ballotsthat federal prosecutors say may belong to noncitizens who fraudulently registered. The DoJ has said the ballots should not be counted until California can confirm their citizenship status. State election leaders have countered that prosecutors’ list and methodology was unreliable and that complying with the demands in the middle of an election would be logistically impossible and would risk disenfranchising US citizens. Multiplejudgeshaverebuffedthe DoJ’s efforts asunconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and the US supreme court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s appeals.Five of the six people charged in the latest round of prosecutions have been arrested, Essayli said at a press conference on Monday. The six defendants include people originally from Mexico, Israel, the Philippines, Canada and Iran, prosecutors said.All six are accused of a single charge each of making false statements on a naturalization application, with affidavits alleging they unlawfully registered to vote, and then when they later applied for citizenship, they falsely claimed that they had never previously registered. The complaints said the defendants cast ballots in recent years, but they are not facing charges specifically relating to fraudulently voting.The defendants are facing a maximum of five years in prison, according to prosecutors. The charges were outlined in initial complaints written by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents. The defendants have not been formally indicted, and it was not immediately clear if any of them had obtained lawyers. The federal public defender’s office in Los Angeles did not immediately respond to an inquiry.One 52-year-old defendant from Canada was accused of voting unlawfully twice, then seeking to cancel his registration. The complaint says he has been in the US for more than 40 years. A 43-year-old defendant from the Philippines has been in the US since 1992 and was accused of voting several times since 2020.Experts have said it was extraordinary for the DoJ to bring these cases in the middle of an election, with federal prosecutors traditionally avoiding taking steps that could be seen as politically motivated or potential interference with an upcoming race. Former prosecutors and defense lawyers have said it was especially galling to see the government present the arrests in such a showy manner, blasting mugshots and parading defendants in front of news cameras.The Associated Press and other news outlets were present for a pre-dawn arrest of the 72-year-old last month on a quiet residential street, and a Fox News reporter on Mondayposted photos of two arrests, including one who appeared to be an Amazon worker handcuffed on the sidewalk. Democrats have accused the DoJ of trying to sow doubt in the results of the election and create a false impression that voter fraud is widespread.Essayli said the newly arrested defendants were on federal prosecutors’ list of 20,000 voters who might be fraudulently registered, arguing the cases further supported their push to stop ballots from being counted. But an immigrants’ rights group, which sued the government over its use of federal immigration data to challenge voters, analyzed the list and said in a filing over the weekend thatmore than 40%of the people flagged as potentially fraudulent voters could not be found on the state’s voter rolls.The 20,000 names represent a tiny fraction of the more than23 million registered votersin California.County election officials who have received threatening letters from the DoJ with demands that they set aside certain ballots have also said the lists handed to them wereriddled with errors.When questioned about the prosecutors’ list on Monday, Essayli told reporters the government had used “third-party databases” to identify potentially fraudulent voters, and that it “may not be 100%” accurate, but there was a “very, very high confidence rate”. At a press briefing during the first round of arrests last month, Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, said: “There may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens.
