We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve askedCaliforniato cooperate with us.”The DoJ in recent days has also repeatedly threatened to criminally prosecute election officials who process fraudulent ballots, prompting arebuke from a federal judgeon Friday, who said the DoJ’s “intimidation, threats, and attempts at coercion force election workers daily to choose between acceding to [the DoJ’s] unlawful demands or adhering to their duties and thereby subjecting themselves to a serious risk of criminal investigation and prosecution”. The judge blocked the administration from continuing to threaten election officials.Essayli has continued his crusade against California’s elections even after a federal judge ruled last week thathe was “unlawfully” servingas the head of the US attorney’s office since he was not formally appointed and confirmed by the Senate. The DoJ is appealing that ruling.Sam Levine contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaTrump administrationWest CoastUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Washington state resident dies from ‘severe illness’ after contracting bird flu | Washington state | The Guardian
description: Individual, who also had underlying conditions, was hospitalized after being exposed to avian influenza
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Individual, who also had underlying conditions, was hospitalized after being exposed to avian influenza
Content: A colorized electron microscope image shows avian influenza A H5N1 virus particles (yellow), grown in epithelial cells (blue).Photograph: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/APView image in fullscreenA colorized electron microscope image shows avian influenza A H5N1 virus particles (yellow), grown in epithelial cells (blue).Photograph: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/APWashington stateWashington state resident dies from ‘severe illness’ after contracting bird fluIndividual, who also had underlying conditions, was hospitalized after being exposed to avian influenzaAnna BettsMon 2 Nov 2026 16.59 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAWashington stateresident has died after being hospitalized with “severe illness” after contracting bird flu, local health officials said on Sunday.The individual was exposed to avian influenza, also known as bird flu, at a dairy with infected cattle in Yakima county, according to anews release. The person was subsequently hospitalized with severe illness and died on Sunday. Health officials said that the individual, whose identity had not been released, had underlying health conditions.“The Yakima health district offers its heartfelt condolences to the individual’s family, friends, and loved ones during this difficult time,” the district said in a statement.This is the first person in the United States to die from complications from bird flu this year, according to theAssociated Press. It comes as officials in Yakima county have reported that sinceearly October, 33 dairy herds havetested positivefor “highly pathogenic avian influenza”.‘It’s clear they are under-vaccinated’: Amish under spotlight amid Pennsylvania measles outbreakRead moreThe Yakima health district has said that it, in coordination with the Washington state department of health, is monitoring human cases of bird flu in Yakima county. So far, the district has recordedthree confirmedhuman cases in the county.In Sunday’s statement, the health district announced the county’s third confirmed human case of bird flu. The individual was “exposed to infected dairy cattle at a Yakima county dairy”, but has not experienced severe illness or required hospitalization.Officials said they are working with public health partners to identify and contact any individuals “who may have been in close contact with the person to monitor for symptoms”.County officials have stressed that “the risk of avian influenza infection to the general public remains low” and that “people at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus”.Human-to-human transmission of bird flu is “extremely rare and has never been documented in the United States”, they said.The USCenters for Disease Control and Prevention(CDC) has recorded 72 human cases of bird flu across the country since 2024, according to agency data. The CDC has maintained that there is no known person-to-person spread and that the risk to the general public remains low.The CDCannouncedthe first death in the US due to complications from bird flu in January 2025.Explore more on these topicsWashington stateBird fluHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
Content: The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year.Photograph: ReutersOilOil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran warBrent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeksGraeme WeardenMon 2 Nov 2026 12.14 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.37 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end theIranwar.Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.Over the weekend,Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets, so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break inthe inflationary pressures gripping the global economy.Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranShipping industryIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Texas voters on high gas prices under Trump: ‘Probably made me go more Democrat’ | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: In state where driving is part of life, president’s pledge to lower prices at the pumps cuts little ice
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: In state where driving is part of life, president’s pledge to lower prices at the pumps cuts little ice
Content: A gas station in Houston earlier this month.Photograph: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA gas station in Houston earlier this month.Photograph: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Texas voters on high gas prices under Trump: ‘Probably made me go more Democrat’In state where driving is part of life, president’s pledge to lower prices at the pumps cuts little iceGaya Guptain Dallas, TexasMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBehind the granite countertops of Fuel City, a gas station in Dallas where taxidermy deer flank the entrance and hot tacos are served 24/7, Alina Cardenas sees first-hand that Texans are stretched thin.Drivers are filling up less, she said, while ringing people up for cigarettes and beer, and fewer people are buying a full tank. Some stop once they’ve reached $10 or $20 worth of gasoline.Cardenas, 19, who is studying radiology at a local college, said she’s been cutting back on gas herself by staying home more and driving only to go to work and school.“It’s just getting really expensive,” she said. “Things got harder this year.”In a state nearly three times the size of the UK, with hundreds of thousands of miles of road, driving is an essential part of life. Commuters can spend as much as six hours a day on the road going to and from their jobs. Over much of the past year, soaring energy costs brought on by the war in Iran has made it all the more expensive.Higher gas prices are expected to play a major role in howTexasvoters will decide a key battle in the upcoming midterms. James Talarico, a state representative, is trying to best Republican Ken Paxton, a former state attorney general, to become the state’s first Democratic senator in over 30 years.View image in fullscreenA sign with ‘Gas Prices Are Too Damn High’ written on it.Photograph: Gaya Gupta/The GuardianRepublicans across the country are fighting an uphill battle against widespread frustration, especially among independent voters, over the economy. Recentpollingshows Talarico with a slight edge over Paxton, who has been embroiled in scandals.On Tuesday, a week before election day, Donald Trump stood in front of an oil tanker docked in Corpus Christi, Texas toannouncethat the first million barrels of oil from his deal with Venezuela had arrived in the state.“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” Trump said at a rally for Paxton in Lubbock later that day.At another rally in Georgia later in the week, Trump touted the “hundreds of billions of dollars” that higher gas prices are bringing to American gas companies. Two of the largest, Exxon and Chevron, are based in Texas.“We’re making a frickin’ fortune,” hetold the crowd.But in Texas, voters seem unconvinced. In the Dallas-Fort Worth area, where bumper stickers declaring “my country, not your church” speed past billboards for gun shows, drivers who spoke to the Guardian expressed deep frustration over gas prices.Cardenas said inflated gas prices has “probably made me go more Democrat” and that she will vote for Talarico.Tom L, 40, who declined to give his last name, said he commutes nearly six hours each day to get to his job as a data analyst in Dallas. He spends about $400 a month on gas, double what he was spending a year ago. The diesel truck that he uses for farm work now costs him around $200 a week.“I’ve definitely had to budget tighter to compensate,” he said.He voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election, but said he is “not sure if that was the right decision” and is unsure which Senate candidate he will support as both have their benefits and flaws.Because Texas is a top oil producer, its residents often enjoy cheaper gas prices than the rest of the US. But the state has not been immune to the rising cost of gas amid the war in Iran. On average, a gallon of gas now costs $3.68, compared to $2.59 a year ago, according toAAA.Diesel, which fuels the big rigs and tanker trucks that transport Texan oil, has shot up by more than 80%, from $3.18 to $5.79.View image in fullscreenGas is pumped into a car at a Love’s truck stop in Shamrock, Texas.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty Images“Texans are paying less than the national average, yes, but they are also paying a lot more than they were a year ago,” said Tom Seng, a professor of energy finances at Texas Christian University. “Texans are feeling the pain just like everyone else.”Though gas prices are just part of a slate of costs that make up everyday expenses, they tend to be the most noticeable, especially in a state where residents heavily rely on their cars for transportation.“People on Tuesday morning, before they go to the polls … they’re not opening up their electric utility bill. They probably aren’t grocery shopping that morning,” Seng said. “But what’s the last thing that they’re probably going to see before they get to the polling place? The price of gasoline.”Kobe Montgomery, a security guard at Fuel City in Dallas, said he uses his car to get to his job in security and to deliver for UberEats and Domino’s on the side. He has no choice but to fill up his tank whenever he needs to.“It beats walking,” he said.But even though he hasn’t noticed the higher cost of gas, he doesn’t plan to vote at all in the upcoming midterms, out of fear for voting for the wrong person and regretting it.Diamond M, who declined to give her last name, said spends at least three hours on the road to get to her job as a warehouse worker. Gas, she estimates, is taking up about 20% of her take-home pay. She only fills up her tank on Friday – pay day –and forces herself to make the tank stretch the whole week.She plans to vote for Talarico, who she believes has the best shot of lowering costs for her.“He has a voice,” she said. “Seems like he’ll get it done.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US economyTexasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The content creator election’: digital streamers and TV networks face off for midterms coverage | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballs
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Journalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballs
Content: Steve Kornacki during primary night coverage on 19 May 2026.Photograph: NBC NewsView image in fullscreenSteve Kornacki during primary night coverage on 19 May 2026.Photograph: NBC NewsUS midterm elections 2026‘The content creator election’: digital streamers and TV networks face off for midterms coverageJournalists such as Jim Acosta and Scott MacFarlane are now competing against their former employers for eyeballsJeremy Barrin WashingtonMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Tuesday, for the first time in more than 20 years, Jim Acosta, a formerCNNstalwart, will not be working for a mainstream television network on election night.Acosta, who left CNN last year after nearly 18 years at the network, is putting on his own live broadcast at the University of Virginia that will air on YouTube and his Substack platform.And in a sign of the times, Acosta will be joined for the broadcast, hosted by the university’s Center for Politics, by another star of linear television – Katie Couric, a former Today show co-host. (Don Lemon, another CNN alum and converted new media player, may also drop by, Acosta said.)“If folks are looking for fresh faces and a different way of doing this kind of coverage, I think it’s going to deliver that,” Acosta said.Acosta said he will be doing his best Steve Kornacki impression, giving analysis using aninteractive, touch screen battleground mapjust like the NBC News data guru. “Yeah, I’m going to have to go to J Crew and get some new khakis.”Rashida Jones, who serves as chief executive of Piers Morgan’s media company Uncensored, predicted that Tuesday’s midterms will come to be remembered as “the content creator election”, when independent journalists hosting streaming broadcasts give traditional networks a run for their money.View image in fullscreenPiers Morgan on the Football Uncensored TV show.Photograph: Ken McKay/Football UncensoredJones was running one of those television networks, MSNBC (now called MS Now), during the 2024 presidential election, a role she held for four years. She is working to expand Morgan’s company by launching new shows and verticals beyond the “Piers Morgan Uncensored” streaming broadcast, which has about 4.5 million subscribers on YouTube.The plan for election night is a several-hour-long live show hosted by Morgan from Washington DC, part of a three-day stint broadcasting from the US capital city.“Our focus is going to be making sense of what’s happening in real time,” she said in an interview. “People aren’t coming to us because they’re looking for how this part of Michigan voted. It’s more the big picture themes and takeaways. Ultimately by the end of the night, people care about where did we land, less about the individual races.”Jones said that traditional television networks will be facing more competition than past election cycles. “If I’m a network that’s got a guy at a board and a ticker at the bottom, and I just assume people are going to come, I don’t know that that’s baked in and that’s a given this cycle. And I think what we see [on Tuesday] will be on a smaller scale what we see for the general election … I think it’ll be the content creator election.”Scott MacFarlane, a veteran reporterwho resigned from CBS News in Marchseeking “some independence”, joined the progressive MeidasTouch network as its chief Washington correspondent and will be co-hosting its live election broadcast.MacFarlane says the streaming show will lack the bells and whistles of a traditional television election broadcast, which is the point. “There will be no teleprompters and no scripts,” he said. “It’s straight to the point, direct, conversational and heavy on original reporting.” He added that “dramatic theme music and theatrical presentations would miss the moment”.Still, many millions of Americans will be watching a traditional television network – or their streaming off-shoot – to keep tabs on the elections. On election night 2024, an estimated 42.3 million viewers watched television coverage – though viewership is obviously lower for non-presidential years.“There are more places than ever for people to get their news and information, but there’s no place that has the depth, the scope, and the breadth that NBC News has,” said Hallie Jackson, an NBC News anchor, who is penciled in for nine hours of live coverage as part of the network’s election team, along with Savannah Guthrie, Tom Llamas and Kristen Welker behind the desk (along with Kornacki).Jackson said the key to election night is hydration, and a regimen of healthy eating that she began last week. “You have to pace yourself. You have to stay hydrated. You have to have a secret pack of M&Ms for your blood sugar that you can come back to every hour.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeni Tienabeso, vice-president of ABC News Live and Specialized Units, said the network has planned for a seven-hour-long broadcast, but could go much longer if a key call – perhaps for control of the US Senate or House – is on the horizon.Asked how much effort is put toward the traditional television broadcast compared with digital and social media offerings, ABC News executives said the network is fully integrated. “For us, it’s about reaching the audience where they are,” Tienabeso said. “We don’t leave any of those arenas as secondary.” (The network’s coverage will also be aired on its ABC News Live digital channel, on Hulu, and on the Disney+ streaming service.)Like most major networks and news organizations, ABC News relies on election results from the Associated Press –as well as a new voter surveyconducted by the polling firm SSRS – to help make projections about key elections. Those decisions are made by a desk that is “holed off” from the rest of the newsroom, Tienabeso said, and is not primarily focused on beating rival networks. “We don’t pay attention to what competitors are doing,” he said. “Our decision desk makes the decision when they feel comfortable with their analysis of the race that they’re covering.”On Tuesday, viewers watching CNN will be able to see the network’s decision desk in action, and will also have access to a new tool called CNN Sightline that will give insights into how a contest is leaning, based on both data and demographics. “I think it’s probably more transparency than we’ve ever had,” said David Chalian, CNN’s political director and Washington bureau chief.CNN’s decision desk makes calls when they have at least 99.5% confidence that a certain candidate will win. “Speed is not part of that at all,” he said.“In a time when voter confidence in elections is something that we constantly look at and is called into question, it only ups the seriousness of purpose with which we take this mission in projecting races,” Chalian added.Chris Stirewalt, who serves as political editor for the cable network NewsNation and anchors the weekly show The Hill Sunday, said he doesn’t think that Republicans will be happy with the election results. He said that early returns from Ohio will be a good indication of whether “the rout is on” for Democrats.Stirewalt is no stranger to election night, having been part of Fox News’ decision desk for several cycles before leaving the network in 2021. He said he values the finality of the process: “The conversation goes on and on and on, and then it’s over. And you count, look at the scoreboard, and then it’s done. I love that.”While Acosta is best-known for his television work, he said he doesn’t miss CNN and is happy to be “starting something at the beginning” by working in creator-driven media. “And that’s kind of the exciting part of it, because who knows where this thing is going to take us?”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026CNNTelevision industryNBC UniversalCBSfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Content: A worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAView image in fullscreenA worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPASwedenShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackChains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shopsWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?Jon HenleyEurope correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.39 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.12 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland,Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.The incidents follow anattack in France last monthin which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.Sweden’s Coop chain toldthe daily Aftonbladetthat six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southernSwedenposted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.View image in fullscreenWorkers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ReutersThe head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.View image in fullscreenEmpty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near  russels.Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty ImagesBelgium’sLe Soir newspaper reportedthat dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read more“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.Ikea,famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.View image in fullscreenA customer surveys an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket in Dublin.Photograph: ReutersMany cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.The agency subsequently reportedthat supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.Explore more on these topicsSwedenSupermarketsCybercrimeRetail industryEuropeBelgiumLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Newcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headache | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Everton beat Newcastle, who finished with 10 men, for the second time in five days as Thierno Barry’s strike sealed a 1-0 win
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Everton beat Newcastle, who finished with 10 men, for the second time in five days as Thierno Barry’s strike sealed a 1-0 win
Content: Thierno Barry wheels away after his poacher’s finish put Everton a goal up in the second half.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarView image in fullscreenThierno Barry wheels away after his poacher’s finish put Everton a goal up in the second half.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarPremier LeagueNewcastle unrest grows as Barry and Everton give Jaissle another headacheMiles Starforth at St James' ParkMon 2 Nov 2026 17.04 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.48 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Grealish will do well to get back into theEvertonstarting lineup when he returns to the squad – as David Moyes’s side are doing just fine without him.Newcastle were condemned to a second defeat in five days by Moyes’s young team, with a second-half goal from Thierno Barry giving Everton victory against 10 men at St James’ Park after the substitute Jacob Ramsey’s late red card.And there are still more questions than answers about Matthias Jaissle’s new-look side following a summer of transition at the club, and supporters again voiced their disapproval at the end of the game.Newcastle United 0-1 Everton: Premier League – liveRead moreMoyes was reluctant to talk about Grealish’s situation, stating simply that the winger was “unavailable” for a second successive game followinga breach of club discipline. But, pressed if there was a way back for the winger, he added: “Of course there is.”Asked about the resilience of his youthful team, Moyes added: “They’re so good, they give everything they’ve got. They’re a brilliant group of players. We beat Newcastle on Thursday night, and to beat them again today, it’s not an easy thing to do for any club.”Jaissle acknowledged the reaction of Newcastle supporters to the performance and the result. “Big frustration, big disappointment,” he said. “Of course, the fans, they get frustrated like we are. We need to analyse it now in detail. It’s also clear that I have the responsibility, and I also take that as manager of this club. We need to do things better.”Newcastle fans had made their feelings aboutthe 3-1 Carabao Cup defeataway to Everton last Thursday clear to Jaissle, who has found himself under pressure early in his tenure. By the time he had gone on to the pitch at Hill Dickinson Stadium to acknowledge their backing, most of the 7,732 travelling supporters had headed for the exits, and St James’ Park emptied just as quickly after the home loss.Eddie Howe was always going to be a hard act to follow given what he achieved in his first four years as head coach at St James’ Park, but the summer departures of big-name players, and his own 11th-hour arrival, has made the job even harder for Jaissle.View image in fullscreenMatthias Jaissle struggles to get his message across to his Newcastle players.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersFrustration bubbled away beneath the surface at St James’ Park, a stadium which can be a cauldron when fans are given something to shout about. But the decibel levels were rarely raised in the first period. Newcastle’s Harvey Barnes cut inside late in the half, and an awkward deflection off Jarrad Branthwaite momentarily had Jordan Pickford worried, but, in truth, neither he nor Lukas Hornicek in the home goal were troubled in the first 45 minutes. Jake O’Brien and Harrison Armstrong had chances for Everton late in the half, but both shot wide.Hornicek, however, was finally tested early in the second half – and a mistake from him handed Barry a goal. The goalkeeper let a shot from the left from Tyrique George squirm under his body, and Barry gratefully tapped the ball into an empty net.Newcastle have given a number of soft goals away this season, and Jaissle conceded that his team had been caught “sleeping” by Everton, who pressed for a second goal before Yoane Wissa and Sean Steur were sent on by Jaissle.Steur, after a hugely promising start to life at St James’ Park, has found himself on the bench in recent games to the bemusement of some supporters given how well he performed early in the season following his move from Ajax. Soon after Steur’s introduction, Barnes delivered a ball from the left which was met by Anthony Elanga at the back post. The ball rolled along the line, but did not fully cross it, and Everton cleared the danger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJacob Ramsey sees red in stoppage time after coming on as a substitute for Newcastle.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersBy now, St James’ Park had livened up, but the home team’s performance still lacked conviction in the final third.Jaissle sent on Ramsey and Jacob Murphy for the last 15 minutes, but Newcastle found themselves pinned back by Everton, who were a threat on the break.Half-chances came and went for Newcastle – who did not have a shot on target until the 86th minute, and also had Ramsey sent off for two stoppage-time yellow cards – as the travelling fans made themselves heard high up on Level 7.The question some Newcastle fans are asking is just how high this team can finish above the Premier League’s relegation zone, as there are still big issues for Jaissle to address at both ends of the pitch ahead of what looks like being a challenging winter.“The only way is togetherness, showing unity, and then the belief comes,” said Jaissle.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNewcastle UnitedEvertonmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Zero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways? | Tampa Bay Buccaneers | The Guardian
description: In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved right
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved right
Content: Baker Mayfield had a busy day handing the ball on Sunday.Photograph: Jason Behnken/APView image in fullscreenBaker Mayfield had a busy day handing the ball on Sunday.Photograph: Jason Behnken/APTampa Bay BuccaneersZero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways?In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved rightDave SchillingMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.21 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t think I’m being cheeky when I say that passing is the most exciting part of football. A solid hit is nice, and a big run can thrill you, but this is a quarterback-centric game. When a QB is bad, teams usually lose and fans get bored. So, Sunday’s performance by Baker Mayfield and theTampa Bay Buccaneershad me positively gobsmacked. I wouldn’t say their 16-0 win over the Atlanta Falcons was thrill-a-minute, but it certainly was historic. By completing a grand total of zero passes out of a paltry three attempts, Baker Mayfield led the Bucs to the first game with no passing offense since the Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 16-12 on 29 September 1974. If you are miraculously old enough to remember the NFL before the advent of the forward pass in 1906, first off, congratulations on being over 120 years of age. Please email me your full diet and exercise regimen. You’re probably on your feet (if standing is still something physically possible), cheering a bit of hard-nosed, classic football. The rest of us young whippersnappers still grinding through our first century are holding our noses.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueNFL roundup: Cowboys and Chiefs suffer late collapses; Lamar Jackson’s season could be overRead moreOf course, Mayfield – a former No 1 overall pick –canthrow. As recently as 2024 he threw for 41 touchdowns and 4,500 passing yards in a season. But Sunday’s game was played in pouring rain thatled to farcical moments like this, and Tampa Bay clearly decided that the ground game was the only way to go. That the Bucs could score at all, let alone 16 points, is a credit to Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell running as though their lives depended on it. Irving finished the day with 170 rushing yards and one touchdown, while Gainwell had 140. Combined with Mayfield, they rushed 56 times for 324 yards – the most ever in a single game for the Bucs. They more than made up for Mayfield’s borderline irrelevance in the pocket. Mayfield made himself useful blocking for his runners, but otherwise, I probably could have started at QB for the Buccaneers and the game would have been the same, other than the high likelihood of me suffering at least one gruesome injury.“If I’m not going to throw the ball, I have to get active somehow,” Mayfield said after the game. He certainly was more valuable for his team than Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr, who had a game that would be front-page terrible if not for the historic passing futility on the other side. Penix went 8-for-24 with four interceptions. The field was wet and as slippery as a greased-up ferret with a sugar rush. But even a wet playing surface wasn’t enough to stop Tampa’s run game, or kicker Chase McLaughlin’s three field goals. Having said that, McLaughlin didn’t even need to make one – Atlanta were just that bad. Next week, the Falcons face the Bengals in Spain. If Atlanta play like this in Madrid, they’ll be the worst American export to Europe sinceDavid Hasselhoff’s first album.MVP of the weekJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.We’ll start with the positives: Burrow threw for five touchdowns, ran for another, racked up 462 passing yards and led his team back from 13 points down to a 43-36 overtime win on Sunday. On the downside, he threw three interceptions and all this came against the Tennessee Titans. But Burrow gets MVP this week for a refusal to do anything dull. And the Bengals are off to their best start since the 2021 season, when they made the Super Bowl.View image in fullscreenJoe Burrow accounted for six touchdowns on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Mack/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockVideo of the weekThe Chiefs-Broncos game was absorbing until the final moments. Kansas City, down 28-24, looked set to pull of a late victory when they had a first and goal on the Denver 4-yard line with 35 seconds left. But stout Broncos defending and a sloppy penalty from the Chiefs when they thought they had scored the winning touchdown meant they needed to score on the final play of the game. When Patrick Mahomes is under center in this type of situation, a Chiefs win is automatic. Not this time, though.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueStat of the week259. That’s the number of career touchdown passes across the regular season and playoffs by Josh Allen for the Bills after his pair during his team’s victory over the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday. In reaching that milestone, he broke the record set by Buffalo legend Jim Kelly. The victory moved the Bills to 6-1 and they now have the best record in the AFC. Sadly, the game was also marked by a thumb injury to the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson. It may end his season, a sad turn of events for one of the most thrilling players in the league.Elsewhere around the leagueThe Vikings are undefeated no more. The Lions pulled out a thriller to end Minnesota’s hopes of a perfect season. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams for a score with 4:35 left in the game to squeak home 19-15. This was Detroit’s third straight victory, but they also lost linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury. Campbell had to be carted off the field on a backboard early in the fourth quarter, which put an undeniable damper on the post-victory celebrations. Instead of reveling in his late-game heroics, Goff wassomber and reflective when speaking about Campbell. “That was definitely scary. He’s a husband and a father.”There’s more heartbreak on display at AT&T Stadium this year than a Kazuo Ishiguro novel. The Dallas Cowboys looked to be in the driver’s seat against Arizona as the fourth quarter began. They led 24-10 and their defense was looking well-prepared to lock down a win. Except, folks, they weren’t. Arizona exploded for 20 points in the fourth, as Gardner Minshew took over from an underperforming Jacoby Brissett. Minshew marched the Cardinals down the field in 63 seconds late in the fourth to tie the game at 30. A simple Chad Ryland extra point would have been enough to win the game, but the PAT flew wide left. This was Ryland’s first extra-point miss in the last 58 tries. To overtime they went. Ryland was able to rescue his no-good, very-bad day by hitting a 42-yard field goal to finally clinch the comeback. The Cowboys are 3-5, and a brutal 1-3 at home as we near the halfway mark of the season. Lucky for Dallas that they play in a division where only one team is above .500.View image in fullscreenGardner Minshew and the Cardinals celebrate a touchdown in their wild comeback.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APAre the Rams back? Or are the Chargers just awful? Time will tell, but in the Battle of Los Angeles, it was the Rams who took care of business, 24-9. The game was close until a pivotal second-half period in which the Rams scored two touchdowns. The Chargers are 0-7. They’re the only team in theNFLwho haven’t scored 100 points or more combined this season – 99 points for, versus 175 against. All this with alleged offensive mastermind Mike McDaniel at OC.The Jacksonville Jaguars remain the most pleasant surprise in the NFL, destroying Indianapolis at home, 42-7. The Jags are top of the AFC South, above three teams with sub-.300 winning percentages. Trevor Lawrence was superb for Jacksonville, sporting a 153.3 rating, 210 yards on 10-of-14 passing and three touchdowns. The Jags’ defense forced three turnovers – two interceptions and a fumble – and surrendered just one pity touchdown in the third quarter. Jacksonville are at the top of a terrible division. Is there any reason to think they won’t stay there?As someone who has dated both a woman from Cleveland and a woman from Pittsburgh (not at the same time), I can attest that Steelers v Browns is one of the most heated rivalries there is, primarily because Pittsburgh and Cleveland are cities with chips the size of dinner plates on their shoulders. Personally, I prefer the food in Pittsburgh (specifically the giant hotdog they sold at Pirates games that has pierogies on top), and so I was pulling for the Steelers on Sunday. They did not let me down. This was the 23rd straight home win for the Steelers over the Browns. Pittsburgh sacked Deshaun Watson eight times. Eerily, the last time I did this column, Deshaun wassacked … eight times by the Jets in Week 5. Maybe next time I’m writing this, I’ll give the Browns a heads-up.View image in fullscreenNick Herbig sacks Deshaun Watson during the Steelers’ win over Cleveland.Photograph: Brent Gudenschwager/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Raiders pulled off another of the day’s improbable comebacks, scoring 24 points in the second half to beat the New York Jets 38-33. Las Vegas broke a four-game losing streak and are 4-4 on the year. Kirk Cousins threw for 247 yards on 19-of-26 passing and three touchdowns, plus a TD run in the third quarter that he punctuated with a peculiarArrested Development-stylechicken dance that he called his “wellness celebration”. The 38-year-old said, “We do a lot of tissue work here. At my age, it’s especially helpful. … So I said someday if I run a touchdown in, I’m going to give a shoutout to all the staff that works so hard to help us feel good and be one of the healthier teams in the league.” Cousins almost forgot to do this peculiar celly, butBrock Bowers reminded him. Perhaps the first and last time anyone will ever say “Hit them with the wellness celebration!” on an NFL field. Or at least I hope so.As for the Jets, they were content to make jokes about themselves. “I think we had some bad penalties, bad mistakes,” their veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick said. “Jets being Jets.”Explore more on these topicsTampa Bay BuccaneersAtlanta FalconsNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lions’ Jack Campbell remains hospitalized after ‘scary’ neck injury but initial signs are positive | Detroit Lions | The Guardian
description: The Detroit Lions have said the initial signs for Jack Campbell are ‘positive’ after the linebacker was carted off the field
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Detroit Lions have said the initial signs for Jack Campbell are ‘positive’ after the linebacker was carted off the field
Content: Jack Campbell was carted off the field on Sunday.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreenJack Campbell was carted off the field on Sunday.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APDetroit LionsLions’ Jack Campbell remains hospitalized after ‘scary’ neck injury but initial signs are positiveTeam say they will not release further information26-year-old will remain in hospital for time beingGuardian sportMon 2 Nov 2026 16.15 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.16 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Detroit Lions have said the initial signs for Jack Campbell are “positive” after the linebacker was carted off the field and taken to hospitalwhen he suffered a neck injuryduring Sunday’s win over the Minnesota Vikings.The 26-year-old was treated for nine minutes on the field after making a tackle during Sunday’s game. Players from both teams were visibly distraught as Campbell received medical attention before he was taken for further treatment at a nearby facility.Zero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways?Read more“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the Lions said in a statement on Monday. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”Lions coach Dan Campbell also gave a brief update on the linebacker’s condition on Monday. “It’s positive news on Jack,” said Dan Campbell. “So your prayers are working. Please continue to do that and we’ll leave it at that.”The Lions coach also paid tribute to the former first-round pick’s contributions to the team.“I don’t even know if I can put it into words. You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy. He’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back,” said Dan Campbell. “He’s just all heart, all effort. And just an unbelievable person. Down to earth. Very genuine. There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him.”On Sunday, Lions quarterback Jared Goff spoke about the anxiety that had surrounded the injury.“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff said. “It just brings you back to reality for a moment that he’s a husband and a father.“Scary. We’re praying for him and hope he’s going to be all right. If anyone is tough enough to get through something like that, it’s going to be him.”Campbell was named an All-Pro last season and is in his fourth year in the league. In May, he signed a four-year contract extension with the Lions worth $81m.Explore more on these topicsDetroit LionsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Longtime host Michael Wilbon steps away from ESPN due to ‘health issues’ | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The NBA commentator and co-host of Pardon the Interruption did not give detail on the issue but said he hopes it is not an ‘extended’ leave of absence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The NBA commentator and co-host of Pardon the Interruption did not give detail on the issue but said he hopes it is not an ‘extended’ leave of absence
Content: Michael Wilbon has co-hosted ESPN’s Pardon the Interruption for the last 25 years.Photograph: Susan Walsh/APView image in fullscreenMichael Wilbon has co-hosted ESPN’s Pardon the Interruption for the last 25 years.Photograph: Susan Walsh/APUS sports mediaLongtime host Michael Wilbon steps away from ESPN due to ‘health issues’Pardon the Interruption co-host to take leave of absenceWilbon did not go into detail but cited ‘worrisome signs’Associated PressMon 2 Nov 2026 14.51 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 14.59 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Wilbon, the co-host of ESPN’s popular Pardon the Interruption talkshow alongside good friend Tony Kornheiser announced on Monday he is taking a leave of absence because of what he described as “multiple health issues”.Wilbon, who turns 68 later this month, wrote in a post on X that he is taking a trip to “the injured list” but added he hopes it is “not an extended one”.While Wilbon, who is also featured on ESPN’s NBA coverage, declined to go into detail about his situation, he added that there are people in his personal life who noticed “worrisome signs” in recent years that he largely ignored. Wilbon did make a point to note the issues are not alcohol or gambling-related.“I have no idea how exactly this part of my journey will wind up,” Wilbon posted. “The goal is to come out of it feeling much better than I do now and ready to return to sparring with Tony.”Wilbon’s last appearance on PTI, which recently celebrated its 25th anniversary and is credited with revolutionizing television’s “sports debate” format, was on 26 October.The show, in part, is a byproduct of the friendship of Wilbon and Kornheiser, who became colleagues at the Washington Post in the 1980s.“I have loved sparring and hosting PTI with Tony every single day these past 25 years,” Wilbon wrote. “And I’m incredibly grateful for the support and encouragement of my colleagues as I take this time away to concentrate on me, especially my well-being.”Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaUS sportsESPNnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture
Author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
Headline: Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture
Content: An aerial view of La Bombonera before kick-off in Sunday’sSuperclásico.The absence of away fans have been a fixture of Argentinian football since 2013. Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/Getty ImagesAttending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixtureByMarcela Mora y Araujoat La BomboneraMon 2 Nov 2026 15.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.39 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since the Observer Sport Monthly publisheda listof 50 sporting things you must do before you die withWatch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Airesat No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.Exciting, right?Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the firstSuperclásicowithout away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press areaMoores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.View image in fullscreenFans of Boca cheer from beneath their umbrellas.Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty ImagesOver the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known asLa Doceleads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in byLa Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.Barritta was the infamous leader ofLa Docedecades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with twoRiver Platefans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.View image in fullscreenRiver Plate fans clash with riot police outside the Monumental prior the final of the Copa Libertadores against Boca Juniors in 2018. The match was rescheduled after the bus carrying Boca players was attacked, injuring several players.Photograph: Sebastian Pani/APDeath at theSuperclásicowas not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm ofLa Docein 1981, by which time the rupture was total.In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle theSuperclásicomight be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of theSuperclásicohas remained,if it hadn’t been sucked out already.Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.“I’ve seen betterSuperclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.View image in fullscreenLeonel Flores of Boca celebrates with teammates following the team’s victory in theSuperclásico.Photograph: Marcelo Endelli/Getty ImagesThat must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch theSuperclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.View image in fullscreenRiver Plate’s Gonzalo Montiel leaves the pitch under police protection against Boca.Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty ImagesMaybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all thisSuperclásicononsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to aSuperclásicowith my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.Explore more on these topicsBoca JuniorsRiver PlatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How Kimi Antonelli saw off the grid to become F1’s youngest world champion | Kimi Antonelli | The Guardian
description: Mercedes driver made history at 20 years old by exceeding all expectations to win the title in only his second season
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Mercedes driver made history at 20 years old by exceeding all expectations to win the title in only his second season
Content: Kimi Antonelli celebrates with his team after winning the Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka in March to provide an early indication something special was brewing.Photograph: Philip Fong/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli celebrates with his team after winning the Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka in March to provide an early indication something special was brewing.Photograph: Philip Fong/AFP/Getty ImagesKimi AntonelliHow Kimi Antonelli saw off the grid to become F1’s youngest world championMercedes driver makes history at 20 years old by exceeding all expectations in only his second seasonGiles RichardsMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.36 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore the 2026 season had begun there was something of a consensus within Formula One. Mercedes appeared to have the fastest car and George Russell was favourite for the title. Beside him in what was indeed a dominant Mercedes, his teenage teammate,Kimi Antonelli, was the prodigious talent who was expected to require honing after a tricky rookie season. Said consensus lasted one race, by the sixth it had been turned on its head and Antonelli was squarely on his way to being champion.Few had doubted that the then 19-year-old Italian would prove to be strong in a car that for the first two-thirds of the season was the class of the field but for Antonelli to come out of the blocks with such verve, aggressive skill and also the judgment and at times maturity of a veteran was revelatory. As the youngest F1 world champion and Italy’s first since Alberto Ascari in 1953, Antonelli made history this year but it was the way he did it which truly caught the eye.Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GPRead moreAs the sport’s youngest world champion at 20 years old crossed the line in tears, wracked with emotion at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, what it meant to him was clear, as it was for his mother, father and sister, the family with whom he is so close and who have played a key part in his success. They embraced and shed their own tears too.It might have been an inevitability for some time but when he climbed from his car to the roaring approval of the fans in the hugely atmospheric stadium section it was understandable that the Italian, only just out of his teens, could barely take it in.“We did it,” he said. “I wouldn’t be here without Mercedes, without my family. This moment is one that will live for ever. I am speechless. I am just trying to process this moment.”In his rookie season Antonelli had struggled with the ground-effect cars as he came to terms with F1 and endured a run of poor performances mid-season. Questions were asked about whether he had been promoted too soon. They were answered emphatically this year but not quite from the off.At theseason opener in Australia he crashed outin final practice with an air of the over-eager charger that was costly and familiar from 2025. The repairs to his car meant he almost missed qualifying and Russell went on to win. The bookies it seemed had called it right.View image in fullscreenAntonelli became F1’s youngest driver to claim pole before his debut grand prix win at the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.Photograph: Sam Bloxham/LAT ImagesWhat followed, for all that it was so early in the season, was nonetheless gamechanging. Fifth place in the sprint in China including a penalty for hitting Isack Hadjar was not entirely auspicious but it was the last foot put wrong in Shanghai. Having becomeF1’s youngest driver to claim polehe converted with an inch-perfect run to take his debut grand prix win by five seconds from Russell.With a handle on how to maximise the driving style required by the energy management of the new cars and a feel for it that was tantalisingly out of reach for his teammate, Antonelli was on another level. Victory in Japan after dropping to sixth at the start followed, albeit with good fortune from a safety car call, and with it a championship lead he would not relinquish again.Miami fell to the Italian, then Canada. The narrative had changed, Russell and the rest of the grid were being schooled by the kid with only one season under his belt.If emphasis were needed as to the who was calling the shots Antonelli performed emphatically in Monaco. He saw off a fierce charge from Max Verstappen to claim pole and then made an indelible mark with victory on the streets of the principality. He held his lead from the off and was flawless beneath the looming walls before having to hold his nerve to see off two restarts that had eradicated the 30-second lead he had built.The second, a standing start alongside the seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton was as nervy a test as one might ask of any driver, let alone one in only his second season. Antonelli passed with flying colours, held his line, the place, and the lead to the flag.View image in fullscreenAntonelli is congratulated by seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton after his win in Canada.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesQuestions were asked of him repeatedly and every time he had the answers. If there were weaknesses in his game, that he might be impetuous or overexcitable, by Monaco they had been banished by the calm, cold commitment of a champion in waiting.It was his fifth consecutive win, a record run after a debut victory and with it he had amassed a lead of 66 points over Hamilton and 68 over Russell.Russell to be fair had endured more than his fair share of bad luck and it was undeniably a factor but not decisive. The safety car at Suzuka which benefited Antonelli cost the British driver, he was unfairly penalised for pit lane speeding at Monaco and then had an engine failure while leading in Canada, a body blow. Yet he admitted at the time that he was not as at home with the car as Antonelli and it was visible on track, the Italian often quicker even when behind his teammate.This was demonstrated in Barcelona when he had passed Russell to take second place with five laps to go. However, the Italian too had to weather his own share of misfortune. Having taken second place he ground to a halt with an electrical shutdown to his immense disappointment and that of some observers missing the good old days when engines used to at least give out with a bang.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat ill luck was followed by a wheel shield failure at Silverstone dropping him out of contention just as he had been challenging for the lead. The resulting points swing put Russell within 25 points but that was as close as the British driver was to come.McLaren and Ferrari both came at Mercedes taking two wins apiece but while Mercedes no longer had it all their own way Antonelli consistently performed. His brief mid-season frustration behind him, a dominant win in Belgium was followed by two podiums. Russell did cop some more bad luck but there were two further races which defined why the season belonged to the 20-year-old.View image in fullscreenThe Italian produced the most memorable of drives after starting at 19th and going on to win his home grand prix in Monza.Photograph: Daniel Dal Zennaro/EPAThe first at his home race in Monza where he started from 19th after an engine change-prompted grid penalty butwent on to take the winwas a masterclass, proving he had the race craft, control and judgment to scythe through the field from a seemingly impossible position. It was another blow to Russell who had started from second and was expectant of clawing back points yet dropped a further seven.Only one driver has come back to win from further down the grid, John Watson from 22nd at the Long Beach GP in 1983. Watson’s drive is long remembered, as will be Antonelli’s.The second was of a similar vein; it indicated the depth of his talent and what greater heights the Italian may go on to reach. In a season marked by only marginal errors, misreading yellow flags in qualifying in Austria, and a penalty for failing to slow under yellow in qualifying in Hungary among them, the most egregious by far was his crash in qualifying at Baku, where Russell went on to take pole by a huge margin.Antonelli admitted the mistake was unnecessary and started from 16th. Yet how he dealt with it illustrated a champion’s mindset. Instead of charging at the race trying to make up places and taking chances on a circuit he knew could bite, he played the percentages, moved through the field with care and decisiveness, even as chaos and crashes at a restart caused him to pick up floor damage making the car a brute to handle. He kept his head and his nerve to grind out fifth, despite still castigating himself for the accident in qualifying.View image in fullscreenAntonelli is mobbed by his Mercedes teammates after clinching the world title in Mexico.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty ImagesHe had accepted the blame and learned from it, then assessed his position, how to handle it and what course was best in the bigger picture of the title fight. Not all titles are won with derring-do, but they can be lost. Antonelli had dropped points but with as much damage limitation as might reasonably be expected, the title inched inexorably closer.A similarly cool head saw off a late resurgence from Verstappen in an impressively improved Red Bull as Antonelli ground out podiums behind him. Indeed, grabbing third in Singapore with a dash past Lando Norris and Hamilton as they fought each another typified why the title was all but in his hands.An emphatic victory in Austin followed, his ninth, which Wolff hailed as one of his best, which was not quite enough to seal the deal but it left him so far ahead that ninth or better would suffice this weekend here in Mexico, where he duly closed it out with a nerveless run to take third place.Better than anyone had anticipated, perhaps even than his Mercedes team might have hoped, Antonelli delivered on his promise in emphatic style and prompted a new consensus: that there is surely only more to come.Explore more on these topicsKimi AntonelliFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMercedes GPfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Goals, guests and 6,561 scenarios: inside ESPN on the biggest NWSL Decision Day yet | NWSL | The Guardian
description: The final day of the regular season gave fans Gotham’s Shield win, a farewell to a Seattle hero and a new part-whiparound, part-watchalong show to take it all in
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The final day of the regular season gave fans Gotham’s Shield win, a farewell to a Seattle hero and a new part-whiparound, part-watchalong show to take it all in
Content: Gotham clinched the NWSL Shield for the first time in club history in the headlining match of ESPN’s Decision Day slate.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGotham clinched the NWSL Shield for the first time in club history in the headlining match of ESPN’s Decision Day slate.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockNWSLGoals, guests and 6,561 scenarios: inside ESPN on the biggest NWSL Decision Day yetThe final day of the regular season gave fans Gotham’s Shield win, a farewell to a Seattle hero and a new part-whiparound, part-watchalong show to take it all inElla Brockwayin Bristol, ConnecticutMon 2 Nov 2026 12.28 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.46 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a player, Ali Krieger went intoNWSLDecision Day focused on one result. She was Gotham FC’s captain in 2023, the first time the league played all of the final games of the regular season simultaneously. The job, she remembers, was to not worry about the other games going on.Three years later, Krieger spent Decision Day with eyes on not one game but eight. For the first time, all of the final games of the NWSL season were aired by the same network. Krieger, now a lead analyst forESPN, and host Kelsey Riggs Cuff anchored the coverage from headquarters in Bristol with a show that was part whiparound, part watchalong, and ultimately wholly new for the 14-year-old league.There was no shortage of storylines. With 16 teams in action, the slate of simultaneous kickoffs was the largest in the league’s history. San Diego and Gotham were fighting for the Shield; four teams were jousting for home-field advantage; three were vying for the final playoff spots. The league simulated Sunday’s games 50,000 times and found more than 200 possibilities for playoff brackets, with 6,561 ways the results could go.How do you prepare for the way that the storydoesspin? The network deployed 60-plus cameras and more than 150 staffers around the United States, plus about 20 in Bristol. Cuff and Krieger met with researchers, rewatched games and assembled a 12-page Google Doc of notes.“You know that it’s going to be chaos. You lean into the breaking news feel of it,” Cuff said in the green room, about an hour before the games began. “And then you just sit back and enjoy it, because this is the biggest day that we have on the calendar right now, with so much on the line from top to bottom.”First-place Gotham’s home match against Utah was the headliner on ESPN’s main channel, with the other seven on the streaming service ESPN+ and Krieger and Cuff’s studio show on ESPN2. It wasn’t ESPN’s first time producing a whiparound-style soccer studio show – the network has done so for the Bundesliga and US Open Cup – but it was the first for the NWSL.“This is like a fresh canvas,” said Manuel de la Fe, vice-president of production at ESPN. “We’re going to paint, and we’re going to see how it comes out.”View image in fullscreenESPN staged its studio show for NWSL Decision Day at headquarters in Bristol.Photograph: Ella Brockway/The GuardianA mantra for live television is to expect the unexpected, and the hosts quickly learned Sunday that the unexpected includes surprise women’s college volleyball upsets. A Tennessee-Missouri five-setter meant the start of the Gotham match was pushed to the ESPN2 slot, and the studio show did not actually begin until about 25 minutes into the games.By the time it kicked into gear, there was plenty to talk about. San Diego, in second place and facing Bay FC in San Jose, scored the day’s first goal in the ninth minute; Gotham scored in their own game seconds later.For those who prefer their whiparound shows to have the cadence of NFL RedZone’srollercoaster, this wasn’t exactly that. Earlier Sunday, Krieger mentioned Diana Taurasi and Sue Bird’s women’s basketball watchalongs as inspiration for this show, and it called on special guests in the style of the Manningcast.While the interviews did occasionally push the game action itself off screen, they also provided some of the day’s highlights. Lead reporter Jeff Kassouf added insights into the changing table. Olivia Moultrie, recovering from an ACL injury, reacted live as her Portland Thorns scored their first goal. Megan Rapinoe called in from a suite at Seattle’s Lumen Field. (“I’m not in the closet, but I am in the bathroom,” Rapinoe quipped.)There were still some snafus. During the Portland game, the feed cut while Sophia Wilson was in the run-up to a penalty kick, jumping to an interview with Heather O’Reilly and a stream of the North Carolina game. Some viewers online spoke of audio-synching issues in certain games.But after just six first-half goals across the eight games, the second half brought more action. Angel City poured three goals on Boston Legacy; Washington scored while their game was in a triple-box display.
