title: Guardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup | Melbourne Cup | The Guardian
description: Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’
Content: More than two-thirds of Australian polled now say they have low or zero interest in the annual Melbourne Cup horse race.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than two-thirds of Australian polled now say they have low or zero interest in the annual Melbourne Cup horse race.Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty ImagesMelbourne CupGuardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne CupGrowing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 14.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA record number of Australians are turning their backs on theMelbourne Cup, with more than two-thirds surveyed saying they have low or zero interest in the annual horse race.Support for the Melbourne Cup has been sliding consistently for a number of years, butthe Guardian Essential pollfound just 9% of Australians said they had high interest in the race now – nearly half the proportion in 2025.“The race that once stopped the nation is now just white noise for many,” said Peter Lewis, the chair of Essential Media.The Guardian Essential poll of 1,003 Australians in late October highlights thelatest erosionin popularity of the eventamid growing ambivalence to the event.Guardian Essential poll: One Nation and Labor’s primary vote on par as discontent with Albanese risesRead moreJust 9% of people said they had high interest in the Cup, down seven percentage points from 2025, with another 23% professing moderate interest, also down three points. About 29% of voters said they had low interest (up five points from last year), while another 39% said no interest at all (up eight points).The combined high and moderate interest came to only 32%, the lowest on record since Essential began asking this question in annual polling in November 2022. The combined low and no interest vote was 68%, jumping 12 points from last year to its highest on record.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn November 2022, the low and no interest vote came to a combined 52%; it was 62% in 2023, 52% in 2024, and 56% in 2025.The“Nup to the Cup” movement, backed by some high-profile politicians and celebrities, has contributed to declining support for the race.But 62% of Australians nonetheless agreed the Melbourne Cup was a unique part of Australia’s national identity. That number remains a strong majority view, despite falling from 78% agreement when Essential asked this question in 2019.Half of Australians (50%) believe the Cup promotes unhealthy gambling behaviour, up 3% since 2025, while 36% say they feel the Cup normalises animal cruelty, down three points from 2025.Another 48% said they were less interested in the Cup than they used to be.“The key driver appears to be a growing disdain for gambling, although concern for animal cruelty comes a close second,” Lewis said.“More broadly this reflects the decline in unifying atonal moments in a world where more and more people have their experiences mediated by targeted advertising algorithms.”Just 12% of voters in October’s poll said they regularly wagered on horse races and would bet on Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, down five points from 2025. In contrast, 46% of people said they were not interested in the Cup and would not place a bet, up six points from last year.Another 25% said they rarely bet on horses but would watch the race and place a bet, while 17% said they would watch but not bet.Explore more on these topicsMelbourne CupEssential pollOpinion pollsHorse racingAnimal welfareGamblingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We had to dig in’: Arsenal’s Anfield win was performance of champions, says Rice | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Declan Rice says Arsenal are ready for more grinding wins as he hailed the 1-0 success at Liverpool on Sunday as the performance of champions
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Declan Rice says Arsenal are ready for more grinding wins as he hailed the 1-0 success at Liverpool on Sunday as the performance of champions
Content: Declan Rice celebrates at the final whistle.Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice celebrates at the final whistle.Photograph: Matt West/ShutterstockArsenal‘We had to dig in’: Arsenal’s Anfield win was performance of champions, says RiceMidfielder praises his side’s grit and determinationSzoboszlai says there are fine margins between teamsDavid HytnerandAndy HunterMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDeclan Rice says Arsenal are ready for more grinding wins as he hailedthe 1-0 success at Liverpoolon Sunday as the performance of champions. The midfielder set up Kai Havertz for the only goal on 16 minutes but his physicality and reading of the game on the defensive side were arguably more impressive.Liverpool were unhappy at the non-award of a penaltyfor a Jurriën Timber shirt-pull on Alexander Isak in the 21st minute and it was a day when the Kop fumed about Arsenal’s streetwise tactics, especially how they won free-kicks – albeit their own players were also guilty of going down too easily at times. The Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya was booked for time-wasting in the 92nd minute as his team closed out the victory.Arsenal won 1-0 at Nottingham ­Forestin their previous Premier League away match – after which they were criticised for their lack of ­creativity. This time, the barbs centred on their gamesmanship because they were a threat on the ­counterattack. They are not about to trouble ­anybody connected to the club.Liverpool’s work in progress fizzles out in the face of streetwise champions | Andy HunterRead more“No game is plain sailing; it is always going to be tough,” Rice said. “Looking back at that Forest game, it wasn’t the best performance but we ground it out, we won and there’s going to be more of that this season. But results like this one [at Liverpool] just make it that extra bit special so we are delighted.”It was Arsenal’s first league ­victory at Anfield since 2012 and so far this season they have won at four grounds where they did not win when ­securing the title in the last campaign, the ­others being Villa Park, the Stadium of Light and the City Ground. “Any team who has won at Anfield in the past has never had it easy,” Rice said. “We had to dig in and give it everything because they throw so many attacks at you. We had to be resilient and strong. It was a great win.”Asked whether it was a match in which ­Arsenal had played like ­champions, Rice replied: “For sure. It’s just drilled into us. What the manager [Mikel Arteta] has built at this club and the ­togetherness of the lads – you don’t get that ­performance without the lads being all together.View image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai said the penalty incident involving Jurriën Timber was crucial.Photograph: David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty Images“The way the manager has ­every­thing under control, the way everyone works towards everything he wants is not like anything I’ve ever seen before. So credit to us for what we have been doing for the last few years. Now it’s a massive thing to deliver again this year.”Dominik Szoboszlai said ­Liver­pool’s defeat demonstrated that there were only fine margins between Andoni Iraola’s side and the ­Premier League champions.According to Opta, Liverpool failed to register a shot on target in a ­Premier League home game for the first time since records began in 2003-04, as Arsenal moved three points clear at the summit. Szoboszlai believes the contest turned on the Isak shirt‑pull incident and that there was little between the teams.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are just one penalty less and that’s a big difference,” the ­midfielder said. “You know Anfield, you know our quality. I know they are a great team but it wouldn’t be easy for them [to have come back from a ­successful penalty].”Iraola claimed that he would tell ­Liverpool players to go down in the box – but Szoboszlai said that was not their style. “I don’t think in this moment you can think: ‘Oh, let me wait for someone touching me and I’ll fall down,’” he said.“No, Alex is focusing on the ball and he wants to head the ball in the net … It’s a penalty. I don’t know what they expect from us, to dive or ­something? I don’t think we are the type of team or players to do that but from now on we might need to do it. If Alex falls down it’s a clear penalty. Timber doesn’t really care about the ball and maybe if he doesn’t pull Alex’s shirt Alex can head it in the goal.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalLiverpoolPremier LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Lions shaken after All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell taken to hospital with ‘scary’ neck injury | Detroit Lions | The Guardian
description: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was taken to a local ⁠hospital after being injured during the fourth quarter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was taken to a local ⁠hospital after being injured during the fourth quarter
Content: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta in thought as Jack Campbell is treated on the field.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreenDetroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta in thought as Jack Campbell is treated on the field.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APDetroit LionsLions shaken after All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell taken to hospital with ‘scary’ neck injury26-year-old injured making tackle in fourth quarterLinebacker treated for nearly 10 minutes on fieldReutersSun 1 Nov 2026 19.09 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 19.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDetroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell sustained a neck injury and was taken to a local ⁠hospital after being injured during the fourth quarterof his team’s 19-15 victoryover the Minnesota Vikings.“Thoughts and ⁠prayers are ​with Jack and his family,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said after the game. “He’s being ⁠taken care of. We don’t have any new information. We’ll keep you updated as this thing goes. But ⁠we are thinking about him. We are thinking about him.”The Lions later said that Campbell would be kept in hospital overnight.“Jack Campbell is resting and will remain in a local hospital tonight, for continued evaluation and monitoring,” the Lions said in a statement. “The team will provide further updates as we have them.”NFL roundup: Cardinals’ comeback stuns Cowboys; Lamar Jackson’s season could be overRead moreJack Campbell, ​a first-team All-Pro last ‌season, was injured while ‌tackling Vikings tight end TJ Hockenson in the fourth quarter.The 26-year-old lay motionless facing the ground and was surrounded by medical personnel for nine minutes while being strapped to a board. He did not signal to the Ford ‌Field crowd as he was driven off on a cart toward the tunnel.“He’s breathing, he’s alert when ​he left,” Dan Campbell told the Lions Radio Network.Lions quarterback Jared Goff was shaken up while observing the situation.“Jack’s deal was definitely scary,” Goff said. “It just brings ⁠you back to reality for a moment that he’s a ​husband and a ​father. Scary. We’re praying for ​him and hope he’s going to be alright. ​If anyone ‌is tough enough ​to get through ​something like that, it’s going to be him.”Campbell, a fourth-year pro, was credited with three tackles prior to the injury. He has 57 this season after a career-high 176 last season. The Lions picked him in the first round of the 2023 draft.Explore more on these topicsDetroit LionsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores
Content: A worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPAView image in fullscreenA worker at ICA’s Sjöbo supermarket in southern Sweden throws away spoiled goods after its cooling units overheated.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPASwedenShop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attackChains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shopsWho is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?Jon HenleyEurope correspondentMon 2 Nov 2026 11.39 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.12 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSupermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland,Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.The incidents follow anattack in France last monthin which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.Sweden’s Coop chain toldthe daily Aftonbladetthat six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southernSwedenposted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.View image in fullscreenWorkers at ICA’s Sjöbo shop empty fridges of spoiled produce.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ReutersThe head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.View image in fullscreenEmpty fridges in a Delhaize supermarket near  russels.Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty ImagesBelgium’sLe Soir newspaper reportedthat dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Read more“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.Ikea,famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.View image in fullscreenA customer surveys an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket in Dublin.Photograph: ReutersMany cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.The agency subsequently reportedthat supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.Explore more on these topicsSwedenSupermarketsCybercrimeRetail industryEuropeBelgiumLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Unions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaul | Trade unions | The Guardian
description: Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company
Content: The Google headquarters at King's Cross in London.Photograph: coldsnowstorm/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Google headquarters at King's Cross in London.Photograph: coldsnowstorm/Getty ImagesTrade unionsUnions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaulProspect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech companyJessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 2 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.48 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplacescame into force, with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday.The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excludingDeepMind.Google DeepMind is expected to strike a separate agreement, with the Communication Workers Union and the Unite union seeking recognition there. The deal follows a similar agreement between Prospect and Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram and employs about 5,000 people in the UK.The agreements willallow unions to communicate with non-unionised workersand encourage them to join.The union, which represents more than 160,000 UK workers across several sectors, will now be able to run sessions inside Google’s workplaces, including the flagship headquarters in King’s Cross, London.Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said: “Prospect has been organising tech workers for many years, and this access agreement is a powerful signal of intent that we can successfully negotiate agreements with even the biggest global tech companies.“Tech workers deserve a stronger voice at work, whether that is over bread-and-butter trade union issues like pay and flexibility, AI deployment or workplace culture. I am pleased that Google has struck this agreement with us, and hope it sends a clear signal to other tech companies that having a relationship with trade unions is the new normal in the sector.”He said workers would have a stronger voice as more employees at Google andMetajoined trade unions. “With our track record of delivering wins for members, I am looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.”Google said it had signed the access agreement to comply with the new UK workplace legislation, although it maintained that it already had good internal employee relations.“This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfil these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on,” a spokesperson said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPaul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said last week that he expected a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as the “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces came into force.The Employment Rights Act gives unions the right to enter workplaces to meet workers or communicate with them electronically. From January, employers will be required to inform workers of their right to join a union.Previously, unions seeking recognition have sometimes had to organise workers from outside their workplaces – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to gain recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.Explore more on these topicsTrade unionsUniteGoogleDeepMindMetaAlphabetEmployment lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health official
Content: The trusts said that the Palantir system was either not live or they were not using any of its applications.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe trusts said that the Palantir system was either not live or they were not using any of its applications.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersPalantirPalantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from itExclusive: Gap between NHS claim and trusts’ comments described as ‘very misleading’ by senior health officialRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 2 Nov 2026 05.19 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.58 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.The 29 hospital trusts that NHS Englandpublicly lists as “realising benefits”from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024.It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”.The contrast between the number of hospitals theNHSclaims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps.Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.”Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.”She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal.The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS,and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?”Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.”Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems. He rebutted criticism from the Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it was “beyond ridiculous” that Lord Watson was a life peer.Watson and Mosley have also been writing directly to critical MPs in letters that have counted the times they have spoken out against the company, which one recipient, Labour’s Clive Lewis, described as “very Big Brother”.Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said: “I am concerned to hear that there are 29 trusts reported as receiving benefits but when asked are not actually using the tool. It is great that a number of trusts that have adopted the FDP are benefiting from this nationally funded programme, but it is crucial for public support … that benefits are reported accurately, transparently and in a way that can be properly verified.”A Palantir spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”Explore more on these topicsPalantirNHSAI (artificial intelligence)HealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer | The Guardian
description: We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future
Content: ‘The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers, and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers, and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionairesNaomi Klein and Ilana GlazerWe cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our futureMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.02 ESTShareAmerica is a divided country in crisis. Despite the sunny economic forecast coming from the Trump administration, millions of Americans are struggling to find and keep jobs, getting crushed under the rising cost of living, and losing health insurance when they need it the most.Meanwhile, via corporate consolidation and political corruption, the billionaire class is getting richer faster than ever before: a40%increase in wealth in just the last two years. Today, the combined wealth of nearly 3,000 global billionaires equalsone-fifth of the entire world’s yearly output. Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States.The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist,IPOs. When a company goes public, its founders and investors win the capitalist lottery. And instead of paying their fair share of taxes and redistributing resources back into society, most turn around and fund even more corporate consolidation and political corruption to extend their dominion.The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreElon Musk became an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, on the backs of workers’ pensions – and is bankrolling theRepublican midterm campaignswith a small percentage of his egregious gains. Oracle’s Larry Ellison – currently seventh on theForbes billionaireslist – backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger that is destroying the film industry and the livelihoods of the Americans who labor in it. Google’s Sergey Brin spent$100m opposing California’s Prop 40, a one-time wealth tax that would put the funds toward healthcare and other public services.To pay for essential services, we must tax billionaires, and pass legislation to do so starting in California and New York, but that is clearly not enough. We cannot allow more billionaires – or trillionaires – to be made in this country, further expanding the inequality chasm that’s turning a dignified life into a luxury in this country. We must also block the impending tech IPOs and preserve what’s left of our economy and our society.The Trump administration and tech investors have positioned IPOs as market success stories: when a company goes public, US investors could gain from their valuations. But regular Americans also shoulder a company’s risks – and risk their own futures when that stock ends up in their retirement accounts without consent.Problems with a private company or its products become problems for everyone invested in that company once it goes public, whether they’ve made the choice or not. And when the speculative investment bubble pops – such as with the 2008 crisis – regular people end up holding the bag.It’s no secret that the AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI are intending to go public in the near future. Both of these players also had major security flaws exposed recently, and openly acknowledge mind-bogglingly huge amounts of debt. If these companies are allowed to go public, their cofounders and investors – some of whom are already billionaires – will rise to whole new strata of private wealth.Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midtermsRead moreAmericans, meanwhile, will be financially crushed if the technologies fail or if these companies prove unable to make good on their extravagant financial promises. Already, the10 most valuable public companiesare in tech, which means the country’s economy depends on the stability of a single industry, one with an undeniable history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, outright fraud.June’s highly contentious SpaceX IPO already carries great risk for regular investors. If more speculative tech companies with staggering risk profiles are allowed to follow suit, the results will become too much for the market to bear.If and when the AI bubble bursts, it will take all of us with it, investors or not. Recessions level lives indiscriminately, and globally. The one exception will be the billionaires, who will have sufficient resources to walk away from the wreckage relatively unscathed.We cannot let the billionaire class take these kinds of risks with our future. To stop these reckless IPOs we must stand together, take collective action, and push for real change. We must find legal and legislative avenues to stop the new tech IPOs from minting new billionaires and transferring the AI industry’s enormous risks onto us.The first step is passing wealth taxes on billionaires to keep them in check. Today, let’s send a message to the billionaires that Americans will not lie down and let them bulldoze working people and the environment on their way to the bank. Tax the billionaires. Block the IPOs.Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia. Her latest book is End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra TaylorIlana Glazer is a comedian and video-podcaster who co-created the comedy series Broad City, wrote and starred in the movie Babes, made her Broadway debut last year in Goodnight, and Good Luck and, now, hosts the comedy and socio-political video-podcast, It’s Open With Ilana GlazerExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionStock marketsIPOscommentShareReuse this content

title: Ryanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costs | Ryanair | The Guardian
description: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures
Content: Ryanair says European short-haul fares could ‘increase materially’ next year amid warnings of a €2bn rise in its annual fuel bill.Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRyanair says European short-haul fares could ‘increase materially’ next year amid warnings of a €2bn rise in its annual fuel bill.Photograph: Pier Marco Tacca/Getty ImagesRyanairRyanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costsAirline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measuresBusiness live – latest updatesMark SweneyMon 2 Nov 2026 07.57 ESTFirst published on Mon 2 Nov 2026 04.06 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by theMiddle East conflict.The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive.Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices byup to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive ofRyanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $106 a barrel on Monday.Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire.“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.He said the company had several pay deals that would come up for renegotiation from March.However, theUniteunion said it had a multiyear pay deal in place that covered 2027, and in any case was not linked to company performance.“Unite hasn’t been advised of any such proposals and we have a multiyear pay deal in place which covers next year,” said Oliver Richardson, a national officer at the union. “A number of unions across Europe have the same. Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured.”O’Leary also said Ryanair was “slowing down hiring meaningfully” for new pilots, cabin crew and across its training courses.The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions.O’Leary said AI had already been used to increase capacity by 4%.“When you’re running 650 aircraft, it’s too big for a human to be able to do it,” he said. “The machines can actually design the schedules better than we know [how to do], so we are getting more productivity out of the aircraft.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRyanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. Twenty-five per cent of its fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are hedged at $95 a barrel.“It’s beginning to dawn on everybody that we [the industry] are not well hedged,” O’Leary said.The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said. “[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending in September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter.Ryanair has taken delivery of about 30 aircraft annually over the last two years, but the delivery rate is set to drop to 15 annually for the next few years.The airline said it was to take deliveries of the Boeing 737 Max 10 aircraft in January, which has about 20% more seats but burns a fifth less fuel than its current fleet.Explore more on these topicsRyanairAirline industryMichael O'LearyUS-Israel war on IranIrelandEuropeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Police use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrests | Western Australia | The Guardian
description: Deployments of surveillance vans over five months resulted in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Deployments of surveillance vans over five months resulted in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders
Content: Western Australia police used cameras with facial recognition technology on marked vans at 43 locations across the state including the Perth royal show.Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAPView image in fullscreenWestern Australia police used cameras with facial recognition technology on marked vans at 43 locations across the state including the Perth royal show.Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAPWestern AustraliaPolice use facial recognition to scan one million faces in WA trial leading to 122 arrestsDeployments of surveillance vans over five months resulted in nine false alerts and led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offendersGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastIma CaldwellandPenry BuckleyMon 2 Nov 2026 01.12 ESTFirst published on Sun 1 Nov 2026 21.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a million people have had their faces scanned in a trial of real-time facial recognition technology inWestern Australia, resulting in 122 arrests and nine incorrect alerts.WA police said under the five-month trial, which concluded on Saturday, the technology scanned 1,380,882 faces after 100 deployments across 43 regional and metropolitan locations.Alongside the 122 arrests, the alerts led officers to engage with 146 registered sex offenders and locate 10 people for a welfare check.Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposalRead moreThe deployments included three operations at the Perth royal show, where 223,749 faces were scanned, resulting in 15 alerts, three arrests and seven “interactions” with registered sex offenders.A police spokesperson confirmed the system generated nine incorrect alerts against the total 1.38m scans, meaning there was an error rate of 0.00065%.Addressing the false matches at a media conference on Sunday, the WA police commissioner, Col Blanch, confirmed officers engaged with each individual.“I want to be very clear on those false alerts,” he said. “No one was arrested. No one made a complaint. Each one did result in an interaction with that person and asking them relevant questions.“It’s a very, very, very low number. It’s not zero. We’d love it to be zero. But I think the important thing for us is to engage with our community just like we would if a human thought someone was a wanted person.”Blanch acknowledged the technology was “not perfect” and that authorities “knew this going into this trial”, but maintained that officers followed up on alerts in the same way they would if a member of the public raised suspicions.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHowever, civil liberties advocates have criticised how the WA police framed the error rate.The chief executive of Civil Liberties Australia, Bill Rowlings, said WA police were “severely gilding the lily” by claiming the incorrect alert rate was 0.00065% and suggested it should instead be calculated by comparing how many of the arrests resulted in convictions.“We will only know what the incorrect rate is when the 122 people arrested have their day in court,” he said.“If half the 122 arrested … are not convicted, the ‘incorrect’ rate will be 50%,” he said in a statement, saying police had performed the almost 1.4m scans “with no reasonable suspicion whatsoever”.Sarah Schwartz, legal director at the Human Rights Law Centre, said every false match is “a real person who may be stopped, questioned or investigated because an algorithm got it wrong”.“The consequences of those mistakes have real consequences for the people of Western Australia.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe questioned if it was “proportionate in a democratic society” to conduct “biometric surveillance on an extraordinary scale” of more than a million people – and raised particular concern over the deployment of surveillance vans at public demonstrations.When the trial was announced, the state’s independent privacy watchdog, the office of the information commissioner WA (OIC WA), said it was not involved in implementing the trial, warning of “collective privacy harms”in a statement. The OIC WA was contacted for comment.View image in fullscreenThe police surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the trial is evaluated.Photograph: Aaron Bunch/AAPOn Sunday, Blanch said the trial “focused on using modern technology responsibly to identify people who presented a risk, while allowing the vast majority of people to go about their day without any impact”.Under the trial guidelines, cameras mounted on or positioned near marked police vehicles scanned faces in designated public areas, matching them against an alert list drawn from police databases. Police said images of people who weren’t on the list were pixelated in real time and deleted immediately without being stored.The trial previouslytriggered backlashover concerns about privacy and algorithmic bias. Experts say the technology could disproportionately affect marginalised groups who are already overrepresented on police watchlists, with facial recognition algorithms historically having higher false-match rates for people with darker skin tones.Schwartz said the governance framework surrounding the technology remained opaque.“WA police have provided remarkably little detail about the safeguards governing this technology,” she said. “Their publicly available policies on the use of this technology appear heavily borrowed from overseas models, while leaving critical questions unanswered about misuse, bias and accountability.”The surveillance vans have now been removed from public deployment while the force conducts an internal evaluation into how the technology performed on the ground and its community impacts, including “reviewing the safeguards and whether all requirements were met”.Explore more on these topicsWestern AustraliaAustralian police and policingFacial recognitionAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: From a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right now | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Casserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party season
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleFrom a life-changing garlic press to a super-glowy serum: 12 buys you’re loving right nowCasserole dishes, electric heaters and silk shirts: your autumnal favourites show you’re hunkering down – with one eye on party seasonDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereJane HoskynMon 2 Nov 2026 05.45 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAutumn, we’ve been expecting you. After a September that seemed to miss the memo about changing seasons, October made up for it withserial stormsand nights that drew in faster than you could say “fall back”. Time to hunker down and, whisper it, even put the heating on – or at least fire up anelectric heaterif you’re still holding out on the radiators.But while you were drawn to the indoor pleasures of heaters, hotcasserolesand hottercoffee, you’ve also had your eye on party season, or at least been thinking about venturing into those corners of your wardrobe that haven’t seen daylight since March. From aclothes steamerto breathe new life into your threads, apencil skirtandsheer silk shirtto update your wardrobe, to avitamin C serumto keep your skin glowing all winter, these were your favourite things in October.Our favourite electric heaterView image in fullscreenDreofan heater£139.99 at Dreo“Within a few seconds of activation, it had begun to make a chilly room feel cosy,” wrotePete Wiseof the overall winner in his test to find thebest electric heaters. Five minutes later, on the highest setting, his “jumper was well and truly off”. Better yet, with a power rating of up to 2kW, you’d expect it to make a right racket – and it doesn’t. At a maximum of 46dB, Pete said it’s “far quieter than any other fan heater I tested”.A classic casserole dishView image in fullscreenHabitat 5.3lcast iron casserole dish£45 at Sainsbury’sSophie Wyburdpainted an irresistible picture in her roundup of thebest casserole dishes: “Tinkering over a pot in the kitchen, glass of wine in hand … while the scent of beef shin ragu wafts through the house.” Yep, that’s me sold. At about a fifth of the price of the winningLe Creuset, Habitat’s chic oven-safe pot provides “brilliant heat retention at an excellent price”. It comes in autumnalorange, too (£47.50).A life-changing garlic pressView image in fullscreenDreamfarm Garject garlic press with peel ejector£41.95 at AmazonWhere there’s a casserole, there’s got to be garlic. ReaderStuart Hatcherrecommended three things inLucy Pavia’srundown of15 everyday items that make your life a teeny bit better, and all three made it into your top 20 products of October. Your favourite was this garlic press that ended Stuart’s “time-consuming chopping”. (The other two, in case you’re wondering, are apair of wrist wraps for weightliftingand aportable air pumpthat can blow up an air bed “effortlessly”.)The five-starbean-to-cup coffee machineView image in fullscreenDe’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60£400 at Argos“It makes espresso. It makes black coffee. It makes cappuccino. It produces hot water on demand,” wroteSasha Mullerin his five-starDe’Longhi Magnifica Start review. “Simple to use, sensibly designed … For everyday coffee drinkers, it’s a great buy.” And many everyday coffee drinkers among you did indeed buy it – the fact that it’s suddenly dark at 5pm may have helped fuel your desire for a decent caffeine fix.The best budget clothes steamerView image in fullscreenPhilips 1000 Series handheld steamer£24.99 at AmazonFree yourself from the iron with this lightweight handheld steamer from Philips –Zoë Phillimore’stop budget pick in our guide to thebest clothes steamers. “This is a great model if you’re just dipping your toes into the iron-free life,” she wrote. It’s not powerful enough to blast through a whole pile of creased laundry, and Zoë found it “a bit spitty” to use on silk, but it made short work of her cotton items and linen trousers.A time-saving egg cookerView image in fullscreenSalter Aspen egg steamer£10 at ArgosGo to work on an egg, or half a dozen of them, with this brilliantly affordable egg cooker that can quickly boil up to six eggs or poach two at a time. ReaderAmanda Nieurzyla-Johnchose hers as hereveryday item that makes your life better, writing that it “takes the guesswork out of cooking while you concentrate on the rest of the meal. I don’t know how I have cooked all these years without it.”A super-glowy vitamin C serumView image in fullscreenCeraVe skin renewing vitamin C serum, 30ml£30 at Boots“I was astounded when, after a week of using it, people started commenting on how ‘glowy’ my face looked,” wroteZoë Phillimorein the Filter’s second-birthday roundup of31 things we loved this year. Zoë bought the serum after reading about it inDanielle Wilkins’sguide to thebest vitamin C serums, and says she hopes “it keeps me looking alive all the way through the grey winter months”.The‘near miracle’hair loss treatmentView image in fullscreenHair+Me hair regrowth subscription£34.99 a month at Hair+MeForSali Hughes’sfriends who barely use moisturiser, let alone Botox, age-related hair thinning is “their line in the sand”, she wrote in herbeauty column. Judging by how many of you heeded Sali’s advice about “a treatment that actually works”, you feel the same. The clinicians at subscription service Hair+Me dispense proven hair-loss medications such as minoxidil and oral treatments, which can reduce the risk to pets.A relaxed pencil skirtView image in fullscreenAlbarayskirt£79 at John Lewis“The pencil skirt is back,” wroteMelanieWilkinsonin her roundup of52 women’s autumn wardrobe updates, and she must be on to something because it was your favourite of the lot. The combination of timeless tailoring, elasticated back waist and side pockets has proved so irresistible that the size 14 had sold out at the time of writing.A sheer shirt for day and nightView image in fullscreenArketsilk organza shirt£54 at Arket“Sheer clothes aren’t just for red-carpet exhibitionists any more,” wrote fashion editorJess Cartner-Morleyin herOctober style essentials. A sheer shirt is particularly versatile because you can “wear it over a tank top during the day” then pair it with something less modest for evening (“a lace bra if you are feeling slightly racy,” suggested Jess). This shirt is now reduced to £54 in all sizes, making it an excellent buy ahead of party season.The best lunch box for kidsView image in fullscreenMunchkin Kids’ bento lunch box£22.99 at John LewisAfter testing 40 boxes for her guide to thebest lunch boxes,Zoë Phillimorechose this colourful plastic caddy as the best option for children. It “feels seemingly indestructible, surviving a school day and a night in lost property”, and, unusually for kids’ lunch boxes, has a silicone seal that encloses each compartment separately. Zoë loved that it included a spoon and fork, but wished replacements were available to buy.The best cheap(ish) iPhoneView image in fullscreenApple iPhone 16e£599 at John LewisYou might not expect to see a new iPhone in a guide to thebest cheap phones, and indeed £599 stretches the definition of cheap, but it’s affordable for an iOS device – especially now that“RAMageddon”(a shortage of memory chips, as opposed to a sheep crisis) has hiked phone prices. The 16e has only one rear camera and no MagSafe, but it packs “great performance and battery life” for its price, wroteThomas Deehan. Look out for it in the Black Friday deals in the coming weeks.View image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs.
