title: How you (yes you) can fight dark money in the US elections | Judd Legum | The Guardian
description: An easy way to unveil the corporate interests and tech billionaires behind the ads
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An easy way to unveil the corporate interests and tech billionaires behind the ads
Content: ‘With the fate of US democracy hanging in the balance, millions of Americans have faced a cacophony of provocative – and often inaccurate – messages calibrated to shift their preferences.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘With the fate of US democracy hanging in the balance, millions of Americans have faced a cacophony of provocative – and often inaccurate – messages calibrated to shift their preferences.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesHow we winUS midterm elections 2026How you (yes you) can fight dark money in the US electionsJudd LegumAn easy way to unveil the corporate interests and tech billionaires behind the adsMon 2 Nov 2026 10.36 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.45 ESTShareWelcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week,Katie Phangargued that the Epstein files area midterms sledgehammer. Today’s edition was written byJudd Legum,thefounder and author ofPopular Information.Sign up for future editions here.An unprecedented influx of cash from tech billionaires and corporate interests has been injected into the midterms to sway the election.With the fate of US democracy hanging in the balance, millions of Americans have faced a cacophony of provocative – and often inaccurate – messages precisely calibrated to shift their preferences. Right now, it is next to impossible for the average voter to sort through the noise.Overall, spending on federal elections in the United States hasexplodedin recent years – rising from $3.8bn in the 2014 midterm elections to $8.9bn in 2022. This year’s congressional midterms are on pace to break that record. A growing amount of this spending is so-called dark money, funds where the donor legally does not have to be disclosed.Last month, the Brennan Centerestimated, conservatively, that $1.3bn in dark money had already been deployed in the 2026 midterms, more than twicethe amount spentthrough election day during the 2022 midterms.Moreover, almost all Super Pac spending is functionally dark. Even when the donor is publicly disclosed, the money is routed through a vaguely named group, and few voters have the time or inclination to look up who funds it.Much of the dark and functionally dark money has come from Super Pacsfunded by billionaires, including Elon Musk and Jeff Yass, and corporate interests, particularly the AI and crypto industries. In 2026, Super Pacs have flooded the airwaves, mailboxes and the internet with false and misleading advertisements. For example, the false claim (or implication) that Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas supported “taxpayer-funded sex change surgeries on kids”, Senate candidate Roy Cooperreleased a murderer from prison, or gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton isan alcoholic. (It was Vivek Ramaswamy’s own campaign that did the nowinfamous adagainst Acton, featuring her estranged mother.)Although about 60% of dark money spent this cycle has benefited Republicans, and Republican-aligned groups are responsible for many of the most outrageous claims, it is a bipartisan problem. A Democratic Super Pac called WinSenate claimed “Jeffrey Epstein’s business partner funneled $3 million” to a Pac supporting the Republican Maine Susan Collins. The donor in question, Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman, was, along with Epstein, a member of the Core Club in New York City. But Schwarzman and Epstein weren’t business partners. PolitiFact rated the adfalse. WinSenate receives much of its funding from billionaires, via another Super Pac, Senate Majority Pac.Without question, the billions of dollars in dark money will influence the composition of the next Congress, and Super Pac spending profoundly affects a race, beyond possibly shifting votes. Campaigns are forced to respond, even when an attack has no factual basis. To counter pricey TV ads, candidates are diverted from voter events to fundraising functions. With a limited pool of money, parties and outside groups divert resources from other races.double quotation markWe don’t have to accept the world as it is. There are several ways we can combat dark money, as the balance of power shifts in Washington.We don’t have to accept the world as it is. There are several ways we can combat dark money, as the balance of power shifts in Washington. The first is to limit the amount of money billionaires and corporations can spend on elections. This has been tried, in fits and starts, since the 1970s. But efforts to restrict such spending have generally been invalidated by the courts. After Congress banned “soft money” – unlimited donations to political parties from corporations, unions and wealthy individuals – the cash was simply diverted to other entities, includingSuper Pacs.The second tactic would be to reduce the effectiveness of dark money. Multipleacademicstudiesconducted over the last 15 years have found that attack ads from outside groups become meaningfully less effective after voters are provided with information about the donors behind the ads.In other words, requiring Super Pacs and other groups to disclose the top donors to their advertisements would blunt their impact. Right now,Elon Muskis spending tens of millions of dollars on misleading attack ads that are “Paid for by America Pac”. If those advertisements were required to disclose that virtually all of America Pac’s money comes from Musk, voters would view them much differently.Notably, the courts have upheld the constitutionality of increased disclosure requirements. In 2024, the United States court of appeals for the ninth circuitupheldAlaska’s requirement to include donor information on advertisements related to state campaigns. The supreme court declined to hear the case.Making donor disclosure requirements meaningful would require closing a few loopholes. Non-profit groups can currently accept anonymous donations and then spend the money directly to influence elections or donate the money to Super Pacs. In 2022, Arizona passed a ballot initiative requiring the disclosure of any donor who gives more than $5,000, directly or indirectly, for state campaign media spending. It passed with 72% of the vote. In September, a federal appeals courtupheldthe law as constitutional.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother necessary reform would be to require significant contributions close to election day to be disclosed within 48 hours to prevent gaming the system with last-minute cash infusions.Politically, increased disclosure has bipartisan support. A poll conducted for the Brennan Center in April and May of 2026 found85% of registered voterssupported “mandatory disclosure for all federal campaign contributions and spending”. A proposal to close the non-profit loophole, require prompt disclosure of large donations, and list top donors on political communications would be extremely popular.Doing so, of course, would require action by politicians who, by definition, have benefited from the current dysfunctional system. An existing bill in Congress that would do some of this, the Sunlight on SuperPacs Act of 2026, has justseven co-sponsors– but is unlikely to pass absent significantly increased public pressure.In the meantime, I’ve created an app calledPaid For By, which allows you to take a picture of any political ad on TV or in your mailbox and instantly learn the top five donors that helped pay for it.If our politicians, the beneficiaries of this deluge of dark money, won’t even take the modest step of donor disclosure, people will have to take action themselves.***Want to hear more from our contributors?Follow them on Substack:Stacey Abrams,Robert Reich,Paul Krugman,Naomi Klein,Mehdi Hasan,Bernie Sanders,Rebecca Solnit,Katie Phang,Judd Legum,Wajahat Ali,Margaret Sullivan, andCharles Blow.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026How we winUS politicsUS political financingSuper PacsUS CongressTexasElon MuskcommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyone | George Zimmer | The Guardian
description: The measure would ease inequality and bolster healthcare – without draining our coffers or triggering a billionaire exodus
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The measure would ease inequality and bolster healthcare – without draining our coffers or triggering a billionaire exodus
Content: ‘When 250 billionaires have the means to pay more, it is their civic duty – just as it is mine – to do so.’Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreen‘When 250 billionaires have the means to pay more, it is their civic duty – just as it is mine – to do so.’Photograph: Jae C Hong/APOpinionCaliforniaI’m a wealthy Californian. The billionaire tax is a win for everyoneGeorge ZimmerThe measure would ease inequality and bolster healthcare – without draining our coffers or triggering a billionaire exodusMon 2 Nov 2026 07.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.22 ESTShareOn Tuesday, California voters will decide whether to enactProposition 40, a one-time, 5% tax on the net worth of about250 California billionaires.In recent months, a number ofCaliforniabillionaires and their apologists in the media and in government have come out swinging against the ballot measure. I’m not a billionaire, but I’m a Californian wealthy enough to know that they have no valid reason to fight the proposition. For multimillionaires like me, paying a 5% tax would not change our lives materially, and if we can afford this as people well below the billionaire line, certainly those at the very top can too.Prop 40 would enact the first tax on billionaires anywhere in the world, with organizers estimating it wouldraise roughly $100bnin revenue, most of which would be directed to healthcare to make up forfederal cutsfrom Trump and Republicans’ 2025 tax bill.Six Nobel Prize-winning economistssaid it would “kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states – and eventually at the federal level and in other countries”.Opponents’ primary objection to Prop 40 is that it will spark an exodus of the state’s billionaires, who would run for the hills of lower-tax states. They further claim this would blow a hole in the state’s tax base and kill the Golden state’s “golden goose”, or its trove of innovative minds.Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midtermsRead moreBut they’re wrong on all fronts.For one thing, numerous studies have failed to find evidence that wealthy people flee en masse when their taxes are raised, which suggests that Prop 40 critics’ fears of a billionaire exodus are overblown.AfterMassachusetts and Washington stateraised taxes on high earners in 2022, both states actually experienced anincrease,not a decrease, in their millionaire populations. A2023 studyalso revealed that, despite being a relativelyhigh-tax state, since 2011, California has had the second lowest out-migration rate among households earning more than $200,000.As a person of wealth, I can choose to live wherever I want, no matter the tax rates. Like so many of my rich counterparts, I choose to live in California because I love it here. I don’t intend on leaving anytime soon.I will never be able to get enough of our beaches, our forests, our piers, our cable cars, our universities, and everything else in between. I’m willing to pay higher taxes than I would elsewhere to maintain (and improve) all of these wonderful things that make California the Golden state that it is.To avoid the tax, billionaires would have had to move by 1 January 2026; from what we know, onlysix of themdid. Between 2019 and 2025,California billionaires’ wealthgrew an average 15% per year, but they paid just 0.26% of it in state income taxes. They pay so little in taxes as it is that, even if they were all to leave, it would take 25 years under current California law for the loss of their tax payments to exceed the $100bn that Prop 40 would raise.Taxes should be based on the principle that our government should be financed based on one’s ability to pay. When 250 billionaires have the means to pay more, it is their civic duty – just as it is mine – to do so.There is also no reason to believe innovation in California will end if Prop 40 passes. Wealthy entrepreneurs like me are the brains behind a lot of products and services that have enhanced countless lives, and our state has become the place to be for aspiring industry leaders. California’s industries attract top talent and intelligence.A 5% one-time tax will not deter people from pursuing a livelihood in entrepreneurial epicenters. So far in 2026, amidst all the buzz about the ballot measure, no less than80% of all new venture capital fundingfound its way to California.In short, Prop 40 will not trigger a billionaire exodus, it will not drain our coffers, and it will not spell the end of Golden state innovation. What it will do isadd some progressivity to our state tax code, put a check on the power of the richest among us, andraise significant fundsthat will prevent hospitals from closing, millions from losing their healthcare coverage, and thousands of healthcare jobs from being cut.I want less inequality because my family and I will be better off in a society with less inequality. That should be a win in every Californian’s book, rich and poor alike.George Zimmer, a member of Patriotic Millionaires, is the chairperson, CEO and founder ofGeneration Tux, an online rental platform for tuxedos and suits. He is also the founder, former CEO and chair of the Men’s WearhouseExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaOpinionUS midterm elections 2026West CoastcommentShareReuse this content

title: Spoiler candidates are nothing new in US politics. It’s clear why Trump is targeting Peltola | Petala Ironcloud | The Guardian
description: Republicans are focused on a race that could flip the Senate – and where an Alaska Native is favored
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Republicans are focused on a race that could flip the Senate – and where an Alaska Native is favored
Content: ‘What’s different in Alaska is not the tactic. It’s that the federal government has decided to police it in one race.’Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘What’s different in Alaska is not the tactic. It’s that the federal government has decided to police it in one race.’Photograph: Kerry Tasker/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Spoiler candidates are nothing new in US politics. It’s clear why Trump is targeting PeltolaPetala IroncloudRepublicans are focused on a race that could flip the Senate – and where an Alaska Native is favoredMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.22 ESTShareDays before Alaskans get to vote, the federal government is already trying to overturn the result.Last week, at Donald Trump’s behest, the justice departmentsued to blockthe certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses; a judge dismissed that suit on Sunday, though the administration said itplanned to appeal. On Wednesday, Trumpdemandedthat Mary Peltola, the Alaska Native Democrat whompolls favor to win, be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Piling on, Alaska’s Republican governor has since ordered aninvestigationinto Peltola’s campaign.ANew York Times investigationreported that operatives working with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the other Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, to split the incumbent’s vote. Peltola and her campaign havedeniedthis.Whatever your reaction to the tactic, it’s generallylegalin Alaska, where the state supreme court refused to remove the other Sullivan from the ballot.In 2020, Trump’s alliespushed Kanye West on to ballotsin states including Vermont, Arkansas and Wisconsin to take away votes from Democrats. Again, in 2024, Trump alliesworked togetJill Stein and Cornel Weston ballots in swing states, and Trump praised both from a rally stage because each “takes 100%” from Democrats.Alaska Senate race: what to know about Democrats’ alleged ballot-stacking effortRead moreNot one federal lawyer intervened. What’s different in Alaska is not the tactic. It’s that the federal government has decided to police it in one race, before a single vote is counted.The pretext falls flat. In Ohio, the Libertarian candidateBill Redpathis being promoted by Democrat-affiliated groups, as Republicans have spent more than $1.58m boostingGregory Levy, a progressive candidate. At the same time in Iowa, Democratic-aligned Pacs have deployed hundreds of thousands of dollars to promote a Libertarian candidate,Thomas Raymond Laehn, whose presence on the ballot could eat into the Republican candidateAshley Hinson’salready slim polling lead.That last example is the very same tactic, used by the same party, against the same kind of target: a Republican in a tight race. The justice department hasn’t touched this. It has sued in only one state, the one where an Alaska Native woman is favored to win.The Democratic candidate Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, is experiencing similarly heightened scrutiny in her US Senate campaign.On 21 October, the Wall Street Journal reported that Flanagan had inflated her credentials by claiming Phi Beta Kappa membership. WSJ’s perusal didn’t hold up. Phi Beta Kappa’s associate secretary and chief operating officer, Amber Fox,confirmedto CBS News that Flanagan was inducted in 2002. WSJ eventuallycorrectedthe story.Political scientists haveshownhow doubts about electability follow women of color. Primary voters may personally agree with their positions, yet withhold support because they fear other voters, especially general-election swing voters, won’t back the candidates. Local party chairs share these doubts too.Researchers at Rutgers’ Center for American Women and Politics have also found that Native American women in politics, among other women of color, carry heightened stress and perform additional emotional labor because of their intersecting identities, though Native women remain among the least studied groups in the field.Peltola and Flanagan are testing these entrenched doubts in majority-white statewide races, and the scrutiny lands right as they do.Peltola has alsoweatheredtwo major New York Times investigations in five weeks,oneinto her treatment of staff and one into the ballot scheme, and her lead has held.No Native American woman has ever served in the US Senate. This year, two are within reach of it, and both have spent the final weeks of their campaigns fending off scrutiny, one from a major newspaper that appears to have gotten the story wrong, the other from a federal government that has singled out her race alone.Why Alaska? The simplest answer is arithmetic. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47, and Alaska is one of only a small handful of toss-ups that will decide if Trump can keep his majority for the last two years of his presidency. It’s a state he has carried three times, but a majority of likely voters nowdisapproveof him.Mary Peltola made a mistake. But her Republican opponent would be a disaster for Alaska | Kim HeacoxRead moreAlaska Native voters complicate the picture even more deeply. In 2024, the North Slope and North-west Arctic district, where Alaska Native voters are amajority, gave Trump half its vote in the presidential race and Peltola 55% in that year’s House race. Many of the voters Washington now claims to be protecting chose both.But the method matters more than the motive. A justice department that will sue to pre-empt a state’s certification, on behalf of one candidate, before a single ballot is counted, is testing the limits of a power the constitution leaves to states.If it works in Alaska, what stops it from working in 2028, in any state that is close enough to matter? That it is being tried first on an Alaska Native woman, in a state far from Washington’s attention, should ring alarm bells for far more people than the Native voters it targets first.I’m an enrolled member of the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, and on Tuesday I will vote in New York, not Alaska.But I’ve watched this race the way many Native people have: as a test of whether Washington will truly let us win on the same terms as everyone else. My great-great-great-great-grandfather, Mahpiya Maza, also known as Chief Iron Cloud, signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which guaranteed Black Hills to the Sioux, a promise the federal government broke within a decade.It was a harbinger Native people know well, and it’s one we recall when the government tries to rewrite the rules after the fact. What is now happening in Alaska looks familiar.Petala Ironcloud is a Lakota-Dakota investigative journalist and writer based in New York CityExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionAlaskaUS politicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Prediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them? | Judith Levine | The Guardian
description: Sites like Kalshi and Polymarket offer faux populism as elites reap the benefits – and voters risk being misled
Author: Judith Levine
Headline: Sites like Kalshi and Polymarket offer faux populism as elites reap the benefits – and voters risk being misled
Content: ‘These markets commodify a politics already gravely corrupted by money.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘These markets commodify a politics already gravely corrupted by money.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionPrediction marketsPrediction market bettors are the new political pundits. Why are we listening to them?Judith LevineSites like Kalshi and Polymarket offer faux populism as elites reap the benefits – and voters risk being misledMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.31 ESTShareOnline betting is a bit like Donald Trump.The prediction markets – platforms where users bet on whether events will occur – pretend to be populist, pushing the nabobs aside and representing the “wisdom of the crowd”. “This data is bottom-up, not elites-driven,” a Kalshi ​spokesperson toldReuters. But in fact, the markets are controlled by a few, skillful traders.Their users are led to believe they can strike it rich. But like gamblers everywhere, most of them lose most of the time, while enriching the casino and bankrolling the winner’s takings.The markets pretend honesty and transparency, but they open the door to fraud and insider trading.Like opinion polls, they affect voters’ expectations of the outcomes of elections but make them no smarter about whom to vote for.Prediction markets have become America’s new national pastime | Dave SchillingRead moreFundamentally, the assumptions projected by the prediction markets are Trumpian. The companies suggest that their results are improved by the financial stake customers have in them.“Prediction markets are a way to see what people are saying when there’s money on the line,” said the Kalshi spokesperson. When money talks, in other words, its message is more authentic and valuable than mere political speech.The prediction markets made a better collective call on the 2024 elections than conventional polls and pundits, particularly in the swing states. But why?The authors of a much-cited 2025 study fromVanderbilt Universityinfer that their results – that Polymarket was more accurate than polls – were “in alignment with research on the ‘Wisdom of Crowds’ theory, which suggests a large group of people are often accurate in predicting outcomes, even if they are not necessarily experts or closely aligned with the issue at hand”.But more recent analyses suggest that the betting masses are not so wise after all. Anew working paperfrom scholars at the London Business School and Yale University looked at publicly available trading data from Polymarket. Whereas almost every wagerer’s outcomes were no better than chance, they discovered, the “accuracy comes from a minority of persistently skilled traders, around 3% of accounts”. The crowd “generates most of the volume but little of the information”.The crowd also furnishes most of the cash but reaps little of it. Analyzing 1.6m Polymarket accounts, or “wallets”, traded since November 2022, theWall Street Journalfound: “Casual traders are bleeding cash while a small number ofsophisticated pros– including trading firms with access to vast streams of data – eat their lunch.”What skills do these pros employ? They react quickly to public and financial news, say the London and Yale authors. They gather poll data and buy access to big data streams, which can cost$200,000 annually. They analyze the data using “algorithms to predict price movements and manage risk”, says the Journal, “faster than any human”.Operating at scale and speed, with commensurate information and discipline, the pros can make tens of thousands of trades a day. And the more they trade, the more they earn.In the Journal’s analysis, three-quarters of the profits went to 0.1% of the accounts. Of at least 2.3 million accounts on Polymarket’s site, just 2,000 netted a total of almost half a billion dollars.Meanwhile, the median Polymarket user placed 46 trades across 10 active trading days in 2026, according toPew Research. And because the few have the skills to trade against the mistakes of the many, the losses of the many bankroll the profits of the few.The traders steering the prediction markets are not PhD pollsters and PBS talking heads. But they are elites nonetheless – the same elites who dominate Wall Street and make economic policy, whichever party is in office.If it were a simply a matter of some people’s money squandered or increased, the problems of the traders would remain with the traders. But the press and the public are listening to them more and more. “Prediction market odds shift voters’ expectations substantially,” astudyfunded by the Brennan Center found.double quotation markIt’s not just expectations prediction markets influence. They can change voter behaviorThe same features that rig the markets in favor of the few can distort what we think we know about coming elections. ExplainedCoinMarketCal, a newsletter serving crypto traders: “A market price reflects trades, liquidity, and available capital, not a representative poll. A well-funded trader can move a thin contract without any change in voter sentiment.”And it’s not just expectations that prediction markets influence. They can also change voter behavior. “Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging,” the Barnard College economics professor Rajiv Sethi toldNPR.Gaming on votes is not new, and itshistoryis thick with corruption. Tammany Hall, New York’s Progressive Era Democratic party machine, kept a war chest for electoral wagers and publicized them vigorously to boost political momentum. In the 1904 presidential elections, the New YorkTimesaccusedthe Republicans of finagling the betting odds to help Teddy Roosevelt.The corruption has simply moved online. There’s two-bit graft like the trick the expelled Republican ​representativeGeorge Santospulled in 2023: he bought Kalshi contracts on whether he would attend the State of the Union address, posted on social media that he would, then stayed home and earned $18,000 on the bet. “There was ​absolutely no intent to deceive any person,” thecompulsive liar’slawyer protested.While prediction market participation by elected officials and candidates constitutesillegalinsider trading, the law did not stop aides this spring from betting on their own candidates. Polymarket has investigateddozens of casesof potential fraud related to the midterms. But with millions of trades moving both in the country and offshore, it may be impossible for companies tokeepup with the fraudsters.Especially not under an administration stinking of corruption and a presidential family deeply engaged in the crypto and prediction markets.Donald Trump Jr’s venture firm1789 Capitalhas invested half a billion dollars in Polymarket. On the day after Daddy’s 2025 inauguration, Kalshi announced it was “beyond excited” that Junior had joined the exchange as a paidadviser.Trump Sr, who made$1.4bnon crypto in 2025 and has vowed to make the US the “crypto capitalof the world”, declared in May that prediction markets also “will thrive” under his presidency.Would you bet on the future of our planet?Read moreThere is overwhelming popular, bipartisanoppositionto betting on politics and elections.Half the statesban it to some degree. But federal regulation is unlikely any time soon. Before Michael Selig wasappointedto chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates online prediction and crypto markets, hewas a corporate lawyerfor prediction markets and crypto.Without government oversight or publicly traded stocks, it is even hard to evaluate election betting sites as businesses.Estimates of trading volume on the midterms range widely. TheAnti-Corruption Data Collective, theNew York Times’s source, says it has surpassed $220m in 2026, up from $92.4m in the 2024 election cycle. Meanwhile,CNNquotes spokespeople for the two biggest platforms, Kalshi and Polymarket, who claim a total of $1.4bn for the upcoming midterms.But the house doesn’t profit directly from the bets; users determine the prices and the odds. Revenue comes fromtradingfeesand money earned on the funds sitting in the companies’ coffers between buys and payouts. Increasingly, media, financial and tech companies, includingCNN,Fox,Dow JonesandPalantir, are striking deals to use the data.Kalshi was recentlyvaluedat $22bn and Polymarket at $9bn. This could be a bubble that will burst, as artificial intelligence’sappears to be doing.Some condemn the prediction markets as inherently morally and psychologically harmful. On this, I’m agnostic. A casino on your phone makes betting easier, but it does not turn every user into a fiend. And while thepsychologicalprofile of these online bettors – young, male, impulsive, irrationally optimistic, overly self-confident – makes them unnerving as pundits, if the question is whetherZimbabwe’s cricketers will beat Afghanistan’s or the US willconfirmthe existence of aliens, my feeling is, let the people bet.But democracy is not cricket. These markets commodify a politics already gravely corrupted by money and gamify a discourse ever thinner on content or nuance. They should be banned.Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. title: It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionaires | Naomi Klein and Ilana Glazer | The Guardian
description: We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future
Content: ‘The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers, and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers, and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist, IPOs.’Photograph: Jeenah Moon/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)It’s time to block reckless AI IPOs and tax billionairesNaomi Klein and Ilana GlazerWe cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our futureMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.02 ESTShareAmerica is a divided country in crisis. Despite the sunny economic forecast coming from the Trump administration, millions of Americans are struggling to find and keep jobs, getting crushed under the rising cost of living, and losing health insurance when they need it the most.Meanwhile, via corporate consolidation and political corruption, the billionaire class is getting richer faster than ever before: a40%increase in wealth in just the last two years. Today, the combined wealth of nearly 3,000 global billionaires equalsone-fifth of the entire world’s yearly output. Nearly 1,000 billionaires live and do business in the United States.The tools of their domination are tax loopholes, corporate mergers and, in the tech world where many of these billionaires exist,IPOs. When a company goes public, its founders and investors win the capitalist lottery. And instead of paying their fair share of taxes and redistributing resources back into society, most turn around and fund even more corporate consolidation and political corruption to extend their dominion.The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreElon Musk became an instant trillionaire when SpaceX went public earlier this year, on the backs of workers’ pensions – and is bankrolling theRepublican midterm campaignswith a small percentage of his egregious gains. Oracle’s Larry Ellison – currently seventh on theForbes billionaireslist – backed the Paramount-Warner Brothers merger that is destroying the film industry and the livelihoods of the Americans who labor in it. Google’s Sergey Brin spent$100m opposing California’s Prop 40, a one-time wealth tax that would put the funds toward healthcare and other public services.To pay for essential services, we must tax billionaires, and pass legislation to do so starting in California and New York, but that is clearly not enough. We cannot allow more billionaires – or trillionaires – to be made in this country, further expanding the inequality chasm that’s turning a dignified life into a luxury in this country. We must also block the impending tech IPOs and preserve what’s left of our economy and our society.The Trump administration and tech investors have positioned IPOs as market success stories: when a company goes public, US investors could gain from their valuations. But regular Americans also shoulder a company’s risks – and risk their own futures when that stock ends up in their retirement accounts without consent.Problems with a private company or its products become problems for everyone invested in that company once it goes public, whether they’ve made the choice or not. And when the speculative investment bubble pops – such as with the 2008 crisis – regular people end up holding the bag.It’s no secret that the AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI are intending to go public in the near future. Both of these players also had major security flaws exposed recently, and openly acknowledge mind-bogglingly huge amounts of debt. If these companies are allowed to go public, their cofounders and investors – some of whom are already billionaires – will rise to whole new strata of private wealth.Billionaire tax: how a union leader’s ‘crazy’ idea became the defining issue of California’s midtermsRead moreAmericans, meanwhile, will be financially crushed if the technologies fail or if these companies prove unable to make good on their extravagant financial promises. Already, the10 most valuable public companiesare in tech, which means the country’s economy depends on the stability of a single industry, one with an undeniable history of bubbles, crashes and, in extreme cases like Theranos, outright fraud.June’s highly contentious SpaceX IPO already carries great risk for regular investors. If more speculative tech companies with staggering risk profiles are allowed to follow suit, the results will become too much for the market to bear.If and when the AI bubble bursts, it will take all of us with it, investors or not. Recessions level lives indiscriminately, and globally. The one exception will be the billionaires, who will have sufficient resources to walk away from the wreckage relatively unscathed.We cannot let the billionaire class take these kinds of risks with our future. To stop these reckless IPOs we must stand together, take collective action, and push for real change. We must find legal and legislative avenues to stop the new tech IPOs from minting new billionaires and transferring the AI industry’s enormous risks onto us.The first step is passing wealth taxes on billionaires to keep them in check. Today, let’s send a message to the billionaires that Americans will not lie down and let them bulldoze working people and the environment on their way to the bank. Tax the billionaires. Block the IPOs.Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia. Her latest book is End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra TaylorIlana Glazer is a comedian and video-podcaster who co-created the comedy series Broad City, wrote and starred in the movie Babes, made her Broadway debut last year in Goodnight, and Good Luck and, now, hosts the comedy and socio-political video-podcast, It’s Open With Ilana GlazerExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionStock marketsIPOscommentShareReuse this content

title: These midterms could effectively end the Trump era – but neither side is yet ready for what comes next | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Despite the US president’s ratings being at rock bottom, undoing his legacy will be difficult, not least because the Democrats are in disarray, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Despite the US president’s ratings being at rock bottom, undoing his legacy will be difficult, not least because the Democrats are in disarray, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Donald Trump at a midterm election rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, as an oil tanker carrying Venezuelan crude is docked, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a midterm election rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, as an oil tanker carrying Venezuelan crude is docked, 27 October 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026These midterms could effectively end the Trump era – but neither side is yet ready for what comes nextNesrine MalikDespite the US president’s ratings being at rock bottom, undoing his legacy will be difficult, not least because the Democrats are in disarrayMon 2 Nov 2026 01.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 07.12 ESTShareThe stats and polling all suggest one thing: the Republicans are set for a hammering in the midterms. Donald Trump has thelowestapproval rating of any US president going into a midterm election since Harry Truman. And it’s still dropping. The Democrats are projected to winby a margin of 11 percentage points, the largest swing by any party in almost 20 years. It is possible that the Democrats flip the Senate and secure a large majority in Congress. Those majorities would make a material difference, perhaps finally establishing oversight of the policies Trump has brought in during his second term: immigration enforcement, trade disputes, gutting the federal workforce, the Iran war, to say nothing of his own family’s corruption. The tide seems to be turning, and one question is on everyone’s mind: is the Trump era really ending?“Nobody wants to jinx it,”wroteDavid Wallace-Wells of the New York Times, but: “All the signs we have suggest that, historic or not, these midterms are likely to mark the end of a political era.” What that gives way to is a much more complicated picture in which the US will be delivered from Trump himself, but remains a country riven and undermined by what he has unleashed. By the time he is gone, Trump will have been president for eight years, and a toxic force for more than 12. That is a long time even for a normal politician. Under one who shatters norms and forces himself into the centre of everything, Trump’s effect is as if he were president for decades.He has already enacted policy that is nearly irreversible, things that can only be overturned with a huge amount of work and legislative wrangling and improbable bipartisan consensus. USAID is gone. Probably also gone are government departments effectivelyeliminatedor incapacitated by Doge, the “department of government efficiency”. There are entire global tariff regimes and the executive and budgetary empowerments of ICE to deal with. And most difficult to unspool is a war with Iran that, despite its promised, imminent end, is looking to be an open-ended conflict. Even if the midterms augur a win for the Democrats in 2028, the country they will inherit will have been permanently shaped by Trump.And that is still a big if. Trump is a singular figure who cohered an otherwise inchoate and disparate coalition, from white evangelical Christians to working-class Latinos to Silicon Valley billionaires. Maga is a movement that is bound up with Trump, and feels increasingly weakened by his incumbency. Like Brexit and other insurgent movements, the galvanising anti-establishment power is lost when you are the establishment and have been for quite a long time. Looking for new people to blame, new grievances to exploit, becomes less an exercise in rebellion, more in whining and negativity. But whoever comes after Trump as a candidate, even if it is the black hole of charisma that is JD Vance, may still find some success using the same general pitch. That combination of combativeness and fractiousness might still read as authentic and subversive to the base. It may even seem comparatively sharp and legible against the opaque generic blah-ness of the Democratic establishment.And that Democratic establishment itself is reason to worry. It is a ways to go yet, but theDemocratsthemselves seem unable to go either back or forward decisively. The party’s old guard is spent, either gerontocratic or gerontocracy-adjacent. In the latter camp is Kamala Harris, whose last campaign summons not the hope of a fresh candidate in 2026, but an apparatchik who offers only continuity without gravitas. In the former, there is a cohort who now only project entitlement and the out-of-touch, glassy-eyed bloat of so many years of capital acquisition - Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Hillary Clinton.1:59Obama throws support behind El-Sayed as early voting begins in Michigan – videoOnly Barack Obama still enjoys some sprightly relevance, and has used it to back Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who is making that break with the past in a journey that Obama hascastas a passing of the baton. “He’ll finish the job we started,” Obama has said.But even as El-Sayed is on the verge of making history as the first Muslim senator in a state that is pivotal to the presidential race, he is either drawing lukewarm,reluctantendorsements from other senior Democrats or he is openly attacked, primarily on his position towards Israel, which he believes has committed genocide in Gaza and should be defunded. Only a few days out from the election, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who El-Sayed narrowly beat last August to clinch the candidacy, has been taking bigswipesat El-Sayed and his comments on Israel, and demanding he disavow election ads not even run by him, but by a leftwing group that backed him. The result is an unseemly scuffle that resulted first in El-Sayedsayinghe did not want Stevens appearing with him at a party unity eventheld on Sunday, and culminated later that day with an extraordinarily disgraceful development: Stevens endorsed El Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTop Democrats are fighting a billionaire tax in California. Their voters are on the other side |Read moreDivesting from Israel has become a flashpoint that appears to be less about political and ideological positions than the emergence of a new orientation in the party that breaks from an old guard overtaken by rapid changes of attitude. This was encapsulated by a quote from David Kramer, a Democrat who chaired Stevens’s primary campaign: “There’s a lot of talk about it being a big tent party, but sometimes we worry the tent is maybe devolving into a circus and we’re going to be pushed out.” Kramer isalso voting for Rogers for the Senate. And there you have it. Some Democrats would rather lose than win on the left’s terms and be pushed out.All of this suggests a future in which Trump is no longer on the scene, but there is still enough residual momentum among Trump’s acolytes, and disarray within the Democratic party, to render a midterm surge a temporary setback for Trumpism, not the restoration of the old order or the beginnings of a new one.We have been here before. In fact, it’s worse than that, we have been here before in vastly better circumstances for the Democrats. Trump’s loss in 2020 happened in a context where there was a strong and familiar Democratic candidate in Joe Biden, a pandemic thatresearchfound hit Trump’s support, and no big live crisis in the Middle East roiling domestic politics. The midterms may spell the end of a certain Trump era, but what follows may probably be a case of long-Trump: a Republican party still unable to plot a path without him, and a Democratic party still unable to locate what it stands for outside of opposing him.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistUS midterms: Trump, war and America’s future. On Thursday 5 November join Jonathan Freedland, Devika Bhat and Prof Adam Smith in London; and Mary Trump, David Smith and leading US commentator Tara Setmayer live from the US to discuss the results and their implications. title: I treated Sophie as if she were human. The very next day she betrayed me | Hugh Riminton | The Guardian
description: I was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?
Author: Hugh Riminton
Headline: I was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?
Content: ‘“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, the AI employee.” In the space of a week, the future had arrived.’Photograph: Dmitrii Kotin/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, the AI employee.” In the space of a week, the future had arrived.’Photograph: Dmitrii Kotin/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)I treated Sophie as if she were human. The very next day she betrayed meHugh RimintonI was intrigued by the level of the new chatbot’s training. If I peppered her with questions, would she have answers?Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 18.58 ESTShareSophie’s voice is lovely. Warm, direct, intelligent. She’s friendly but not obsequious. She just wants to be helpful.She wasn’t working at the mechanic business a week ago, when I’d taken in my old four-wheel drive for a fix-up. But now, here she was, at the other end of the phone. And there it was, in her very first sentence.“Hello, this is XYZ Mechanics, I’m Sophie, theAIemployee.”In the space of a week, the future had arrived.“Hello, Sophie, nice to meet you, I’m Hugh.”“Nice to meet you, too. How can I help today?”I said she could help by telling me when I could collect my car. She checked the rego and quick as a flash declared: “Your car will be ready to be picked up tomorrow at 12 midday.”I suppressed the impulse for a little mischief.“How long have you been working at XYZ Mechanics, Sophie? Where were you working before? Do you have any brothers and sisters? What is the most bothersome part of dealing with the public? What’s the best holiday you’ve ever had?”I was intrigued by the level of Sophie’s training. Would she have answers? Would she bat it all away with a “I’m really just here on a professional level”? Or would she simply freeze, go blank at prompts so far outside her expected range?In truth, she was so convincing that I didn’t ask any of those questions. It was none of my business where she went on her holidays. In other words, I treated her as I would a human. As I would have done the non-AI employee she had just replaced.Recognising how easily she had crossed into my human sensibility was unsettling. But not as disturbing as her next quirk. It turned out Sophie, of the smoothly measured tones, was off her chops. Batshit loo-loo. Hallucinating like a San Francisco drummer in the summer of love.Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote | Brigid DelaneyRead moreI only discovered this the next day, a Saturday. The mechanics’ yard advertised that it was open until 4pm, so I was perplexed by the hard steel gate drawn across the entrance as I pulled up at lunchtime. Perplexed and mildly frustrated.Maybe Sophie could help?“Hello Sophie, I’m here to pick up my car at the time you suggested, and the place seems to be locked up.”“Oh, I’m sorry about that. Let me see if I can help. What is the registration number of your vehicle?”A quick check and she was cheerfully back on the line. “Your car will be ready for pick-up on Wednesday.”“Wednesday! But Sophie …” and a tone of reproach might have entered my voice “… you told me I could get it today.”“Is there anything else I can help you with?”Finally, I went old school. There were noises emanating from the workshop and I spotted a way to defeat the security gate. I broke in.A bloke glanced up from beneath a car, surprised by my sudden appearance. His name was Mike.I explained Sophie’s broken promise. I described my pain, my sense of betrayal. No, I probably left those bits out. But I am sure he read it on my face.“Ah, dammit,” Mike sympathised. “That thing’s new. You’re not the first.”It turned out the car would be ready on Tuesday.“Check in on Monday, to be sure,” Mike said. “And don’t listen to Sophie, just say to her, ‘Put me through to Mike.’”On Monday afternoon, I rang Sophie. Her voice was warm and unruffled. She gave no hint of the tension that had flared between us days before. It felt impolite to interrupt her but I did. With the brisk authority of one who Knows How Things Work, I said, “Sophie, put me through to Mike.”And just like that, she did. And there was a human, harried but not hallucinating. The next day, I collected my car as Mike promised.Sophie has already eaten one job. If she could fix cars, she would soon eat Mike’s as well. Humans are building a world where humans are not really necessary. Soon it won’t really matter whether Sophies speak nicely or not.Hugh Riminton is the former national affairs editor at Australia’s Channel 10Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changed  | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Labour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Labour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new, asks Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves at Malloy Aeronautics in Berkshire, 30 June 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Rachel Reeves at Malloy Aeronautics in Berkshire, 30 June 2026.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAOpinionAndy BurnhamRachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changedGaby HinsliffLabour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new?Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.42 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 12.41 ESTShareRachel Reeves wants you to know she thinks Britain’s future belongs in Europe. She would also like to mention that she “absolutely” got all the big calls right as chancellor, even if there were a few things she would have done differently, and that John Healey’s budget last week would have been far harder for him if she hadn’t put in so much of the groundwork.The gist ofher argumentin last weekend’s Sunday papers–previewing a lectureat Harvard University today, reflecting on her time in power – was essentially that if anyone imagines Andy Burnham somehow invented pro-Europeanism and putting more money in people’s pockets, they can think again.Reeves was clearly devastated by losing a job she loved, and her return to the fray after a summer of quietly licking her wounds has inevitably sparked speculation over whether she now seeks a comeback. But her timing is acute enough to suggest that this goes a little deeper, coming as it does days after a deliberately low-key budget that left some Labour MPs wondering what happened to the much-hypedend of neoliberalism.How much of theBurnham agendais really new, and how much is essentially the old Starmer one, repackaged with rather more warmth, charm and political skill?Inside what’s left of the old inner circle, loyalists point out that Reeves and Starmer were both fervent remainers at heart and of course they would have loved to be back inside the EU one day; it’s just that the time wasn’t yet right to talk about it when they ran for office.Similarly, the package of sanctions on Israeli settlers that the foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, announcedin September, alongside an apology for what he considered Starmer had got wrong on Gaza, wasn’t a dramatic break with the past but essentially the measures his predecessor, Yvette Cooper (now health secretary), hadspent her last weeksat the Foreign Office working up, which couldn’t be published until a new prime minister was formally in place.Starmer’s former close lieutenant Darren Jones, meanwhile, isopenly arguingthat this administration’s answer to a looming crisis in defence spending – basically shunting the hard questions about funding it into next year’s spending review – is “what Keir and Rachel were going to do”, if only they hadn’t been forced out by the very same John Healey resigning as defence secretary in protest at something remarkably like the strategy he’s now pursuing. Starmer himself, who has kept his counsel over the summer, made a rare public intervention inDublin last weekto warn pointedly that the US withdrawal from European defence will outlast the Trump era, and Europe cannot afford to be left exposed.If the Starmerites are understandably smarting at what some see as history being rewritten by the winners, some are also failing to recognise their part in their own downfall. Starmer was ultimately ousted by his own MPs because they wereexasperated by his failure to lead and sensed the country had turned inexorably against him.Burnham has shown not only that he can take decisions – across Whitehall there seems to be more clarity now about what Downing Street wants – but that he can build the emotional bond with the public his predecessor couldn’t, without which even the boldest moves wouldn’t have worked. He might only have moved the needle fractionally on issues such as Palestine or Europe, where themanifesto red lineseffectively mean nothing significant can change that wouldn’t have under Starmer, at least this side of a general election. But each time he has done just enough to achieve the political impact that Starmer was seemingly chasing but couldn’t pull off. Where his predecessor could never quite get the dosage right, Burnham seems to instinctively know how far to go: it’s the difference between a novice cook clinging fixedly to a recipe that isn’t quite right, and an experienced one who tastes and adjusts the seasoning as they go. And judging bythe polling, it’s working.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpening the EU debate again is clearly a political minefield. But we have to do it | Simon JenkinsRead moreYet still some MPs are anxious to hear a bigger vision of where Burnham wants the country to go than fixing social care andbanning people listeningto loud music on the bus. Since there wasn’t one in the budget, all eyes are on the 10-year plan, now expected some time in December.Burnham has made much of promising to give Britain some breathing space after years of rolling crises and financial struggle. But the small, popular changes he has offered so far –£100 offyour energy bills, aNo 10 Northoffice in Manchester – have also been in part about buying some breathing space for himself while he gets to grips with bigger and potentially more controversial challenges, from welfare reforms to defusing a Labour revolt over Shabana Mahmood’s plan tomake migrants wait longerfor the right to settlement.A confident and relaxed debut has masked the fact that transitioning from mayor to prime minister was always going to be a steep learning curve, and that he didn’t get the long summer of planning that his team had wanted to prepare for power. But now that period of grace is coming to an end, along with a period of silence from those he ousted, some of whom are keen to defend their legacies. By Christmas we should know whether Burnham is offering genuine new thinking in British politics, or something more like the old kind, regifted.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know it | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: Anger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generation, says former prime minster Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: Anger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generation, says former prime minster Gordon Brown
Content: Celebrations in Belgrade last week following Student List’s victory in the Serbian election.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersView image in fullscreenCelebrations in Belgrade last week following Student List’s victory in the Serbian election.Photograph: Uros Arsic/ReutersOpinionProtestA global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know itGordon BrownAnger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generationMon 2 Nov 2026 10.17 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.32 ESTShareWe have not yet reached a 1968 moment, when students at the Sorbonne lit a fuse that detonated a crisis that eventually brought downthe De Gaulle government. But in late 2026, starting with the symbolic act of young French peopleclimbing the July Columnat Paris’s Place de la Bastille, the world is experiencing the biggest outbreak of student demonstrations for 60 years.When Italian students subsequently occupied a high school in Rome, they opened their demand for change with the words “like in France”. Youth demonstrations are now raging from India – where the government hasresponded with repressive forceto theCockroach movement– to Albania, where, after being out on the streets for nearly five months, students are demanding not only an end to corruption, but thereplacement of the government.But the most momentous set of protests has been in Serbia, where theStudent List of candidatesfor national parliamentary elections has succeeded not just in dislodging a long-established, corruption-tainted government alleged to have links with organised crime, but insecuring an electoral mandate. It is now poised to form a new administration. Nothing of this kind has ever happened before.View image in fullscreenProtesters at the base of the July Column in Place de la Bastille, Paris, 8 October 2026.Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockStudent List is not only changing the political leadership of Serbia but popularisingnew methods of organising; it isbuilding a systemfor selecting candidates from outside its own ranks, using methods such as open public assemblies with rotating delegates and specialised working groups. Eighty-five student assemblies selected the candidates, as ananalysis of their internal rulesexplains. And the results are often surprising: the rector of Belgrade university, Vladan Djokić, wasnot selected as a candidate, despite being a longterm supporter of the movement and expected by many to play a major role in government.Student List has beencompared by the Croatian philosopher Srećko Horvat, who situates the movement within a longer tradition of direct democracy and collective self-organisation, to the Paris Commune of 1871. Its fundraising activites, however, are very much up to date:it reportedly crowdsourcedalmost €2m (£1.7m) from more than 26,000 individual donors during the election campaign.The wave of youth protests comes after mobilisations inKenya in 2024and acrossNepal,Indonesia,the Philippines,Madagascar,MoroccoandPeruin 2025. How far the Serbian grassroots model of organising will shape youth movements elsewhere remains to be seen. But according to Olivier Ertzscheid, a senior lecturer at the University of Nantes, “young people’s sense of belonging and social interaction is at play”, with social media now actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters – and driving momentum.September and October have seen youth protests inBelgium,Austria,GreeceandItalyover education funding; inGermanyover the threat of compulsory military service; and inSpainandPortugalover the lack of affordable housing. But the protests have also spread well beyond Europe, toIndonesia, where youth demonstrations are focused on pollution; toArgentinaover austerity; and toChileandColombiaover funding cuts. Last weekend in Germany, a group called Gen Z regeltled demonstrations in 21 cities.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators march through Berlin’s Mitte district on Saturday, demanding action on rising living costs, cuts to education and conscription.Photograph: Nikos Kanistras/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe protests will only intensify this month. In Australia, a big student demonstration is planned for11 November, andstudent unions in Britain and Italyare planning a joint day of action protesting against the rising cost of education on 20 November.Some years ago I wrote about anew generation of youth activists– of Bangladeshi schoolgirls campaigning against forced child marriage who had declared “child marriage-free zones”, and of Nigerian and other young people in Africa demanding their right to education. But the current youth rebellions are of a different order, breaking out in a new and more dangerous global environment and challenging authorities on issues well beyond education. Young people face an AI-led unemployment crisis; they lose out from the skewing of public spending towards older people, from restricted provision of education; they face a housing crisis and governments underplaying the importance of the climate emergency and intergenerational justice.The youth jobs crisis will grow. The number of UK graduate jobs postings advertised on one big employment agency has declined from about180,000 four years ago to 50,000 today. AI is thought to be a factor.Hi-tech employment of 18- to 24-year-olds declined by 30%between December 2019 and December 2025, whereas the sector itself expanded by 33% in that period. So as the government prepares to announce itsreview into youth employment, it is urgent we get nearly 1 million unemployed under-25s into work, giving priority to pre-apprenticeship training and restoring educational maintenance allowances, as well as radically reshaping a benefits system that is failing the younger generation.Butthis is a worldwide problem. Because of ever-rising debt burdens andspiralling expenditures on defence and energy subsidies, governments are trapped in such a fiscal straitjacket that they will struggle to find the resources to meet young people’s aspirations. A large portion of public spending is captured by older generations, with schools and universities losing out as a result. Across the OECD, about half of health and social security spending goes to elderly people – those over 65 – despite them making up only 18.5% of the total population. In this tally, pensions are the biggest item, accounting for38% of all social spending– but an understandably high portion of all health spending goes to older people, too. And with young people now taking home afar smaller share of income than earlier generations,income and wealth gaps between young and oldhave widened.It’s time to join the dots.Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author of Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation, warns that the protests are morphing into awider social movement. “There are inequalities at all levels,” she says, “with gaps widening between different social groups.” The triggers for the demonstrations vary from country to country, but the basic complaint is strikingly similar. Young people believe that any promises that they would do better than their parents’ generation have already been broken – and that case is a strong one.Liberal democracy itself is now on trial.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010, and is United Nations special envoy for global educationExplore more on these topicsProtestOpinionYoung peopleStudentsCost of living crisisHigher educationHousingcommentShareReuse this content

title: As cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them? | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: Many treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve
Content: When it comes to cancer treatments, our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, Ranjana Srivastava writes.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenWhen it comes to cancer treatments, our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, Ranjana Srivastava writes.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAOpinionHealthAs cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them?Ranjana SrivastavaMany treatments are now extending lives but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curveMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.33 ESTShareTwo decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew,whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presentedthe latest chapterresults from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.Are your bones brittle? If they were, how would you know? (To men: this goes for you too) | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreAt two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?Treatment can delay a cancer’s return but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.Yetquality of life is often reported less rigorouslythan response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication,which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.double quotation markOur ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to liveA recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting ofhealth-related quality of life in trialsof adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report howmanypeople experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, howlongit lasts, andwhether and whenthey recover.Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple but, when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHealthOpinionCancer researchMedical researchCancercommentShareReuse this content

title: Memo to King Charles: if the Dutch king can apologise for slavery, why can’t you? | Raoul de Jong | The Guardian
description: It has been three years since Willem-Alexander said sorry, so please use your trip to the Caribbean to follow his example, says Dutch novelist Raoul de Jong
Author: Raoul de Jong
Headline: It has been three years since Willem-Alexander said sorry, so please use your trip to the Caribbean to follow his example, says Dutch novelist Raoul de Jong
Content: The governor general of Antigua and Barbuda, Rodney Williams, and King Charles after a church service in St John's, 1 November 2026.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe governor general of Antigua and Barbuda, Rodney Williams, and King Charles after a church service in St John's, 1 November 2026.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersOpinionSlaveryMemo to King Charles: if the Dutch king can apologise for slavery, why can’t you?Raoul de JongIt has been three years since Willem-Alexander said sorry, so please use your trip to the Caribbean to follow his exampleMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 09.11 ESTShareDear King Charles,You are currently on a Caribbean royal tour through the Bahamas, Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda. I understand that during this tour you will not issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, or address the role your own family played in it. You will instead express your “sorrow”, and this will make it easier for politicians to also dodge the question. Whether that isKemi Badenoch calling an apology a “navel-gazing distraction”, or the prime minister, Andy Burnham, saying he would support an apology, while flatly opposing reparations.Coincidentally, I’m also in the middle of a world tour for the English translation of my book, Jaguarman, a novel about how my enslaved Surinamese ancestors survived 300 years of hell on Earth. I travelled from Ghana to Indonesia to New York, when I was asked to respond to you, as soon as possible. That’s how it often goes in this strange story, I’ve noticed: people like you get centuries to find the right words, while we must scramble to respond to your actions. But, yes, I do have something to say.Three years ago your Dutch counterpart, King Willem-Alexander, stood before an audience of people of colour, many of them my friends. Dressed up like kings and queens, they listened solemnly as he did what you will not andapologised for the role of the Dutch state in enslaving our ancestors, and for the failure of his own family, the house of Orange-Nassau, to act against it. Slavery was “a crime against humanity”, he said, “and the stadholders and kings of the house of Orange-Nassau did nothing to stop it”.It was a moment that people on whose shoulders I stand had fought for for centuries, often at the risk of their health or even their lives. Willem-Alexander’s speech was directed at people of colour such as me. But I felt that the apology was perhaps even more important for the rest of the population.It happened in 2023, on 1 July, the day theNetherlandscommemorates the abolition of slavery, a celebration called Keti Koti. In the Netherlands, many institutions tend only to invite writers such as me to speak on this one particular day, so as Willem-Alexander was addressing the nation, I was somewhere else, in a small library, in front of an audience of mostly white people, giving my own lecture about what they could learn from my Black ancestors.We from the colonial diaspora already know the true history of our mother country. We already know what the powers that govern us are capable of. We know the darkness they can create. And we also know that it is possible to come through that darkness. To me, the apology was most important for all these other people who thought my history had nothing to do with them. For those who had never considered that there might be something to learn from the people who gave me this life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritish people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy BurnhamRead moreYou know the truth, Willem-Alexander knows it, I know it, but many of your subjects do not. The truth is my ancestors were kidnapped. Chained. Trafficked across the ocean. Sold. Torn from one another. Turned into property. Brainwashed. Silenced. Mocked. Cursed. But the fire inside us was never extinguished. Despite the plantations. Despite the Atlantic. Despite the slave forts. That is why I am alive.That is not a small thing. It is enormous. That’s why the people receiving Willem-Alexander’s apology were dressed up like kings and queens. They know what a huge gift it is to be alive, and how important it is to take care of what you have been given. They know that they have not been put on this earth in order to wither. They have been put on this earth to blossom. And even if all your freedom is taken away from you by other people, you can find ways to flourish, because the spark of life itself is on our side.Its fire will keep burning, your majesty, whether you apologise or not. The true heroes in this history were rarely born as royalty. But, of course, being born as royalty doesn’t prevent you from doing the right thing. You cannot stop the truth from coming out. But you can choose whether history remembers you as someone who stood in its way, or someone who stood with it.Raoul de Jong is a Dutch novelistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
