title: Radical-right youth groups are at the root of Europe’s populist surge | Cas Mudde and Duncan McDonnell | The Guardian
description: From France’s Jordan Bardella to Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, organised youth politics has produced many rightwing leaders, say the political scientists Cas Mudde and Duncan McDonnell
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: From France’s Jordan Bardella to Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, organised youth politics has produced many rightwing leaders, say the political scientists Cas Mudde and Duncan McDonnell
Content: Giorgia Meloni speaking in Rome at the National Congress of Notaries, 22 October 2026.Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGiorgia Meloni speaking in Rome at the National Congress of Notaries, 22 October 2026.Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockOpinionThe far rightRadical-right youth groups are at the root of Europe’s populist surgeCas MuddeandDuncan McDonnellFrom France’s Jordan Bardella to Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, organised youth politics has produced many rightwing leaders. Democrats must catch upMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 05.16 ESTShareThe leaders of the most successful populist radical right parties in western Europe have one thing in common that is often overlooked. Italy’sMatteo Salvini, Jordan Bardella from France, Jimmie Åkesson from the Sweden Democrats, and Tom Van Grieken from Belgium’s Vlaams Belang all led the youth wing of the parties they now run. These movements shaped the politicians they are today, and they are now shaping Europe’s political future.As Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, another former radical right youth-wing leader,put it: “Even more than my growth as a politician, I owe my growth as a person and as an Italian to my youth-wing activism. There is no more formative training ground than this.” And yet, until recently, we knew little about these incubation chambers of populist radical right parties.‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answeredRead moreIn researching our new book,Youth Wings of the Populist Radical Right, we looked at 10 such organisations from across Europe. From the youth wing of Austria’s Freedom party to that of France’s National Rally, we found they help to recruit, train and promote the radical right’s grassroots members, their representatives and leaders of the future. They also perform important functions for their parties in the present, encouraging young people to vote for them, providing a key source of labour during election campaigns, running party branches and influencing policy.In particular, we found that youth-wing leaders and their rank and file members are helping to achieve three key goals for the radical right as their parties expand in the 2020s: internationalisation, professionalisation and normalisation.First, these youth wings go even further than their older equivalent organisations in building new transnational alliances. Away from the spotlight, there has been a proliferation of international far-right workshops and conferences, such as theTransatlantic Patriot Summit, held each year in Budapest since 2022. These and similar events have brought together youth leaders from Europe, India, Israel, Latin America and the US, to talk about common aims and establish ties that will last through their careers. Many of the youth leaders we spoke to talked openly about how these international ties will benefit them “when we are the ones in government”.View image in fullscreenThe National Rally’s Jordan Bardella poses for a selfie with supporters.Photograph: Patrick Hertzog/AFP/Getty ImagesSecond, they are heavily involved in political training at international, national and local levels. Once derided as a bunch of amateurs (and with good reason, in some cases), the populist radical right now invests considerably in professionalisation. The young people who join are taught not only about policies and history, but also rhetoric and media communications. They are being trained as future politicians, and the likes of Åkesson, Bardella, Meloni and Salvini are proof of concept.Third, the recruitment of university-educated young people – who look and sound very different from the stereotypical media image of the angry far-right youth – feeds into the growing normalisation of the populist radical right. Producing more articulate, professional and presentable leaders can help their parties be seen by voters as legitimate political actors. And the more distance they can put between themselves and previous generations of uncouth leaders, such as Jean-Marie Le Pen in France or Umberto Bossi in Italy, the more they can attract young people like themselves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStickers offered at the refounding of the AfD youth organisation in Giessen, Germany, 29 November 2025.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APBut this smartening up of the radical right’s public image does not reflect a softening of the message. The young leaders we spoke to will not lead their parties down a path to moderation. They may have found ways to smooth down their movements’ rough edges, but the ideology is still an exclusionary, nationalist one. In other words, the regeneration of the radical right through its youth wings makes it an even more significant challenge to liberal democracy.How can mainstream parties respond to this challenge? One way would be to stop focusing on the radical right as the root of their problems, and to look at themselves and their own youth wings.Recentresearchinto youth-wing membership has found that centre-left and centre-right youth groups are dominated by men, people from political families and careerists. If mainstream parties are to regain ground with young people, this needs to change.Governing parties could also do far more to address the problems that young people are facing in the 21st century. For most of the postwar period, younger generations in western Europe grew up with the implicit promise that they would have better life prospects than their parents. That promise has been broken. In fact, with the rise of insecure employment, compounded by the housing crisis, a significant minority of young Europeans arestill livingwith their parents into their late 20s and early 30s. It is no surprise that many have little faith in the capacity of mainstream parties to change their lives.By contrast, the young populist radical-right activists we interviewed talked about how their parties spoke to them in clear terms about the issues that concerned them, and offered them solutions. Mainstream parties should be doing the same.Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author ofThe Far Right Today; Duncan McDonnell is professor of politics at the Jeff Bleich Centre in Flinders University in Adelaide, Australia.Youth Wings of the Populist Radical Right, co-authored by Duncan McDonnell, Sofia Ammassari, Ann-Cathrine Jungar, Anders Ravik Jupskås, and Cas Mudde, is published by Oxford University PressExplore more on these topicsThe far rightOpinionGiorgia MeloniYoung peopleMatteo SalviniEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)commentShareReuse this content

title: Conservatives like me embrace conservation. Why the Coalition’s chainsaw approach to climate?  | Andrew McLachlan | The Guardian
description: The radical assault on longstanding measures to drive down Australia’s emissions and facilitate decarbonisation seems almost pathological
Author: Andrew McLachlan
Headline: The radical assault on longstanding measures to drive down Australia’s emissions and facilitate decarbonisation seems almost pathological
Content: The recent climate announcement from the Coalition and its leader Angus Taylor (pictured) ‘is an abandonment of the Liberal traditions and values that have long sustained the party’s success.’Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe recent climate announcement from the Coalition and its leader Angus Taylor (pictured) ‘is an abandonment of the Liberal traditions and values that have long sustained the party’s success.’Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPOpinionCoalitionConservatives like me embrace conservation. Why the Coalition’s chainsaw approach to climate?Andrew McLachlanThe radical assault on longstanding measures to drive down Australia’s emissions and facilitate decarbonisation seems almost pathologicalSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereSun 1 Nov 2026 20.49 ESTLast modified on Sun 1 Nov 2026 23.17 ESTShareTheCoalitionis repudiating its longstanding policy positions on climate, even to the extent of disowning many of the structures it created when in government. Such thinking is not from the conservative tradition and has more in common with the radical. In my view, it is an abandonment of the Liberal traditions and values that have long sustained the party’s success.The Coalition wants to remove net zero targets from Australian law, abolish the Net Zero Economy Agency, reform (read diminish) the Australian RenewableEnergyAgency and the Clean Energy Finance Corporation as well as remove the electric vehicle tax concession, battery rebates and Scope 3 emission reporting requirements. It intends to cancel the annual Climate Change Statement to Parliament and remove the statutory mandate of the Climate Change Authority to advise on future targets.The good news for those of us who want to hand over a better world to the next generation is that many of these extreme measures will have to navigate the Senate. Depending on the Senate’s disposition, the Coalition is unlikely to find much support.It is the opposition’s role to question government spending. The institutions, policy settings and expenditures must always be questioned to ensure they are fit for purpose and public funds are invested wisely. In the name of reducing the cost of living and protecting the Australian way of life, the Coalition is walking away from any serious attempt to reduce pollution or invest in the natural world that sustains our lives.Angus Taylor pledges to repeal swathe of climate policies, saying ‘Australia has done its bit’Read moreThe unabashed assault on longstanding measures to drive down emissions and facilitate decarbonisation seems almost pathological rather than rational. More concerning, it is implicit that a future Coalition government will not want to even understand the environmental impact of its policies.Being of a conservative disposition myself, there is nothing in these announcements that finds any favour with me. I am committed to ensuring generations that follow will enjoy a healthier planet and sustainable economy. A deep love of nature, place and community demands that you ensure nature’s interests are at the heart of all decision making. This includes internalising the cost of carbon pollution into our economy, as we do with pollution more generally.Sadly the longstanding tradition of conservation in the right inAustralian politicshas now been abandoned. It has been replaced with a deep dislike, even hate in some quarters, of all things considered “environmental”. The past achievements of the Liberal party in the environmental portfolio are now looked upon with embarrassment.Leaving aside the fact that building a sustainable economy that is in harmony with nature is the moral path, such is the revolutionary zeal of the Coalition for tearing down the structures created to transition our economy, it appears little to no thought has been given to the very real adverse consequences of these policies.Pacific nations are looking to Australia for leadership. The impact of climate change is existential for these beautiful island states. If the Coalition approach is adopted, we will not be a credible nation in our own region and this will allow other actors to increase their influence.There are incredible economic benefits in the green industrial transformation. Recently the South Korean government invested1,000 tn won (A$1.1 tn)into its transition. China is exporting up to US$30 bn per month of clean technology, up 100% year on year. All major economies are pivoting and we risk being left behind.The desire of some in the Coalition to mimic One Nation or adopt the language of the Maga movement should not be allowed to prevent Australia from aligning with our key Asian trading partners. Nor should it prevent the EU trade agreement from coming into force. That deal is especially great for our exporters, yet is being criticised by the Coalition for mentioning the Paris agreement, which we are already a signatory to.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Coalition says it wants cheaper power, not ideology. But its evidence-free plan is all ideology | Adam MortonRead moreInternational capital primarily looks for the best returns on investment. When mainstream political parties float radical measures sovereign risk is heightened and, even if never realised, the impacts will be felt today. Fund managers seeking to invest for the long term and drive innovation will now hesitate, uncertain of the direction of our decarbonisation journey.No government policy settings are perfect and all require review and adjustment from time to time. A wiser approach would have been to announce sensible reforms of extant structures in order to improve outcomes for the nation – both for its people and the natural world that sustains them.However, to devise those policy advances or adjustments, you have to accept that climate change is real. Further, that it will be more expensive in the long term to respond to the consequences than to invest in prevention and adaptation now. Sensible national investment requires climate system knowledge and upgrading infrastructure ahead of time.At its core, the Coalition plan suggests that to seek prosperity you must abandon the journey to net zero. Net zero is being used as a scapegoat to explain away our declining productivity and is wilfully blind to the impact of pollution. To blame net zero for every national woe might be easy to sell alongside One Nation, but it undermines the Coalition’s reputation of being serious economic managers.The economic credentials of the Coalition are further diminished by wanting to muzzle the Climate Change Authority and dissolve any accountability frameworks such as setting targets and measuring performance against the same. The “shooting the messenger” approach can never be justified. Pollution will not magically disappear because it is not being reported upon.There has never been a more important time for conservatives to stand up for nature and advocate for policy settings that support an economic transition to a cleaner economy through encouraging innovation and free markets.All this brings to mind Giulio Boccaletti’s thesis in his book The Environmental Republic: the environmental challenges we face are not from a lack of scientific knowledge or understanding but are essentially political. He dreams of a society where caring for the natural world is the foundation of our freedom. My own vision for the future has no place for the political chainsaw. Rather I advocate for investment in our body politic and its institutions that will preserve, renew and enrich our world, especially for those that will come after us.Andrew McLachlan is a Liberal senator in South AustraliaExplore more on these topicsCoalitionOpinionLiberal partyClimate crisisEnergyAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’
Content: ‘I’m still carrying the scars of her creation’ … a later incarnation of Lara Croft.Photograph: AspyrView image in fullscreen‘I’m still carrying the scars of her creation’ … a later incarnation of Lara Croft.Photograph: AspyrHow we madeCultureTomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’Interviews by Sean ColeMon 2 Nov 2026 09.40 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 16.11 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Douglas, lead programmer and co-creatorI joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches forTomb Raider. He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols.I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life.double quotation markWe worked till 2am every day for a year – and managed to bottle lightningWe had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis.Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefactsjust for fun.Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints.View image in fullscreen‘I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of how Lara was sexualised’ … the 1996 Tomb Raider title screen.Photograph: MobyGamesIt was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress.We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised.We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation.Heather Stevens, level designerWe developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life.View image in fullscreen‘Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that’ … Heather Stevens’ level concept sketches.Photograph: Heather StevensToby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before.Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together.double quotation markI was able to buy a house with the royaltiesBefore designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru!Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her.I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties.Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog. Feeling as if you’ve left a mark, and connected with millions of people through something you’ve created, is amazing.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madeTomb RaiderGamesAdventure gamesPlatform gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art icon | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at Tate
Author: Kat Lister
Headline: The artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at Tate
Content: ‘She’s making the moves’ … Wilhelmina Barns-Graham’s Protest, 1967.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustView image in fullscreen‘She’s making the moves’ … Wilhelmina Barns-Graham’s Protest, 1967.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustArt and designBeaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art iconThe artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at TateKat ListerMon 2 Nov 2026 07.30 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 07.32 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the centre of Tate St Ives’ newly opened retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, her monumental altar-piece Glacier (Blue Cave) pulls viewers into its frozen tendons of turquoise and white. Its mouth is agape and the blue slit of its eye casts downwards to the rest of its body. The glacierfeelshuman: a vivisection of rock, ice and snow that brings to mind the fragmented facial features of Picasso’s Weeping Woman.Standing in front of this glassy colossus, the exhibition’s curator, Katy Norris, talks about these “mangled” and “twisted” forms – so alive on the canvas. “Barns-Graham was so distinct in her approach,” Norris says. “There are always questions of: what am I seeing? What is in front of mereally?And how does that relate to what I feel inside?”View image in fullscreen‘Feels human’ … Glacier (Blue Cave), 1950.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustGlacier (Blue Cave) was painted not far from this gallery space in 1950 – only 10 years after the Scottish-born painter moved 500 miles south to the tiny fishing town of St Ives – but it goes some way to showing just how radical she was over the course of her eight-decade career. From her early 20s, Barns-Graham’s quest for connection saw the self-described “lone wolf” become a key player in the St Ives school which congregated in and around the Cornish harbour during the second world war. She continued to experiment relentlessly with colour, geometry, kineticism and repetition until her death in 2004, aged 91.Anne Barlow, director of Tate St Ives, points out this major retrospective – the first to span Barns-Graham’s full career – is a “long-overdue celebration” of an expressive master. The art historian Virginia Button wrote that “Barns-Graham clearly felt that as a woman she had been unfairly sidelined from the history of St Ives” with its focus on Ben Nicholson, Peter Lanyon and Patrick Heron. She had a brief period of fame in the 1950s, but it waned in the 1960s as her landscape modernist work became increasingly “hard-edged” (as Rob Airey, director of the Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust, puts it) and more daring; less commercial and harder to categorise.View image in fullscreenIn Barns-Graham’s beloved St Ives … The Blue Studio, 1948.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust. Courtesy of The Fleming Collection.With her “blue eyes that flashed like knives” (so her husband, the writer David Lewis, remarked) and her delight in toying with gender stereotypes (she took great pleasure in the sexual ambiguity of her preferred nickname “Willie”), Barns-Graham ploughed her own furrow from the beginning. Born into an upper-class family in the seaside town of St Andrews in 1912, Barns-Graham’s resistance was tested early when her stern father became hostile towards her plan to pursue artmaking as a profession.Nonetheless, ignited by her love of Cézanne, at the age of 18 Barns-Graham started studying at Edinburgh College ofArt. “She had a single-mindedness,” Norris says. “She didn’t see any limitations, she just saw the path ahead.” It’s a focus you can sense in her 1945 oil painting Froth and Seaweed. Painted in her beloved St Ives, the artist homes in on the spidery tendrils of algae and slithery copper rock. “It’s almost as if she has no peripheral vision, she’s just seeing beauty at her feet.”View image in fullscreenBarns-Graham in Cousins’ A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things.Photograph: Publicity imageFilm-maker Mark Cousins first encountered Barns-Graham’s paintings in late-80s Edinburgh. Whether depicting the silvery shorelines of St Ives and St Andrews or the crystalline glaciers of Switzerland, he says, “she just leapt off the walls”. He made a pilgrimage to her St Andrews house during lockdown, and in 2024 released A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things, which delves into the artist’s distinctive gaze and synesthesia. Barns-Graham associated colours with people, places, emotions and even letters of the alphabet – something she called a “total experience”. “If we think of Turner’s relationship to landscape, he saw a vortex. And Leonardo da Vinci saw a machine. She was like that as well; she saw a living thing,” Cousins says.View image in fullscreenGlacier Knot, 1979.Photograph: © Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustHer encounter with the Grindelwald glacier in Switzerland came in 1949. “That day was almost like a rebirth, a kind of rapture,” Cousins says of her life-defining hike and the 60-odd paintings and drawings that followed over a three-year period documenting the glacier’s “many moods”. In a letter to the Tate in 1965, she wrote: “It seemed to breathe!” This wasn’t an artist above the landscape, Norris says, butofthe landscape. The glacier’s interiority was her interiority – a close symbiosis that intensified for the rest of her life as she pushed further into abstraction, moving away from figurative landscape painting in favour of “systems, rhythm, repetition and spatial tension”.Yet the underlying presence of nature was still there: “bird flights, dancing diamonds on water, dots inside foxgloves, cell formations,” Norris writes. For the curator, Barns-Graham’s work in the 1960s-70s (titled Things of a Kind in Order and Disorder) is where she truly pioneered a new way of experiencing the world – “like chaos theory, really” – by laying out small cardboard squares in neat rows on her studio floor before randomly nudging them with her foot. On a stormy morning on the golden stretch of Porthmeor beach, I got to see this paint-splattered studio for myself; its floor-to-ceiling window looking out on to fast-moving clouds and ferocious waves.Like Merce Cunningham’s “choreography by chance”, Barns-Graham was thinking about “how things hold together” – not least her marriage, which ended in divorce in 1963. Referring to her 1968 oil painting on board Olive Green Squares on Vermillion, she compared the erratic block of squares against a rage of red to “a broken marriage” – herown. Yet with Protest – another volatile blockwork which was made in 1967 as the Vietnam war raged and a year after the Beatles had released Revolver – “she was [also] thinking about participation and action and what you can do as an artist or viewer. She’s making the moves, she’s a part of it, she’s no longer in awe of a natural phenomenon that’s doing its own thing.”View image in fullscreen‘Are they soundwaves?’ … Eight Lines, Porthmeor, 1986.Photograph: Tate Photography/© Wilhelmina Barns-Graham TrustWhen the Beatles came along, “working-class men were cool and posh women weren’t,” says Cousins. “But she just kept going.” In the 1980s, Barns-Graham’s tumult of squares made way for the thumbprint pen-and-ink lines of her Small Energy Drawings. “Are they soundwaves? Is it the wind?” Norris ponders. “Sometimes she’d look out from the cathedral-esque window of her studio in St Ives and turn her back to it, playing music and drawing lines that replicated the sea.” Another “choreography by chance”: first you observe, then you listen, then you feel. That precision and intuition can exist in such harmony in these artworks speaks profoundly to Barns-Graham’s own particular genius.“At my age there’s no time to be lost,” Barns-Graham said in the 1990s. “I say to myself: ‘Do it now, say it now, don’t be afraid.’” Drawn to the late works of Picasso and Joan Miró, and incensed by the environmentally ruinous decade in which she was living (“the most appalling time of abuse of living things,” she remarked), the octogenarian slapped colour on to the canvas with an energy that was both urgent and physical. “The St Ives narrative flattened her,” Cousins says of this late flourish. “It saw her as one of many. It is important to extract her from St Ives and see her as a singular imaginative person.”Wilhemina Barns-Graham is at Tate St Ives until 3 MayExplore more on these topicsArt and designTate St IvesPaintingArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Gilded Age review – what did we do to deserve such a terrible stinker? | Television | The Guardian
description: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful show
Content: Looking as if someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle … Cynthia Nixon (right) as Ada Brook, with Christine Baranski as Agnes van Rhijn.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenLooking as if someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle … Cynthia Nixon (right) as Ada Brook, with Christine Baranski as Agnes van Rhijn.Photograph: HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Gilded Age review – what did we do to deserve such a terrible stinker?Julian Fellowes’ high-society period drama has, somehow, picked up Emmys and reached its fourth series. Poor Meryl Streep must feel so awkward watching her daughter Louisa Jacobson in such a uniformly awful showLucy ManganMon 2 Nov 2026 17.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdoctor with a fully qualified moustache races up a carriageway towards an immaculate stately home. “I fear we should have sent for you sooner!” says the lady who greets him on the doorstep as the screams of a woman in drug-free labour rattle the windows in their frames.Oh, ya think?is not Dr Moustache’s reply.When this many cliches assemble so quickly, it can only mean one thing: Brownstone Abbey – AKA Julian Fellowes’ Revenge, AKA What Did We Do to Deserve This?, AKA The Gilded Age if you insist on its official title – is back for a fourth and, no one has said let alone promised, final season.The labouring woman is Gladys (Taissa Farmiga), daughter of the nouveau riche Russells of Fifth Avenue and now married to Hector (Ben Lamb – I’m sorry, actors, it’s Guardian policy to identify you), 5th Duke of Englandshire and living in England Hall in England after some plot last season. “She’s bleeding!” cries an astute maid, staring at a blood-soaked bed. “What’s wrong?” cries someone crackingly stupid. “She’s haemorraghing!” says the doctor, which is medical moustache for “She’s bleeding!”, so really, we are no further along. That’s the Gilded Age dialogue promise.‘We could have had good fun a few decades ago’: Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatreRead moreMeanwhile, back in America, the costume budget is assembling in church for the wedding of Oscar (Blake Ritson – again, I’m sorry but I don’t make the rules), scion of the old-money Van Rhijn family, and Enid (Kelley Curran), wealthy widow of Mr Winterton and former lady’s maid to Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon). Enid has mastered the constipated diction of the US aristocracy enough to fool Oscar’s mother, Agnes, into thinking that she is a suitable wife for Oscar. (Agnes is played by Christine Baranski, whom one imagines praying nightly before a shrine to Maggie Smith, the patron saint of actors’ retirement funds, begging for a sign that she has done the right thing.)“At last my son is married!” says Agnes, for viewers who have just watched the wedding but still need a bit of help. “And to a fine-looking woman with enough money for them to live well! And soon I shall entertain the president of the United States!” She’s not having a stroke – Grover Cleveland is indeed due to be hosted at Brownstone Abbey. All signs point to it being the equivalent of the opera house wars from season one, so do hold on to your hats.Enid has not, however, fooled either herself or Oscar into thinking she is the right woman for him. He is a dedicated homosexual; theirs is a marriage of convenience and much the healthiest setup of the bunch.View image in fullscreenJack Gilpin (Mr Church), Carrie Coon (Bertha Russell), Taissa Farmiga (Gladys de Vere) and (Ashley Atkinson) as Mamie Fish.Photograph: HBORight, what else is happening? Cynthia Nixon’s Ada is wealthier than Agnes now, since her rich reverend died, but she remains in constant facial rictus, a smile-thing happening beneath a permanently wrinkled nose so she looks as though someone has stuffed a slowly rotting rat up her bustle. Her niece Marian (Louisa Jacobson, daughter of Meryl Streep and honestly, family Thanksgivings must be so awkward whenever this is airing) is still yearning after the Russells’ (heterosexual) scion Larry (Harry Richardson), and I’m afraid no good comes of them being forced to stay in a hotel overnight after a coach accident. (Thunder, lightning, shot of horse rearing, wheel breaking, Larry saying “The horse must have been spooked by the storm!”, fealty to the dialogue promise rewarded by later nakedness with Marian.)Peggy (Denée Benton) is engaged to William (Jordan Donica) and happily so, apart from his interfering mother (Phylicia Rashad). If my bingo card of as-yet-unused-tropes does not deceive me, Peggy is soon to experience problems in terms of reconciling her professional success with her imminently increasing domestic duties. She and the Kirklands remain a conduit for Fellowes’ and his co-typer Sonja Warfield’s take on turn-of-the-century race relations, which is as subtle as their take on class distinctions, Anglo-US relations and human relations, on which we shall not dwell.George Russell (Morgan Spector plus beard, such a beard!) is still in financial difficulties: “And if I deal with him, I have to pay most of the transportation costs of the oil?” “Without his business, your railroad cannot survive!” He is also busy trying to track down the person who shot him before the Newport ball at the end ofthe last series. Something to do with copper mines, I think. I cannot be expected to remember everything.Bridget, the Irish maid (Taylor Richardson), still hasn’t mastered her accent (“Halp me get the kek!”) and is still pining for Jack, the young inventor (Ben Ahlers). He is following up on his alarm-clock success with an electric mixer he assures potential investors will take the world by storm. Meanwhile, Gladys loses her uterus (“What’s wrong?” “The script using the word ‘uterus’”) and – do you know what? I’m too exhausted to go on. In short, all is as it was. Uniformly terrible and likely to outlive us all.This stuff won an Emmy. America is a failed state. E pluribus zilch.The Gilded Age aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now in the UK, and on HBO in the US and Paramount+ in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewJulian FellowesCynthia NixonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jail | Music | The Guardian
description: Young, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UK
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: Young, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UK
Content: ‘The energy was there – tons of energy!’ ... HR, centre, performs with Bad Brains in Wetlands in New York in 1999.Photograph: Steve Eichner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The energy was there – tons of energy!’ ... HR, centre, performs with Bad Brains in Wetlands in New York in 1999.Photograph: Steve Eichner/Getty ImagesMusic‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jailYoung, black and fuelled by self-help mantras, they were reputedly the best live band on Earth. As their wild first sessions are rereleased, the group talk about scaring club owners – and getting kicked out of the UKAlex DellerMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOld punks might not agree on much – who was first, who was fastest, where to file the Faith/Void split LP in their record collection – but for those who saw them in their prime, Bad Brains were, unequivocally, the best live band on the planet. YouTube footage bears this out: frontman HR, born Paul D Hudson, is equal parts straining sinew and raw electricity as he bucks and contorts, punctuating rapid-fire snarls and otherworldly croons with impeccably timed backflips. The band surge around him, forging blisteringly fast punk informed by everything from the Damned and Dead Boys to P-Funk, Stevie Wonder and Chick Corea’s Return to Forever.Young, black and fuelled by an ideology that united the 1930s self-help mantras of Napoleon Hill with Rastafari, they were outliers in the already outre 70s punk scene. But while Bad Brains helped change the face of American punk as it morphed into hardcore in the early 80s, and inspired artists as diverse as Rage Against the Machine, Deftones, Lil Jon, the Roots and Beastie Boys, defeat was never far from glory as they balanced feted live performances and a scintillating run of records with an excruciating capacity for self-sabotage.double quotation markI cleaned the floors in jail and got time off on Sundays. I said: ‘Let’s give it a try then’The band’s roots thread back to Central High, a school in Maryland where middle-class military kids HR and his younger brother Earl (drums) met Dr Know (AKA Gary Wayne Miller, guitar) and Darryl Jenifer (bass). Jenifer hailed from Washington DC’s south-east projects. “We had an art teacher that would let us bring in records,” he says. “So you’re making papier-mache, or whatever the fuck, and our clique of musicians met by bringing in things like Billy Cobham’s Spectrum rather than Earth, Wind & Fire.”View image in fullscreen‘It wasn’t like being in a band – it was a mission’ ... from left: Dr Know, Earl Hudson, HR and Darryl Jenifer AKA Bad Brains.Photograph: Atiba JeffersonThe quartet, along with Jenifer’s close friend Sid McCray, began making music, rehearsing in a friend’s house when his mother was out playing bingo. “We were very influenced by all kinds of music,” says Miller. “White, black, rock’n’roll, funk – all the flavours, just like Baskin-Robbins.” Jenifer sums things up more pithily: “My female cousins would say, ‘Darryl listens to white boy music that you can’t dance to.’”The group initially aspired to the jazz-fusion of Return to Forever and the Mahavishnu Orchestra, although Jenifer suggests this era was little more than adolescent daydreaming. “We called ourselves Mind Power, but we never played a show, and we only had one song. It was the delusional teenage phase: it never was serious, it never was real.”Things got real, though, when McCray discovered punk, introducing the band to Sex Pistols, Dead Boys and Ramones. “I just remember listening to the music and feeling liberated,” says Jenifer. “Like, damn, I can make some shit like that.”Mind Power was rechristened Bad Brains, and HR inherited the mic from McCray. “Our first poster said: ‘Bad Brains, the greatest punk rock band in the world’,” laughs Jenifer. While easily chalked up to youthful braggadocio, this radical self-belief was largely the product of the band’s adherence to PMA – positive mental attitude – as a guiding credo.“My father would say, ‘Why do you want to be a musician? Be a doctor or a lawyer or something,’” says HR from his Texas home. “He told me to read a book, so I read Think and Grow Rich.” This was by Hill, the personal motivation guru. “I decided to use PMA as a formula, as a vehicle in my music, and to try to use it to help guide me through what I was going through.” Dabbling with hard drugs, working a dead-end security job and on the brink of fatherhood, it’s perhaps no surprise that PMA seemed like a lifeline for HR, but his interest was shared by the rest of the band. “We wanted to have a purpose and a message,” says Jenifer. “It wasn’t like being in a band – it was a mission.”This sense of focus was apparent at the band’s first studio session, when they entered Don Zientara’s Inner Ear Studio in 1979 to record a six-track demo, a pivotal moment that has now been remastered and released by Trust Records under the title Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording. “They were serious,” says Zientara, speaking from his studio. “The songs were there. The energy was there – tons of energy! – and you hear that coming through. At the time, I didn’t have a chance to think about how good they were. They came, they played, they packed up. It was so quick. It was like, did I record these guys?!”View image in fullscreenA force to be reckoned with … Bad BrainsAfter another demo session, Bad Brains hit their stride with a series of landmark releases: 1980’s brief, brilliant 7-inch Pay to Cum was followed by a self-titled album and then by Rock for Light, produced by Ric Ocasek. These years were turbulent, marked by triumph and tribulation: the band were banned from a number of Washington venues. “They said we incited riots,” says Miller. “The club owners said, ‘You’re making the kids go crazy!’” And, although a scorching 1979 gig with the Damned had led to an invitation to tour the UK, the band tried to enter the country without working papers and were immediately sent back to the US – penniless and with their equipment lost en route.For all the chaos, this period cemented the band’s legend as a force to be reckoned with. The excitement of their music was matched by a zeal amplified by their burgeoning Rastafari beliefs. “The intention has always been to excite people and make them exult,” says Jenifer. “We’re not performing a riff or trying to nail a show. We’re giving the crowd the vibration to destroy Babylon. This music is the spearhead – that’s what we go on stage with. If we didn’t have that revolutionary spirit, we’d probably feel stupid playing the shit that we play.” Miller, more succinct, agrees: “We’re not lost in the moment,” he says. “Wearethe moment.”These sentiments are echoed by many who saw Bad Brains perform. “My friend Bruce and the guys in Autistic Behavior kept telling me, ‘Once you see Bad Brains, your life will change,’” says author and educator Nancy Barile. “They were right.” Barile first saw the band play in Philadelphia in 1982 and had a “physical and visceral” response. “Every time I saw Bad Brains in the early 80s, the audience reaction was insane,” she says. “There’s only a handful of bands I’ve seen get that kind of unrestrained – and totally pure – response and Bad Brains lead the pack. It was chaotic but hypnotic. It was clear that we, the audience, wanted – actually needed – to be participatory in the performance.”Photographer and artist Glen E Friedman concurs. “The first time I saw Bad Brains was just after these early demos were recorded,” he says. “I was in high school. In all honesty, I had never seen anything or heard anything like them. They were incredible in so many ways.”View image in fullscreen‘We’re not lost in the moment. We are the moment’ … the band in 1983The band split for the first time after the release of Rock for Light, with HR wary of major label interest and growing tensions within the band due to his and Earl’s increasing fondness for all-reggae sets. There were also abusive, homophobic clashes with members of the hardcore scene’s gay community – notably with Texas punks Big Boys, whose frontman was gay. The former Hüsker Dü frontmanBob Mouldhas also recalled incidences where his band were subject to homophobia by Bad Brains. And then there was the roundly condemned (and subsequently disowned) 1989 song Don’t Blow Bubbles – perceived to be anti-gay – which continues to cast a pall over the band’s legacy. Neither Williams nor Jenifer are keen to rake over these incidents, though the latter suggests youthful and misguided zealotry were at play. “I was taught to love all people,” he says now. “I’m no homophobe. I respect life. If you got life, I’m loving you.”The band reunited for 1986’s blistering I Against I, which saw them expanding their palette into soul, funk and heavy metal, securing the talents of super-producer Ron Saint Germain despite their label’s limited budget. As well as providing the record with oomph, Saint Germain’s technical skill helped overcome certain logistical difficulties – like HR serving time for a marijuana bust.“I was doing stupid things,” says the singer, “jeopardising my future, and I had to learn the hard way. I was in jail when Sacred Love was recorded. Ron suggested I try to sing some vocals to it over the phone. I was working as a mop, cleaning the floors, and I got in time off on a Sunday. I said, ‘OK, well, I’ll give it a try.’”From the late 1980s onwards, the band existed in fits and starts. Releases were punctuated by breakups, lineup changes and violent incidents that sank both a series of high-profile gigs with Beastie Boys and a deal with Madonna’s Maverick Records. “Everybody can be a handful,” is how Miller rather plainly sums things up. “When we hit the stage, though, all that stuff doesn’t mean anything because the spirit takes over.”With Miller still recovering from a severe stroke and cancer, and HR being treated for both Sunct syndrome and schizoaffective disorder, it’s unlikely Bad Brains will perform again. But their deal with Trust Records at least puts their recorded legacy in safe hands – a legacy the band are very much aware of. “When we first started, we knew it was something unique and not what people expected,” says Miller. “It was like, ‘Who’re these brothers playing some rock’n’roll?’ But what they should’ve done was go to the history of rock’n’roll. It’s all Muddy Waters and them guys, not Elvis Presley.”Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording is out on 6 November via Trust RecordsExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPunkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ashanti: ‘I’ve had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment’ | Music | The Guardian
description: Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skill
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skill
Content: ‘What gets on my nerves about my husband Nelly? Definitely the thermostat’: Ashanti, who is touring Australia this month.Photograph: Michael Simon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What gets on my nerves about my husband Nelly? Definitely the thermostat’: Ashanti, who is touring Australia this month.Photograph: Michael Simon/Getty Images10 chaotic questionsMusicAshanti: ‘I’ve had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment’Before her Australian tour, the Grammy-winner talks about her marriage to Nelly, fans rushing the stage and her secret skillGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailSian CainMon 2 Nov 2026 09.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 17.40 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour debut album, Ashanti, turns 25 next year and you’re in the process of re-recording it.How do you feel about that album now?We are re-recording it so I will own my masters. Sonically, it will be a lot clearer. It was 25 years ago so it’ll sound a little more new, obviously, but with the same classic vibe. I’m very excited. What I’ve learned is that I’m just really grateful to have written records that stand the test of time. Foolish is turning 25! That I can still go to an arena and hold the mic in the air and hear everyone sing those lyrics is a beautiful feeling. And a blessing.Owning my masters is really important to me. Nowadays, obviously, things are a lot different compared with back when I first came out as an artist. But after 20 years, you get the right to go in and legally re-record your masters … and take back what’s yours, so to speak. Hopefully it inspires artists to try and take control from the beginning – hopefully you don’t have to wait 20 years! But if you do, you go in, you get it done and you have fun with it.You and your husband, Nelly, have been together for decades. What do you like most about him and what gets on your nerves?He has got to have the biggest heart I know. He is so generous and genuine – he will literally take the shirt off of his back and give it to you. He’s really a beautiful person. And he taught me a lot about staying positive and looking at the glass half full, as opposed to half empty. He has an amazing heart.What gets on my nerves? Definitely the thermostat. He likes it to be cold and I like it to be warm and toasty and cozy. A lot of our beef happens over the thermostat. Our compromise number is 70 degrees fahrenheit (21C) because I would prefer 80, 85 and he would prefer, like, 60. I’m like, “Bro, come on!” So we agreed on 70.What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?Obviously 20 years ago it was very different – you are a new artist so people would come up to me, crying and shaking. And I’m very grateful for that. But being in the game for 20-plus years, teenagers that weren’t even born back then come up to me now. I met a young girl recently and I was like “How do you even know Foolish?” I saw her singing every word in the audience with her mom. It was the coolest thing.Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morningYou want to hear something crazy? This young girl did an interview with me at SiriusXM recently and she said, “Oh my God, I love you! My dad named me after you!”As a millennial, John Tucker Must Die is a very important film to me. Do you find acting easy? How does it compare to making music?It’s just another muscle to flex. I really enjoy acting. I think the difference is you have a lot more control in music, especially if you write your own music. If you’re on stage, you know people are there to see you. When you’re acting, you’re portraying a character that someone else has written and you’re being directed … so although it’s really cool to dip into another version of yourself, it’s kind of limiting because you’re there to portray what they want you to.What’s the most chaotic thing that’s ever happened to you on stage?I definitely have had some – I guess we’re going to call them very excited fans – jump on stage and give me a hug mid-performance. I’ve also had a bodysuit snap off on stage. That was not my coolest moment. We had to have the band play for a second. I went into the wing and got it together.When you get to a hotel, what’s the first thing you do?I wipe down the phone and the remote with disinfectant wipes – always!If you could collaborate with another artist you haven’t already worked with, who would it be and why?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI like a lot of the newer R&B girls; they are really cool. I love SZA, I think she’s really, really dope. She’s shown me so much love since the beginning. Summer Walker is dope too. And I like women empowerment. Nothing against the guys!What is the best lesson you’ve learned from someone that you’ve worked with?Michael Theo: ‘I want to be on Dancing with the Stars! Would a top hat be too much?’Read moreUsually your gut is right. Sometimes, as artists, we second guess ourselves – but usually your gut is right and you’ve got to follow it. My husband has definitely said that to me, because he’s always like, “You second guess yourself!” But we all do that.Is your baby boy coming along on the Australia tour?Yes, he’s coming to Australia with me. I really thought long and hard about it but I can’t go that long without seeing him. I’m very grateful and blessed to have an amazing nanny. It definitely takes a village. Being a working mom and travelling all over the world definitely takes its toll. And I’m a mom that cooks all of his food from scratch. Everything is organic. Most people have liquor, chips, candy on their rider – and mine is just, like, organic sweet potatoes!What are you secretly really good at?I don’t know if it’s a secret, but I’m actually a really good cook. My go-to dish is Chilean sea bass with rice and vegetables. And I am good at impressions.Who’s your best impression?[In a very convincing Australian accent]Well, I think my best imitation might be you at the moment.Ashanti’s Australian tourkicks off in Perth on 9 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusic10 chaotic questionsR&BfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama | Movies | The Guardian
description: Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say
Author: Craig McLean
Headline: Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say
Content: Balancing act … Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney.Photograph: BBC/Hilltop ScreenView image in fullscreenBalancing act … Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney.Photograph: BBC/Hilltop ScreenMoviesInterview‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s dramaCraig McLeanWritten by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they sayMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhead of production on their first job together, Rhys Ifans andLaura Linneydidn’t undergo the standard “chemistry read” to make sure they got on. Which is remarkable, given what their characters would have to do to each other in Onwards and Sideways.In the Norfolk-set BBC film directed by John Madden (Shakespeare in Love), Ifans would have to nearly throttle Linney while in the grip of night terrors, she’d have to collapse in his arms in a weeping mess having bankrupted herself with a gambling addiction; both situations arising from the neurological condition afflicting their characters: Parkinson’s disease.But despite being thrown into the deep end in this hugely emotional, often hilarious film, both actors acknowledge an immediate feeling of safety around each other as they embarked on a project that would require them to strip themselves bare. “It’s odd,” says Ifans, “you learn so much about each other so quickly. I couldn’t tell you what kind of car Laura drives. What her home looks like. But we both know how we feel about death and dying.”Linney, 62, is a triple-Oscar-nominated star with a diverse array of roles on her CV, from her breakthrough in The Truman Show (1998) onwards through Clint Eastwood’s Mystic River and Richard Curtis’s Love Actually (both 2003), then the TV series Ozark and The Big C. Ifans, 59, franklyburstthrough in 1997’s Twin Town, AKA the “Welsh Trainspotting”, and went on to play Hugh Grant’s scraggly flatmate Spike in Curtis’s Notting Hill (1999), Daniel Craig’s stalker in Enduring Love (2004) and drug smuggler Howard Marks in Mr Nice (2010).Divergent backgrounds, then. But equally time-served, too. So the actors were able to dive in, no chemistry read required. They did, though, do dance classes. They waltzed together in London, and separately nearer their respective homes, the better to understand one popular form of recreational therapy for people with Parkinson’s. In Brooklyn, Linney was introduced to David Leventhal at the Mark Morris Dance Group. He runs a programme there called Dance for PD.“That’s the mothership of this wonderful organisation that now has offshoots all over the world, including here,” the New Yorker says when she, Ifans and I meet in the central London offices of the producers behind Onwards and Sideways. Both are dressed casually and low-key, each clearly easy in the other’s company, their conversation frequently erupting into gales of laughter.View image in fullscreenIfans and Linney in Onwards and Sideways.Photograph: Jonathan Birch/BBC“I spoke with David for a long time – and then I learned that Juilliard has classes for this once a week,” Linney says of the acting school that’s her alma mater. “So I just started hanging out there. It’s incredibly moving what the arts will do,” she says – in this case, how dance and music could relax people grappling with a condition that, among its 40-plus symptoms, causes uncontrollable shaking, stiffness of gait and involuntary freezing in doorways and thresholds. “How brave it makes people. How it opens up the imagination, and then the body follows somehow, when it shouldn’t. And the difference between someone moving in a dance class and then, when the music stops, to see what happens to their bodies – it’s shattering in a good and a sad way. So … it gets right to the bone of things.”Ifans, meanwhile, attended weekly sessions with a group who meet in Pontio, an “arts and innovation centre” in Bangor, north-west Wales. “There was a harpist accompanying the dance,” says the Pembrokeshire native. “Then there was a support dog running around the room who happened to be a sheepdog.”“Herding!” adds Linney, laughing.“It was peak Welshness!” acknowledges Ifans, to hoots all round. Then, quietly again: “They were so inspiring, these classes. And a great leveller. You’d be sitting next to a nuclear scientist and a school cleaner. Both dancing to the same tune and wrestling with the same diagnosis.”The writer of Onwards and Sideways is Paul Mayhew-Archer. He’s an actor, writer – he co-created The Vicar of Dibley with Richard Curtis – and accidental activist. The 73-year-old is a founder member of the Movers and Shakers podcast, which raises both awareness and laughs, alongside fellow “Parky people”, including journalists Jeremy Paxman and Mark Mardell. He was diagnosed with the disease at 58, with the canary in the coalmine, symptoms-wise, being that “my handwriting was very small and unclear”.His experiences directly inform the experiences of the fiftysomething characters played by Ifans (Tony, a teacher) and Linney (Emma, a musician). They also, full disclosure, inform my writing of this feature: my dad has Parkinson’s and I’m in the age bracket Mayhew-Archer was when he was diagnosed. My handwriting is appalling.View image in fullscreenLove is the drug … Linney with Jason Bateman in Ozark.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyTrue to Mayhew-Archer’s mission, Onwards and Sideways is painfully, honestly funny. The scene where Rory Kinnear’s doctor rather cavalierly informs Tony that he has the condition features a joke lifted from Mayhew-Archer’s own diagnosis.“My neurologist told me one of the symptoms is the difficulty of smiling, and that I seemed to have difficulty smiling,” Mayhew-Archer relates to me when we meet on another day in the same office. “And I said: ‘Well, that could be because you just told me I’ve got Parkinson’s.’ As soon as I said that, I knew I wanted to be funny about Parkinson’s, because I saw no point in being serious.”double quotation markThere’s a mercurial element to this illness – it’s bespoke. No one has the same Parkinson’sIfans – who’s been staunchly committed to this project for the duration of its lengthy gestation, stretching back pre-Covid – seconds that emotion. “I loved the way Paul’s story about a life-changing diagnosis was handled, funny and devastating all at once. My attraction to it was also that I have friends and family who’ve been impacted by Parkinson’s. That gave me a fast track into the telling of a story like this.”“You don’t have to scratch very far to find someone somewhere who knows someone who has Parkinson’s,” echoes Linney of a condition that, in the UK, 166,000 people are living with, with one person being diagnosed every 20 minutes according to Parkinson’s UK. “I certainly have friends who do.”To “act” Parkinson’s, Ifans and Linney were aided by the Neuro Heroes, “remarkable women who do physio for people with Parkinson’s and various related conditions”, says Linney. “They helped us with our basic understanding of Parkinson’s, and then also the physicalisation. [Because there’s] a mercurial element to this condition – it’s bespoke. No one has the same Parkinson’s.” Or even the same side-effects from the drugs prescribed to help manage the incurable condition: they can cause increased libido, appetite, and compulsive spending and gambling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThrones is where the heart is … Ifans in House of the Dragon.Photograph: HBO“Parkinson’s was like a physical dialect for us,” continues Ifans. “We had to learn its physical language. They [the Neuro Heroes] could say what was happening at the muscular level, or the skeletal impact, of Parkinson’s. But we needed poetry to understand what that felt like. Whether it felt like moving through tar or sand. Just to be able to arrive at an image that you could apply to the body, that you could take with you to set each day, to help you achieve the shapes and positions that Parkinson’s puts people in.”And those people, ultimately, were always in the actors’ minds. Mayhew-Archer knew the film had to honour those with the condition, but that that noble aim did have its bluntly practical limits. “We knew we couldn’t cast people with Parkinson’s in those two central roles,” he says. “Partly because Laura’s character has [a medical procedure] done which means she stops doing certain things. And it would be very hard for people with Parkinson’s to stop doing some things!” he adds with a laugh. “Once you start freezing, you can’t stop!”“We had the added responsibility in getting Parkinson’s right,” says Ifans. “Not just right, but bang-on. Because there’s a whole demographic watching that deserves to be represented. That was the scary bit, wasn’t it?”Linney, staring intently at her co-star across the table, nods. It was, she says, fundamentally about “doing it justice”. And then, “the possibility of failing at that?” says Ifans. “Huge responsibility. That brought us closer together. That’s the stuff that woke us up at night.”When we meet, Linney is about to be unveiled as one of the cast of DC superhero TV series Lanterns. She’s a Guardian of the Universe, “or so I’ve been told”, she says with spoiler-savvy diplomacy. “But a green beam might come down and evaporate me if I utter a word!” She’s also two weeks into filming, alongside Colin Firth and Julianne Moore, Comfort and Joy (formerly The Joy of Sex), a romcom about the north London throuple who helped produce Alex Comfort’s groundbreaking 1972 illustrated sex manual. So, another unconventional midlife drama but lighter, certainly, than Onwards and Sideways.“There was something about this world of Parkinson’s that forced me to be very present in a way that I normally am not, particularly while working,” she admits. “It forced me to be over my skis a bit. And off-balance, and vulnerable, and experiencing things in very different ways. “This movie rearranged my cellular structure!” she adds, beaming in gratitude. “Most movies don’t do that. I love my work. But very few experiences have literally rearranged my soul. This one certainly did.”As for Ifans, this year we’ve seen him alongside Anna Maxwell Martin in Apple TV’s cold war-era sci-fi thriller Star City. When I meet him, he’s just been beheaded on House of the Dragon. Onwards and Sideways, in stark contrast, is acting in the raw, with no high-concept narrative or CGI to hide behind. Acting of a different order.“Yes. You can have spaceships, lunar landscapes, swords and castles, but you ain’t gonna have a co-star like this,” Ifans says, beaming at Linney. “That’s where the money is. Not the coin … That’s why we go to work. As Laura says: all these [roles] are different and thrilling and enjoyable in their own way. But this film is particularly nourishing.”Having seen Onwards and Sideways in the company of my mum, who cares 24/7 for my dad, I couldn’t agree more. We watched it bathed in both tears and smiles. It’s a beautiful achievement; empowering, educational entertainment, and Ifans and Linney deserve all the credit in the world for how they’ve portrayed the multiverse of Parkinson’s. I would send them a personal note to thank them for what they’ve done for those with, and connected with, the disease. But I’m not sure they’d be able to read my handwriting.Onwards and Sideways is inUKcinemas from 6 November, and on BBC One and iPlayer later this year.Explore more on these topicsFilmRhys IfansLaura LinneyDrama filmsParkinson's diseasefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It still preys on my mind’: readers on their scariest non-horror movies | Movies | The Guardian
description: After Guardian writers picked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman Show
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: After Guardian writers picked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman Show
Content: A still from Never Let Me Go.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from Never Let Me Go.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyMovies‘It still preys on my mind’: readers on their scariest non-horror moviesAfter Guardian writerspicked their choices for Halloween, readers have responded with films that send chills down their spines – from Never Let Me Go to The Truman ShowGuardian readersMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Short Film About KillingThe murder of the taxi driver is utterly excruciating and the hanging at the end equally so. Both are shown in full, in close up and in real time. The condemned man’s last cigarette is smoked in full. The unease (to put it mildly) of the audience was palpable.WiscotAftersunNot horror but horribly tense. I was convinced when he went into the sea at night that he wasn’t going to come out. A personal response from me, but I found it almost unbearable to watch.annarachel‘I left shellshocked’: writers on their scariest non-horror moviesRead moreThe Manchurian CandidateThe brain washing sequence scared the living daylights out of me: never could watch Angela Lansbury in any thing after that without a shiver going down my spine!JobsworthWilkinsLilya 4-everLilya 4-Ever for me, a harrowing journey through a young girl’s experience of being seduced and then sex-trafficked. It’s excellent, but grim – oh, so grim – and it left me feeling hollowed out afterwards and disgusted with the human race.AdamKView image in fullscreenStill from Melancholia.Photograph: Magnolia Pictures/AllstarMelancholiaThe existential dread of an extinction level event – so lyrically and beautifully evoked. It embodies the desolate inevitability of the end of all things.RishiSamboraSalvationIts portrayal of mountain village clan feuds, superstition and the mass delusion that might enable a charismatic individual to dehumanise others, with mass-murderous consequences, was very scary. Even more frightening was that the film was roughly inspired by a real-life massacre, in Bilge in 2009.appealforsanityThe Truman ShowIt’s one of the best horror-non-horrors ever made. The premise is pure terror. Your friends, family, job are all lies. You have no secrets. Every moment of your life, every lesson you thought you learnt in private is seen, recorded, witnessed forever. Your deepest paranoia is real. Yes, even the sky is fake. The Truman show was so ahead of its time with the horrors of digital life. Scary as fuck!materofviriiWatership DownI was six when Watership Down came out, and saw it in the cinema (Birkenhead Odeon, no less, scary in itself in 1978). I don’t think anything has ever had a greater long-term effect on me than the images of the rabbits crushed together in plugged and gassed burrows, blood-red eyes and gasping desperately for air. That evil Woundwood rabbit wasn’t much better; that night I wouldn’t go upstairs to bed in case the fucker was hiding in my wardrobe.WrighthanesThe most frightening, nightmare inducing film for me will always be Watership Down. First saw it in the cinema aged around nine, it has some very memorable scenes.FlowerpottyView image in fullscreenA still from Wake in Fright.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWake in FrightAn Australian movie about a young teacher who gets stranded in an outback town while trying to get home for the holidays. Gradually the dark side of the town and of a certain type of Australian culture is revealed, until it ends in utter bleakness. Not a horror movie, but horrifying. The sort of movie that sticks with you. Good acting too.RabbigatorStill can’t sit through it even after all these years. “The Australian Experience” distilled down to its nasty, toxic, alcohol soaked chauvinistic worst.cantgettakickNever Let Me GoNever Let Me Go is ostensibly a sci-fi (alternative reality) drama, I suppose, but its central premise is terrifying. As is the ultimate acceptance of their fate (after some inevitably failed resistance) by all the characters. It still preys on my mind.boavisteiroThe TribeThere was a Ukrainian film set in a deaf school and told entirely in sign language with no subtitles called The Tribe that really was particularly grim and shattering. Not seen it since it was in the cinema, don’t want to revisit it as I don’t think it would have the same impact on a TV set-up. One of those films you come out of and you can hardly speak.vammypUnited 93United 93 was as horrific a film as I’ve seen – needed nonstop cartoons and a lie down after that film, the mundanity of the run up to it, not showing the villains as pantomime characters and knowing the outcome all feed in to the feeling of it.RobRoy1975View image in fullscreenA still from Compliance.Photograph: Bad Cop Bad Cop Film Productions/Sportsphoto/AllstarComplianceWorth watching if you get the chance – basically just about someone crank-calling a fast food restaurant and convincing the duty manager to do some pretty terrible things, all just with the power of assumed authority. It’s very uncomfortable and to find out that everything in it happened –multipletimes – is truly chilling.getoutofmydreamsYellow SubmarineThere’s something about the animation style which was absolutely skin-crawling, and the image of people being apparently turned to stone, but still with an occasional tear running down their frozen cheek, was deeply unsettling.1AngryManGoodfellasI had spent my life since early childhood watching horror films that I was probably too young for, but I’d never felt so frightened watching a film until, aged 18, I saw GoodFellas – my first Scorsese in the cinema. I thought it was absolutely terrifying. It certainly didn’t make me want to be a gangster.TheManWithoutFearView image in fullscreenA still from Kiss Me Deadly.Photograph: Allstar Collection/Cinetext/United/Sportsphoto/AllstarKiss Me DeadlyTakes the disillusionment and fatalism of noir to its logical endpoint in the age of atomic anxiety. Becomes something more akin to cosmic horror in its final stretch, just leaves you haunted by the spectre of an unleashed and irrevocable annihilation.penny_lane00Dreams of a LifeThe docudrama about Joyce Vincent who lay dead for nearly three years in her London flat before being discovered is one of the saddest and most troubling films I have ever seen and all the more disturbing because it is true. That nobody could miss her or not care about not seeing her for three years highlights the hidden horror of social isolation and the cracks through which the lonely and mentally troubled can fall. Truly haunting and unforgettable.lilactimeBlue VelvetHow could you not give a nod to Blue Velvet, in which Dennis Hopper plays Frank Booth, who’s got to be one of the scariest villains ever. Every time he’s onscreen, I tense up, knowing that he’s so strung out & malevolent that only pain or death will ensue. Dennis Hopper plays him to the hilt, especially after he sucks in his nitrous oxide.BobManchesterCTExplore more on these topicsFilmGoodfellasDavid LynchWake In FrightMelancholiaLars von TrierNever Let Me GofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg review – a BBC reporter’s howl of frustration  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: After more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politics
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: After more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politics
Content: Laura Kuenssberg.Photograph: Jonathan Callery/BBC/October FilmsView image in fullscreenLaura Kuenssberg.Photograph: Jonathan Callery/BBC/October FilmsBook of the dayPolitics booksReviewPay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg review – a BBC reporter’s howl of frustrationAfter more than two decades of studied neutrality, the journalist delivers some home truths about modern politicsGaby HinsliffMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLaura Kuenssberg always swore she would never write a book. Amid all the vitriol hurled her way, the BBC’s political editor turned presenter has largely kept her counsel. She rarely complained even when she needed security to do her job unobstructed at Labour party conference under Jeremy Corbyn, or had to run the gauntlet of aggressive Brexit protesters outside parliament, or when a creepy unnamed minister tried to inveigle her into his hotel room for what an appalled Kuenssberg concluded was intended to be a threesome. Knowing everything she does is minutely parsed for bias, she keeps her cards close to her chest. Until, apparently, something snapped.Pay Attention is a muted but heartfelt howl of frustration with politicians “who have looked like an absolute shower for a long time” but also,sotto voce, with voters, who she evidently wishes would occasionally take things more seriously. Having covered Westminster since the late noughties, Kuenssberg brings all that weight of experience to bear in spelling out just how far the abnormal is now becoming normalised in British politics.double quotation markShe deconstructs the techniques Farage has developed to dodge questions he dislikesOnce, she points out, there was a cross-party understanding not to inflame racial tensions at sensitive times; now masked men can roam Belfast seeking foreign-born people to burn from their homes, and still Nigel Farage says they shouldn’t be called far right. The Greens, Tories and Reform all selected candidates for this year’s council elections who had previously expressed startlingly flaky views. The rapid turnover of prime ministers over the last decade isn’t normal either, she argues, but nor was the behaviour causing it – from the boozy loucheness of Boris Johnson’s Downing Street to Keir Starmer securing a whopping great majority but no mandate, having never really made a case for what he actually wanted to do.This is a serious and earnest book, not a gossipy insider’s tale, focused on the failures of governance that have radicalised what she argues isn’t naturally a radical country. Kuenssberg describes a politics paralysed by fear, with MPs afraid of telling an angry public the hard truths they’ll happily discuss with her once the camera stops running. (Nobody she talks to, apparently, thinks government operates effectively or spends money well.)
