But there are glimpses too of journalism struggling to hold politicians accountable, in an era of shrinking audience attention spans – Kuenssberg is notably sniffy about fluffy interviews that focus on a politician’s colourful backstory, not their policies – and Trumpian resistance to scrutiny.She deconstructs the techniques Farage has developed to dodge questions he dislikes: expressing total conviction even when he doesn’t know the facts; turning questions back on his interviewer; and claiming to be persecuted by the media when cornered – an incendiary tactic Corbyn also adopted and which Zack Polanski is beginning to use, though Kuenssberg says at least Polanski has a “swagger and a bluntness” which means he’ll usually answer a straight question. When a politician lashes out at the mainstream media, she argues, pay extra attention to what they’re actually doing: often it’s a distraction tactic.But she also identifies the weaknesses in mainstream politics that she believes gave Farage his opening. Ten years ago, she argues, it would have sounded “distressing and insane” to say there would soon be mass small boat crossings of the Channel: if that reality has changed, alongside the numbers of legal immigrants arriving and arrangements for housing them, perhaps it’s unsurprising that the public mood has changed, too. For Kuenssberg, it started with a wave of eastern European migration in the 2000s that some communities struggled to absorb, followed by the 2015 exodus of refugees from war-torn Syria and European leaders’ apparent impotence in the face of what she calls a “massive migration crisis”.Politicians reacted first too slowly then too bombastically, promising to stop the boats and smash the gangs even when that wasn’t realistically possible, and fuelling the idea that immigration was beyond their control. What’s interesting about this argument – with which readers may agree or disagree – is that itisan argument, one of the few times she seemingly feels strongly enough to advance one.There is a discernible tension here between Kuenssberg’s professional duty as a BBC journalist to remain politically neutral, and the need for a book to say something beyond the bleeding obvious. At times, I wondered if she wouldn’t have been better saving it all for a post-BBC memoir where she could let rip.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs it is, some readers will be outraged that she isn’t taking a stronger stand against extremism, while others will doubtless think she has outed herself as a moderate centrist merely by pointing out that ideas now advanced by both Reform and the Greens would once have been considered completely off the wall. As Kuenssberg knows better than most, you can’t win – though that doesn’t mean it isn’t worth trying. Sadly, I think she’s right that our politics is neither normal nor healthy, and that saying so in plain English is an important part of holding the line. But it will take more than paying attention, I suspect, to bring sanity back.Pay Attention by Laura Kuenssberg is published by Little, Brown (£22). title: ‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disaster | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higher
Content: Taika Waititi at the Klara and the Sun premiere at  London film festival last month.Photograph: Zak Hussein/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTaika Waititi at the Klara and the Sun premiere at  London film festival last month.Photograph: Zak Hussein/Variety/Getty ImagesMovies‘Sad lost souls’: Taika Waititi lambasts critics after Klara and the Sun box-office disasterThe Jojo Rabbit director blamed the dismal numbers for his film of Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel on ‘obsolete’ reviewers’ notices, adding that he works ‘for the people’ – whose Rotten Tomatoes ratings are much higherAndrew PulverMon 2 Nov 2026 06.38 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 13.14 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaika Waititi has launched a furious broadside at “critics” following the disastrous commercial performance of Klara and the Sun, his new film adapted from aKazuo Ishiguronovel.‘I’d consider replacing one of my children’: Taika Waititi on robot kids, his cheese-o-meter and Klara and the SunRead moreIn a post on social media, Waititi wrote: “This Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus settled, and became critics.”He added: “The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit … Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”Pointing to the disparity of thefilm’s audience and critics’ score on review aggregator site Rotten Tomatoes, which currently stands at 74% for the former and 26% (from 90 reviews) for the latter, Waititi also wrote: “I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people.”Klara and the Sun, which costa reported $44m(£32.8m) to make, achieved adismal $701,000(£523,000) on its first weekend at the North American box office, working out at just under $800 (£596) per theatre from 880 venues. It came in at 16th place, well below other similarly aimed films such as Wicker, which opened with $5.7m in North America from 1471 venues at an average of $3,906 per cinema. In contrast, You Can See Everything, the celebrated documentary about Elizabeth Holmes scored $18.7m on its second weekend andhas reached a cumulative total of $63.8m.In the UK, the film recordedcomparable figures to Klara and the Sun’s North American results, with an opening weekend of £176,000 from 368 venues, for an average of £477.Klara and the Sun review – Taika Waititi’s manic pixie dream robot sci-fi is a sentimental messRead moreThe Guardian’s chief critic Peter Bradshaw described Klara and the Sun as “unbearably mannered” and “unspeakably acted” in a one-star review, adding: “[It] is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy.” Bradshaw alsonegatively reviewed Waititi’s 2019 film Jojo Rabbit, calling it a “terrible film … a pointless Hitler-spoofy YA adventure with a 12A certificate, obtusely accentuating little-kid cuteness and optimism amid the quaintly imagined non-horror.”Other reviewers have been equally negative towards Klara and the Sun:in the Observer, Wendy Ide called it “a thin and cloying thing that strips away any profundity in the source material and replaces it with self-conscious quirkiness”, whilethe LA Times’ Tim Grierson said: “[Waititi] lacquers the film with a calculated gooeyness that’s stultifying before it becomes downright exasperating”.Its second weekend at the North American box-office saw Klara and the Sun enter a steep decline, dropping 79% to $145,000 (£108,000) from a similar number of venues.Explore more on these topicsFilmTaika WaititiScience fiction and fantasy filmsFilm adaptationsKazuo IshiguroFilm industryFilm criticismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Steve Ellis, frontman of Everlasting Love hitmakers Love Affair, dies aged 76 | Music | The Guardian
description: Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul Weller
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul Weller
Content: Steve Ellis pictured in 1982.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSteve Ellis pictured in 1982.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockMusicSteve Ellis, frontman of Everlasting Love hitmakers Love Affair, dies aged 76Singer hit No 1 with pop-rock band in 1968 and scored three more Top 10 hits with them, before solo career featuring collaborations with Paul WellerBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 2 Nov 2026 06.29 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.31 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSteve Ellis, the singer who found fame as the frontman of 60s pop-rockers Love Affair, has died aged 76. A message on social media announced that Ellis died “peacefully” on 30 October, after “complications from a chronic illness”.With his stirring, heartfelt croon, Ellis gave voice to one of the most enduring hits of the 1960s: Everlasting Love, which topped the UK chart in 1968.Born in Edgware, north-west London, in 1950, Ellis formed the band Soul Survivors when he was 15 years old, inspired by Black US soul and R&B acts including James Brown who Ellis saw perform live: “He blew our socks off, he was phenomenal. I thought, that’s how a singer has to be, so I started doing gymnastics,” he told the Express in 2021.Soul Survivors morphed into Love Affair in the mid-1960s. They were signed to Decca and their debut single, She Smiled Sweetly, was released almost concurrently with the original version by the Rolling Stones, and flopped.But the follow-up Everlasting Love, another cover version, was a major hit – recorded by Ellis between shifts on a building site. Written by Buzz Cason and Mac Gayden and originally recorded by US singer Robert Knight, Ellis’s vocal was arguably more spirited, really selling the song’s pledge of eternal fealty: “Need you by my side, girl, to be my bride / You’ll never be denied everlasting love.”It spent two weeks at No 1 in the UK, and while other versions of the song would become more successful in the US – including Carl Carlton’s No 6 hit in 1974 – Love Affair’s version has endured as the most popular on streaming services, and a staple of wedding ceremonies.Buoyed by bombastic symphonic backings, Love Affair would go on to have three more UK Top 10 hits in the next two years. Rainbow Valley repeated the Everlasting Love formula – a Cason-Gayden song first performed by Knight, anchored by an emotionally wracked Ellis performance – and spent 11 weeks in the Top 40, and it was followed by A Day Without Love and Bringing on Back the Good Times.View image in fullscreenLove Affair perform at Revolution Club, London, in 1970.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesEllis became disillusioned with Love Affair after their fame began to wane later in the decade: “The band wanted to go progressive rock and that wasn’t for me,” he later said. “I’d always been a soul-boy. The main reason we broke up though was the screaming [fans]. We couldn’t hear what we were playing.” In 1972 he formed the band Ellis – their debut album was produced by Roger Daltrey – and then Widowmaker, which also featured ex-Hawkwind member Huw Lloyd Langton and others, recording their self-titled debut in 1976 before they continued without him.He released solo album The Last Angry Man in 1977, followed by Basement Days in 1983. Ellis returned in 2008 with the album Best of Days, which reunited him with Daltrey who appeared on two tracks.That album also kickstarted an enduring collaboration withPaul Weller, who appeared on two tracks including a live acoustic version of Everlasting Love. Ellis and Weller rejoined for 2018’s Boom! Bang! Twang!, with Weller co-writing two tracks and co-producing the album, followed by a one-off co-written song in 2022, Just to Simplify. His most recent album is Baby Faced Assassin, released in September, featuring another three songs co-created with Weller.Weller was among those paying tribute, writing on Instagram: “God bless ya Stevie safe travels everlasting love for sure.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockPaul WellernewsShareReuse this content

title: John Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83 | Doctor Who | The Guardian
description: Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T Davies
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T Davies
Content: John Leeson holding up a picture of K9 at a Doctor Who convention in 2005.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJohn Leeson holding up a picture of K9 at a Doctor Who convention in 2005.Photograph: ShutterstockDoctor WhoJohn Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83Actor, who appeared in Dad’s Army and Rainbow, remembered as ‘true gent’ by TV producer Russell T DaviesMartin BelamMon 2 Nov 2026 04.13 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.04 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Leeson, the actor best known as the voice of K9, the robot dog inDoctor Who, has died at 83.Leeson’s son, Guy Ducker, shared the news on Facebook. He wrote: “I regret to announce the death of my father … after a summer of illness. The end was peaceful.”In a separate post on social media, Ducker said: “Many thanks to the Whovian community for the love they showed to my father over the decades, it meant a lot to him and me.”Born John Ducker in 1943, he trained at Rada before embarking on a successful career on stage and screen. He was known for his character work across a range of TV shows such as Dad’s Army, Sorry!, Crown Court and Longitude, while other credits included The Bill, Vanity Fair, Doctors and Blake’s 7. He was also a continuity announcer on Channel 4.But Leeson was best known for K9, created by Bob Baker and Dave Martin, who was introduced to Doctor Who in 1977 in a Tom Baker-led story called The Invisible Enemy.Originally only intended to appear in that single script, the production team believed the character would be popular with younger viewers, and decided to have the metallic mutt join the Tardis team. He stayed until 1981 – although K9 was also voiced for a period by David Brierly – establishing the catchphrase “Affirmative, Master” when addressing the Doctor.View image in fullscreenLeeson with wife Judy Griffiths on their wedding day in 1969.Photograph: Gary Weaser/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenK9 flanked by the stars of Doctor Who in 1977.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyView image in fullscreenLeeson standing amid an ITV audience in 1993.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockLeeson reprised the role in the 20th anniversary special of Doctor Who and in a spin-off K-9 and Company, which featured Elisabeth Sladen as popular companion Sarah Jane Smith. Sladen and Leeson were reunited in Doctor Who in 2006 in a David Tennant episode calledSchool Reunion, before featuring in the CBBC spin-off Sarah Jane Adventures, which aired from 2007 until Sladen’s death in 2011.In an Instagram post after Leeson’s death, the former Doctor Who showrunner Russell T Davies said: “There was no question that we’d ask John to provide the voice” when the robot returned. “A posh dog, uppity, haughty, wry, but somehow innocent too, and so funny. Pitched perfectly so that kids could impersonate him. That’s not easy. A true gent, and a great loss.”Keith Barnfather, who first worked with Leeson in the 1980s and who produces behind-the-scenes documentaries about Doctor Who, described the actor as “kind, considerate, professional, charming, talented, unassuming”. Lisa Bowerman, who has credits for work across the Doctor Who universe, remembered him as “an utterly lovely man, excellent company and – and I don’t hesitate to use this word for once – a truly iconic voice”.After leaving school, Leeson worked as a hospital porter before auditioning for Rada. Talking about his career in interviews, Leeson described it as being in two parts: “Half of my career has been pretty much as a stage actor and the television half of my career arose pretty much by accident.”View image in fullscreenThe stars of Rainbow, from left: Bungle, Zippy, George and Geoffrey Hayes. Leeson said he felt ‘really ill inside this bear suit’.Photograph: Rex/ShutterstockLeeson had a stint playing Bungle on the children’s show Rainbow, a job in which he described being “poured out of this costume every evening into a taxi”, because a day’s work in a small studio under the hot lights left him “really ill inside this bear suit”.He also once lamented the haircut he was given when appearing on Dad’s Army, saying: “I was livid because they gave me an army haircut, a real basin job, and then of course put me in a balaclava and a tin hat, so nobody could see the hair anyway.”He was still working as K9, providing voices for Big Finish audio dramas last year. This was despite, he once said, being told by producers at theBBCafter his debut that “under no circumstances would there be anything after the first episode has been shot and is in the can. So don’t expect too much. And here I am in 2025 still attached to Doctor Who … I got to meet a tremendous number of knees doing K9.”View image in fullscreenLeeson with K9.Photograph: ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsDoctor WhoTelevisionBBCChildren's TVFantasy TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meeting Elvis was ‘my biggest day with the Beatles’, says road manager’s book | The Beatles | The Guardian
description: Mal Evans’s tale of historic meeting among revelations in forthcoming memoir unpublished before his death in 1976
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Mal Evans’s tale of historic meeting among revelations in forthcoming memoir unpublished before his death in 1976
Content: Mal Evans at the Hollywood Bowl in August 1965 with Beatles Paul McCartney and George Harrison.Photograph: Malcolm Frederick Evans ArchivesView image in fullscreenMal Evans at the Hollywood Bowl in August 1965 with Beatles Paul McCartney and George Harrison.Photograph: Malcolm Frederick Evans ArchivesThe BeatlesMeeting Elvis was ‘my biggest day with the Beatles’, says road manager’s bookMal Evans’s tale of historic meeting among revelations in forthcoming memoir unpublished before his death in 1976Dalya AlbergeMon 2 Nov 2026 03.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeeting Elvis Presley was “the biggest day of all the years I have spent with the famous Beatles”, the band’s loyal road manager wrote.It is among recollections in a memoir that Mal Evans had planned to publish, with the band’s permission, before his death in 1976, aged 40, in a shooting by the Los Angeles police. Distraught over the breakup of his marriage, it is believed to have been “suicide by cop” after he repeatedly pointed an air rifle at police.Now, 50 years later, that memoir is to be published for the first time, having been made available by Evans’s family to Kenneth Womack, one of the world’s foremost Beatles experts and author of numerous books on them.View image in fullscreenMal Evans accompanying Paul McCartney on his arrival at Maharishi Mahesh Yogi’s transcendental meditation centre in India in February 1968.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveEvans became the Beatles’ roadie from their early days at Liverpool’s Cavern Club, where he had been a bouncer.He wrote of working with John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr in diaries and notebooks, while taking thousands of photographs and scooping up discarded lyric sheets, receipts and other ephemera when they were on the road and in the recording studio.For his memoir, he had hired a stenographer. Womack has all the recordings that Evans dictated into a portable cassette recorder in 1975. The memoir manuscript spans about 95,000 words. Although Womack drew on it for his Evans biography in 2023, the text itself will finally be published in December, titledWith the Beatles.Describing Evans as the Beatles’ first archivist, Womack told the Guardian: “It’s the book Mal was going to publish, taking us into the heart of Beatlemania, reminding us how electrifying it was. He pulls no punches. He shows us the Beatles. It’s very powerful. It’s a treasure trove of new material.”View image in fullscreenMal Evans (top right) and the Beatles descend aircraft steps at Heathrow after flying in from Spain in July 1965.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesIts passages include Evans’s first-hand account of the fabled meeting between the Beatles and Elvis – “rock’s greatest heavyweights of all time”, Womack said.He added: “Mal loved Elvis more than he loved the Beatles, in terms of music. So, for that reason, when they meet Elvis in Bel Air in August 1965, Mal writes page upon page about the experience and what happened.“There’s been so much debate among writers about that meeting – and now we have this complete record of Mal saying: ‘Here’s exactly what happened.’”Evans idolised Elvis, writing in one passage: “If there is one day in my life I shall never forget, it is the day when the two biggest phenomena in showbiz met for the one and only time.“The day the Beatles met Elvis Presley. I was there that day in El’s palatial Hollywood home. And that will always be the biggest day of all the years I have spent with the famous Beatles.”He recalled that Elvis played them Beatles LPs before finding guitars for each of them. Evans listened in awe as “they began to make the place rock with … improvised beat music”.Evans’s memoir follows the group from the Help! album through the Magical Mystery Tour EP to the Get Back single sessions and the final studio years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn one chapter, he wrote of the band’s perilous tour of the Philippines, after they caused unintentional insult in turning down an invitation to an official event with the first lady, Imelda Marcos.“A large number of the promoter’s staff were wearing automatic pistols in their back pockets … this was brought home to me personally the morning of our departure,” he wrote.“I had just finished packing when one of the gentlemen entered my room asking for autographed pictures.“I was in the middle of explaining that I had given away most of the photographs, keeping a few for the plane crew on the way home, when I was cut short by the same gentleman brandishing a gun in my face and repeating the demand. I couldn’t give them to him fast enough.“This was the prelude to a morning of terror … I waited for the Beatles to arrive, then we proceeded to immigration. We were climbing a stairway inside the airport when suddenly … a dozen men appeared to impede our progress, and started to jostle us.“It was obvious that they were looking to cause trouble … because of the fiasco the previous evening with the first lady.“They were standing on our toes, jabbing us with elbows, generally giving us a bad time … I would give my right arm for any of those boys but, under these circumstances, it was most inadvisable to retaliate in any way whatsoever. To stand there and see my beloved Beatles treated so roughly was heartbreaking.”Womack has pieced together the memoir from material that Evans had stored in “six massive boxes”. It will feature about 400 photographs, including some that have never been seen before.Explore more on these topicsThe BeatlesnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ glory | Television | The Guardian
description: High-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: High-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Period piece … The Gilded Age.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenPeriod piece … The Gilded Age.Photograph: HBOTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: The Gilded Age returns in all its glossy Julian Fellowes’ gloryHigh-society plotting is afoot as nouveau riche arrivistes threaten the old order. Plus, David Harewood’s dogged Pierre won’t let a spot of angina slow him down. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Jack SealeandGraeme VirtueMon 2 Nov 2026 01.15 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 03.06 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Gilded Age9pm, Sky AtlanticJulian Fellowes’ glossy, airy period confection returns. The Gilded Age has now happily embraced its own lack of real nutritional value and, towards the end of the third season, its ratings swelled as a result. In the opener, Agnes is scheming to retain her position in society and there’s a subplot of real modern resonance as old money starts being threatened by crass, arriviste monopolists.Phil HarrisonA Place in the Sun6pm, Channel 4Now that it’s dark before dinnertime, the show about upping sticks from the UK feels like perfect vicarious viewing. The Dordogne and a gorgeous Greek island feature later in the week but the new run kicks off with a couple contemplating retirement on the balmy Costa Blanca. What can a £450k budget get them?Graeme VirtueEscaping Idi Amin9pm, BBC TwoIn the context of the current hysteria around migration, thistwo-part documentary has been sobering. As it concludes, it’s 1972 and a month after Uganda’s swaggering dictator Idi Amin issued an ultimatum to the country’s Asian population. They must leave within 90 days, taking nothing more than one suitcase and £50 each. Will Britain take them?PHView image in fullscreenDogged … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4 / Olly CourtneyPierre9pm, Channel 4It’s the penultimate chapter of David Harewood’s suave legal drama, and if you think collapsing would keep this dogged duty solicitor down, think again (“It wasn’t a heart attack, it was angina”). He escapes his hospital bed to get back on the case following a new lead on Michael’s death.Hollie RichardsonTrauma: My Broken Brain10pm, Channel 4The documentary’s concluding half follows Dan, Saskia and Dec – all in their 20s – as they recover from life-threatening strokes. As Dan endures surgery to repair a hole in his skull, Saskia goes to great lengths to overcome her neurological fatigue. Dec, meanwhile, finds his psychological recovery more challenging than the physical.Jack SealeDispatches: The Taliban’s War on Women11pm, Channel 4The 2021 US and UK withdrawal from Afghanistan, allowing the Taliban to take control, felt like a shameful betrayal. And the stories that emerge from this remarkable Dispatches documentary confirm that impression. It follows Afghans in exile as they attempt to rescue loved ones from the theocracy; a story of torture, sexual violence, erasure and extraordinary courage.PHLive sportTennis: Paris Masters. title: The Rhyl Poster by Tom McCarthy review – is this avant-garde spy drama worth the riddles? | Tom McCarthy | The Guardian
description: The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating reading
Author: Anthony Cummins
Headline: The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating reading
Content: Prank-adjacent vibe … Tom McCarthy.Photograph: Johannes SchriekView image in fullscreenPrank-adjacent vibe … Tom McCarthy.Photograph: Johannes SchriekTom McCarthyReviewThe Rhyl Poster by Tom McCarthy review – is this avant-garde spy drama worth the riddles?The hallucinatory crisis of a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency makes for frustrating readingAnthony CumminsMon 2 Nov 2026 04.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf the cohort of experimental novelists whose renown grew in the wake of the 2008 financial crash – names includeDeborah Levy,Eimear McBrideandClaire-Louise Bennett– it was Tom McCarthy who first demonstrated the benefit of bypassing orthodox routes to market. When British publishers rejected his 2005 novel,Remainder, about an amnesiac who spends a windfall restaging his past, he released it in a limited edition from a Paris art collective. Three years later, Zadie Smith wrote an essay celebrating it as a path-breaking overthrow of establishment-sanctioned “lyrical realism”. The literary press soon began finding more room for McCarthy, whose regular denunciations of English fiction – not least for its “middlebrow” ignorance of challenging ideas from the continent – did much to shape bookish conversation at the turn of the decade.If his zeal wasn’t to everyone’s taste – the New Statesman once called him Britain’s “most galling interviewee” – anyone lately stepping into a bookshop might well feel the last laugh belongs to McCarthy. Witness the success of Fitzcarraldo Editions: innovative Europeans are hot property. Risk-rewarding ventures such as the Goldsmiths prize, established in 2013 to spotlight formally daring fiction amid panic about the philistinism of award panels, feel a little less urgent when a novel as inscrutable as M John Harrison’sThe End of Everythingsits comfortably on this year’s Booker shortlist, a bestseller to boot. When the mainstream and the avant garde are now kissing cousins, where does it leave McCarthy?The Making of Incarnation(2021), a dense, Pynchonesque espionage yarn about motion capture technology, suggested that he saw the Booker-shortlisted success of both 2010’sCand 2015’sSatin Islandas a green light to push readers harder. Further evidence for the theory is supplied by his riddling new novel, The Rhyl Poster, another abstruse spy drama, this time set deep inside the polyglot operations of Luxembourg’s Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). It’s as if McCarthy – a longtime Berliner who, post-Brexit, holds a Swedish passport – had determined to immerse himself in the minutiae of the institution his native Britain elected to leave.We’re in the company of a pill-popping jurist, Stanton, scarred by his past as a military geographer with the British army in Iraq. Memories of that time, opaque to the reader, don’t help him at work, where he’s meant to be drafting a landmark opinion on a privacy suit against a data analytics firm. His desire for relief from his various war wounds makes him prey to an approach from a shadowy criminal seeking EU documents in exchange for unapproved painkillers from a lab in Rotterdam – home, handily, to Stanton’s long-distance Dutch-Surinamese girlfriend, one among a catalogue of lovers whose pillow talk greases the story’s cogs.double quotation markReading The Rhyl Poster is like trying to fill in a crossword using the wrong cluesThe ensuing double-dealing zigzag around northern Europe plays out as a genre-curious mashup of trauma plot and heist narrative, steadfastly averse to closure. Suspense derives less from events than from the disorientingly stretchy syntax of McCarthy’s narration, a dry blend of legal lingo and lower-slung idiom, like a lecturer wearing a blazer with Nikes. “Interpretation,” we’re told, isn’t the same thing as “advancing to a conclusion from a set of givens guided by parameters that, fixed, are also given: that’s induction. No:interpretation, understood in its profoundest sense, is the plumb opposite … If law in general is the realm where language shapes the world, the European Court of Justice pimps this logic to thenth.”The novel’s interest in law, or its “fundamental propensity for repeatability, its driving imperative towards self-duplication”, eventually reveals itself as another iteration of McCarthy’s abiding preoccupation with repetition. Even the most dramatic scene, a revelatory flashback to Stanton’s days in Iraq, is a replay of sorts, evoking Zadie Smith’s observation about the role Remainder gave to a black man’s fatal shooting (experimental or not, she said, “the non-white subject is still the bad conscience of the contemporary novel”).Remainder remains McCarthy’s best book, its multifunctional concept delivering old-school psychological intrigue while poking fun at literary realism’s mimetic aspirations. Reading The Rhyl Poster, by contrast, is like trying to fill in a crossword using the wrong clues. The endeavour isn’t devoid of quixotic frisson: it’s not unfun to note, for instance, that the defendant in Stanton’s case is named Elrond – like Palantir, a lift from Tolkien – or that the claimant, Kohlhas, described as a “one-man operation”, echoes the wronged justice-seeker Michael Kohlhaas in Heinrich von Kleist’s 1810 novella of that name.Yet these are keys tinkling, not doors unlocked, and while there’s a measure of page-turning urgency in Stanton’s increasingly hallucinatory personal crisis, he’s too plainly a parody of a girl-getting hardman-savant to carry much by way of emotional weight. The mystifying title, poised between enigma and bathos, refers (no spoiler, this) to the protagonist’s half-memory of riding a train in north Wales while watching someone paste up an advert – blank, naturally.The prank-adjacent vibe hardly subsides once the novel’s 240 pages of high-pressure buildup conclude with the word “begin”. Any takeaway perhaps lies in the acronym of the court at the book’s heart, blinking like a beacon through its pages – CJEU,c’est jeu, a game – and if you don’t get a kick out of that, be sure McCarthy does.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsTom McCarthyFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: One in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting again | Movies | The Guardian
description: Following a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformed
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Following a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformed
Content: Superb … Syrian refugee Israa in One in a Million.Photograph: Keo Films/Jack MacInnesView image in fullscreenSuperb … Syrian refugee Israa in One in a Million.Photograph: Keo Films/Jack MacInnesMoviesReviewOne in a Million review – deeply moving film about displacement, freedom and the upheaval of starting againFollowing a Syrian mother and daughter over a decade, Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes capture a family transformedPhil HoadMon 2 Nov 2026 08.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 08.02 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a startling moment in this BBC refugee documentary when Syrian mother Nisreen – in the apparently miserable situation of hiking across the Balkans towardsGermany, four kids in tow – suddenly explodes with joy. “This is the best holiday I’ve ever had! It’s an amazing adventure. Now I have the chance to walk in the rain – I love it!” Shunted off early into an arranged marriage, never having left Syria until forced out of Aleppo by the civil war, for Nisreen this running jump into the unknown represents total liberation.Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ superb, forthright and highly moving film bypasses the usual refugee dichotomies, that they’re either external threats or history’s victims. Instead of flat abstractions, we get the knotty reality. Focused over a 10-year period from 2015 to 2025 principally on Nisreen’s eldest daughter Israa, it presents an intimate chronicle of how geographical displacement and cultural dislocation reshape families and lives from the inside.Eleven years old in the Turkish city of Izmir, Israa is a quick-smiling street vendor waiting to cross the Aegean; cheery despite the upheaval because of seemingly unbreakable family solidarity. Just a few years later in Cologne, she is a Justin Bieber-worshipping, football-playing teenager who lauds democracy for giving her the freedom to do whatever she wants. Which is increasingly too much for her dad, Tarek, who approves of change “with limits” – so is unaware of her secret boyfriend. He puts his foot down when Israa and Nisreen apply makeup in front of the film-makers’ cameras on the latter’s birthday. Israa is distraught. But soon he has no one to control; Nisreen, who has fanatically embraced western feminism, kicks him out of the house.It’s a wrenchingly immediate demonstration of the neglected flip side to discussions of how immigrants alter host countries – and how the immigrants themselves are also changed in the process. Through the young man who becomes her husband, Israa slowly comes to a rapprochement with her Syrian and Muslim identity – and finally makes an Ithacan return to Aleppo. But the damage is harder to repair for once-respected shawarma chef Tarek, who in his own moment of truth admits he made his family pay for his loss of status. As his daughter says at the start: “War is not as hard as what comes after.”Azzam and MacInnes’ film is so deft at sifting the debris of the years to highlight these breakthroughs for maximum effect, you wish there was another hour to pore over the path leading there. But it stays the course impressively on external and internal journeys as it highlights the family’s hard-won transformations.One in a Million is in UK and Irish cinemas from 6 November.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMigrationSyriaIslamGermanyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dead Howling review – werewolf hunts zombies in tough-love apocalypse horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: Every bog-standard cliche is employed – and fails – in this moribund Aussie thiller, which entirely lacks both bite and bark
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Every bog-standard cliche is employed – and fails – in this moribund Aussie thiller, which entirely lacks both bite and bark
Content: Dead on arrival … Joel Jackson in Dead Howling.View image in fullscreenDead on arrival … Joel Jackson in Dead Howling.MoviesReviewDead Howling review – werewolf hunts zombies in tough-love apocalypse horrorEvery bog-standard cliche is employed – and fails – in this moribund Aussie thiller, which entirely lacks both bite and barkPhil HoadMon 2 Nov 2026 04.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 04.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen talk here turns to what would happen if the film’s werewolf hero were bitten by a zombie, the term coined is “wombie”. Sadly, this inter-species thought-experiment never comes to pass in this otherwise lifeless and crushingly derivative Aussie post-apocalyptic slog, the only point of note in which is a very brief cameo from Mr Once Were Warriors and Jango Fett himself, Temuera Morrison. He drops off his niece and nephew, Megan (Téa Heathcote-Marks) and Billy (Riley Stiles), before succumbing to a zombie pile-on.The pair quickly encounter Carter (Armie Hammer lookalike Joel Jackson), a hulking former scientist turned one-man undead clean-up squad who still can’t get his head around this bog-standard apocalypse: rampant virus, flesh-eating zombie hordes, overwhelming guilt over not saving his wife and child, etc. But this whiskey-slugging misanthrope is also a lycanthrope, thanks to a super-serum he developed while trying to counteract the plague. Able to metamorphose at a second’s notice into a rabid canine, and seemingly equipped with an infinite supply of new black T-shirts for afterwards, he is the perfect protector for the teens as they attempt to reach a safe zone they insist exists inside Perth’s city limits.The brief flicker of interest on their journey is Carter’s tough-love approach to survival: he forces Megan and Billy to make their first kills unprotected in a derelict school gymnasium. But the daft werewolf gambit (possibly something to do with this sharing a producer with British horror classic Dog Soldiers) kicks the legs out from under this attempt at flinty realism.Otherwise, Dead Howling is saddled with dreary pity-party discussions when it isn’t shambling into every apocalypse-film cliche trap going, from the emotionally shut-down journeyman, to agonised euthanising of soon-to-be-zombie colleagues, to a closing message of hope somehow more dispiriting than the complete collapse of civilisation. The zombies are evolving, we are told – but it only highlights this moribund movie genre’s urgent need to evolve itself.Dead Howling is on digital platforms from 2 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsZombiesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Blockhead review – struggling novelist embraces his inner monster in comic thriller of literary machismo | Movies | The Guardian
description: Writer-director Matt Harlock looks into ego and insecurity in a smart film about a BritLit bad boy who goes down a grisly road
Author: Mike McCahill
Headline: Writer-director Matt Harlock looks into ego and insecurity in a smart film about a BritLit bad boy who goes down a grisly road
Content: Hitchcockian … Joe Sims (left) and Danny Horn in Blockhead.View image in fullscreenHitchcockian … Joe Sims (left) and Danny Horn in Blockhead.MoviesReviewBlockhead review – struggling novelist embraces his inner monster in comic thriller of literary machismoWriter-director Matt Harlock looks into ego and insecurity in a smart film about a BritLit bad boy who goes down a grisly roadMike McCahillMon 2 Nov 2026 06.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis has nothing to do with Ian Dury; rather, it is a brisk, effective British indie thriller informed by the legend of Robert Louis Stevenson wrestling his shadow self while writing Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. The present-day equivalent proposed by writer and director Matt Harlock is BritLit posterboy Will Mercer (Danny Horn), much admired for his debut novel A Random Act yet presently mired in indecision over a follow-up that seems likely to cost him relationships, representation and reputation alike. Retreating to a friend’s garret, he is woken by a builder: bullet-headed, charismatic hulk Mikey (Joe Sims), who merits and invites closer literary study. Mikey is unarguably an arresting character – a very handy golem in overalls – even if we worry about the path he’s leading our man down.No prizes, then, for guessingwhich David Fincher filmprovides the template here. Typing to a soundtrack of his own best reviews (“The world needs to hear your story”), an emboldened Will is soon exploring grislier avenues, including home invasion and murder, while his increasingly unhinged rants to creative-writing students attract a rapt protege. Evoking a world where publishers push books with unequivocally positive pull quotes like “confrontational” and “dangerous”, Harlock is taking a red pencil to hackneyed notions of bad-boy writers. There is, he posits, only so much muscle one can wield while hunched over a laptop.Crucially, Harlock matches literary smarts with cinematic elan: suggestive use of masks and screens; a stark contrast between the blank-page sparseness of Will’s lodgings and the night he strays into; a symmetricalmise en abymetying everything together. (One nicely Hitchcockian touch: the string of fairylights following one victim over a balcony.) Horn nails the writer’s tempestuous mix of bravado and insecurity, while Sims’ Mikey revels in skewering Will’s loftier pretensions. A few first-feature wobbles aside – a mid-film drug trip is only partly justified by a Coleridge namedrop – we’re walking similar streets to Christopher Nolan’s microbudget breakthrough Following, but this time with wittier, satirically minded company.Blockhead is in UK cinemas from 5 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmThrillersLondonFilm criticismDrama filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Funny and self-aware’: why (500) Days of Summer is my feelgood movie | (500) Days of Summer | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaning
Author: Charlie Lindlar
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaning
Content: Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of SummerPhotograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenJoseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in (500) Days of SummerPhotograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMy feelgood movie(500) Days of Summer‘Funny and self-aware’: why (500) Days of Summer is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers detailing their most rewatched comfort films carries special romantic meaningCharlie LindlarMon 2 Nov 2026 05.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 11.13 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is September 2009. Barack Obama is settling into the White House. The global economy is hauling itself gingerly out of the financial crisis. And Keisha has just left the Sugababes.But more importantly, I am on a first date.‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movieRead moreFans of indie music and cinema, both myself and the woman I’m seeing – I still remember the black dress and gold-glitter eyeshadow she chose – are seated to take in (500) Days of Summer, a quirky-looking romcom starring a youthful Joseph Gordon-Levitt and the doe-eyed, Ur-manic pixie dream girlZooey Deschanel.If you’ve not seen the film, how dare you, but here’s a recap: diehard romantic Tom (Gordon-Levitt) meets mysterious lone wolf Summer (Deschanel) in a lift at their workplace, and instantly falls in love when, first, she sings along to the Smiths song she can hear emanating from his headphones, and then, fatally, praises his taste in music. The film then – skipping around in non-linear fashion – recounts the 500 days in which Tom and Summer become close, fall into a relationship of some kind, fall apart in a seemingly sudden argument over what they mean to each other, and ultimately come to part forever as Summer moves jobs and, out of nowhere, marries another man.The heart of the film is the grey area of Tom and Summer’s relationship: were they ever a couple, like Tom believes? Or were they just friends, as Summer insists? While each readily acknowledges they mean something significant to each other, the Rorschach test quality of their dynamic drives the drama.The film is a success: the time-hopping format is a thrill, the rise and fall of their relationship plausible, funny and self-aware. The performances are nuanced career bests from a pair of leads with tangible chemistry. The production is gorgeous too: it combines a glorious indie-poptimist soundtrack, timeless yet squarely 2009 costuming and a sepia-tinged portrayal of Los Angeles which focuses not on the Hollywood Hills and golden beaches but instead on the city’s under-loved downtown, with its plazas, art deco high-rises and many, many car parks.The date, by the way, was a success too. My wife and I have been together ever since, and (500) Days of Summer remains a shared love. Far too many lines have slipped into our lexicon, we have visited a number of key locations on visits to LA, and I at least regularly look back to Tom for office-wear inspo. (Bring back ties and cardigans, but perhaps not those Puma trainers just yet).Most meaningfully, on every anniversary of that 2009 date, we rewatch the film together. We know the thing frame-by-frame now, but the reason we insist on coming back to the story every year stems from something deeper than just loving the script or the setting. To us, each annual rewatch is a chance to look again at the shape, direction and even nature of true love – and perhaps by extent our own relationship.It’s an opportunity to reconsider Tom’s position: is he a true romantic, or just deeply naive? Is his desire to fix a label to what he has with Summer reasonable, or insecure? It’s a chance too to look anew at Summer’s philosophy: is she a woman of principled boundaries, or someone who locks others out to protect herself? Is her desire to avoid labelling things independence, or is it carelessness with the feelings of others?Some years, we like to approach the rewatch with an agenda: last year, we tried to be Summer stans and see only Tom’s foibles. Other times, we theorise if things ever could have worked, or pinpoint the precise moment their relationship goes wrong. This year, we focused only on who was “worse” to the other (it’s Summer, sorry – you can’t invite your ex-lover to an intimate gathering at your apartment andnottell them it’s a party celebrating your engagement to an entirely different man!).The beauty of the film to us is that, though it tends to be more sympathetic to Tom, it forces few conclusions upon you. In the film’s closing moments, when Tom and Summer part for the final time, they find one shared conclusion: he’s right about the existence of true love … but he just wasn’t meant to find it with her.Each year, as we watch and litigate and re-litigate this wonderful film, I too find myself sure of one thing. While Tom was wrong about having found his true love, I know what I knew at that first viewing in 2008: I have found mine.(500) Days of Summer is available on Hoopla and to rent digitally in the US and on Disney+ in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topics(500) Days of SummerMy feelgood movieJoseph Gordon-LevittZooey DeschanelComedy filmsRomance filmsDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I Died review – moving portrait of Tzotzil women confronting patriarchal violence in the Mexican highlands | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ana Ts’uyeb’s poetic film celebrates the resilience of Indigenous women while exploring the possibility of a different future
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Ana Ts’uyeb’s poetic film celebrates the resilience of Indigenous women while exploring the possibility of a different future
Content: Sobering … Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary, I Died.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenSobering … Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary, I Died.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewI Died review – moving portrait of Tzotzil women confronting patriarchal violence in the Mexican highlandsAna Ts’uyeb’s poetic film celebrates the resilience of Indigenous women while exploring the possibility of a different futurePhuong LeMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 02.01 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShot in her home village of Naranjatic Alto in the Mexican highlands, Ana Ts’uyeb’s documentary debut is a stirring ode to the courageous women of theIndigenous Tzotzil community. The film centres on three important figures in her life: her mother, Margarita; her aunt, Juana; and her sister-in-law, Faustina. Each is from a different generation, yet they have all suffered at the hands of patriarchal violence.The patterns of systemic abuse and disenfranchisement are startlingly similar. All three women recall past opportunities to advance their education, hopes and dreams that were squashed by fathers and other male relatives. Also rampant are physical and psychological abuse. There’s a sobering matter-of-fact tone to their reminiscence; their unfortunate experiences appear to be a common reality endured by many Tzotzil women.In place of conventional sit-down interviews, Ts’uyeb dynamically captures her subjects at work, lending a dose of cinematic poetry to everyday rituals. From weaving cloth and sieving grain to the back-breaking toil of harvest, these diaristic vignettes not only speak to a collective resilience but also act as a visual archive of Indigenous customs and traditions. Previously exploited for their labour but excluded from land inheritance, these brave women can now pour their blood, sweat and tears into their own land, thanks to the Zapatista movement.Unfortunately for those unfamiliar with this Indigenous-led insurgency, the film doesn’t provide much context around Zapatista activism over land reform. But despite this lack of background, the focus on the women’s interior lives still packs an emotional punch. In one moving scene, we see Margarita clear an uneven path ahead of Ts’uyeb with great tenderness. It seems that years of generational trauma may have finally come to an end, and a new future awaits the women of Naranjatic Alto.I Died is on True Story from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMexicoWomenAmericasWorld cinemaIndigenous peoplesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief | Jo Brand | The Guardian
description: The comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaper
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaper
Content: ‘Maybe anarchy needs to come back’ … Jo Brand.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Maybe anarchy needs to come back’ … Jo Brand.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe big interviewJo Brand‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and griefThe comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaperEmine SanerMon 2 Nov 2026 00.00 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHadJo Brand, who turns 70 next year, been spending a long time thinking about getting older? Had it become the subject that consumed her, and the reason why, now, she felt impelled to write a book about the vagaries of ageing? No, she says, laughing. She was simply asked if she’d like to do it.Still, it encouraged introspection about what she wanted her future to look like. “Now’s the time, if you want things, to get them in place. I think a lot of people say, ‘I really want to do that, but I’ll forget it for now.’ And then they get to a stage where they can’t.” Does she mean bucket-list things? “No, I mean … what do I mean?” Brand pauses. “I mean the ability to perhaps end your own …” She doesn’t go there, but the end to that sentence is obviously: life.“I know it’s not legal yet, but I think it will be, sooner rather than later.” Her mother had procured drugs to end her own life when she was ill, though she didn’t use them. Two minutes in, and we’re already talking about assisted dying. Off-duty comedians – such a laugh.I’m being unfair. Of course Brand is fun, but ageing isn’t, sometimes. In her book, Decline and Falling Over, she calls the point past middle age “your shitter second half”. The book is funny, as you’d expect, but also surprisingly sober, covering such cheering topics as the decision to go into a care home and, yes, assisted dying.double quotation markI’ve never really been a grumpy person. I’ve been a bit friendly, and tried to be pleasant to everyoneDespite thinking about what she wants her future to look like, Brand has not yet come to any solid conclusions. As a teenager, she worked in a residential home (for adults with learning disabilities, rather than older people), and complained after she witnessed some “appalling behaviour” by male staff. It was not investigated; instead, she was sacked. She was left with a fear of care homes. “That was in the 70s. Are they that different now? Who knows?” But, she adds, “I can’t imagine I can persuade any of my family to get interested in looking after me.” (She has two grown-up daughters.)Are there any benefits of getting older? “Being rude to people.” She laughs. “No, not really. But saying what you think, I suppose. I like the whole ‘grumpy old woman’ sort of thing. I do quite like being grumpy. I’ve never really been a grumpy person. I’ve been a bit friendly, and tried to be pleasant to everyone – not on stage, I accept that, because a lot of people think I’m probably horrible, but in my personal life.” It is, she says, “that whole thing that a lot of women suffer from, which is putting everybody first and themselves last”.Brand writes several times that she’s a “people pleaser” – which, given her bolshie stage persona and unflinching attitude, surprises me (although she has always seemed thoughtful, and very kind). “It surprises me as well,” she says. We’re in a meeting room at the Guardian offices, Brand glorious in layers of black with dark pink hair, looking queenly but punk. “I have always been one because … well, why? I’ve no idea. My dad was quite hard to please, so maybe I spent quite a lot of time doing that.”Did the on-stage version of her character not influence the way she was in real life? “I don’t think it really did,” she says. “I think that was because there weren’t many women comics around when I started – you needed a sort of shield.” If she could be more vulgar, more aggressive than the drunk men who heckled her, they’d back off – or at least, she hoped, word would get around that she wasn’t to be messed with. “If you’re heckled, you have to deal with it because audiences lose faith in you if you don’t, so I had a sliding scale of pleasant through to soul-destroying. I never wanted to use soul-destroying, but I occasionally would.”View image in fullscreenHecklers beware … at the Sadler’s Wells theatre in London, 1995.Photograph: Michael Le Poer Trench/ShutterstockGrowing up in Hastings, where the family ended up after moving from London and Kent, the teenage Brand was rebellious rather than people-pleasing. She had unsuitable boyfriends, stayed out, discovered drugs. “But that was more to do with the circumstances we were in,” she says. “At the time my dad was in a very bad place, and so he was really difficult to live with.” He could be violent. “I mean, not as bad as some poor women have it on a regular basis, but quite a few times. Mainly when I answered back to him, or my little brother did.” Brand, I notice, tends to downplay a lot, but it must have been scary. “It makes you a bit jumpy, hypervigilant. So I was only too delighted to get out of home.”She moved into a bedsit at 17. It was quite exciting, looking back. “We had the freedom to behave appallingly, if we wanted to.” Was she in danger of going out of control? “I always had a sense of when the brakes should be applied. So I was never in danger of, let’s say, becoming a heroin addict, even though I was around a lot of people that used drugs. I think I would have quite happily drunk a lot more if I could drink.” But she couldn’t hold it. “When I was at university, I was very cheap to get pissed.”Becoming a comic had been Brand’s ambition since she was a teenager. “I liked making people laugh, but not in any well-formed sense of doing an act.” She became a psychiatric nurse instead, trying standup at 29. “I imposed a pointless line on my life: that you can’t get to 30 and not have tried comedy.” It helped that she was older, she thinks, and that no heckler could ever be as shocking or as aggressive as some of the patients she had dealt with, who suffered with psychosis. “I was a bit hardened.”Still, how did she not let it get to her, listening to drunk men making personal attacks? “My self-esteem had gone as low as it probably could. It’s hard, because it’s embarrassing if someone says something really gross and awful to you in front of a big group of other people. And the way to deal with it, to me, is to come back with something better. It’s like a battle. If we’d had to fight each other, obviously I wouldn’t have done terribly well.” She smiles. “But I might have done.”What was it like to be a young woman on the circuit? Was sexual harassment part of her experience? “Not the way I looked,” Brand laughs. Then she reconsiders: “Actually, there were a few comics occasionally trying to get in my room at two o’clock in the morning. I just shouted through the door, told them to fuck off, and they did. So it was nothing that I couldn’t deal with.”View image in fullscreenWith Joanna Scanlan, left, and Vicki Pepperdine, the cast of Getting On.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianStill, the 80s comedy circuit sounds as if it must have been thrilling. It was, she says. “There was such a variety of people doing such weird things, like melting a block of ice or whatever it was they did,” she says, referring to the performance artist Anthony Irvine, known as the Iceman. “These days, it’s much more uniform. I think there are some really brilliant comics around, but it’s become very stand-uppy.” It’s expected to be more polished now, I venture, less anarchic. “Yes, maybe anarchy needs to come back.”The birth of alternative comedy in the 80s must also have felt exciting, politically, after decades of old-style comedians with their racist and sexist jokes. For a while it must have felt as if a generation of progressive comics could change, or at least help change, society. But it doesn’t feel like that now. “Yeah, the world is in a mess,” says Brand. “But there are an awful lot of good people, and I just hope the good people win out. I’m not an optimist, but then again, I’m not a terrible pessimist, either.”By 1993 Brand had her own show, Jo Brand Through the Cakehole. It was a mix of standup and sketches. In one segment – Drudge Squad, her spoof cop show – two female detectives worn down by domesticity try to fight crime amid laundry baskets and useless husbands.There were men in the tabloids who were unforgivably awful about Brand, especially about the way she looked. But as for the teenage girls (myself among them) who watched her Friday night Channel 4 show, it’s hard to overstate the thrill of seeing Brand, a woman who looked and spoke differently from everyone else: hilariously rude and unapologetic.View image in fullscreenBrand presented The Great British Bake Off: An Extra Slice from 2014.Photograph: Channel 4Is she envious of female comedians starting now? Does she think they get an easier time? “I’m not, actually. There’s a lot more really good competition these days, and because we were quite unusual – I think there were 15 of us out of, like, 200 male comics – we were a bit of a novelty act, so that was a help. And people didn’t quite know what to make of us, and that was a help, too.”Until last year, Brand presented the Great British Bake Off after-show, An Extra Slice, and this year she is doing a book tour. She has already won a Bafta for her role as a kind but harassed nurse in Getting On, the BBC comedy she co-wrote with Vicki Pepperdine and Joanna Scanlan, set in an NHS geriatric ward. Over the years, she has – for television – learned to play the organ at the Royal Albert Hall, performed as Britney Spears and, for Comic Relief in 2016,walked 140 milesfrom Hull to Liverpool.One aspect of getting older, she says, is that she is less adventurous than she used to be. “I used to do quite a lot of stupid things, like jump off things or learn how to rally drive. I couldn’t imagine being a rally driver now. I love a bit of madness like that, but I’m much less mad than I used to be, physically.”Brand also doesn’t do as many live shows. She thinks her memory took a hit during the pandemic, which makes remembering long sets a bit harder. But she has been doing some “work-in-progress shows”, which takes the pressure off a polished performance. “I was so delighted that I could use that tag, which basically means: most of this might be rubbish.”One of the worst things about ageing, she says, particularly as a woman, is that “you get ignored. Putting my job for a moment out of the equation, older men still get much more respect than older women, because we all think older women are just one big blob that looks the same. I think it’s going to take a while longer to cherish older women for the fantastic variety that they are.”Brand has experienced tragedy in the last 10 years – she lost her parents, both brothers, and two of her three best friends. How has she dealt with it? “I’ve been very good at suppressing my emotions,” she says. “I was always taught not to show any weakness in public, which used to be just a bloke’s thing, didn’t it? So I probably haven’t handled it all very well – I just pretended it wasn’t happening for a long time because I couldn’t believe how awful it was.”View image in fullscreen‘Being angry is very good for me.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn her book, she writes about being stuck at the “angry stage” of grief for a while. “I like the angry stage,” she says. “I think anger is just as valid as crying – you can be angry about people leaving you. I think being angry is very good for me.” As for denial, another part of the so-called five stages of grief, Brand says she could probably do it for the rest of her life. “So yes, I’m not terribly good at grief, because I’m not terribly good at acceptance, either – I don’t think I’ve done that yet at all.” Sometimes she’ll think she hasn’t heard from one of those best friends for a while. “And then I remember. That weird stuff happens with grief all the time, doesn’t it?”Has it made her agonise about her own mortality more? “Less! I refuse to think about it. I’m a massive avoider of those sorts of things. I know it’s a bad thing to be, but what’s the point of thinking about it? It’s far too late for me to go down the gym every 10 minutes. At least, I did give up smoking, but now I’m a champion vaper.”Best just to get on with things. Or at least take a tip on ageing from her great-grandmother, “who just went to bed and ate chocolate all day”. Not that retirement holds any appeal. Brand is lucky, she says, in that her job is not one she has to retire from. “There are still enough people to come and see me at shows, so I can do that if I want to.” Long may she reign.Decline and Falling Over is published by Penguin (£22). title: BBCSO/Stasevska review – Caroline Shaw’s cosmic visions meet Barber’s lyrical brilliance | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but occasionally underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall Goosby
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but occasionally underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall Goosby
Content: Violinist Randall Goosby with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Dalia Stasevska in the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenViolinist Randall Goosby with the BBC Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Dalia Stasevska in the Barbican, London.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewBBCSO/Stasevska review – Caroline Shaw’s cosmic visions meet Barber’s lyrical brillianceBarbican, LondonThe Golden Record and the vastness of space inspire a fascinating but underdeveloped new work, alongside a richly rewarding performance from Randall GoosbyErica JealMon 2 Nov 2026 06.09 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 06.25 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs it hurtles away from Earth – 16bn miles and counting – theGolden Recordon board the Voyager spacecraft continues to fascinate us.Caroline Shaw’s The Listeners – written for San Francisco’s Philharmonia Baroque in 2019 and here receiving its London premiere from the BBCSO as part of Shaw’s Barbican residency – features one of its tracks: spoken greetings in 55 languages. Heard via record player, these resonate through the hall while Shaw’s music forms haltingly underneath, from a pulsing keyboard note to briefly sweeping choral phrases. At times, the music almost eclipses the speech – which somehow emphasises its wonder. Later, Carl Sagan’s “pale blue dot” speech is heard, this time unadorned, via cassette player.Using a wordless choir to express wonderment is a cliche that Shaw skirts deftly, her harmonies avoiding sentimentality even though they often feel simple. Lasting 35 minutes and styled like a miniature classical oratorio, The Listeners starts and ends with movements that grow from a wordless lullaby, sung here hauntingly by the mezzo-soprano Lotte Betts-Dean. There’s a prominent role for keyboard; a harpsichord at the premiere, but an electric piano here, lending the whole thing an aptly Tomorrow’s World feel reinforced by the sight of the audio hardware on a table at the front. A baroque-style orchestral interlude conjures interstellar velocity; as for the texts Shaw sets to music, these include poetry by Whitman and Tennyson along with a striking 2017 meditation on the arbitrariness of borders by Yesenia Montilla.View image in fullscreenLotte Betts-Dean and Florian Störtz with Dalia Stasevska and the BBC Symphony.Photograph: Mark AllanBetts-Dean and the baritone Florian Störtz were communicative soloists, and the BBC Symphony Chorus put the choral passages across compellingly. The movements aren’t necessarily too short – Haydn managed to conjure the vast unknown in just six minutes at the start of The Creation – yet they didn’t all feel developed to full capacity. Given the immensity of its subject, it’s perhaps unsurprising that Shaw’s piece should be enjoyable, thought-provoking and slender all at once.Stasevska and her orchestra had warmed us up with a lyrical first half. Grazhyna, a 1955 tone poem by the Ukrainian composer Borys Lyatoshynsky, was a worthwhile discovery, telling a 15th-century Lithuanian tale in sonorously dramatic style. And Randall Goosby gave us a gratifyingly rich yet unsentimental performance of Barber’s Violin Concerto. His encore, Coleridge-Taylor Perkinson’s Louisiana Blues Strut, was a toe-tapping evocation of bluegrass and slide guitar.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicBarbicanChoral musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rob Delaney and Bel Powley star in a knotty rehab drama: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Sharon Horgan executive produced this moreish road trip story about addiction, mishaps and revelations. Plus, the new one from Serial’s Sarah Koenig
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Sharon Horgan executive produced this moreish road trip story about addiction, mishaps and revelations. Plus, the new one from Serial’s Sarah Koenig
Content: Road show … Rob Delaney and Bel Powley star in Sober Companion.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenRoad show … Rob Delaney and Bel Powley star in Sober Companion.Photograph: BBCBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioRob Delaney and Bel Powley star in a knotty rehab drama: best podcasts of the weekSharon Horgan executive produced this moreish road trip story about addiction, mishaps and revelations. Plus, the new one from Serial’s Sarah KoenigHollie Richardson,Phil HarrisonandHannah J DaviesMon 2 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Mon 2 Nov 2026 03.41 ESTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekSober Companion“I never thought I’d be back here with the fluorescent lights and lukewarm coffee,” says recovering addict Tim (Rob Delaney). “But then Lucy Green ruined my life.” So begins this intriguing 10-part drama of bite-size episodes, executive produced by Sharon Horgan. It rewinds to Tim escorting millennial pop star Lucy (Bel Powley) to rehab in Arizona on an eventful road trip. Jameela Jamil and Greg James complete a cracking cast.Hollie RichardsonBBC Sounds, all episodes out on Monday 2 NovemberMetro With Sarah KoenigView image in fullscreenNative New Yorker … Sarah Koenig.Photograph: Sandy Honig“I feel like something is happening.” The New York Times’ Sarah Koenig is excited about her city. The Knicks have won the NBA and the city has elected a popular socialist mayor. This podcast hears her hitting the streets and bars to capture the city’s current essence. She doesn’t force hot-button issues so the conversations can spiral in unpredictable directions.Phil HarrisonWidely available, episodes weeklySold a StoryAfter the first series of Emily Hanford’s podcast, revealing why so many US schools were struggling to teach kids to read, teachers told her: “It’s not just reading.” She now delves wider and deeper and looks at teaching itself – how it has changed and, ultimately, what works best.HRWidely available, episodes weeklyTell Me WhyProspect Magazine’s new series is hosted by staffers Alona Ferber and Imaan Irfan, and takes an intelligent approach to the news without laying its intellect on trowel-thick. Episodes cover Silicon Valley-fuelled tech authoritarianism (with insights from Astra Taylor and Naomi Klein), and AI’s relationship to authorship.Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSevered MindsThis investigative series tells the story of a deeply unsettling chapter in mental health history, and the lobotomies that Walter Freeman performed in the US between the 1930s and 60s. It’s a difficult listen but one that is meticulously researched, exploring the lives of Gretchen Reb and others who were altered for ever by these brutal, experimental procedures.HJDAudible, all episodes out nowWhat are you listening to this week?
